| `^`      | XOR                    | 1 where the bits differ                     |
| `~`      | Complement             | Flips every bit                             |
| `<<`     | Left shift             | Shifts left, filling with 0                 |
| `>>`     | Signed right shift     | Shifts right, filling with the sign bit     |
| `>>>`    | Unsigned right shift   | Shifts right, filling with 0                |

```java
int a = 0b1100;   // 12
int b = 0b1010;   // 10

System.out.println(Integer.toBinaryString(a & b));   // 1000  = 8
System.out.println(Integer.toBinaryString(a | b));   // 1110  = 14
System.out.println(Integer.toBinaryString(a ^ b));   // 0110  = 6
System.out.println(~a);                              // -13   (see below)
```

`~a` is `-13` because Java integers are two's complement: `~x == -x - 1`.

**Shifts.** Left shift by `n` multiplies by 2 to the power n; signed right
shift divides by 2 to the power n, rounding toward negative infinity.

```java
int x = 8;                 // 0000...1000
System.out.println(x << 2);   // 32     0000...100000
System.out.println(x >> 2);   //  2     0000...0010

int neg = -8;              // 1111...1000
System.out.println(neg >> 2);    // -2   sign bit copied in: 1111...1110
System.out.println(neg >>> 2);   // 1073741822  zeros shifted in
```

```text
  -8 as 32-bit two's complement:  11111111 11111111 11111111 11111000

  >> 2  (arithmetic, keeps sign): 11111111 11111111 11111111 11111110  = -2
  >>> 2 (logical, fills zeros)  : 00111111 11111111 11111111 11111110  = 1073741822
```

Shift distances are taken modulo 32 for `int` and modulo 64 for `long`, so
`1 << 32` is `1`, not `0` — a genuine trap.

**Bit flags.** The classic application packs many booleans into one integer:

```java
public class Permissions {
    public static final int READ    = 1 << 0;   // 0001
    public static final int WRITE   = 1 << 1;   // 0010
    public static final int EXECUTE = 1 << 2;   // 0100
    public static final int DELETE  = 1 << 3;   // 1000

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int perms = READ | WRITE;                    // set two flags: 0011

        boolean canWrite = (perms & WRITE) != 0;     // test a flag: true
        perms |= EXECUTE;                            // add a flag:  0111
        perms &= ~WRITE;                             // remove a flag: 0101
        perms ^= READ;                               // toggle a flag: 0100

        System.out.println(Integer.toBinaryString(perms));  // 100
    }
}
```

Useful idioms worth recognising on sight:

```java
boolean isEven    = (n & 1) == 0;           // test the lowest bit
boolean isPowerOf2 = n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0;  // clears the lowest set bit
int     swapped   = a; a = a ^ b; b = a ^ b; a = a ^ b;  // XOR swap (a curiosity)
int     bitCount  = Integer.bitCount(n);    // population count, prefer the library
int     highest   = Integer.highestOneBit(n);
```

In application code, prefer `EnumSet` over hand-rolled bit flags: it is
type-safe, readable, and internally just as compact.

> Key Takeaways
> - Bitwise operators act per bit; `~x` equals `-x - 1` under two's complement.
> - `>>` preserves the sign, `>>>` fills with zeros; there is no `<<<`.
> - Shift distances wrap modulo 32 for `int` and 64 for `long`.
> - Flag sets use `|` to add, `& ~` to remove, `&` to test, and `^` to toggle.
> - `EnumSet` is the idiomatic alternative in application code.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write methods to set, clear, toggle, and test bit `n` of an `int`.
> 2. Implement `isPowerOfTwo(int n)` using a single bitwise expression and
>    explain why it works.
> 3. Interview: What is the difference between `>>` and `>>>`, and for which
>    input do they produce the same result? (Hint: think about the sign bit.)

#### Ternary Conditional Operator

The conditional operator is Java's only ternary operator, taking three
operands. Unlike an `if` statement, it is an *expression*: it produces a value
and can therefore appear anywhere a value is expected.

```java
condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse
```

```java
int a = 5, b = 10;
int max = (a > b) ? a : b;          // 10

// The same logic as a statement takes four lines and needs a mutable variable
int max2;
if (a > b) { max2 = a; } else { max2 = b; }
```

Its real advantage is enabling `final` declarations and inline use:

```java
final String label = count == 1 ? "item" : "items";   // cannot do this with if
System.out.println("Found " + count + " " + label);

System.out.println("Status: " + (isActive ? "on" : "off"));  // inline in an expression

return value != null ? value : "default";   // though Objects.requireNonNullElse is clearer
```

Only the selected branch is evaluated, so it short-circuits like `&&`:

```java
String name = null;
int length = (name != null) ? name.length() : 0;   // safe, length() is skipped
```

**Nesting.** Chained ternaries are legal and associate right to left. They
remain readable only with disciplined formatting:

```java
// Acceptable when formatted as a decision table
String grade = score >= 90 ? "A"
             : score >= 80 ? "B"
             : score >= 70 ? "C"
             : score >= 60 ? "D"
             :               "F";

// Unacceptable: unformatted and mixing conditions on different variables
String s = a ? b ? "x" : "y" : c ? "z" : d ? "w" : "v";
```

**The type trap.** The result type is computed by promoting both branches to a
common type, which can produce surprises when branch types differ:

```java
Object o = true ? Integer.valueOf(1) : Double.valueOf(2.0);
System.out.println(o);        // 1.0 -- not 1: both branches promoted to double

Integer i = null;
int result = true ? 0 : i;    // fine here, but if the condition flips,
                              // unboxing null throws NullPointerException
```

Use a ternary when both branches produce a value of the same conceptual type
and each branch is short. Use an `if` statement when the branches perform
actions rather than produce values, or when either branch needs more than one
expression.

Java 14's switch expressions cover the multi-branch case far more legibly than
a chain of ternaries, which is the topic that follows.

> Key Takeaways
> - The conditional operator is an expression, so it can initialise a `final`
>   variable and appear inline.
> - Only the chosen branch is evaluated.
> - Chained ternaries associate right to left and need table-style formatting
>   to stay readable.
> - Mixed numeric branch types are promoted to a common type, which can change
>   the printed result.
> - Prefer `if` for actions and switch expressions for many branches.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Rewrite an `if`/`else` that assigns a variable as a ternary, then mark the
>    variable `final`.
> 2. Write a ternary chain mapping a numeric score to a letter grade, formatted
>    as a decision table.
> 3. Interview: What does `true ? 1 : 2.0` evaluate to, and what is its type?
>    (Hint: both branches must share one type.)

#### Operator Precedence and Associativity

Precedence decides which operator binds tighter when an expression mixes them;
associativity decides the order among operators of equal precedence. Java's
table is inherited from C, with a few entries removed.

| Level | Operators                                 | Associativity |
| ----- | ----------------------------------------- | ------------- |
| 1     | `()` `[]` `.` `::`  method call           | Left to right |
| 2     | `++` `--` (postfix)                       | Left to right |
| 3     | `++` `--` (prefix) `+` `-` (unary) `~` `!` | Right to left |
| 4     | `(cast)` `new`                            | Right to left |
| 5     | `*` `/` `%`                               | Left to right |
| 6     | `+` `-`                                   | Left to right |
| 7     | `<<` `>>` `>>>`                           | Left to right |
| 8     | `<` `<=` `>` `>=` `instanceof`            | Left to right |
| 9     | `==` `!=`                                 | Left to right |
| 10    | `&`                                       | Left to right |
| 11    | `^`                                       | Left to right |
| 12    | `\|`                                      | Left to right |
| 13    | `&&`                                      | Left to right |
| 14    | `\|\|`                                    | Left to right |
| 15    | `? :`                                     | Right to left |
| 16    | `=` `+=` `-=` `*=` `/=` `%=` `&=` `^=` `\|=` `<<=` `>>=` `>>>=` | Right to left |

The rows that actually cause bugs are few, and they are worth memorising:

**Bitwise operators bind looser than comparison.** This is the single most
common precedence bug in Java, inherited from C:

```java
int flags = 0b0110;
// if (flags & 0b0010 != 0) { }   // ERROR: parsed as flags & (0b0010 != 0)
if ((flags & 0b0010) != 0) { }    // correct: parenthesise the mask
```

**`&&` binds tighter than `||`.** So a condition mixing them groups the ANDs
first, exactly like `*` before `+`:

```java
if (a || b && c)      // means: a || (b && c)
if ((a || b) && c)    // different meaning -- parentheses required
```

**Assignment is right-associative and lowest**, which makes chained assignment
work and means the entire right-hand side is evaluated first:

```java
int x, y, z;
x = y = z = 5;        // z = 5, then y = z, then x = y
```

**Unary operators bind tighter than arithmetic:**

```java
int i = 5;
int r = -i + 3;       // (-i) + 3 = -2, not -(i + 3)
int s = 2 + 3 * 4;    // 14, not 20
int t = (2 + 3) * 4;  // 20
```

Worked examples, resolved step by step:

```text
  2 + 3 * 4 - 6 / 2
= 2 + 12 - 3          (* and / first, left to right)
= 14 - 3
= 11

  true || false && false
= true || (false && false)    (&& before ||)
= true || false
= true

  1 + 2 + "x" + 1 + 2
= "3x" + 1 + 2                (+ is left-associative throughout)
= "3x1" + 2
= "3x12"
```

The practical rule: memorise the four or five relationships above, and
parenthesise anything else. Explicit parentheses cost nothing at runtime, and a
reader should never have to consult a precedence table to review your code.

> Key Takeaways
> - Precedence selects the binding operator; associativity orders equals.
> - Bitwise `&`, `^`, `|` bind looser than `==` and `!=`, so masks need
>   parentheses.
> - `&&` binds tighter than `||`, mirroring `*` before `+`.
> - Assignment and the conditional operator associate right to left.
> - Parenthesise for the reader rather than relying on the table.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Evaluate by hand, then verify: `10 - 4 - 3`, `2 * 3 % 4`,
>    `true || true && false`, `1 + 2 + "3" + 4 + 5`.
> 2. Find and fix the precedence bug in `if (value & MASK == MASK)`.
> 3. Interview: Why does `a || b && c` not mean `(a || b) && c`, and how would
>    you make the intent unambiguous? (Hint: compare with arithmetic.)

<a id="15-control-flow"></a>
### 1.5 Control Flow

Control flow statements decide which code runs and how often. Java's set is
small and conventional, with modern additions that turn some of them into
expressions.

#### if, else if, and else

The `if` statement executes a block when a condition is `true`. The condition
must be a `boolean` expression — Java accepts nothing else, which eliminates
the C family's most infamous typo.

```java
int temperature = 25;

if (temperature > 30) {
    System.out.println("Hot");
} else if (temperature > 20) {          // only tested if the first was false
    System.out.println("Warm");
} else if (temperature > 10) {
    System.out.println("Mild");
} else {
    System.out.println("Cold");
}
```

There is no `elseif` keyword: `else if` is simply an `if` statement nested in
the `else` branch. The conventional formatting hides that nesting, which is
why long chains stay readable.

```text
if (c1) { A }          is really      if (c1) { A }
else if (c2) { B }                    else {
else { C }                                if (c2) { B }
                                          else { C }
                                      }
```

**Braces are optional for a single statement, and omitting them is a known
hazard.** The compiler binds only the next statement to the `if`:

```java
if (isValid)
    log("valid");
    process();        // ALWAYS runs -- indentation lies, this is not in the if

if (isValid) {        // always use braces
    log("valid");
    process();
}
```

A dangling `else` binds to the nearest unmatched `if`, which is another reason
braces are not optional in practice:

```java
if (a)
    if (b) x();
    else y();        // belongs to 'if (b)', despite what the indentation suggests
```

**Conditions must be boolean**, so these classic errors cannot occur:

```java
int count = 0;
// if (count) { }        // ERROR: int cannot be converted to boolean
// if (count = 1) { }    // ERROR: the assignment yields int, not boolean
if (count == 1) { }      // correct
if (flag = true) { }     // compiles! both sides are boolean -- the one real trap
```

Style matters more here than anywhere else in the language, because deep
nesting is the most common readability failure in Java code. Guard clauses
flatten it:

```java
// Nested: the happy path is buried four levels deep
public String process(Order order) {
    if (order != null) {
        if (order.isPaid()) {
            if (order.hasStock()) {
                return ship(order);
            } else { return "out of stock"; }
        } else { return "unpaid"; }
    } else { return "no order"; }
}

// Guard clauses: handle failures first, keep the happy path unindented
public String process(Order order) {
    if (order == null)      return "no order";
    if (!order.isPaid())    return "unpaid";
    if (!order.hasStock())  return "out of stock";
    return ship(order);
}
```

Comparing a boolean to a literal is redundant: write `if (isReady)`, not
`if (isReady == true)`.

> Key Takeaways
> - Conditions must be `boolean`; numbers and references do not convert.
> - `else if` is a nested `if`, not a distinct keyword.
> - Always use braces; without them only the next single statement is bound,
>   and a dangling `else` attaches to the nearest `if`.
> - `if (flag = true)` compiles when `flag` is boolean, and is the one
>   assignment-in-condition trap that survives.
> - Guard clauses flatten nesting and keep the primary path visible.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a method classifying a `char` as vowel, consonant, digit, or other,
>    using an `if`/`else if` chain.
> 2. Take a method nested three levels deep and rewrite it with guard clauses.
> 3. Write code where omitting braces causes a bug, then fix it and describe
>    what the indentation implied versus what the compiler did.

#### switch Statements and switch Expressions

`switch` selects among many branches by comparing one value against constant
labels. Java has two generations of it, and knowing both is necessary because
old code is everywhere.

**The classic switch statement** falls through from one case into the next
unless stopped by `break`. Fall-through was inherited from C, is occasionally
useful, and is far more often a bug:

```java
int day = 3;
switch (day) {
    case 1:
        System.out.println("Monday");
        break;                          // forget this and Tuesday prints too
    case 2:
        System.out.println("Tuesday");
        break;
    case 6:
    case 7:                             // intentional fall-through: grouped labels
        System.out.println("Weekend");
        break;
    default:
        System.out.println("Midweek");
}
```

Permitted selector types are `byte`, `short`, `char`, `int` and their wrappers,
`String` (since Java 7), and `enum`. Notably absent are `long`, `float`,
`double`, and `boolean`. Case labels must be compile-time constants, so a
variable or a method call cannot be a label.

**Switch expressions** (standard since Java 14) fix the design. The arrow form
takes no fall-through, requires exhaustiveness when producing a value, and can
be assigned directly:

```java
String dayType = switch (day) {
    case 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 -> "Weekday";     // multiple labels, comma separated
    case 6, 7          -> "Weekend";
    default            -> "Invalid";      // required: the switch must be exhaustive
};                                        // note the terminating semicolon
```

For a branch needing several statements, use a block and `yield` to supply the
value:

```java
int numLetters = switch (day) {
    case 1, 2 -> 6;
    case 3 -> {
        System.out.println("Computing for Wednesday");   // side effect
        yield 9;                                         // yield, not return
    }
    default -> 0;
};
```

| Aspect             | Classic statement            | Arrow expression                |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Fall-through       | Yes, unless `break`          | Never                           |
| Produces a value   | No                           | Yes                             |
| Multiple labels    | Stacked `case` lines         | Comma-separated                 |
| Exhaustiveness     | Not required                 | Required when returning a value |
| Scope of variables | Shared across all cases      | Per branch                      |
| Multi-statement    | Naturally                    | Use a block with `yield`        |

The scope difference is worth seeing, because the classic form shares one scope
across every case, so a variable declared in one case is visible (though
unassigned) in the others:

```java
switch (x) {
    case 1:
        int v = 10;        // v is in scope for case 2 as well
        break;
    case 2:
        // int v = 20;     // ERROR: v is already defined
        break;
}
```

With `enum` selectors the compiler knows every possible value, so an arrow
switch covering all constants needs no `default` — and if someone later adds a
constant, the code stops compiling, which is exactly the reminder you want:

```java
enum Status { ACTIVE, SUSPENDED, CLOSED }

String describe(Status s) {
    return switch (s) {
        case ACTIVE    -> "running";
        case SUSPENDED -> "paused";
        case CLOSED    -> "finished";
        // no default: adding a constant becomes a compile error here
    };
}
```

Pattern matching for `switch`, which allows type patterns and guards in case
labels, builds on this and is covered with polymorphism in a later chapter.

> Key Takeaways
> - The classic switch falls through unless each case breaks; the arrow form
>   never falls through.
> - Switch expressions produce values, must be exhaustive, and use `yield`
>   inside blocks.
> - Selector types are integral types, `String`, and `enum` — not `long`,
>   floating point, or `boolean`.
> - Case labels must be compile-time constants.
> - Omitting `default` over an `enum` turns a future added constant into a
>   compile error, which is desirable.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a classic switch that deliberately relies on fall-through to group
>    months by quarter, then rewrite it as an arrow expression.
> 2. Convert an `if`/`else if` chain over a `String` command into a switch
>    expression.
> 3. Interview: Why can a switch not use `long` or `double`? (Hint: think about
>    how labels are matched and what a jump table requires.)

#### while and do-while Loops

Both loops repeat while a condition holds. The difference is when the condition
is tested, which decides whether the body can run zero times.

```java
// while: test first, so the body may never execute
int i = 0;
while (i < 5) {
    System.out.print(i + " ");   // 0 1 2 3 4
    i++;                         // forgetting this is the classic infinite loop
}

// do-while: body first, so it always runs at least once
int j = 10;
do {
    System.out.println("runs once even though 10 < 5 is false");
    j++;
} while (j < 5);
```

```text
   while                          do-while

   +-> test condition             +-> execute body
   |      |                       |       |
   |   true|  false -> exit       |    test condition
   |      v                       |       |
   +--- body                      +--true |  false -> exit
```

`while` is the natural choice when the number of iterations is unknown in
advance, which is why it dominates input reading, searching, and consuming
iterators:

```java
Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in);
String line;
while (!(line = scanner.nextLine()).equals("quit")) {   // assign, then test
    process(line);
}

// Consuming an iterator explicitly
Iterator<String> it = list.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) {
    String value = it.next();
    if (value.isEmpty()) it.remove();   // the only safe way to remove while iterating
}
```

`do-while` fits when at least one pass is required by the problem itself:
menus, retry loops, and input validation.

```java
int choice;
do {
    System.out.println("1) Deposit  2) Withdraw  3) Exit");
    choice = scanner.nextInt();
} while (choice < 1 || choice > 3);     // re-prompt until valid
```

Note the semicolon after the `while` in a `do-while`; it is required, and
omitting it is a common syntax error.

**Infinite loops** are written deliberately with `while (true)` and exited with
`break` or `return`. This is idiomatic for event loops and servers:

```java
while (true) {
    Request request = queue.take();     // blocks until work arrives
    if (request.isShutdown()) break;
    handle(request);
}
```

Three habits prevent most loop bugs: make sure some statement in the body can
change the condition, be careful that the change is reachable on every path
(an early `continue` that skips the increment causes a hang), and never test
`double` values for exact equality in a loop condition.

```java
// Hangs: the accumulated value never equals 1.0 exactly
for (double d = 0.0; d != 1.0; d += 0.1) { }

// Correct: compare with an inequality
for (double d = 0.0; d < 1.0; d += 0.1) { }
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `while` tests before the body, so it may run zero times; `do-while` always
>   runs at least once.
> - `do-while` requires a terminating semicolon.
> - `while` suits unknown iteration counts; `do-while` suits menus and
>   validation.
> - Ensure the condition variable changes on every path, including after
>   `continue`.
> - Never use exact equality on floating-point loop conditions.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write the same countdown twice, once with `while` and once with
>    `do-while`, starting from a value that makes the condition initially
>    false, and compare the output.
> 2. Write a number-guessing loop that keeps prompting until the guess is
>    correct, reporting "higher" or "lower".
> 3. Write a `while` loop with a `continue` placed so that the loop never
>    terminates, then fix it.

#### Classic and Enhanced for Loops

The classic `for` loop packs initialisation, condition, and update into one
header, keeping the loop's mechanics in one place.

```java
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    System.out.print(i + " ");     // 0 1 2 3 4
}
// i is out of scope here
```

```text
for ( init ; condition ; update ) { body }

  1. init        runs once, before anything else
  2. condition   tested before each iteration; false -> exit
  3. body        executes
  4. update      runs after the body
  5. back to 2
```

All three parts are optional, and the initialiser and update may contain
several comma-separated expressions:

```java
for (int i = 0, j = 10; i < j; i++, j--) {   // two counters converging
    System.out.println(i + " " + j);
}

for (;;) { }                    // no parts at all: an infinite loop
```

**The enhanced for loop** (or "for-each", since Java 5) iterates over arrays
and anything implementing `Iterable`, removing the index bookkeeping entirely:

```java
int[] numbers = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
for (int n : numbers) {
    System.out.print(n + " ");
}

List<String> names = List.of("Ada", "Grace", "Alan");
for (String name : names) {
    System.out.println(name);
}

Map<String, Integer> ages = Map.of("Ada", 36, "Alan", 41);
for (Map.Entry<String, Integer> entry : ages.entrySet()) {   // iterate a map
    System.out.println(entry.getKey() + " is " + entry.getValue());
}
```

It is pure syntactic sugar. The compiler desugars the collection form into an
iterator loop and the array form into an indexed loop:

```java
// for (String s : list)  becomes:
for (Iterator<String> it = list.iterator(); it.hasNext(); ) {
    String s = it.next();
    ...
}
```

That desugaring explains both its limitations and its one notorious runtime
error:

```java
List<String> items = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
for (String item : items) {
    if (item.equals("b")) {
        items.remove(item);       // ConcurrentModificationException
    }
}

items.removeIf(item -> item.equals("b"));   // correct and concise
```

| Situation                          | Loop to choose            |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| Need the index                     | Classic `for`             |
| Iterate backwards or by a step     | Classic `for`             |
| Modify the collection while looping| Classic `for` or iterator |
| Read every element in order        | Enhanced `for`            |
| Iterate several collections at once| Classic `for`             |

The enhanced form also cannot modify the array or list element itself, because
the loop variable is a copy of the value or reference:

```java
int[] values = {1, 2, 3};
for (int v : values) { v *= 2; }          // no effect on the array
for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) { values[i] *= 2; }   // works
```

Prefer the enhanced form whenever it suffices: it cannot go out of bounds, it
cannot get the termination condition wrong, and it states the intent plainly.

> Key Takeaways
> - The classic `for` collects init, condition, and update in one header and
>   scopes its variable to the loop.
> - The enhanced `for` works on arrays and `Iterable`, and is desugared to an
>   iterator or indexed loop.
> - Structurally modifying a collection inside an enhanced `for` throws
>   `ConcurrentModificationException`; use `removeIf` or an explicit iterator.
> - The loop variable is a copy, so assigning to it does not change the source.
> - Use the enhanced form by default, the classic form when you need the index.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Print an array forwards with an enhanced `for` and backwards with a
>    classic one.
> 2. Trigger a `ConcurrentModificationException`, then fix it three ways:
>    `removeIf`, an explicit `Iterator`, and collecting into a new list.
> 3. Write nested loops printing a multiplication table from 1 to 9, aligned
>    with `printf`.

#### break, continue, and Labeled Statements

`break` exits a loop or switch entirely; `continue` skips the rest of the
current iteration and proceeds to the next one. Both apply to the innermost
enclosing loop unless a label directs them elsewhere.

```java
for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {
    if (i == 5) break;           // leaves the loop at once
    System.out.print(i + " ");   // 1 2 3 4
}

for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {
    if (i % 2 == 0) continue;    // skips the println for even numbers
    System.out.print(i + " ");   // 1 3 5 7 9
}
```

A critical detail: in a classic `for` loop, `continue` still runs the update
expression, so the counter advances. In a `while` loop it does not, which is
how `continue` causes infinite loops:

```java
int i = 0;
while (i < 5) {
    if (i == 2) continue;    // INFINITE: i++ below is never reached when i == 2
    System.out.print(i);
    i++;
}
```

**Labels** name a statement so that `break` or `continue` can target an outer
loop. A label is an identifier followed by a colon, placed immediately before
the loop.

```java
outer:                                    // the label
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
        if (i * j > 2) {
            break outer;                  // leaves BOTH loops
        }
        System.out.println(i + "," + j);
    }
}

search:
for (int[] row : matrix) {
    for (int value : row) {
        if (value == target) {
            found = true;
            break search;                 // stop scanning the whole matrix
        }
    }
}
```

```text
   break;              break outer;          continue outer;

   +--outer------+     +--outer------+       +--outer------+
   |  +-inner-+  |     |  +-inner-+  |       |  +-inner-+  |
   |  |  X----+--+     |  |  X-----+--+----> |  |  X-----+--+--+
   |  +-------+  |     |  +-------+  |  exit |  +-------+  |  | next
   |   continues |     |             |       |             |<-+ outer
   +-------------+     +-------------+       +-------------+    iteration
```

`continue label` is rarer and restarts the labelled loop's next iteration,
skipping the remainder of both bodies.

Labels are the closest thing Java has to `goto` — and `goto` is a reserved but
unused keyword precisely so that nobody adds it. Labels are constrained: they
can only break out of or continue an enclosing statement, never jump forward
into arbitrary code.

Use them sparingly. A labelled break out of a double loop is legitimate and
clear; three or more nested labelled jumps usually mean the inner loops should
become a method, where a plain `return` does the same job more legibly:

```java
// Often better than a labelled break
private boolean contains(int[][] matrix, int target) {
    for (int[] row : matrix) {
        for (int value : row) {
            if (value == target) return true;   // returns from the method
        }
    }
    return false;
}
```

One more use: `break` inside a `switch` nested in a loop exits the *switch*,
not the loop. To leave the loop from inside a switch, you need a label.

> Key Takeaways
> - `break` exits the innermost loop or switch; `continue` skips to the next
>   iteration.
> - In a classic `for`, `continue` still runs the update; in a `while` it does
>   not, which can hang the loop.
> - Labels let `break` and `continue` target an enclosing loop.
> - `break` inside a switch within a loop exits only the switch.
> - Extracting a method and using `return` is usually clearer than deep
>   labelled jumps.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write nested loops that find the first pair of numbers in two arrays
>    summing to a target, stopping both loops immediately.
> 2. Construct a `while` loop where `continue` skips the increment, observe the
>    hang, and fix it two different ways.
> 3. Write a loop containing a switch, and make `break` exit the loop rather
>    than the switch.

#### Nested Control Structures

Real logic combines these constructs, and the combination is where readability
is usually won or lost. Nesting itself is not the problem; unnecessary nesting
is.

A standard nested loop walks a two-dimensional structure, with the outer loop
over rows and the inner over columns:

```java
for (int row = 1; row <= 3; row++) {
    for (int col = 1; col <= 3; col++) {
        System.out.printf("%4d", row * col);
    }
    System.out.println();          // end the line after each row
}
```

```text
   1   2   3
   2   4   6
   3   6   9
```

Complexity compounds multiplicatively: two nested loops over n items perform
n squared iterations, three perform n cubed. A triple-nested loop over ten
thousand records is a hundred trillion operations — which is why recognising
nesting depth is a performance skill, not just a style one.

Combining loops with conditionals produces the classic drift toward the right
margin. Four techniques reverse it.

**1. Invert conditions and use `continue`** to keep the body flat:

```java
// Before
for (Order order : orders) {
    if (order.isPaid()) {
        if (order.getTotal() > 100) {
            applyDiscount(order);
        }
    }
}

// After
for (Order order : orders) {
    if (!order.isPaid())        continue;
    if (order.getTotal() <= 100) continue;
    applyDiscount(order);
}
```

**2. Extract the inner loop into a method**, which also names the operation:

```java
for (Department dept : departments) {
    totalPayroll += payrollFor(dept);      // inner loop moved inside
}

private double payrollFor(Department dept) {
    double sum = 0;
    for (Employee e : dept.getEmployees()) {
        sum += e.getSalary();
    }
    return sum;
}
```

**3. Return early** rather than nesting the remainder in an `else`.

**4. Replace the loop with a stream** when the operation is a filter, map, or
reduce. Streams are covered in depth later, but the contrast is instructive:

```java
double total = departments.stream()
        .flatMap(d -> d.getEmployees().stream())
        .filter(Employee::isActive)
        .mapToDouble(Employee::getSalary)
        .sum();
```

A worked example combining everything — validating a grid and reporting the
first problem:

```java
public static String validate(int[][] grid) {
    if (grid == null || grid.length == 0) {
        return "grid is empty";                 // guard clause
    }
    for (int row = 0; row < grid.length; row++) {
        if (grid[row].length != grid[0].length) {
            return "row " + row + " has a different length";   // early return
        }
        for (int col = 0; col < grid[row].length; col++) {
            int value = grid[row][col];
            if (value < 0) {
                return "negative value at " + row + "," + col;
            }
        }
    }
    return "valid";
}
```

As a rule of thumb, three levels of nesting inside a method is a signal to
extract; four is a defect waiting to be found.

> Key Takeaways
> - Nested loops multiply their iteration counts, so depth is a performance
>   concern as well as a readability one.
> - `continue` with inverted conditions flattens filtering loops.
> - Extracting an inner loop into a well-named method both flattens and
>   documents the code.
> - Early returns remove `else` branches entirely.
> - Treat three levels of nesting as a prompt to refactor.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Print a right-angled triangle of asterisks of height n using nested loops.
> 2. Take a triple-nested loop with two conditionals and flatten it using
>    method extraction and `continue`.
> 3. Write a method that finds the first duplicate in a two-dimensional array,
>    returning its coordinates, and stop scanning as soon as it is found.

<a id="16-arrays-and-strings"></a>
### 1.6 Arrays and Strings

Arrays and strings are the two aggregate types you meet before learning to
write classes. Both are objects, both are fixed in size once created, and both
have behaviour that surprises people who assume otherwise.

#### One-Dimensional Array Creation and Access

An array is a fixed-length, ordered container of values that all share one
type. Unlike the primitives, an array is an object: it lives on the heap, a
variable holds a reference to it, and that reference can be `null`.

```java
int[] numbers;                        // declares a reference, no array yet
numbers = new int[5];                 // allocates 5 slots, all zero-initialised

int[] combined = new int[5];          // the usual one-line form
int[] literal  = {10, 20, 30};        // initialiser shorthand, size inferred
int[] explicit = new int[]{10, 20, 30};  // needed when not at a declaration

String[] names = new String[3];       // three null references, no String objects
```

Put the brackets after the type, not the variable. `int[] a` is idiomatic Java;
`int a[]` is legal C-style syntax that Java tolerates and nobody uses.

```text
   int[] numbers = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};

   numbers ---> +------+------+------+------+------+
                |  10  |  20  |  30  |  40  |  50  |
                +------+------+------+------+------+
  index            0      1      2      3      4
                                            length = 5
                                            last valid index = length - 1
```

**Access is zero-based and bounds-checked.** Every read and write verifies the
index at runtime, and an out-of-range index throws rather than corrupting
memory. That check is the reason Java does not have buffer overflow
vulnerabilities in ordinary code.

```java
int[] numbers = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};

System.out.println(numbers[0]);        // 10
System.out.println(numbers[4]);        // 50
numbers[2] = 99;                       // arrays are mutable

System.out.println(numbers.length);    // 5 -- a FIELD, not a method
// numbers[5];                         // ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
// numbers[-1];                        // same exception
```

Note `length` is a field on arrays, `length()` is a method on `String`, and
`size()` is a method on collections. The inconsistency is historical and you
simply have to remember it.

**Fixed size.** An array's length is set at creation and can never change.
"Growing" an array means allocating a new one and copying:

```java
int[] grown = Arrays.copyOf(numbers, numbers.length * 2);   // new array, padded with 0
int[] slice = Arrays.copyOfRange(numbers, 1, 4);            // indices 1,2,3
```

If you need a container that grows, use `ArrayList`, which does exactly this
copying internally.

**Default values** are the same zero values used for fields: `0`, `0.0`,
`false`, `'\u0000'`, or `null`. An array of objects contains null references
until you fill it, which is a frequent source of `NullPointerException`:

```java
String[] words = new String[3];
System.out.println(words[0]);           // null
// System.out.println(words[0].length()); // NullPointerException
Arrays.fill(words, "");                 // fill before use if you need non-null
```

Iteration uses either form of `for`, depending on whether you need the index:

```java
for (int i = 0; i < numbers.length; i++) {      // index available
    System.out.println(i + ": " + numbers[i]);
}
for (int value : numbers) {                     // values only
    System.out.println(value);
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Arrays are fixed-size heap objects holding one element type, and the
>   reference can be `null`.
> - Elements are zero-initialised; object arrays start full of `null`.
> - `length` is a field on arrays, `length()` a method on `String`, `size()` on
>   collections.
> - Indexing is zero-based and bounds-checked, throwing
>   `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`.
> - Resizing means allocating and copying, which is what `ArrayList` automates.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write methods computing the minimum, maximum, and average of an `int[]`,
>    handling the empty array explicitly.
> 2. Reverse an array in place using two indices moving toward each other.
> 3. Interview: Why is `array.length` a field while `string.length()` is a
>    method? (Hint: what kind of object is an array, and what can it declare?)

#### Multidimensional and Jagged Arrays

Java has no true multidimensional array. What it has is arrays of arrays, and
understanding that distinction explains everything else about them.

```java
int[][] matrix = new int[3][4];       // 3 rows, each an int[4]
matrix[1][2] = 7;                     // row 1, column 2

int[][] literal = {
    {1, 2, 3},
    {4, 5, 6},
    {7, 8, 9}
};
```

```text
   matrix ---> +-----+-----+-----+
               |  •  |  •  |  •  |     an array of THREE references
               +--|--+--|--+--|--+
                  |     |     |
                  v     v     v
        [0]-> +---+---+---+---+
              | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |       each row is a separate int[4] object
              +---+---+---+---+
        [1]-> +---+---+---+---+
              | 0 | 0 | 7 | 0 |
              +---+---+---+---+
        [2]-> +---+---+---+---+
              | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
              +---+---+---+---+
```

Because rows are independent objects, they need not be the same length. An
array with rows of differing length is called *jagged* (or ragged):

```java
int[][] triangle = new int[4][];       // 4 row slots, no rows allocated yet
for (int i = 0; i < triangle.length; i++) {
    triangle[i] = new int[i + 1];      // row i has i+1 columns
}

int[][] jagged = {
    {1},
    {2, 3},
    {4, 5, 6}
};
```

This is why `matrix.length` is the number of rows and `matrix[i].length` is the
length of *that specific row*. Iterating correctly means asking each row for
its own length:

```java
for (int row = 0; row < jagged.length; row++) {
    for (int col = 0; col < jagged[row].length; col++) {   // per-row length
        System.out.print(jagged[row][col] + " ");
    }
    System.out.println();
}

// Enhanced form, which avoids the mistake entirely
for (int[] row : jagged) {
    for (int value : row) {
        System.out.print(value + " ");
    }
    System.out.println();
}
```

Only the leftmost dimensions may be specified when allocating, and they must be
contiguous:

```java
int[][][] cube   = new int[2][3][4];   // fully allocated
int[][]   partial = new int[3][];      // legal: rows allocated later
// int[][] invalid = new int[][4];     // ERROR: cannot skip a leading dimension
```

Printing needs the right helper, because an array's own `toString` prints a
type name and a hash code:

```java
System.out.println(jagged);                      // [[I@1b6d3586 -- useless
System.out.println(Arrays.toString(jagged[0]));  // [1]
System.out.println(Arrays.deepToString(jagged)); // [[1], [2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
```

Performance note: because rows are separate objects, they can be scattered
across the heap. Iterating row by row (following the memory layout) is faster
than column by column for large matrices, an effect that grows with size.

> Key Takeaways
> - Multidimensional arrays are arrays of array references, not contiguous
>   blocks.
> - Rows may have different lengths, producing jagged arrays.
> - Use `matrix[i].length` for the row length, never assume a uniform width.
> - Only leading dimensions may be given at allocation time.
> - Use `Arrays.deepToString` to print nested arrays.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build and print Pascal's triangle for ten rows using a jagged array.
> 2. Write a method that transposes a rectangular `int[][]`, and decide what it
>    should do with a jagged input.
> 3. Interview: What does `new int[3][]` create, and how does it differ from
>    `new int[3][4]`? (Hint: count the objects allocated.)

#### Array Utility Methods

`java.util.Arrays` provides the operations arrays lack as objects. Knowing this
class saves writing loops that are easy to get subtly wrong.

```java
import java.util.Arrays;

int[] data = {5, 2, 9, 1, 7};
```

**Printing and comparing.**

```java
System.out.println(Arrays.toString(data));           // [5, 2, 9, 1, 7]
System.out.println(Arrays.deepToString(matrix));     // for nested arrays

int[] a = {1, 2, 3};
int[] b = {1, 2, 3};
System.out.println(a == b);              // false -- different objects
System.out.println(a.equals(b));         // false -- Object.equals, identity again
System.out.println(Arrays.equals(a, b)); // true  -- element by element
System.out.println(Arrays.deepEquals(nested1, nested2));   // for nested arrays
```

`a.equals(b)` returning `false` for identical contents catches almost everyone
once. Arrays do not override `equals` or `hashCode`, so they inherit identity
semantics from `Object`.

**Sorting and searching.**

```java
Arrays.sort(data);                                   // [1, 2, 5, 7, 9], in place
Arrays.sort(data, 1, 4);                             // sort a subrange only

String[] words = {"pear", "Apple", "fig"};
Arrays.sort(words, String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER);   // custom Comparator
Arrays.sort(words, Comparator.comparing(String::length));

int pos = Arrays.binarySearch(data, 7);              // 3 -- REQUIRES a sorted array
int missing = Arrays.binarySearch(data, 6);          // negative: -(insertion point) - 1
```

`binarySearch` on an unsorted array does not throw; it returns a meaningless
result. Sorting first is your responsibility.

**Filling, copying, and converting.**

```java
int[] filled = new int[5];
Arrays.fill(filled, 42);                             // [42, 42, 42, 42, 42]
Arrays.fill(filled, 1, 3, 0);                        // fill a subrange

int[] copy  = Arrays.copyOf(data, 3);                // first 3, or pad with 0
int[] range = Arrays.copyOfRange(data, 1, 4);        // indices 1..3
System.arraycopy(data, 0, copy, 0, 3);               // lower-level, fastest

List<String> list = Arrays.asList("a", "b", "c");    // FIXED-SIZE view, not a copy
// list.add("d");                                    // UnsupportedOperationException
List<String> mutable = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList("a", "b"));   // real list
```

**Streams and aggregates.**

```java
int sum = Arrays.stream(data).sum();
OptionalInt max = Arrays.stream(data).max();
double avg = Arrays.stream(data).average().orElse(0);
long evens = Arrays.stream(data).filter(n -> n % 2 == 0).count();
```

| Task                    | Use                                   |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| Print contents          | `Arrays.toString` / `deepToString`    |
| Compare contents        | `Arrays.equals` / `deepEquals`        |
| Sort                    | `Arrays.sort`                         |
| Search a sorted array   | `Arrays.binarySearch`                 |
| Resize                  | `Arrays.copyOf`                       |
| Fast block copy         | `System.arraycopy`                    |
| Aggregate               | `Arrays.stream(...)`                  |

One caution on `Arrays.sort`: primitives are sorted with a dual-pivot quicksort
(fast, not stable, which does not matter for primitives), while object arrays
use a stable merge sort called TimSort. The distinction matters when sorting
objects by several keys in sequence.

> Key Takeaways
> - Arrays do not override `equals` or `toString`, so use `Arrays.equals` and
>   `Arrays.toString`.
> - `binarySearch` silently misbehaves on unsorted input.
> - `Arrays.asList` returns a fixed-size view backed by the array, not an
>   independent list.
> - `Arrays.copyOf` resizes by allocating and copying; `System.arraycopy` is
>   the fastest block copy.
> - Primitive sorts use quicksort; object sorts use a stable merge sort.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Demonstrate the difference between `==`, `.equals`, and `Arrays.equals` on
>    two arrays with identical contents.
> 2. Sort an array of strings by length and then alphabetically, using a
>    comparator chain.
> 3. Show what `Arrays.binarySearch` returns for an absent element and use that
>    value to compute the correct insertion point.

#### String Immutability and the String Pool

A `String` is an object wrapping a sequence of characters, and its defining
property is that it is *immutable*: once created, the characters can never
change. Every method that appears to modify a string in fact returns a new one.

```java
String s = "hello";
s.toUpperCase();                    // creates "HELLO" and DISCARDS it
System.out.println(s);              // hello -- unchanged

s = s.toUpperCase();                // reassigning the reference is the only way
System.out.println(s);              // HELLO
```

Immutability is not an accident; it buys four concrete things. Strings can be
shared safely between threads with no synchronisation. Their hash code can be
computed once and cached, which makes them ideal `HashMap` keys. They can be
pooled and deduplicated. And security-sensitive values such as file paths or
class names cannot be changed by another thread between validation and use.

**The string pool** is a region of memory holding one shared instance of each
distinct string literal. Because strings cannot change, sharing is safe.

```java
String a = "java";          // creates the pooled instance
String b = "java";          // reuses the SAME pooled instance
String c = new String("java");   // explicitly forces a new heap object
String d = c.intern();      // returns the pooled instance

System.out.println(a == b);        // true  -- same object
System.out.println(a == c);        // false -- different objects
System.out.println(a == d);        // true  -- intern() found the pooled one
System.out.println(a.equals(c));   // true  -- contents are equal
```

```text
   String pool (inside the heap)        Regular heap
   +---------------------+              +---------------------+
   |  "java"  <--- a     |              |  "java"  <--- c     |
   |          <--- b     |              +---------------------+
   |          <--- d     |
   +---------------------+              a == b  true
                                        a == c  false
                                        a.equals(c)  true
```

Compile-time constant expressions are folded and pooled; anything computed at
runtime is not:

```java
String x = "ja" + "va";              // folded by the compiler -> pooled literal
System.out.println(x == a);          // true

String part = "ja";
String y = part + "va";              // computed at runtime -> new object
System.out.println(y == a);          // false
System.out.println(y.equals(a));     // true

final String cpart = "ja";           // a compile-time constant
String z = cpart + "va";             // folded again
System.out.println(z == a);          // true
```

The practical rule follows directly: **compare strings with `equals`, never
with `==`.** For case-insensitive comparison use `equalsIgnoreCase`, and to
avoid a `NullPointerException` when the variable may be null, call `equals` on
the literal or use `Objects.equals`:

```java
String input = null;
// input.equals("yes")            // NullPointerException
"yes".equals(input);              // false, safe
Objects.equals(input, "yes");     // false, safe and symmetrical
```

Since Java 9, strings are stored internally as a `byte[]` with an encoding flag
("compact strings"), using one byte per character for Latin-1 text instead of
two. This halved the memory footprint of typical applications and required no
code changes, a good illustration of why encapsulating the representation
matters.

> Key Takeaways
> - Strings are immutable; every "modifying" method returns a new string.
> - Immutability enables safe sharing, cached hash codes, and pooling.
> - Literals are pooled and shared; `new String(...)` always allocates.
> - Compare with `equals`; `==` compares identity and works with literals by
>   coincidence.
> - Call `equals` on the known-non-null side, or use `Objects.equals`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a program producing three strings with identical contents where
>    `==` gives different answers, and explain each case.
> 2. Show that `s.replace('a', 'b')` leaves `s` unchanged unless reassigned.
> 3. Interview: Why does Java make `String` immutable, and what would break in
>    `HashMap` if it were not? (Hint: think about when a hash code is computed
>    and where the entry is stored.)

#### Common String Operations

`String` exposes a large API. These are the methods that cover the vast
majority of real use, grouped by purpose.

**Inspecting.**

```java
String s = "Hello, World";

s.length();                  // 12 -- a method, unlike array.length
s.charAt(0);                 // 'H'
s.indexOf("World");          // 7, or -1 if absent
s.lastIndexOf('l');          // 10
s.contains("lo, W");         // true
s.startsWith("Hello");       // true
s.endsWith("!");             // false
s.isEmpty();                 // false -- length() == 0
"   ".isBlank();             // true  -- Java 11: empty or whitespace only
```

**Transforming** (all return new strings).

```java
s.toUpperCase();             // "HELLO, WORLD"
s.substring(7);              // "World"          -- from index to the end
s.substring(0, 5);           // "Hello"          -- end index is EXCLUSIVE
s.replace('l', 'L');         // "HeLLo, WorLd"
s.replace("World", "Java");  // "Hello, Java"
"  padded  ".trim();         // "padded"  -- removes ASCII whitespace
"  padded  ".strip();        // "padded"  -- Java 11, Unicode-aware
"ab".repeat(3);              // "ababab"  -- Java 11
```

The exclusive end index of `substring` is the single most common off-by-one
source: `substring(a, b)` yields `b - a` characters, and `substring(i, i)` is
the empty string.

**Splitting and joining.**

```java
String csv = "red,green,blue";
String[] colours = csv.split(",");                 // takes a REGEX, not a literal
String[] parts   = "a.b.c".split("\\.");           // '.' must be escaped in regex
String[] limited = "a,b,c,d".split(",", 2);        // ["a", "b,c,d"]

String joined = String.join(" | ", colours);       // "red | green | blue"
String fromList = String.join(", ", List.of("x", "y"));
```

That `split` takes a regular expression, not a plain delimiter, is a frequent
bug: splitting on `"."` or `"|"` without escaping matches everything or
nothing.

**Comparing.**

```java
"abc".equals("ABC");                // false
"abc".equalsIgnoreCase("ABC");      // true
"apple".compareTo("banana");        // negative: lexicographic ordering
"apple".compareToIgnoreCase("APPLE");  // 0
```

`compareTo` returns a negative number, zero, or a positive number — never
specifically -1 or 1, so test the sign rather than an exact value.

**Formatting and conversion.**

```java
String formatted = String.format("%s scored %.1f%%", "Ada", 92.5);
String modern    = "%s scored %.1f%%".formatted("Ada", 92.5);   // Java 15

int    n = Integer.parseInt("42");        // String -> int, throws on bad input
double d = Double.parseDouble("3.14");
String back = String.valueOf(42);         // int -> String, null-safe
String also = Integer.toString(42);
char[] chars = s.toCharArray();
```

A chained example — normalising user input:

```java
public static String normalise(String raw) {
    if (raw == null) return "";
    return raw.strip()                    // remove surrounding whitespace
              .toLowerCase()              // case-fold
              .replaceAll("\\s+", " ");   // collapse internal runs of whitespace
}
```

Each call returns a new string, so chaining reads naturally but allocates at
every step. For a handful of calls that cost is irrelevant; inside a hot loop,
it is not, which leads directly to the next topic.

> Key Takeaways
> - `substring`'s end index is exclusive, yielding `end - start` characters.
> - `split` and `replaceAll` take regular expressions; `replace` takes literals.
> - `compareTo` returns a sign, not a fixed magnitude.
> - Use `strip` over `trim` for Unicode correctness, and `isBlank` to test for
>   whitespace-only strings.
> - Every transformation allocates a new string.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a palindrome check that ignores case, spaces, and punctuation.
> 2. Write a method counting the occurrences of a substring, and make sure
>    overlapping matches are handled the way you intend.
> 3. Split `"a.b.c"` on the dot, observe the empty result, and fix the regex.

#### StringBuilder and Efficient Concatenation

Because strings are immutable, concatenation in a loop is quadratic: each `+`
allocates a new string and copies every character seen so far.

```java
// Anti-pattern: for n iterations this copies roughly n squared characters
String result = "";
for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
    result += i + ",";        // allocates a NEW String every iteration
}
```

```text
   iteration 1:  ""        + "0,"  -> "0,"            copy 0 chars
   iteration 2:  "0,"      + "1,"  -> "0,1,"          copy 2 chars
   iteration 3:  "0,1,"    + "2,"  -> "0,1,2,"        copy 4 chars
   ...                                                 total ~ n^2 / 2
```

`StringBuilder` holds a mutable `char` buffer and appends in place, growing the
buffer geometrically. The same loop becomes linear:

```java
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
    sb.append(i).append(',');     // append returns 'this', so calls chain
}
String result = sb.toString();    // one allocation at the end
```

On a ten-thousand-iteration loop the difference is typically three orders of
magnitude.

The main API:

```java
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();        // default capacity 16
StringBuilder sized = new StringBuilder(1024); // pre-size when you know roughly

sb.append("Hello").append(", ").append(42).append(true);  // any type
sb.insert(0, ">> ");            // insert at an index
sb.replace(0, 2, "**");         // replace a range
sb.delete(0, 3);                // delete a range
sb.deleteCharAt(0);
sb.reverse();                   // in place
sb.setLength(0);                // clear and reuse the buffer
sb.charAt(2); sb.length(); sb.indexOf("lo");
String out = sb.toString();     // produce an immutable String
```

**When `+` is fine.** The compiler optimises concatenation *within a single
expression*, so these are not a problem:

```java
String message = "User " + name + " logged in at " + time;   // one expression
```

Modern compilers compile this to an efficient `invokedynamic` call that builds
the result in one pass. The rule is therefore narrower than "never use `+`":
avoid `+` when concatenating **repeatedly across separate statements**,
typically in a loop.

| Situation                          | Use                                  |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Joining a few values in one line   | `+`                                  |
| Building in a loop                 | `StringBuilder`                      |
| Joining a collection with a delimiter | `String.join` or `Collectors.joining` |
| Shared across threads              | `StringBuffer` (synchronised)        |

`StringBuffer` is the thread-safe sibling with identical methods and
synchronised access. It predates `StringBuilder` (added in Java 5) and is
slower; use it only when a single builder genuinely is shared across threads,
which is rare because a better design usually avoids sharing it at all.

| Class           | Mutable | Thread-safe | Typical use                |
| --------------- | ------- | ----------- | -------------------------- |
| `String`        | No      | Yes (by immutability) | Values, keys, APIs |
| `StringBuilder` | Yes     | No          | Local building             |
| `StringBuffer`  | Yes     | Yes         | Legacy or shared building  |

For the common case of joining a collection, prefer the dedicated tools, which
handle the delimiter edge cases for you:

```java
String csv = String.join(",", List.of("a", "b", "c"));       // "a,b,c"
String fancy = list.stream().collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "[", "]"));
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Concatenating with `+` inside a loop is quadratic because each step copies
>   the whole accumulated string.
> - `StringBuilder` appends into a growable buffer, making the same work
>   linear.
> - `+` within a single expression is compiled efficiently and is fine.
> - Pre-size the builder when the final length is roughly known.
> - Use `StringBuffer` only for genuine cross-thread sharing; prefer
>   `String.join` for delimited output.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Time building a 100,000-character string with `+` and with
>    `StringBuilder`, and report the ratio.
> 2. Write a method reversing each word in a sentence while preserving word
>    order, using `StringBuilder`.
> 3. Interview: Is `"a" + "b" + "c"` slow? Explain what the compiler does with
>    it. (Hint: are those values known at compile time?)

#### Text Blocks and String Formatting

Multi-line text in source code used to require escape-laden concatenation.
Text blocks, standard since Java 15, let you write it literally.

```java
// Before: escapes, concatenation, and hard-to-see structure
String json = "{\n" +
              "  \"name\": \"Ada\",\n" +
              "  \"age\": 36\n" +
              "}";

// After: a text block, delimited by three double quotes
String json2 = """
        {
          "name": "Ada",
          "age": 36
        }""";
```

The opening `"""` must be followed by a line terminator; content starts on the
next line. Closing delimiter placement controls the trailing newline: on its
own line, the string ends with `\n`; on the content's last line, it does not.

**Incidental indentation is stripped automatically.** The compiler finds the
minimum indentation across all non-blank lines *and* the closing delimiter,
then removes that much from every line. This lets the block stay indented with
the surrounding code without polluting the value:

```text
        String sql = """
                SELECT id, name        <- 16 spaces
                FROM users             <- 16 spaces
                WHERE active = true    <- 16 spaces
                """;                   <- 16 spaces  => strip 16 from each line

        Result: "SELECT id, name\nFROM users\nWHERE active = true\n"
```

Moving the closing delimiter further left preserves more indentation, which is
how you control it deliberately.

Two escapes are specific to text blocks:

```java
String joined = """
        This line continues \
        onto the same line.""";      // trailing \ suppresses the newline

String trailing = """
        Keeps two trailing spaces\s\s
        """;                          // \s is a literal space, protected from stripping
```

Text blocks are ordinary `String` objects: same type, same methods, same
pooling for constant blocks. They are purely a source-code convenience, ideal
for SQL, JSON, HTML, and multi-line messages.

**Formatting.** Three interchangeable routes exist, and `formatted` reads best
with a text block:

```java
String a = String.format("%s is %d years old", name, age);
String b = "%s is %d years old".formatted(name, age);       // Java 15
System.out.printf("%s is %d years old%n", name, age);       // writes directly

String query = """
        SELECT * FROM users
        WHERE country = '%s' AND age > %d
        """.formatted("IT", 18);
```

Format specifier syntax is `%[argument_index$][flags][width][.precision]conversion`:

| Specifier | Meaning                    | Example                  | Output      |
| --------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------ | ----------- |
| `%s`      | Any value via `toString`   | `format("%s", 1.5)`      | `1.5`       |
| `%d`      | Integer                    | `format("%d", 42)`       | `42`        |
| `%f`      | Floating point             | `format("%f", 3.14)`     | `3.140000`  |
| `%.2f`    | Two decimal places         | `format("%.2f", 3.146)`  | `3.15`      |
| `%10s`    | Right-align in 10 columns  | `format("%10s", "hi")`   | `        hi`|
| `%-10s`   | Left-align in 10 columns   | `format("%-10s\|", "hi")` | `hi        \|` |
| `%,d`     | Group digits               | `format("%,d", 1000000)` | `1,000,000` |
| `%05d`    | Zero-pad to width 5        | `format("%05d", 42)`     | `00042`     |
| `%x` `%o` | Hex, octal                 | `format("%x", 255)`      | `ff`        |
| `%b`      | Boolean                    | `format("%b", null)`     | `false`     |
| `%n`      | Platform line separator    |                          |             |
| `%%`      | A literal percent sign     |                          |             |

```java
// A formatted report, combining width, alignment, and grouping
System.out.printf("%-15s %10s %8s%n", "Product", "Price", "Qty");
System.out.printf("%-15s %,10.2f %8d%n", "Keyboard", 1299.5, 3);
System.out.printf("%-15s %,10.2f %8d%n", "Monitor", 24999.0, 1);
```

```text
Product              Price      Qty
Keyboard          1,299.50        3
Monitor          24,999.00        1
```

A mismatch between a specifier and its argument, such as `%d` with a `String`,
throws `IllegalFormatConversionException` at runtime rather than failing to
compile, so format strings deserve a test.

> Key Takeaways
> - Text blocks start after a line break following `"""` and strip incidental
>   indentation based on the least-indented line and the closing delimiter.
> - Closing-delimiter placement decides whether a trailing newline is included.
> - `\` at end of line joins lines; `\s` preserves a trailing space.
> - A text block is an ordinary `String` with no runtime difference.
> - `formatted`, `String.format`, and `printf` share the same specifier syntax;
>   mismatches fail at runtime.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write an HTML fragment as a text block and print it, verifying that the
>    surrounding code indentation does not appear in the output.
> 2. Produce a formatted invoice table with right-aligned, comma-grouped
>    amounts to two decimals.
> 3. Interview: How does a text block decide how much indentation to remove,
>    and how would you keep four leading spaces on every line? (Hint: the
>    closing delimiter participates in the calculation.)


<a id="2-classes-objects-and-encapsulation"></a>
## 2. Classes, Objects, and Encapsulation

This chapter is where Java stops being a procedural language with nice syntax
and becomes object-oriented. It covers how to define a type, how objects are
created and initialised, how methods receive and return data, and how access
control turns a loose bag of fields into a component with an enforced contract.
Everything in the remaining chapters — inheritance, interfaces, collections,
frameworks — is built from the ideas established here.

<a id="21-object-oriented-thinking"></a>
### 2.1 Object-Oriented Thinking

Before any syntax, it is worth understanding what problem objects solve, because
the syntax only makes sense once the motivation is clear.

#### Procedural versus Object-Oriented Paradigms

In procedural programming, data and the functions that act on it are separate.
You define record structures, then write functions that take them as arguments.
This works well at small scale and degrades badly at large scale, for one
specific reason: nothing stops any function anywhere from modifying any field.
When a value is wrong, the list of suspects is every line of code in the
program.

Consider a bank account written procedurally in Java-like syntax:

```java
// PROCEDURAL: data is a passive record, logic lives elsewhere
class AccountData {
    String owner;
    double balance;      // anyone can write anything here
}

class AccountOperations {
    static void deposit(AccountData account, double amount) {
        account.balance += amount;          // no validation enforced anywhere
    }
    static void withdraw(AccountData account, double amount) {
        account.balance -= amount;          // allows a negative balance
    }
}

// Somewhere else, three months later, in a hurry:
account.balance = -5000;                    // perfectly legal, nothing prevents it
```

The rule "a balance may never go negative" exists only in the programmer's head
and in whichever functions remember to check. The object-oriented version moves
the data and its rules into one unit, and closes the door on everything else:

```java
// OBJECT-ORIENTED: the data and the rules that protect it live together
class Account {
    private String owner;          // private: unreachable from outside
    private double balance;

    public void deposit(double amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Deposit must be positive");
        }
        balance += amount;         // the ONLY way balance can increase
    }

    public void withdraw(double amount) {
        if (amount > balance) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient funds");
        }
        balance -= amount;         // the ONLY way balance can decrease
    }

    public double getBalance() { return balance; }
}

// account.balance = -5000;        // now a COMPILE error, not a runtime disaster
```

The gain is not that the code is shorter, because it is not. The gain is that
the set of places capable of producing a negative balance shrank from "the whole
program" to "these twenty lines". That reduction is the entire point.

```text
  PROCEDURAL                          OBJECT-ORIENTED

  +----------+   +----------+         +------------------------+
  |  data    |   |  data    |         |  Account               |
  +----------+   +----------+         |  - balance  (private)  |
       ^   ^          ^                |                        |
       |   |          |                |  + deposit()           |
  +----+ +-+---+ +----+----+           |  + withdraw()          |
  | fn | | fn  | |   fn    |           |  + getBalance()        |
  +----+ +-----+ +---------+           +------------------------+
                                                  ^
  any function may touch any field                |
                                        outside code can ONLY call methods
```

| Aspect             | Procedural                          | Object-oriented                       |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| Unit of decomposition | Function                         | Class                                 |
| Data and behaviour | Separate                            | Bundled together                      |
| Who may change data| Any function with a reference       | Only the owning class                 |
| Invariants         | Enforced by convention              | Enforced by the compiler              |
| Growth behaviour   | Coupling grows with the codebase    | Coupling is bounded by interfaces     |
| Good fit           | Scripts, small tools, pure algorithms | Domains with rules and many collaborators |

Neither paradigm is universally superior. A short data-transformation script is
usually clearer written procedurally, and Java's own `Math` class is a purely
procedural collection of static functions. Object orientation earns its overhead
when the same data is touched by many parts of a system over a long time.

> Key Takeaways
> - Procedural code separates data from behaviour, so any function can violate
>   a data rule.
> - Object orientation bundles data with the operations permitted on it.
> - The benefit is a smaller set of code that can break a given invariant, not
>   fewer lines.
> - Access control is what turns the bundling from a convention into a
>   compiler-enforced guarantee.
> - Small scripts and pure algorithms are often better procedural; long-lived
>   domains benefit from objects.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a procedural `Temperature` record with a `celsius` field plus free
>    functions, then rewrite it as a class that rejects values below absolute
>    zero.
> 2. Find a class in your own code with public mutable fields and list every
>    place in the program that could put it into an invalid state.
> 3. Interview: Name one situation where a procedural design is preferable to
>    an object-oriented one in Java, and justify it. (Hint: think about whether
>    there is any state to protect.)

#### Objects as State and Behavior

An object is the pairing of *state* (the data it currently holds) with
*behaviour* (the operations it can perform). A third property, *identity*,
distinguishes two objects even when their state is identical.

The everyday analogy is a physical device. A television has state (channel,
volume, on or off) and behaviour (change channel, adjust volume, power on). You
interact with it through buttons, never by reaching into the circuitry. Two
identical televisions in a shop have the same state but are distinct objects:
switching one off does not affect the other.

```java
public class Television {
    // STATE: what this particular television currently knows
    private boolean on = false;
    private int channel = 1;
    private int volume = 10;

    // BEHAVIOUR: what this television can be asked to do
    public void powerOn()  { on = true; }
    public void powerOff() { on = false; }

    public void setChannel(int newChannel) {
        if (!on) return;                       // behaviour depends on state
        if (newChannel < 1 || newChannel > 999) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("No such channel: " + newChannel);
        }
        channel = newChannel;
    }

    public void volumeUp() {
        if (on && volume < 100) volume++;      // state constrains behaviour
    }

    public String status() {
        return on ? "Channel " + channel + ", volume " + volume : "Off";
    }
}
```

```java
Television living = new Television();
Television kitchen = new Television();

living.powerOn();
living.setChannel(42);

System.out.println(living.status());    // Channel 42, volume 10
System.out.println(kitchen.status());   // Off -- independent state

System.out.println(living == kitchen);  // false -- distinct identities
```

```text
   Each object has its OWN copy of every instance field.

   living  ---> +-------------------+     kitchen ---> +-------------------+
                | Television        |                   | Television        |
                | on      = true    |                   | on      = false   |
                | channel = 42      |                   | channel = 1       |
                | volume  = 10      |                   | volume  = 10      |
                +-------------------+                   +-------------------+
                         \                                      /
                          \____ both share ONE copy of ________/
                                the METHOD code
```

That diagram captures a crucial implementation detail: every object gets its own
field values, but method *code* exists once per class. When you call
`living.setChannel(42)`, the JVM runs the single shared method body with a
hidden reference to `living` (accessible as `this`) so it knows whose fields to
modify.

The three properties interact in ways worth naming:

| Property  | Question it answers          | Java mechanism                    |
| --------- | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| State     | What does it know?           | Instance fields                   |
| Behaviour | What can it do?              | Instance methods                  |
| Identity  | Which one is it?             | The reference; compared with `==` |

Good object design keeps state and behaviour aligned: an object should own the
data its methods need and expose methods that mean something in the problem
domain. An object with fields but no behaviour is a record, and an object with
behaviour but no state is a function collection. Both are legitimate, but if you
find them everywhere, the design has probably drifted back to procedural.

> Key Takeaways
> - An object combines state, behaviour, and identity.
> - Every object has its own instance fields; method code is shared by the
>   class.
> - `this` is the hidden reference that tells a shared method which object's
>   state to use.
> - State can constrain behaviour, which is how objects enforce rules.
> - Objects that are all state or all behaviour are a signal to re-examine the
>   design.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Model a `Lamp` with state for brightness and power, where brightness can
>    only be adjusted while the lamp is on.
> 2. Create two objects of the same class with identical field values and show
>    that `==` reports false.
> 3. Write a `Counter` class and demonstrate that two counters increment
>    independently.

#### Classes as Blueprints

A class is a *type definition*: it specifies what fields every instance will
have and what methods every instance will support. It is not itself the thing.
The distinction between class and object is the single most important one for a
beginner to internalise.

The standard analogy is architectural. A blueprint describes a house: three
bedrooms, a kitchen of a certain size, a front door. From one blueprint you can
build any number of houses. Each house has its own furniture and its own
occupants, but all share the same layout. You cannot live in a blueprint.

```text
   CLASS (the blueprint)               OBJECTS (the houses)

   class House {                       +------------------+
       String address;        new      | 12 Oak Street    |
       String colour;       ------->   | blue             |
       int occupants;                  | 3 occupants      |
   }                                   +------------------+
       |                               +------------------+
       |                     new       | 47 Elm Road      |
       +-------------------------->    | white            |
                                       | 1 occupant       |
                                       +------------------+

   One definition, compiled once.      Many instances, each with its own state.
```

```java
public class House {
    String address;      // every House will have these three fields
    String colour;
    int occupants;

    void describe() {
        System.out.println(address + " is " + colour
                           + " with " + occupants + " occupants");
    }
}
```

```java
House first  = new House();     // instantiation: build a house from the blueprint
first.address = "12 Oak Street";
first.colour  = "blue";
first.occupants = 3;

House second = new House();     // a second, entirely independent house
second.address = "47 Elm Road";
second.colour  = "white";
second.occupants = 1;

first.describe();               // 12 Oak Street is blue with 3 occupants
second.describe();              // 47 Elm Road is white with 1 occupants
```

Some vocabulary that gets used interchangeably and should not be:

| Term          | Meaning                                                    |
| ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Class         | The definition of a type                                   |
| Object        | A thing built from that definition, existing at runtime    |
| Instance      | Synonym for object, emphasising which class it came from   |
| Instantiation | The act of creating an object with `new`                   |
| Member        | Any field or method declared in a class                    |
| Reference     | A variable holding the address of an object                |

A class exists at compile time and is loaded once by the JVM; objects exist at
runtime and there may be millions of them. This explains why `static` members,
covered later in this chapter, belong to the class rather than to any instance:
there is exactly one class, so there is exactly one copy.

The blueprint analogy has one limit worth flagging. A blueprint is purely
passive, whereas a Java class is itself an object at runtime (of type `Class`),
can hold `static` state, and can execute code in static initialisers. That
nuance matters later; for now, "blueprint" is the right mental model.

> Key Takeaways
> - A class defines a type; an object is an instance of it created with `new`.
> - One class definition supports any number of independent instances.
> - Classes exist at compile time and are loaded once; objects live at runtime.
> - Instance fields are per-object; the class itself is shared.
> - "Object" and "instance" are synonyms; "instantiation" is the act of
>   creation.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `Book` class with title, author, and year, then create three
>    distinct books and print each.
> 2. Explain in one sentence each what is created at compile time and what at
>    runtime when you write `new Book()`.
> 3. Interview: If a class is a blueprint, what does a `static` field
>    correspond to in that analogy? (Hint: what belongs to the blueprint itself
>    rather than to any building?)

#### The Four Pillars Overview

Object orientation is conventionally summarised by four principles. This section
introduces all four so the vocabulary is available; each receives full treatment
later, three of them in the next chapter.

**Encapsulation** — bundling data with the methods that operate on it, and
restricting direct access to that data. It is the subject of section 2.5.

```java
public class Thermostat {
    private double target;                    // hidden

    public void setTarget(double celsius) {   // guarded entry point
        if (celsius < 5 || celsius > 30) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Out of safe range");
        }
        target = celsius;
    }
}
```
