```text
   push  factorial(2)  ->  needs factorial(1)
   push  factorial(1)  ->  BASE CASE, returns 1
   pop                     2 * 1  = 2
   pop                     3 * 2  = 6
   pop                     4 * 6  = 24
   pop                     result 24

   stack depth peaked at 4 frames
```

**Stack overflow.** The stack is finite (typically a few hundred kilobytes to a
megabyte). Recursion that is too deep, or that never reaches a base case,
exhausts it:

```java
public static int broken(int n) {
    return broken(n - 1);        // no base case
}
broken(10);                      // StackOverflowError after thousands of frames
```

`StackOverflowError` is an `Error`, not an `Exception`: it signals a condition
you are not expected to recover from. Typical depth limits are around 10,000 to
20,000 frames, which means recursion over a large list is unsafe while recursion
over a balanced tree (depth about log n) is fine.

**Recursion versus iteration.** Any recursion can be rewritten iteratively, and
the iterative version is usually faster and always bounded in stack use:

```java
public static long factorialIterative(int n) {
    long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;                 // constant stack space
}
```

| Aspect           | Recursion                        | Iteration                  |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| Memory           | One stack frame per call         | Constant                   |
| Speed            | Call overhead per level          | Faster                     |
| Readability      | Excellent for self-similar data  | Better for linear work     |
| Risk             | `StackOverflowError`             | Infinite loop              |
| Natural fit      | Trees, graphs, divide and conquer| Sequences, counters        |

**Where recursion genuinely wins** is tree-shaped data, where the iterative
version needs an explicit stack and is markedly less clear:

```java
public static int depth(TreeNode node) {
    if (node == null) return 0;                              // base case
    return 1 + Math.max(depth(node.left), depth(node.right));
}
```

**Naive recursion can be exponentially slow.** The classic example recomputes
the same subproblems repeatedly:

```java
public static long fib(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return n;
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);     // fib(40) makes ~331 million calls
}

// Memoisation collapses it to linear time:
public static long fibMemo(int n, Map<Integer, Long> cache) {
    if (n <= 1) return n;
    return cache.computeIfAbsent(n, k -> fibMemo(k - 1, cache) + fibMemo(k - 2, cache));
}
```

A final note: Java does not perform tail-call optimisation. A tail-recursive
method still consumes one frame per call, so languages that guarantee that
optimisation permit recursion depths that Java does not.

> Key Takeaways
> - Every recursion needs a base case and progress toward it.
> - Each call consumes a stack frame; exhausting the stack raises
>   `StackOverflowError`.
> - Java has no tail-call optimisation, so deep linear recursion is unsafe.
> - Recursion is clearest for tree-shaped and divide-and-conquer problems.
> - Naive recursion may recompute subproblems exponentially; memoise when it
>   does.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write recursive and iterative versions of summing an integer array, then
>    find the input size at which the recursive one fails.
> 2. Write a recursive method that reverses a string, and identify its base
>    case.
> 3. Interview: Why does `fib(50)` written naively take minutes while the
>    memoised version is instant? (Hint: count how many times `fib(10)` is
>    evaluated.)

#### Method Signatures and Return Contracts

A method's signature and documented behaviour together form a *contract*: a
promise to callers about what inputs are acceptable and what will be produced.
Callers depend on it, so changing it breaks them.

**The signature** is the method name plus the ordered parameter types. Formally,
that is all — return type, parameter names, modifiers, and `throws` clauses are
excluded, though they matter in other ways.

```java
public String format(int value, boolean pad) throws IOException
       ^^^^^^ ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
       |      |
       |      +-- part of the signature: name + (int, boolean)
       +--------- NOT part of the signature
```

**The contract has three parts**, borrowed from design-by-contract:

| Part          | Meaning                                      | Expressed by                  |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Precondition  | What must hold before the call               | Parameter types, Javadoc, validation |
| Postcondition | What holds after a successful call           | Return type, Javadoc          |
| Invariant     | What holds before and after                  | Class design, `final`, validation |

```java
/**
 * Withdraws the given amount from this account.
 *
 * @param amount the amount to withdraw; must be positive and no greater
 *               than the current balance          <- PRECONDITION
 * @return the new balance, always non-negative     <- POSTCONDITION
 * @throws IllegalArgumentException if amount is not positive
 * @throws IllegalStateException    if amount exceeds the balance
 */
public long withdraw(long amount) {
    if (amount <= 0)        throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive");
    if (amount > balance)   throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds");
    balance -= amount;
    return balance;                 // INVARIANT preserved: balance >= 0
}
```

**Return contracts worth designing deliberately:**

```java
// 1. Never return null for a collection -- return empty.
public List<Order> findOrders(String customerId) {
    List<Order> found = repository.search(customerId);
    return found == null ? List.of() : found;
}

// 2. Use Optional when absence is a normal outcome.
public Optional<Customer> findById(String id) { ... }

// 3. Return an immutable or defensive copy when the value is internal state.
public List<String> getTags() { return List.copyOf(tags); }

// 4. Be consistent about failure: either throw or return a sentinel, not both.
public int indexOf(String item) { return -1; }   // documented sentinel
```

**What breaks callers** when you change a published method:

| Change                                   | Source compatible | Binary compatible |
| ---------------------------------------- | ----------------- | ----------------- |
| Rename a parameter                       | Yes               | Yes               |
| Add an overload                           | Usually           | Yes               |
| Widen a parameter type (`int` to `long`)  | Usually           | No                |
| Narrow the return type (covariant)        | Usually           | No                |
| Add a checked exception to `throws`       | No                | Yes               |
| Rename the method                         | No                | No                |
| Reorder parameters of the same types      | Compiles, silently wrong | No         |

That last row is worth pausing on: swapping two `String` parameters produces
code that still compiles at every call site and does the wrong thing. This is a
strong argument for distinct types over primitive obsession — a `CustomerId`
type and an `OrderId` type cannot be swapped by accident, while two `String`s
can.

**Designing a good signature**, in short: as few parameters as possible;
specific types rather than `String` and `int` for everything; no boolean flags
that change behaviour (`setVisible(true)` reads worse than `show()`); and a
return type that makes the absence case explicit.

```java
// Poor: what do these mean at the call site?
public void update(String a, String b, boolean flag, int mode) { }

// Better: types carry meaning, behaviour is named, no mode flag
public void rename(CustomerId id, CustomerName newName) { }
public void archive(CustomerId id) { }
```

> Key Takeaways
> - The signature is the method name plus ordered parameter types; return type
>   and `throws` are not part of it.
> - A contract covers preconditions, postconditions, and invariants, documented
>   in Javadoc and enforced by validation.
> - Prefer empty collections and `Optional` over `null` returns.
> - Reordering same-typed parameters compiles and silently breaks callers.
> - Distinct domain types beat `String` and `int` everywhere, and boolean flags
>   usually want to be separate methods.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a full Javadoc contract for a `divide(int, int)` method, covering
>    the zero-divisor case.
> 2. Take a method with four `String` parameters and redesign it using small
>    domain types.
> 3. Interview: Your library method currently returns `null` when nothing is
>    found. What are the options for improving it, and what does each cost
>    callers? (Hint: consider source compatibility.)

<a id="25-encapsulation-and-access-control"></a>
### 2.5 Encapsulation and Access Control

Encapsulation is the pillar this chapter has been building toward: deciding
what a class exposes, what it hides, and how it guarantees that its data stays
valid.

#### Access Modifiers: private, default, protected, public

Java has four access levels controlling where a member may be referenced. They
form a strict ordering from most to least restrictive.

| Modifier    | Same class | Same package | Subclass (other package) | Anywhere |
| ----------- | ---------- | ------------ | ------------------------ | -------- |
| `private`   | Yes        | No           | No                       | No       |
| (default)   | Yes        | Yes          | No                       | No       |
| `protected` | Yes        | Yes          | Yes                      | No       |
| `public`    | Yes        | Yes          | Yes                      | Yes      |

"Default" (also called package-private) is the absence of any modifier, not a
keyword.

```java
package com.example.shapes;

public class Shape {
    private   String secret    = "only this class";
    /*default*/ String internal = "this package";
    protected String inherited = "package + subclasses anywhere";
    public    String open      = "everyone";

    private void hiddenHelper() { }
    public void render() { hiddenHelper(); }     // fine: same class
}
```

```java
package com.example.shapes;

class Neighbour {                       // same package
    void test(Shape s) {
        // s.secret;                    // ERROR: private
        System.out.println(s.internal); // OK: same package
        System.out.println(s.inherited);// OK: protected includes package access
        System.out.println(s.open);     // OK
    }
}
```

```java
package com.example.other;              // DIFFERENT package
import com.example.shapes.Shape;

class Circle extends Shape {
    void test(Shape other) {
        // other.internal;              // ERROR: different package
        System.out.println(this.inherited);  // OK: protected, through inheritance
        // other.inherited;             // ERROR: protected access is through
                                        //        'this', not an arbitrary instance
        System.out.println(other.open); // OK
    }
}
```

That last restriction surprises people. `protected` grants a subclass access to
*its own* inherited member, not to the member of any other instance of the
superclass. The rule exists so a subclass cannot reach into unrelated sibling
objects.

```text
        Access widens outward

   +---------------------------------------------+
   |  public          anywhere                   |
   |  +---------------------------------------+  |
   |  | protected    package + subclasses     |  |
   |  |  +---------------------------------+  |  |
   |  |  | default   same package          |  |  |
   |  |  |  +---------------------------+  |  |  |
   |  |  |  | private   same class only |  |  |  |
   |  |  |  +---------------------------+  |  |  |
   |  |  +---------------------------------+  |  |
   |  +---------------------------------------+  |
   +---------------------------------------------+
```

**Where each modifier is legal:**

| Element                | Allowed modifiers                           |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Top-level class        | `public` or default only                    |
| Nested class           | All four                                    |
| Field, method, constructor | All four                                |
| Local variable         | None (they have no access level)             |
| Interface members      | `public` implicitly; `private` allowed since Java 9 |

**The default choice should be `private`.** Start every member private and widen
only when a concrete need appears. Widening later is easy; narrowing later
breaks callers, and once a member is `public` in a published library it is
effectively permanent.

```java
public class Cache {
    private final Map<String, String> entries = new HashMap<>();   // hidden
    private int hits;                                              // hidden

    public String get(String key) {          // the deliberate public surface
        String value = entries.get(key);
        if (value != null) hits++;
        return value;
    }

    public void put(String key, String value) { entries.put(key, value); }

    int hitCount() { return hits; }          // package-private: for tests
}
```

That last member shows a common, pragmatic use of package-private: exposing
something to tests in the same package without making it part of the public API.

`protected` deserves caution. It is part of your public API as far as
subclasses are concerned, meaning any protected field becomes a compatibility
commitment. Prefer protected *methods* over protected *fields*, so the
representation remains free to change.

> Key Takeaways
> - Four levels: `private`, default (package-private), `protected`, `public`.
> - Default is the absence of a keyword, not a keyword itself.
> - `protected` allows a subclass access through `this`, not through arbitrary
>   instances of the superclass.
> - Top-level classes may only be `public` or package-private.
> - Start with `private` and widen deliberately; `protected` fields become a
>   permanent commitment.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create two packages and a four-member class, then verify each access rule
>    from a same-package class and from a subclass in the other package.
> 2. Try to declare a top-level class `private` and read the error.
> 3. Interview: Why can a subclass in another package not access
>    `otherInstance.protectedField`? (Hint: think about what protected is meant
>    to enable.)

#### Information Hiding Principles

Access modifiers are the mechanism; information hiding is the principle. The
goal is that a class's *implementation* can change without any caller noticing,
which is only possible if callers never depended on it in the first place.

The classic illustration is a class whose representation changes:

```java
// VERSION 1: temperature stored in Celsius, fields public
public class Weather {
    public double celsius;          // callers write: w.celsius = 21.0;
}
```

Now a requirement arrives: store the temperature in Kelvin internally for
scientific calculations. Every caller breaks, because every caller referenced
the field directly. With the field hidden, the change is invisible:

```java
// VERSION 2: internal representation changed, public surface identical
public class Weather {
    private double kelvin;                        // representation changed

    public double getCelsius()  { return kelvin - 273.15; }
    public void setCelsius(double c) { kelvin = c + 273.15; }

    public double getKelvin()   { return kelvin; }    // new capability, free
}
```

The public surface of a class is a promise; the private part is a free hand.
Every public member you add shrinks the freedom you retain.

**What to hide, in decreasing order of importance:**

1. **Fields.** Essentially always private. A public mutable field surrenders all
   control over the class's state.
2. **Implementation types.** Return `List`, not `ArrayList`, so you can switch
   implementations.
3. **Helper methods.** If it only exists to support a public method, it is
   private.
4. **Constructors.** Making them private and exposing factories keeps creation
   under your control.
5. **Nested classes.** If a nested class is an implementation detail, it should
   be private.

```java
public class OrderBook {
    private final List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>();   // 1. field hidden

    public List<Order> getOrders() {            // 2. interface type returned
        return List.copyOf(orders);             //    and a snapshot, not the field
    }

    public void add(Order order) {
        validate(order);                        // 3. helper is private
        orders.add(order);
    }

    private void validate(Order order) { ... }

    private static final class Index { ... }    // 5. internal structure hidden
}
```

**The leaky abstraction problem.** A class can have all-private fields and still
expose its implementation through its method names and types:

```java
// Encapsulated, but leaks its implementation in the API
public class UserCache {
    private HashMap<String, User> map = new HashMap<>();

    public HashMap<String, User> getMap() { return map; }   // leaks BOTH the
}                                                           // type and the object

// Better: the API talks about users, not about maps
public class UserCache {
    private final Map<String, User> byId = new HashMap<>();

    public Optional<User> find(String id) { return Optional.ofNullable(byId.get(id)); }
    public void store(User user)          { byId.put(user.getId(), user); }
    public int size()                     { return byId.size(); }
}
```

The second version can switch to a `TreeMap`, add an eviction policy, or move
to a database without changing a single caller.

**A useful test.** For each public member, ask: "if I changed how this class
works internally, would I have to keep this member working exactly as it does
now?" If the answer is yes and the member is about *how* rather than *what*, it
should not be public.

| Symptom                                  | What it leaks                    |
| ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| `public` fields                          | The entire representation        |
| Getter returning an internal collection  | The ability to mutate your state |
| Return type `ArrayList` instead of `List`| Your choice of implementation    |
| Method named `getHashMap()`              | The data structure you chose     |
| `protected` fields                       | Representation, to all subclasses |

> Key Takeaways
> - Information hiding lets the implementation change without breaking
>   callers.
> - Every public member is a permanent commitment; keep the surface small.
> - Return interface types, not implementation types.
> - A class can be encapsulated and still leak through method names and return
>   types.
> - Ask whether each public member describes *what* the class does or *how* it
>   does it.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a class storing a full name in one field, then change it to first
>    and last name fields without breaking any caller.
> 2. Find a getter that returns an internal collection and make it safe, then
>    explain the trade-off you chose.
> 3. Interview: A class has all-private fields but a method
>    `public HashMap<String,User> getMap()`. Is it encapsulated? (Hint: what
>    can a caller do with the returned object?)

#### Getter and Setter Design

Getters and setters are the conventional way to expose controlled access to
state. They are also routinely overused: generating a getter and a setter for
every field reproduces public fields with extra typing and none of the benefit.

**The convention:**

```java
public class Person {
    private String name;
    private boolean active;

    public String getName()          { return name; }    // getX for most types
    public void   setName(String n)  { this.name = n; }

    public boolean isActive()        { return active; }  // isX for boolean
    public void    setActive(boolean a) { this.active = a; }
}
```

The `get`/`is`/`set` naming is not a language rule; it is the JavaBeans
convention, and frameworks such as Jackson, Hibernate, and Spring rely on it for
reflection-based mapping. Deviating from it breaks those tools.

**What a getter or setter is actually for** is adding behaviour to access:

```java
public class Account {
    private long balanceCents;
    private String email;

    public void setEmail(String email) {
        if (email == null || !email.contains("@")) {       // validation
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid email: " + email);
        }
        this.email = email.toLowerCase();                  // normalisation
        auditLog.record("email changed");                  // side effect
    }

    public double getBalance() {
        return balanceCents / 100.0;                       // computed, not stored
    }

    public List<Transaction> getTransactions() {
        return List.copyOf(transactions);                  // defensive copy
    }
}
```

If a setter does nothing but assign, it provides no value over a public field
except JavaBeans compatibility and the ability to add behaviour later without
breaking callers. That last point is the real justification in library code, and
is weaker in an application you control entirely.

**Prefer not to generate setters at all.** The modern default is immutability:
set everything in the constructor and omit setters. A class with no setters
cannot enter an invalid state after construction, is thread-safe for free, and
is safe to use as a map key.

```java
// Mutable: five ways to be half-initialised
public class Order {
    private String id;
    private Customer customer;
    public void setId(String id) { this.id = id; }
    public void setCustomer(Customer c) { this.customer = c; }
}

// Immutable: valid from birth, or it does not exist
public final class Order {
    private final String id;
    private final Customer customer;

    public Order(String id, Customer customer) {
        this.id = Objects.requireNonNull(id);
        this.customer = Objects.requireNonNull(customer);
    }
    public String getId()        { return id; }
    public Customer getCustomer(){ return customer; }
}
```

**Records** make this the path of least resistance for pure data carriers, and
are covered fully in chapter 4:

```java
public record Point(int x, int y) { }   // accessors x() and y() generated
```

Note that record accessors are named `x()` and `y()`, not `getX()`, which is a
deliberate departure from the JavaBeans convention.

**Design guidance:**

| Guideline                                          | Reason                          |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Do not add a setter unless something must change it | Immutability by default         |
| Validate in setters and constructors alike          | Invariants must hold always     |
| Return copies of mutable internal state             | Prevent external mutation       |
| Name methods for the domain, not the field          | `deposit()` beats `setBalance()`|
| Avoid a getter for every field reflexively          | Getters are API surface too     |

That fourth row deserves emphasis: `account.setBalance(account.getBalance() +
100)` moves the business rule out of the class and back into the caller, which
is exactly what encapsulation was meant to prevent. `account.deposit(100)` keeps
it where it belongs.

> Key Takeaways
> - `get`/`is`/`set` is the JavaBeans convention, required by many frameworks,
>   not a language rule.
> - A trivial setter adds value only as a future extension point.
> - Prefer immutability: assign in the constructor and omit setters.
> - Return defensive copies of mutable internal state.
> - Domain-meaningful methods beat setter-plus-getter arithmetic in the caller.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `Product` class where the price setter rejects negatives and the
>    getter returns a formatted string.
> 2. Convert a mutable class with five setters into an immutable one, and note
>    what the callers had to change.
> 3. Interview: Is `getBalance()` followed by `setBalance()` in the caller a
>    problem? (Hint: where does the rule about minimum balance now live?)

#### Immutable Class Construction

An immutable object cannot change after construction. This sounds restrictive
and turns out to remove entire categories of bugs, which is why `String`,
`Integer`, `LocalDate`, and the modern collection factories all work this way.

**The five rules** for a correctly immutable class:

1. Make the class `final`, so no subclass can add mutable state or override a
   method to lie about the state.
2. Make every field `private` and `final`.
3. Provide no setters or any other mutating method.
4. Defensively copy mutable objects on the way *in*.
5. Defensively copy mutable objects on the way *out*.

```java
public final class Reservation {                      // 1. final class

    private final String guestName;                   // 2. private final
    private final LocalDate date;                     //    (immutable type)
    private final List<String> requests;              //    (mutable type!)

    public Reservation(String guestName, LocalDate date, List<String> requests) {
        this.guestName = Objects.requireNonNull(guestName);
        this.date = Objects.requireNonNull(date);     // LocalDate is immutable: share
        this.requests = List.copyOf(requests);        // 4. copy on the way in
    }

    public String getGuestName() { return guestName; }
    public LocalDate getDate()   { return date; }

    public List<String> getRequests() {
        return requests;                              // 5. already immutable, safe
    }

    // 3. No setters. Changes produce a NEW object:
    public Reservation withDate(LocalDate newDate) {
        return new Reservation(guestName, newDate, requests);
    }
}
```

The `withX` naming convention for "a copy with one thing changed" is standard
across the JDK (`LocalDate.withYear`, `String.replace` conceptually).

**What immutability buys:**

| Benefit               | Why it follows                                           |
| --------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| Thread safety         | No writes means no race conditions, no synchronisation    |
| Safe sharing          | No defensive copying needed by callers                    |
| Safe as a map key     | The hash code cannot change after insertion               |
| Simpler reasoning     | A reference's value is fixed at every point in the program |
| Failure atomicity     | A failed operation leaves no half-modified object         |

The map-key point is concrete and worth seeing:

```java
// A mutable key silently corrupts a HashMap
class MutablePoint { int x, y; /* equals and hashCode based on x, y */ }

Map<MutablePoint, String> map = new HashMap<>();
MutablePoint key = new MutablePoint(1, 2);
map.put(key, "found me");

key.x = 99;                       // the hash code changes AFTER insertion
System.out.println(map.get(key)); // null -- it is in the wrong bucket now
```

**The cost** is allocation: every modification creates an object. For small
objects this is negligible, since modern JVMs allocate cheaply and collect
short-lived objects almost for free. For a large structure modified in a tight
loop, a mutable builder is the standard remedy — which is precisely the
`String` and `StringBuilder` relationship from chapter 1.

**Common mistakes:**

```java
public final class Broken {
    private final List<String> items;
    private final Date created;

    public Broken(List<String> items, Date created) {
        this.items = items;              // MISTAKE: caller keeps a reference
        this.created = created;          // MISTAKE: Date is mutable
    }

    public List<String> getItems() {
        return items;                    // MISTAKE: caller can now call add()
    }

    public Date getCreated() {
        return created;                  // MISTAKE: caller can call setTime()
    }
}
```

Note that `final` on a field is necessary but not sufficient: it prevents
reassignment of the reference, not mutation of the object, as established in
chapter 1. The whole point of rules 4 and 5 is to cover that gap.

Records, introduced in Java 16, generate most of this automatically but do not
solve the mutable-component problem: a record holding a `List` field still needs
`List.copyOf` in a compact constructor.

> Key Takeaways
> - Immutable classes are `final`, with `private final` fields, no mutators,
>   and defensive copies in both directions.
> - `final` on a field prevents reassignment, not mutation of the referenced
>   object.
> - Immutability gives thread safety, safe sharing, and valid map keys for
>   free.
> - Modification is expressed as a `withX` method returning a new instance.
> - Records automate the boilerplate but still require copying mutable
>   components.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write an immutable `Money` class with amount and currency, plus `plus` and
>    `minus` methods returning new instances.
> 2. Take the `Broken` class above and fix all four mistakes.
> 3. Interview: Why is a mutable object dangerous as a `HashMap` key? (Hint:
>    what does the map use to choose a bucket, and when?)

#### Class Invariants and Validation

A *class invariant* is a condition that must be true of every instance at every
moment an outside caller can observe it. "A balance is never negative", "start
precedes end", "the list never contains null" are all invariants. Encapsulation
exists to make them enforceable.

An invariant holds if two things are true: the constructor establishes it, and
every method that changes state preserves it. Since the fields are private, no
other code can break it.

```java
public final class DateRange {
    private final LocalDate start;
    private final LocalDate end;

    // ESTABLISH the invariant: start is never after end
    public DateRange(LocalDate start, LocalDate end) {
        this.start = Objects.requireNonNull(start, "start");
        this.end = Objects.requireNonNull(end, "end");
        if (start.isAfter(end)) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException(
                    "start (" + start + ") must not be after end (" + end + ")");
        }
    }

    // PRESERVE it: every derived instance is validated by the same constructor
    public DateRange extendTo(LocalDate newEnd) {
        return new DateRange(start, newEnd);      // re-validates automatically
    }

    public long days() {
        return ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(start, end) + 1;   // relies on the invariant
    }
}
```

The payoff is in `days()`: because the invariant is guaranteed, the method needs
no defensive checks and can never return a negative count.

**Where to validate:**

| Location            | What belongs there                                |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Constructor         | Everything needed to establish the invariant      |
| Setter / mutator    | Everything needed to preserve it                  |
| Private helper      | Shared checks, called from both                   |
| Static factory      | Validation plus the choice of what to return      |

**Choosing the right exception** communicates whose fault the failure is:

```java
public void withdraw(long amount) {
    // Bad ARGUMENT from the caller
    if (amount <= 0) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive, was " + amount);
    }
    // Bad STATE of this object for this operation
    if (amount > balance) {
        throw new IllegalStateException("Balance " + balance + " is less than " + amount);
    }
    // Missing required input
    Objects.requireNonNull(currency, "currency must be set first");

    balance -= amount;
}
```

| Exception                   | Use when                                        |
| --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `IllegalArgumentException`  | A parameter value is unacceptable                |
| `NullPointerException`      | A parameter or field is null when it must not be |
| `IllegalStateException`     | The object is in the wrong state for the call    |
| `IndexOutOfBoundsException` | An index parameter is out of range               |
| A custom checked exception  | The caller can reasonably recover                |

**Fail fast.** Validate at the boundary, before any state changes. A method that
modifies three fields and then discovers a problem leaves the object
half-updated:

```java
// BAD: fails after mutating -- the object is now inconsistent
public void update(String name, int age) {
    this.name = name;
    if (age < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("age");   // too late
    this.age = age;
}

// GOOD: validate everything first, then mutate -- failure atomicity
public void update(String name, int age) {
    Objects.requireNonNull(name, "name");
    if (age < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("age must be non-negative");
    this.name = name;
    this.age = age;
}
```

This property is called **failure atomicity**: a failed method call leaves the
object exactly as it was. Immutable classes get it for free, since a failed
construction simply produces no object.

**Useful validation helpers** in the standard library:

```java
Objects.requireNonNull(value, "message");
Objects.requireNonNullElse(value, fallback);
Objects.checkIndex(index, length);                  // Java 9+
if (!condition) throw new IllegalArgumentException("...");
```

Error messages should include the offending value. `"Invalid age"` forces a
debugging session; `"age must be between 0 and 150, was -3"` does not.

> Key Takeaways
> - An invariant is a condition true of every observable instance state.
> - Constructors establish invariants; mutators preserve them; privacy makes
>   that enforceable.
> - `IllegalArgumentException` blames the argument, `IllegalStateException`
>   blames the object's state.
> - Validate before mutating so a failed call leaves the object unchanged.
> - Include the offending value in every validation message.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `Percentage` class whose invariant is 0 to 100 inclusive, and
>    enforce it in the constructor.
> 2. Write a method that violates failure atomicity, demonstrate the
>    half-updated object, then fix it.
> 3. Interview: What is the difference between `IllegalArgumentException` and
>    `IllegalStateException`, and which fits "withdrawing more than the
>    balance"? (Hint: is the amount itself invalid?)

<a id="26-static-members-and-class-level-state"></a>
### 2.6 Static Members and Class-Level State

Everything so far has belonged to individual objects. `static` members belong to
the class itself, existing once regardless of how many instances are created.

#### Static Fields and Shared State

A `static` field is stored once per class, not once per object. Every instance
sees the same variable, and it exists even when no instance has been created.

```java
public class Counter {
    private static int totalCreated;     // ONE copy, shared by all instances
    private final int id;                // one copy PER instance

    public Counter() {
        totalCreated++;                  // every construction updates the shared field
        this.id = totalCreated;
    }

    public int getId()                { return id; }
    public static int getTotal()      { return totalCreated; }
}
```

```java
Counter a = new Counter();
Counter b = new Counter();
Counter c = new Counter();

System.out.println(a.getId());          // 1
System.out.println(c.getId());          // 3
System.out.println(Counter.getTotal()); // 3 -- accessed through the CLASS
```

```text
   CLASS-LEVEL (one copy)              INSTANCE-LEVEL (one per object)

   Counter.totalCreated = 3            a --> [ id = 1 ]
            ^  ^  ^                    b --> [ id = 2 ]
            |  |  |                    c --> [ id = 3 ]
            a  b  c   all share it
```

**Access through the class name**, not an instance. Java permits
`a.getTotal()`, but it is misleading because it suggests instance-specific data,
and most style checkers flag it.

```java
Counter.getTotal();      // correct and clear
a.getTotal();            // compiles, but misleading -- avoid
```

**The dominant legitimate use is constants:**

```java
public class Physics {
    public static final double SPEED_OF_LIGHT = 299_792_458.0;
    public static final int    MAX_RETRIES    = 3;
}
```

`static final` with an immutable value is unambiguously good: one copy, never
changes, no state to corrupt. The JDK is full of these (`Integer.MAX_VALUE`,
`Math.PI`).

**Mutable static state is where trouble begins.** It is effectively a global
variable, with all the classic drawbacks:

```java
public class BadRegistry {
    public static Map<String, User> users = new HashMap<>();   // several problems
}
```

| Problem              | Consequence                                              |
| -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| Global mutability    | Any code anywhere can change it                           |
| Not thread-safe      | Concurrent access corrupts a `HashMap` without locking    |
| Test pollution       | State persists between tests, causing order dependence    |
| Hidden dependency    | A class using it has a dependency invisible in its API    |
| Lifetime             | Lives as long as the class loader, a common leak source   |

The test-pollution point is the one developers meet first:

```java
@Test void testA() { BadRegistry.users.put("x", user); /* ... */ }
@Test void testB() { assertTrue(BadRegistry.users.isEmpty()); }  // fails if A ran first
```

**Legitimate uses of mutable static state** do exist, and share a property: the
state is genuinely global to the process and access is controlled.

```java
public class IdGenerator {
    private static final AtomicLong counter = new AtomicLong();   // thread-safe

    public static long next() { return counter.incrementAndGet(); }
}

public class Logger {
    private static final Logger INSTANCE = new Logger();   // singleton instance
    private Logger() { }
    public static Logger get() { return INSTANCE; }
}
```

Note that both keep the field `private` and expose controlled methods, and both
use a thread-safe type. A `public static` mutable field has essentially no
defence.

The modern alternative in application code is dependency injection: instead of a
class reaching for a static registry, it receives what it needs through its
constructor. That makes the dependency visible, replaceable in tests, and
independently scoped.

```java
// Hidden dependency on global state
public class OrderService {
    public void process(Order o) { BadRegistry.users.get(o.getUserId()); }
}

// Explicit dependency, easy to substitute in a test
public class OrderService {
    private final UserRepository users;
    public OrderService(UserRepository users) { this.users = users; }
    public void process(Order o) { users.findById(o.getUserId()); }
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A `static` field exists once per class and is shared by every instance.
> - Access static members through the class name, not through an instance.
> - `static final` constants with immutable values are safe and idiomatic.
> - Mutable static state is a global variable: unsafe for threads, polluting
>   for tests, and a hidden dependency.
> - Prefer constructor injection over static registries.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a class counting how many instances have been created, and verify
>    the count from three objects.
> 2. Create a mutable `public static` list, modify it from two different
>    classes, and describe why this is hard to debug.
> 3. Interview: Why is mutable static state a problem for unit tests? (Hint:
>    what persists between test methods?)

#### Static Methods and Utility Classes

A `static` method belongs to the class rather than to any instance. It can be
called without creating an object, and consequently it has no `this`.

```java
public class MathUtils {
    public static int square(int n) { return n * n; }

    public static double average(int... values) {
        if (values.length == 0) return 0;
        int sum = 0;
        for (int v : values) sum += v;
        return (double) sum / values.length;
    }
}

int result = MathUtils.square(5);        // no object required
```

**When a method should be static:** when it does not read or write instance
state. If a method never touches a field and never calls an instance method, it
is a function, not behaviour, and marking it static says so.

```java
public class Order {
    private List<Item> items;

    public double total() {                    // uses instance state -> instance method
        return items.stream().mapToDouble(Item::price).sum();
    }

    public static double taxFor(double amount, double rate) {   // pure function
        return amount * rate;                                   // -> static
    }
}
```

**A static method cannot** access instance members directly, because there is no
instance to access:

```java
public class Example {
    private int instanceField = 10;
    private static int staticField = 20;

    public static void staticMethod() {
        System.out.println(staticField);      // OK
        // System.out.println(instanceField); // ERROR: non-static variable
        // this.instanceField;                // ERROR: no 'this' in a static context

        Example e = new Example();
        System.out.println(e.instanceField);  // OK: through an explicit instance
    }

    public void instanceMethod() {
        System.out.println(staticField);      // OK: instances can see static members
        System.out.println(instanceField);    // OK
    }
}
```

**The utility class idiom** groups related static methods in a class that is
never instantiated:

```java
public final class StringUtils {          // final: nothing to extend

    private StringUtils() {               // private: nothing to instantiate
        throw new AssertionError("No instances");   // blocks reflection too
    }

    public static boolean isBlank(String s) {
        return s == null || s.isBlank();
    }

    public static String reverse(String s) {
        return new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString();
    }
}
```

The three elements — `final` class, private constructor, all-static members —
are the standard recipe. The JDK's own `Math`, `Arrays`, `Collections`, and
`Objects` follow it.

**Static methods and polymorphism do not mix.** A static method cannot be
overridden; a subclass declaring the same signature *hides* it instead, and the
version called is chosen by the static type:

```java
class Parent {
    static void greet() { System.out.println("Parent"); }
}
class Child extends Parent {
    static void greet() { System.out.println("Child"); }   // HIDES, not overrides
}

Parent p = new Child();
p.greet();          // "Parent" -- chosen by the STATIC type of p
```

This is examined again in chapter 3; the practical advice is not to hide static
methods, because the result confuses every reader.

**Testability.** Static methods are hard to substitute in tests, since there is
no reference to replace. A pure function such as `Math.max` is fine, but a
static method that performs I/O or reads configuration becomes an obstacle:

```java
// Hard to test: no way to substitute the clock or the file system
public static Report generate() {
    LocalDate today = LocalDate.now();
    String config = Files.readString(Path.of("/etc/app.conf"));
    ...
}
```

The rule of thumb: static is appropriate for pure functions of their arguments,
and inappropriate when the method has dependencies you might want to replace.

> Key Takeaways
> - A static method belongs to the class, has no `this`, and cannot access
>   instance members directly.
> - Make a method static when it uses no instance state.
> - The utility class recipe is a `final` class with a private constructor and
>   only static members.
> - Static methods are hidden, not overridden, and dispatch on the static type.
> - Static methods with dependencies are hard to substitute in tests; pure
>   functions are fine.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `ValidationUtils` class following the full utility-class recipe.
> 2. Try to access an instance field from a static method and read the exact
>    error.
> 3. Interview: Why can a static method not be overridden? (Hint: overriding
>    needs an object to dispatch on.)

#### Static Initializer Blocks

A static initializer is a block marked `static` in the class body. It runs once,
when the class is initialised, and exists for setup that needs more than a
single expression.

```java
public class Registry {
    private static final Map<String, String> CODES = new HashMap<>();

    static {                                  // runs once, at class initialisation
        CODES.put("IT", "Italy");
        CODES.put("FR", "France");
        CODES.put("DE", "Germany");
    }

    public static String lookup(String code) { return CODES.get(code); }
}
```

Without the block, populating that map would require a helper method or the
discouraged double-brace idiom.

**When class initialisation happens.** The JVM initialises a class lazily, on
first *active use*:

| Triggers initialisation                     | Does NOT trigger it                     |
| ------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Creating an instance with `new`             | Declaring a variable of the type        |
| Calling a static method                     | Accessing a compile-time constant       |
| Reading or writing a non-constant static field | Loading the class with `Class.forName(..., false, ...)` |
| Reflective instantiation                    | Referencing an array type of the class  |
| Initialising a subclass                     |                                         |

```java
public class Lazy {
    static { System.out.println("Lazy initialised"); }
    public static final int CONSTANT = 42;              // compile-time constant
    public static int mutable = 42;
}

Lazy ref;                             // nothing printed: declaration only
System.out.println(Lazy.CONSTANT);    // nothing printed: inlined at compile time
System.out.println(Lazy.mutable);     // "Lazy initialised" printed now
```

That middle case catches people out: a `static final` primitive or `String`
initialised with a constant expression is inlined by the compiler, so reading it
does not touch the class at all.

**Multiple blocks run in source order**, interleaved with static field
initialisers:

```java
public class Order {
    static int a = print("1. static field a");
    static { print("2. first static block"); }
    static int b = print("3. static field b");
    static { print("4. second static block"); }

    private static int print(String s) { System.out.println(s); return 0; }
}
```

**Exception handling.** A static block cannot throw a checked exception out of
the class; it must handle it. An uncaught exception during static
initialisation is wrapped in `ExceptionInInitializerError`, and the class is
permanently marked unusable for the rest of the JVM's life:

```java
public class Fragile {
    private static final Properties CONFIG = new Properties();

    static {
        try (InputStream in = Fragile.class.getResourceAsStream("/app.properties")) {
            CONFIG.load(in);                   // IOException is checked
        } catch (IOException e) {
            throw new ExceptionInInitializerError(e);   // fail loudly and clearly
        }
    }
}
```

Any later attempt to use `Fragile` throws `NoClassDefFoundError`, whose message
does not mention the original problem. That is why the first failure must be
logged clearly — it is the only comprehensible error you will get.

**Alternatives.** For a single expression, a field initialiser is simpler. For
lazy expensive initialisation, the holder idiom uses lazy class loading to get
thread-safe laziness with no synchronisation:

```java
public class Heavy {
    private static class Holder {                     // not loaded until referenced
        static final Heavy INSTANCE = new Heavy();
    }
    public static Heavy get() { return Holder.INSTANCE; }   // triggers loading here
}
```

The JVM guarantees that class initialisation is thread-safe and happens exactly
once, which is what makes this idiom correct without any explicit locking.

> Key Takeaways
> - A static block runs once, at class initialisation, for multi-statement
>   setup.
> - Initialisation is lazy and triggered by first active use, not by
>   declaration.
> - Compile-time constants are inlined, so reading one does not initialise the
>   class.
> - Static blocks and static field initialisers run in source order.
> - A failure during static initialisation raises
>   `ExceptionInInitializerError` and permanently breaks the class.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a class with a static block and prove it runs only once no matter
>    how many instances you create.
> 2. Demonstrate that reading a `static final int` constant does not trigger
>    the static block, while reading a non-final static field does.
> 3. Interview: What happens if a static initializer throws an exception, and
>    what error do later callers see? (Hint: the class never becomes usable.)

#### Static versus Instance Context

Many beginner compile errors reduce to one question: does this code have an
object to work with? Static context does not; instance context does.

```java
public class Example {
    private int instanceField;
    private static int staticField;

    public void instanceMethod() {
        instanceField = 1;      // OK: 'this' exists
        staticField = 2;        // OK: static members are always reachable
        staticMethod();         // OK
        helper();               // OK
    }

    public static void staticMethod() {
        // instanceField = 1;   // ERROR: non-static variable cannot be referenced
        staticField = 2;        // OK
        // helper();            // ERROR: non-static method cannot be referenced
        // this.toString();     // ERROR: 'this' cannot be used in a static context
    }

    private void helper() { }
}
```

| From \ To        | Instance field | Instance method | Static field | Static method | `this` |
| ---------------- | -------------- | --------------- | ------------ | ------------- | ------ |
| Instance method  | Yes            | Yes             | Yes          | Yes           | Yes    |
| Static method    | No             | No              | Yes          | Yes           | No     |
| Instance block   | Yes            | Yes             | Yes          | Yes           | Yes    |
| Static block     | No             | No              | Yes          | Yes           | No     |
| Constructor      | Yes            | Yes             | Yes          | Yes           | Yes    |

The asymmetry has one cause: static code may run before any instance exists, so
there is nothing for an instance reference to point at.

```text
   TIMELINE

   class loaded ----> static init ----> [ maybe never any instance ]
                           |
                           |  at this moment there are ZERO objects,
                           |  so 'instanceField' has no meaning
                           v
                      new Example() ----> instance init ----> instance methods
                                              |
                                              +-- now 'this' exists
```

**The most common beginner error** is calling an instance method from `main`,
which is static:

```java
public class App {
    private int counter;

    public void run() { counter++; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // run();                  // ERROR: non-static method run() cannot be
                                   //        referenced from a static context
        new App().run();           // correct: create an instance first
    }
}
```

**Static can be reached from instance context freely**, because the class is
always initialised before any instance exists. The reverse is what needs an
explicit object:

```java
public static void process(Example e) {
    System.out.println(e.instanceField);   // fine: we were GIVEN an instance
}
```

**Choosing between them** comes down to a single question, asked of the method:

```text
   Does this method read or write instance state?
           |
      yes  |  no
           |
    instance    Does it belong conceptually to the type rather than a value?
                        |
                   yes  |  no
                        |
                    static      probably belongs in another class entirely
```

Common static members in practice: factory methods (`List.of`), pure functions
(`Math.abs`), constants (`Integer.MAX_VALUE`), and `main`. Common instance
members: anything that reads or modifies the object's own data.

A final subtlety worth knowing: a *nested* class declared `static` follows the
same logic. It has no reference to an enclosing instance, which is why it can be
created independently. That is the next topic.

> Key Takeaways
> - Static context has no `this`, because it may run before any object exists.
> - Instance code can reach static members freely; static code needs an
>   explicit reference to reach instance members.
> - Calling an instance method from `main` requires creating an object first.
> - Make a method static exactly when it does not use instance state.
> - The same reasoning explains static nested classes.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `main` method that tries to call an instance method directly, read
>    the error, then fix it two different ways.
> 2. Build a table for your own class showing which of its members each other
>    member can access.
> 3. Interview: Why can `main` not access instance fields directly? (Hint: when
>    does `main` run relative to object creation?)

#### Static Nested Classes

A class declared inside another class is a *nested* class. Nested classes come
in two flavours, and the distinction is exactly the static-versus-instance one
from the previous topic.

```java
public class Outer {
    private int outerField = 10;
    private static int staticField = 20;

    static class StaticNested {              // NO reference to an Outer instance
        void show() {
            System.out.println(staticField);   // OK: static member
            // System.out.println(outerField); // ERROR: needs an Outer instance
        }
    }

    class Inner {                            // HOLDS a reference to an Outer
        void show() {
            System.out.println(outerField);    // OK: reaches the enclosing instance
            System.out.println(staticField);   // OK
        }
    }
}
```

```java
// A static nested class is created independently
Outer.StaticNested nested = new Outer.StaticNested();

// An inner class requires an enclosing instance
Outer outer = new Outer();
Outer.Inner inner = outer.new Inner();       // unusual syntax, rarely seen
```

```text
   STATIC NESTED                       INNER (non-static)

   [ Outer.StaticNested ]              [ Outer instance ]
          (independent)                       ^
                                              | hidden reference
                                       [ Inner instance ]

   no link to any Outer object         cannot exist without an Outer object
```

| Aspect                     | Static nested       | Inner (non-static)     |
| -------------------------- | ------------------- | ---------------------- |
| Enclosing instance         | None                | Required               |
| Can access outer instance fields | No            | Yes                    |
| Creation                   | `new Outer.Nested()`| `outer.new Inner()`    |
| Can declare static members | Yes                 | Yes, since Java 16     |
| Memory overhead            | None                | One hidden reference   |
| Typical use                | Helper types, builders, nodes | Iterators, tight coupling to the outer object |

**Prefer static nested classes.** The hidden reference held by an inner class is
a genuine memory-leak risk: if an inner-class instance outlives its intended
scope, it keeps the entire enclosing object alive.

```java
public class DataHolder {
    private byte[] hugeArray = new byte[100_000_000];

    class Listener { }              // each Listener pins hugeArray in memory

    static class SafeListener { }   // independent, no such risk
}
```

This is exactly why Android tooling warns about non-static inner classes used as
callbacks.

**The canonical uses of static nested classes:**

```java
// 1. A builder for its enclosing type
public class Pizza {
    private final String size;
    private Pizza(Builder b) { this.size = b.size; }

    public static class Builder {
        private String size = "medium";
        public Builder size(String s) { this.size = s; return this; }
        public Pizza build() { return new Pizza(this); }
    }
}
Pizza p = new Pizza.Builder().size("large").build();

// 2. An internal data structure
public class LinkedStack<E> {
    private Node<E> top;

    private static class Node<E> {       // needs no LinkedStack instance
        E value;
        Node<E> next;
    }
}

// 3. A grouped, closely related type
public class Http {
    public static class Request  { }
    public static class Response { }
}
```

Note `Node` being both `private` and `static`: private because it is an
implementation detail, static because a node has no reason to reference the
stack that holds it.

**The other two nested forms** are local classes, declared inside a method, and
anonymous classes, declared and instantiated in one expression. Both are covered
in chapter 4 alongside lambdas, which have largely replaced them.

> Key Takeaways
> - A static nested class has no reference to an enclosing instance; an inner
>   class does.
> - Inner classes keep their enclosing object alive, which risks memory leaks.
> - Prefer static nested classes unless you genuinely need the outer instance.
> - Common uses are builders, private data structures such as nodes, and
>   grouping related types.
> - Creating an inner class requires the `outer.new Inner()` syntax.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write an `Outer` class with both a static nested and an inner class, and
>    try to access an outer instance field from each.
> 2. Implement a singly linked list with a private static `Node` class.
> 3. Interview: Why can a non-static inner class cause a memory leak? (Hint:
>    what does each instance hold a reference to?)

#### The this Keyword

`this` is a reference to the object whose method is currently executing. Every
instance method and constructor receives it implicitly, which is how a single
shared method body knows whose fields to touch.

**Use 1: disambiguating a shadowed field.** This is the most common use by far.

```java
public class Point {
    private int x;
    private int y;

    public Point(int x, int y) {      // parameters SHADOW the fields
        this.x = x;                   // this.x = the field, x = the parameter
        this.y = y;
    }

    public void setX(int x) {
        this.x = x;
        // x = x;                     // legal and useless: assigns the parameter
    }                                 // to itself; the field never changes
}
```

Without shadowing, `this.` is optional and usually omitted:

```java
public double distanceFromOrigin() {
    return Math.sqrt(x * x + y * y);       // 'this.' implied
    return Math.sqrt(this.x * this.x + this.y * this.y);   // identical meaning
}
```

**Use 2: passing the current object to something else.**

```java
public class Button {
    public void register(EventBus bus) {
        bus.subscribe(this);                // hand over a reference to myself
    }

    public boolean sameAs(Button other) {
        return this == other;               // identity comparison
    }
}
```

**Use 3: constructor delegation**, covered earlier in this chapter:

```java
public Employee(String name) {
    this(name, "Unassigned");      // must be the first statement
}
```

**Use 4: returning the receiver for fluent chaining:**

```java
public class Query {
    public Query where(String cond) { /* ... */ return this; }
    public Query orderBy(String col) { /* ... */ return this; }
}
new Query().where("active").orderBy("name");
```

**Use 5: reaching the enclosing instance from an inner class**, where the
qualified form is needed because the inner class has its own `this`:

```java
public class Outer {
    private String name = "outer";

    class Inner {
        private String name = "inner";

        void print() {
            System.out.println(name);             // "inner"  -- nearest scope
            System.out.println(this.name);        // "inner"  -- the Inner instance
            System.out.println(Outer.this.name);  // "outer"  -- qualified this
        }
    }
}
```

**Where `this` does not exist:**

```java
public static void staticMethod() {
    // this.something;        // ERROR: no object in a static context
}
```

**A caution: do not leak `this` from a constructor.** Registering an object
before its constructor finishes publishes a half-built object, which other code
(or another thread) may observe in an inconsistent state:

```java
public class Leaky {
    private final int value;

    public Leaky(EventBus bus) {
        bus.register(this);        // DANGER: 'this' escapes before construction ends
        this.value = compute();    // another thread could see value == 0
    }
}

// Safer: finish construction, then register via a factory
public static Leaky create(EventBus bus) {
    Leaky instance = new Leaky();
    bus.register(instance);        // fully constructed before anyone sees it
    return instance;
}
```

This is the same hazard as calling an overridable method from a constructor,
seen earlier: in both cases, code runs against an object that is not yet
finished.

> Key Takeaways
> - `this` refers to the object executing the current instance method or
>   constructor.
> - Its main use is distinguishing a field from a parameter that shadows it.
> - `this(...)` delegates to another constructor and must come first.
> - `Outer.this` reaches the enclosing instance from an inner class.
> - Never publish `this` from a constructor; the object is not yet fully built.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a constructor whose parameters shadow the fields, omit `this.`, and
>    demonstrate that the fields stay at their defaults.
> 2. Write a fluent builder with three methods that each return `this`.
> 3. Interview: What does `Outer.this` mean, and when do you need it? (Hint:
>    how many `this` references are in scope inside an inner class?)

<a id="27-packages-and-code-organization"></a>
### 2.7 Packages and Code Organization

Classes need somewhere to live. Packages provide namespacing, an access-control
boundary, and the primary structure of a Java project.

#### Package Declaration and Directory Structure

A package is a namespace for related types. It prevents name collisions, groups
code by purpose, and defines the scope of package-private access.

```java
package com.example.billing;      // must be the FIRST statement in the file

public class Invoice { }
```

**The directory rule.** The package name must mirror the directory path, with
each dot corresponding to a directory level:

```text
project/
└── src/
    └── com/
        └── example/
            ├── billing/
            │   ├── Invoice.java        package com.example.billing;
            │   └── TaxCalculator.java  package com.example.billing;
            └── shipping/
                └── Parcel.java         package com.example.shipping;
```

```bash
# Compile from the source root, writing classes into out/
javac -d out src/com/example/billing/Invoice.java

# Run using the FULLY QUALIFIED name
java -cp out com.example.billing.Invoice
```

The compiler enforces this for output: `-d out` recreates the package
directories under `out`. It is more lenient about input paths, but every build
tool and IDE assumes the mirror structure, so treat it as mandatory.

**The fully qualified name** is the package plus the class name, and it is the
type's true identity. Two classes with the same simple name in different
packages are entirely distinct:

```java
java.util.Date       // one class
java.sql.Date        // a completely different class
```

**The default package.** Omitting the `package` declaration places a class in
the unnamed default package. This works for scratch files and is unsuitable for
anything else, because a class in the default package cannot be imported by any
packaged class:

```java
// File: Helper.java, no package declaration
public class Helper { }

// File: com/example/App.java
package com.example;
// import Helper;        // IMPOSSIBLE: there is no syntax for this
```

**One public class per file**, named identically to the file, as established
earlier. Combined with the directory rule, this means the compiler can locate
any class from its fully qualified name alone — no include paths, no header
files, no build-order declarations.

```text
   com.example.billing.Invoice
   |__________________| |_____|
           |               |
      directory path    file name
   com/example/billing/ Invoice.java
```

**Packages do not nest for access purposes.** This surprises people: despite the
dotted names, `com.example.billing` and `com.example.billing.internal` are two
unrelated packages. A package-private member of one is invisible to the other.

```java
package com.example.billing;
class Helper { }                        // package-private

package com.example.billing.internal;
// Helper h;                            // ERROR: not visible, despite the name
```

There is no "subpackage" concept in the access rules. The Java Platform Module
System, discussed at the end of this section, was created partly to address this
gap.

> Key Takeaways
> - The `package` declaration comes first and must mirror the directory
>   structure.
> - The fully qualified name is the class's real identity; same-named classes in
>   different packages are unrelated.
> - Classes in the default package cannot be imported and should not be used
>   beyond scratch work.
> - The directory-name correspondence lets the compiler find any class from its
>   name alone.
> - Subpackages are not nested for access control; each package is independent.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create two packages with a class each, compile both with `javac -d out`,
>    and run one by its fully qualified name.
> 2. Put a class in the default package and try to use it from a packaged
>    class.
> 3. Create `com.example.a` and `com.example.a.b`, then verify that a
>    package-private class in the first is invisible to the second.

#### Import Statements and Static Imports

An `import` does not copy code. It is purely a naming convenience, letting you
write a simple class name instead of a fully qualified one. The compiled result
is identical either way.

```java
package com.example.app;

import java.util.List;               // single-type import
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.*;                  // on-demand import: all types in java.util

public class Demo {
    List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();          // thanks to the imports
    java.util.List<String> other = new java.util.ArrayList<>();   // always valid
}
```

**Single-type versus on-demand.** The wildcard form imports every *type* in a
package, not subpackages, and has no runtime cost. Most style guides still
prefer explicit imports, because they document dependencies and avoid the
ambiguity below:

```java
import java.util.*;
import java.sql.*;

// Date d = new Date();      // ERROR: ambiguous, both packages define Date
java.util.Date d = new java.util.Date();      // resolved by qualifying

// Or import one explicitly: a single-type import wins over a wildcard
import java.util.*;
import java.sql.*;
import java.util.Date;       // this one now takes precedence
Date d = new Date();         // java.util.Date
```

**`java.lang` is imported automatically**, which is why `String`, `System`,
`Integer`, `Math`, and `Object` need no import. Classes in the same package need
no import either.

**Static imports** bring in static members rather than types:

```java
import static java.lang.Math.PI;
import static java.lang.Math.sqrt;
import static java.util.Arrays.asList;

double circumference = 2 * PI * radius;        // instead of Math.PI
double d = sqrt(x * x + y * y);                // instead of Math.sqrt
List<String> l = asList("a", "b");
```

They shine in tests, where they make assertions read like prose:

```java
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

assertEquals(expected, actual);        // instead of Assertions.assertEquals(...)
assertTrue(list.isEmpty());
```

Used carelessly, they hurt: a bare `max(a, b)` gives the reader no clue whether
it came from `Math`, a utility class, or the current class. The guideline is to
static-import only where the origin is obvious from context, and never for
members with generic names.

| Import form                  | Example                            | Imports              |
| ---------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| Single type                  | `import java.util.List;`           | One class            |
| On demand                    | `import java.util.*;`              | All types in a package |
| Single static member         | `import static java.lang.Math.PI;` | One static member    |
| Static on demand             | `import static java.lang.Math.*;`  | All static members   |

**What import cannot do:**

```java
// import java.util;              // ERROR: cannot import a package itself
// import java.*.List;            // ERROR: no wildcards in the middle
// import java.util.*.*;          // ERROR: wildcards do not recurse into subpackages
```

That last one matters: `import java.util.*` does not import `java.util.concurrent`,
because subpackages are separate packages.

**Ordering convention**, enforced by most formatters:

```java
package com.example.app;          // 1. package

import java.util.List;            // 2. java and javax
import java.util.Map;

import org.springframework.Bean;  // 3. third-party libraries

import com.example.other.Thing;   // 4. your own project

import static java.util.Arrays.asList;   // 5. static imports last
```

Unused imports are harmless at runtime but are flagged by every linter, because
they misrepresent a file's dependencies.

> Key Takeaways
> - `import` is a naming shortcut with no runtime effect; fully qualified names
>   always work.
> - Wildcard imports cover one package's types, never its subpackages.
> - `java.lang` and the current package are imported implicitly.
> - A single-type import takes precedence over a conflicting wildcard import.
> - Static imports suit tests and obvious constants, and obscure origins
>   elsewhere.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a class using both `java.util.Date` and `java.sql.Date`, resolving
>    the conflict two different ways.
> 2. Rewrite a class that uses `Math` repeatedly to use static imports, and
>    judge whether readability improved.
> 3. Interview: Does an unused import slow a program down? (Hint: what does the
>    compiler actually emit for an import?)

#### Classpath Fundamentals

The classpath tells the JVM and the compiler where to look for `.class` files
and JARs. Nearly every "class not found" error is a classpath problem.

```bash
# A single directory
java -cp out com.example.App

# Several entries: colon-separated on Unix, semicolon on Windows
java -cp out:lib/gson.jar com.example.App
java -cp "out;lib\gson.jar" com.example.App

# Every JAR in a directory
java -cp "out:lib/*" com.example.App

# The default when -cp is omitted is the current directory
java com.example.App        # equivalent to -cp .
```

**How lookup works.** Given the fully qualified name `com.example.App`, the JVM
searches each classpath entry in order for `com/example/App.class`:

```text
   -cp out:lib/gson.jar

   looking for com.example.App
        |
        +--> out/com/example/App.class          <- found here, search stops
        +--> lib/gson.jar!/com/example/App.class

   Order matters: the FIRST match wins.
```

That ordering rule is the cause of "JAR hell": two JARs containing different
versions of the same class produce whichever the classpath lists first, often
with confusing `NoSuchMethodError` failures later.

**The two errors and what they mean:**

| Error                    | Meaning                                                   |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ClassNotFoundException` | A *reflective* lookup failed: `Class.forName("...")`       |
| `NoClassDefFoundError`   | The class was present at compile time but missing at runtime, or its static initialiser failed earlier |

```text
$ java -cp out com.example.App
Error: Could not find or load main class com.example.App
Caused by: java.lang.ClassNotFoundException: com.example.App
```

The usual causes, in order of frequency: the class name is not fully qualified,
the classpath root is wrong (pointing at the package directory instead of the
source root), or the code was never compiled.

```bash
# WRONG: pointing at the package directory
java -cp out/com/example App

# RIGHT: point at the ROOT, name the class fully
java -cp out com.example.App
```

**JARs.** A JAR is a ZIP archive of class files plus a manifest. An executable
JAR names its entry point in the manifest:

```bash
jar --create --file app.jar --main-class com.example.App -C out .
java -jar app.jar          # NOTE: -jar IGNORES -cp entirely
```

The `-jar` flag overrides the classpath, so dependencies must be declared in the
manifest's `Class-Path` attribute or bundled into the JAR. This catches people
out constantly.

**In practice**, build tools manage the classpath. Maven and Gradle resolve
declared dependencies, download them, and construct the classpath for
compilation, tests, and packaging:

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>com.google.code.gson</groupId>
  <artifactId>gson</artifactId>
  <version>2.10.1</version>
</dependency>
```

Understanding the raw mechanism still matters, because when a build tool
produces a classpath problem, the diagnosis happens at this level.

> Key Takeaways
> - The classpath lists directories and JARs searched for compiled classes.
> - Entries are searched in order and the first match wins, which is the root
>   of version conflicts.
> - Point the classpath at the package *root*, and name classes fully.
> - `ClassNotFoundException` is a failed reflective lookup;
>   `NoClassDefFoundError` means it vanished after compilation or failed to
>   initialise.
> - `java -jar` ignores `-cp`; dependencies must be in the manifest or bundled.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compile a packaged class into `out`, then try running it with the
>    classpath pointing at the package directory and observe the error.
> 2. Build an executable JAR and run it with `-jar`.
> 3. Interview: What is the difference between `ClassNotFoundException` and
>    `NoClassDefFoundError`? (Hint: one involves a name resolved at runtime.)

#### Naming Conventions for Packages

Package names are the one part of Java naming that is globally shared, so the
conventions exist to prevent collisions between organisations as well as within
a project.

**The rules:**

1. All lowercase, no underscores or camel case.
2. Start with your organisation's domain name reversed.
3. Continue with project and module names.

```java
package com.example.billing.invoice;
        |_________| |_____| |_____|
             |         |       |
      reversed domain  project component
```

```text
   Organisation domain:  example.com
   Reversed:             com.example
   Plus project:         com.example.shopfront
   Plus component:       com.example.shopfront.checkout
```

Reversing the domain works because domain ownership is already globally unique,
so two organisations cannot accidentally collide. If you own no domain, `io.github.username`
is the conventional choice for open-source projects.

**Reserved and special prefixes:**

| Prefix        | Meaning                                       |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `java.*`      | Reserved for the Java Platform; do not use    |
| `javax.*`     | Standard extensions, historically             |
| `jdk.*`       | JDK-specific implementation packages          |
| `sun.*`, `com.sun.*` | Internal, unsupported, may vanish      |

Writing a class in a `java.*` package is actively blocked by the classloader at
runtime, not merely discouraged.

**Handling awkward domain names.** Domains can contain characters illegal in
identifiers, and may start with a digit or be a Java keyword:

| Domain            | Package                    | Reason                       |
| ----------------- | -------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `my-company.com`  | `com.my_company`           | Hyphen becomes underscore    |
| `123shop.com`     | `com._123shop`             | Cannot start with a digit    |
| `int.example.org` | `org.example._int`         | `int` is a keyword           |

**Structuring packages within a project.** Two broad approaches exist:

```text
   BY LAYER (technical)              BY FEATURE (functional)

   com.example.app                   com.example.app
   ├── controller                    ├── billing
   │   ├── OrderController           │   ├── Invoice
   │   └── UserController            │   ├── InvoiceController
   ├── service                       │   └── InvoiceRepository
   │   ├── OrderService              ├── shipping
   │   └── UserService               │   ├── Parcel
   └── repository                    │   ├── ShippingController
       ├── OrderRepository           │   └── ShippingRepository
       └── UserRepository            └── shared
```

Packaging by feature is generally preferred for anything beyond a small
project. Each package contains everything one capability needs, so a change is
local, package-private access becomes genuinely useful (the repository can be
hidden from other features), and the structure communicates what the
application does rather than which frameworks it uses.

Packaging by layer spreads every change across three packages and makes
package-private access nearly worthless, since collaborating classes are always
in different packages.

**Further conventions** worth following: singular nouns (`com.example.order`,
not `orders`), short segments, and no deep hierarchies for their own sake. A
package named `util` or `common` tends to become a dumping ground; prefer a name
that says what the contents have in common.

> Key Takeaways
> - Package names are lowercase and begin with a reversed domain you control.
> - `java.*` is reserved and enforced at runtime; `sun.*` and `com.sun.*` are
>   internal.
> - Illegal characters become underscores, and digits or keywords need an
>   underscore prefix.
> - Package by feature rather than by layer for all but the smallest projects.
