> - A chain of `instanceof` tests usually indicates missing polymorphism.
> - Legitimate uses include `equals`, deserialization, raw collections, and
>   sealed hierarchies.
> - `instanceof` accepts subtypes; comparing `getClass()` demands an exact
>   match.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write code that triggers a `ClassCastException`, then guard it with
>    `instanceof`.
> 2. Refactor an `instanceof` chain computing areas into a polymorphic
>    `area()` method.
> 3. Interview: When is downcasting unavoidable in well-designed code? (Hint:
>    look at the signature `Object.equals` forces on you.)

#### Pattern Matching for instanceof

The test-then-cast pattern was one of Java's most repetitive idioms: name the
type twice and declare a variable that the compiler already knew the type of.
Pattern matching, standard since Java 16, removes the redundancy.

```java
// Before Java 16
if (object instanceof String) {
    String s = (String) object;        // type named twice, cast is redundant
    System.out.println(s.length());
}

// Java 16 and later
if (object instanceof String s) {      // test, cast, and bind in one construct
    System.out.println(s.length());
}
```

The variable `s` is called a *pattern variable*. It is in scope exactly where
the compiler can prove the test succeeded, which is smarter than it first
appears.

**Flow scoping.** The pattern variable's scope follows the logic of the
condition, not the braces:

```java
// Available in the then-branch
if (o instanceof String s) {
    System.out.println(s.length());
}
// s is not in scope here

// Available after a negated early return
if (!(o instanceof String s)) {
    return;
}
System.out.println(s.length());      // in scope: we only reach here if the test passed

// Available in the right-hand side of &&
if (o instanceof String s && s.length() > 5) {   // s usable immediately
    System.out.println(s);
}

// NOT available after ||, because the test may not have run
// if (o instanceof String s || s.isEmpty()) { }   // ERROR
```

The `&&` case is particularly useful, and it is the reason the operator's
short-circuit semantics matter here.

**Combining with `equals`**, which becomes markedly cleaner:

```java
// Before
@Override
public boolean equals(Object o) {
    if (this == o) return true;
    if (o == null || getClass() != o.getClass()) return false;
    Point point = (Point) o;
    return x == point.x && y == point.y;
}

// After
@Override
public boolean equals(Object o) {
    return o instanceof Point p && x == p.x && y == p.y;
}
```

The second version is a single expression and handles `null` automatically,
since `instanceof` is false for null.

**Pattern matching for `switch`** (standard in Java 21) extends the idea to
multi-branch dispatch:

```java
static String describe(Object o) {
    return switch (o) {
        case Integer i when i > 100 -> "large number: " + i;   // guarded pattern
        case Integer i              -> "number: " + i;
        case String s               -> "text of length " + s.length();
        case int[] arr              -> "int array of " + arr.length;
        case null                   -> "nothing";              // explicit null case
        default                     -> "something else";
    };
}
```

Note three things: patterns bind variables per branch, `when` adds a guard
condition, and `case null` is now expressible — a plain `switch` throws
`NullPointerException` on a null selector.

**Record patterns** (Java 21) destructure records directly:

```java
record Point(int x, int y) { }
record Line(Point start, Point end) { }

static String describe(Object o) {
    return switch (o) {
        case Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(var x2, var y2)) ->
                "line from (" + x1 + "," + y1 + ") to (" + x2 + "," + y2 + ")";
        case Point(var x, var y) -> "point at (" + x + "," + y + ")";
        default -> "unknown";
    };
}
```

**Exhaustiveness with sealed types.** When the hierarchy is sealed (covered in
section 3.6), the compiler knows every possible case and no `default` is needed:

```java
sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square { }
record Circle(double radius) implements Shape { }
record Square(double side)   implements Shape { }

static double area(Shape s) {
    return switch (s) {
        case Circle c -> Math.PI * c.radius() * c.radius();
        case Square q -> q.side() * q.side();
        // no default needed; adding a permitted subtype breaks compilation here
    };
}
```

This combination — sealed types plus pattern switches — gives Java something
close to algebraic data types, and it makes "handle every case" a compile-time
guarantee rather than a hope.

| Version | Feature                                 |
| ------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Java 16 | Pattern matching for `instanceof`       |
| Java 17 | Sealed classes                          |
| Java 21 | Pattern matching for `switch`, record patterns |

> Key Takeaways
> - `instanceof Type variable` tests, casts, and binds in one step.
> - Flow scoping makes the pattern variable available exactly where the test is
>   known to have passed, including after `&&` and after a negated early
>   return.
> - `equals` implementations collapse to a single expression.
> - Pattern switches support guards with `when`, an explicit `case null`, and
>   record destructuring.
> - Sealed hierarchies make pattern switches exhaustive without a `default`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Rewrite three test-then-cast blocks using pattern matching.
> 2. Write an `equals` method as a single expression using
>    `instanceof` with a pattern variable.
> 3. Interview: Why can a pattern variable be used after `&&` but not after
>    `||`? (Hint: which operand is guaranteed to have been evaluated?)

#### ClassCastException Avoidance

`ClassCastException` is an unchecked exception thrown when a cast does not match
the object's actual type. It always indicates a programming error rather than a
recoverable condition, so the goal is to make the cast unnecessary or provably
safe.

```java
Object o = "a string";
Integer i = (Integer) o;       // ClassCastException: class java.lang.String
                               // cannot be cast to class java.lang.Integer
```

**Strategy 1: use polymorphism instead.** The best cast is the one you never
write:

```java
// Requires a cast
public void process(Object item) {
    if (item instanceof Order) { ((Order) item).ship(); }
}

// Requires no cast
public void process(Shippable item) {
    item.ship();
}
```

**Strategy 2: use generics.** Raw types were the main source of cast exceptions
before Java 5, and still are in legacy code:

```java
// Raw type: the compiler cannot help
List list = new ArrayList();
list.add("text");
list.add(42);
for (Object o : list) {
    String s = (String) o;        // ClassCastException on the second element
}

// Generic: the error is caught at compile time
List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add("text");
// list.add(42);                  // ERROR: incompatible types
for (String s : list) { }         // no cast needed at all
```

**Strategy 3: guard with pattern matching.** When a cast is genuinely needed,
never write one unguarded:

```java
// Unsafe
Dog dog = (Dog) animal;

// Safe, and the cast disappears
if (animal instanceof Dog dog) {
    dog.fetch();
}

// Safe with a fallback
String result = (animal instanceof Dog dog) ? dog.fetch() : "not a dog";
```

**Strategy 4: `Class.cast` and `isInstance` for reflective code**, where the
type is not known statically:

```java
public <T> T convert(Object value, Class<T> type) {
    if (!type.isInstance(value)) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException(
                "Expected " + type.getSimpleName() + " but got "
                + (value == null ? "null" : value.getClass().getSimpleName()));
    }
    return type.cast(value);        // checked cast with a clear failure message
}
```

**The generics pitfall: type erasure.** Generic type arguments are erased at
runtime (chapter 6), so an unchecked cast can defer the failure to a surprising
place:

```java
public static <T> T unsafeCast(Object o) {
    return (T) o;                    // unchecked warning; no runtime check happens
}

String s = unsafeCast(42);           // ClassCastException thrown HERE, at the
                                     // assignment, not inside the method
```

The exception surfaces where the value is first used as its declared type, which
can be far from the actual mistake. Treat unchecked-cast warnings as real.

**Diagnosing one when it happens:**

```text
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ClassCastException:
  class com.example.Cat cannot be cast to class com.example.Dog
  (com.example.Cat and com.example.Dog are in unnamed module of loader 'app')
        at com.example.Shelter.walk(Shelter.java:23)
```

The message names both types and the line. A confusing variant reports the
*same* class name on both sides, which means two different class loaders loaded
it — a common situation in application servers and plugin systems.

| Technique                      | Prevents the cast, or makes it safe |
| ------------------------------ | ----------------------------------- |
| Polymorphic method             | Removes it                          |
| Generics                       | Removes it                          |
| `instanceof` pattern           | Makes it safe                       |
| `Class.isInstance` / `cast`    | Makes it safe with a clear message  |
| Sealed types with exhaustive switch | Removes it                     |

> Key Takeaways
> - `ClassCastException` is unchecked and always signals a programming error.
> - Prefer polymorphism and generics so that no cast is written at all.
> - Guard any unavoidable cast with an `instanceof` pattern.
> - Use `Class.isInstance` and `Class.cast` in reflective code for clear
>   failures.
> - Erasure means an unchecked cast fails at the point of use, not at the point
>   of the mistake.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Produce a `ClassCastException` using a raw `List`, then fix it with
>    generics.
> 2. Write an unchecked generic cast and observe where the exception actually
>    surfaces.
> 3. Interview: You see a `ClassCastException` saying `Foo cannot be cast to
>    Foo`. What is going on? (Hint: class identity involves more than the
>    name.)

#### Polymorphic Collections of Objects

Holding many subtypes in one collection and treating them uniformly is where
polymorphism pays off most visibly in everyday code.

```java
public abstract class Shape {
    public abstract double area();
    public abstract String name();
}

public class Circle extends Shape {
    private final double radius;
    public Circle(double radius) { this.radius = radius; }
    @Override public double area() { return Math.PI * radius * radius; }
    @Override public String name() { return "Circle"; }
}

public class Rectangle extends Shape {
    private final double w, h;
    public Rectangle(double w, double h) { this.w = w; this.h = h; }
    @Override public double area() { return w * h; }
    @Override public String name() { return "Rectangle"; }
}
```

```java
List<Shape> shapes = List.of(
        new Circle(2),
        new Rectangle(3, 4),
        new Circle(1));

double total = 0;
for (Shape s : shapes) {
    System.out.printf("%-10s %8.2f%n", s.name(), s.area());
    total += s.area();                     // each call dispatches to the right class
}
System.out.printf("%-10s %8.2f%n", "TOTAL", total);
```

```text
Circle        12.57
Rectangle     12.00
Circle         3.14
TOTAL         27.71
```

The loop contains no type tests and never changes when a new shape is added.

**With streams**, the same idea reads more declaratively:

```java
double total = shapes.stream().mapToDouble(Shape::area).sum();

Map<String, List<Shape>> byType = shapes.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Shape::name));

List<Shape> large = shapes.stream()
        .filter(s -> s.area() > 10)
        .sorted(Comparator.comparingDouble(Shape::area).reversed())
        .toList();
```

**Sorting a polymorphic collection** works through `Comparable` or `Comparator`,
both of which are themselves polymorphic:

```java
List<Shape> sortable = new ArrayList<>(shapes);
sortable.sort(Comparator.comparingDouble(Shape::area));
```

**The variance pitfall.** `List<Dog>` is *not* a subtype of `List<Animal>`, even
though `Dog` is a subtype of `Animal`. Generics are invariant:

```java
List<Dog> dogs = new ArrayList<>();
// List<Animal> animals = dogs;      // ERROR: incompatible types
```

If it were allowed, this would follow:

```java
List<Animal> animals = dogs;    // hypothetically
animals.add(new Cat());         // legal for a List<Animal>
Dog d = dogs.get(0);            // ClassCastException: it is a Cat
```

The remedy is a bounded wildcard, which permits reading as `Animal` while
forbidding unsafe writes:

```java
public double totalArea(List<? extends Shape> shapes) {   // accepts List<Circle> too
    double sum = 0;
    for (Shape s : shapes) sum += s.area();
    // shapes.add(new Circle(1));      // ERROR: cannot add through '? extends'
    return sum;
}

totalArea(List.of(new Circle(1)));     // a List<Circle> is now acceptable
```

Chapter 6 covers wildcards and the PECS rule in full; the essential point here
is that arrays and generics differ:

```java
Object[] array = new Dog[3];      // arrays ARE covariant -- and this is unsafe
array[0] = new Cat();             // compiles, throws ArrayStoreException at runtime
```

Arrays were made covariant before generics existed, and the runtime check is the
price. Generics chose compile-time safety instead.

| Container      | Covariant? | Error detected      |
| -------------- | ---------- | ------------------- |
| `Dog[]`        | Yes        | Runtime (`ArrayStoreException`) |
| `List<Dog>`    | No         | Compile time        |
| `List<? extends Dog>` | Read-only view | Compile time |

**Design guidance.** Declare collections by the most general type that callers
need, and take `? extends T` in parameters that only read. That maximises what
the method accepts without giving up safety.

> Key Takeaways
> - A collection of a supertype holds any mixture of subtypes and dispatches
>   each call correctly.
> - Polymorphic loops need no type tests and survive the addition of new
>   subtypes.
> - Generics are invariant: `List<Dog>` is not a `List<Animal>`.
> - Use `List<? extends Shape>` for read-only parameters to accept subtype
>   collections.
> - Arrays are covariant and therefore fail at runtime with
>   `ArrayStoreException`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a `List<Shape>` with three subtypes and compute the total area with
>    both a loop and a stream.
> 2. Try assigning a `List<Circle>` to a `List<Shape>` variable, then fix the
>    method signature with a wildcard.
> 3. Interview: Why is `List<Dog>` not a `List<Animal>` when `Dog[]` is an
>    `Animal[]`? (Hint: what could you put into each one?)

<a id="34-abstract-classes"></a>
### 3.4 Abstract Classes

An abstract class defines a partial implementation: shared state and behaviour
plus a declaration of what subclasses must supply.

#### Declaring Abstract Classes and Methods

Some classes exist only to be extended. A `Shape` has an area, but there is no
such thing as a generic shape you could instantiate and ask. `abstract` makes
that explicit and lets the compiler enforce it.

```java
public abstract class Shape {              // cannot be instantiated

    protected final String name;           // shared state

    protected Shape(String name) {         // constructors are still needed
        this.name = name;
    }

    public abstract double area();         // no body: subclasses MUST provide one

    public String describe() {             // concrete: shared by all subclasses
        return name + " with area " + String.format("%.2f", area());
    }
}
```

```java
public class Circle extends Shape {
    private final double radius;

    public Circle(double radius) {
        super("Circle");                   // the abstract class's constructor
        this.radius = radius;
    }

    @Override
    public double area() { return Math.PI * radius * radius; }   // required
}
```

```java
// Shape s = new Shape("generic");     // ERROR: Shape is abstract; cannot be instantiated
Shape s = new Circle(2);               // fine: instantiate a concrete subclass
System.out.println(s.describe());      // "Circle with area 12.57"
```

**The rules:**

| Rule                                              | Consequence                      |
| ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| An abstract class cannot be instantiated          | Only subclasses produce objects  |
| It may have zero abstract methods                 | Still uninstantiable             |
| A class with any abstract method must be abstract | The compiler enforces this       |
| An abstract method has no body, only a semicolon  | `abstract double area();`        |
| A concrete subclass must implement every abstract method | Or be declared abstract itself |
| Abstract classes have constructors                | Called via `super(...)`          |
| `abstract` and `final` are contradictory          | Compile error                    |
| `abstract` and `private` are contradictory        | A private method cannot be overridden |
| `abstract` and `static` are contradictory         | Static methods are not dispatched |

```java
public abstract class Example {
    // public abstract final void a();      // ERROR: illegal combination
    // private abstract void b();           // ERROR: cannot be overridden
    // public abstract static void c();     // ERROR: not dispatchable
    public abstract void d();               // correct
}
```

**An intermediate abstract subclass** may leave some methods unimplemented:

```java
public abstract class Shape {
    public abstract double area();
    public abstract double perimeter();
}

public abstract class Polygon extends Shape {
    protected final int sides;
    protected Polygon(int sides) { this.sides = sides; }

    @Override public double perimeter() { return sides * sideLength(); }
    protected abstract double sideLength();      // a new abstract method
    // area() is still abstract: Polygon stays abstract
}

public class Square extends Polygon {
    private final double side;
    public Square(double side) { super(4); this.side = side; }
    @Override protected double sideLength() { return side; }
    @Override public double area() { return side * side; }     // now complete
}
```

```text
        Shape (abstract)
          area()        abstract
          perimeter()   abstract
             |
        Polygon (abstract)
          perimeter()   implemented
          sideLength()  abstract, newly added
          area()        still abstract
             |
        Square (concrete)
          everything implemented -> instantiable
```

**Abstract classes can still be referenced and are used constantly as types:**

```java
List<Shape> shapes = List.of(new Circle(1), new Square(2));   // Shape as a type
Shape s = shapes.get(0);                                      // Shape as a variable
public double total(List<Shape> shapes) { ... }               // Shape as a parameter
```

You simply cannot write `new Shape(...)`. Anonymous subclasses are the one
syntactic exception, and they are creating a concrete subclass, not the abstract
class:

```java
Shape s = new Shape("anon") {          // an anonymous CONCRETE subclass
    @Override public double area() { return 0; }
};
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `abstract` on a class prevents instantiation; on a method it demands an
>   implementation from subclasses.
> - A class containing an abstract method must itself be abstract.
> - Abstract classes have constructors, fields, and concrete methods.
> - An intermediate abstract subclass may implement some methods and leave
>   others.
> - `abstract` cannot combine with `final`, `private`, or `static`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write an abstract `Employee` with an abstract `calculatePay()` and two
>    concrete subclasses.
> 2. Try to instantiate the abstract class and read the error, then do it with
>    an anonymous subclass.
> 3. Interview: Can an abstract class have a constructor, and if so, who calls
>    it? (Hint: what runs when a subclass is instantiated?)

#### Partial Implementation Strategies

The real value of an abstract class is that it can implement the parts it knows
and delegate only the parts it cannot know. Deciding where to draw that line is
the design work.

**Strategy 1: implement in terms of abstract methods.** The abstract class
provides useful behaviour built on top of what subclasses supply:

```java
public abstract class Account {
    protected double balance;

    public abstract double interestRate();      // subclass supplies the rate

    // Everything below is written ONCE, using that one unknown
    public void applyMonthlyInterest() {
        balance += balance * interestRate() / 12;
    }

    public double projectedAnnualInterest() {
        return balance * interestRate();
    }

    public boolean beatsInflation(double inflation) {
        return interestRate() > inflation;
    }
}
```

One abstract method yields three concrete ones. A `SavingsAccount` supplies a
rate and gets all three behaviours free.

**Strategy 2: provide a default with an override point.** A concrete method that
subclasses *may* replace, rather than must:

```java
public abstract class Report {
    public abstract List<Row> rows();            // must supply

    protected String header() { return "Report"; }   // may override
    protected String footer() { return "End";    }   // may override

    public final String render() {               // fixed algorithm
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(header()).append('\n');
        rows().forEach(r -> sb.append(r).append('\n'));
        return sb.append(footer()).toString();
    }
}
```

This is the **template method pattern**: `render()` is `final` so the sequence
cannot change, while `header` and `footer` are hooks.

**Strategy 3: the skeletal implementation.** Pair an interface with an abstract
class that implements most of it, so implementers can either extend the skeleton
or implement the interface from scratch:

```java
public interface Collection<E> {
    int size();
    boolean isEmpty();
    boolean contains(Object o);
    // ... many more
}

public abstract class AbstractCollection<E> implements Collection<E> {
    public abstract int size();                  // left to subclasses
    public abstract Iterator<E> iterator();

    @Override public boolean isEmpty() { return size() == 0; }        // derived

    @Override public boolean contains(Object o) {                     // derived
        for (E e : this) {
            if (Objects.equals(e, o)) return true;
        }
        return false;
    }
}
```

The JDK uses this throughout: `AbstractList`, `AbstractMap`, `AbstractSet`.
Implementing a custom list means extending `AbstractList` and writing two
methods instead of twenty.

```java
public class RangeList extends AbstractList<Integer> {
    private final int from, to;
    public RangeList(int from, int to) { this.from = from; this.to = to; }

    @Override public Integer get(int index) { return from + index; }   // 1
    @Override public int size()             { return to - from; }      // 2
    // contains, indexOf, iterator, subList, equals, hashCode, toString: inherited
}
```

**Choosing what to leave abstract.** A practical test: a method should be
abstract when its implementation genuinely differs per subclass, and concrete
when a sensible shared version exists.

| Make it abstract when                         | Make it concrete when                      |
| --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Every subclass needs a different answer        | A reasonable default exists                |
| There is no sensible default                   | The behaviour is derivable from other methods |
| Forgetting to implement it would be a bug      | Most subclasses want the same thing        |

**A caution about protected fields.** It is tempting for an abstract class to
expose its state to subclasses directly:

```java
public abstract class Account {
    protected double balance;      // every subclass can now corrupt it
}

public abstract class Account {
    private double balance;                            // better
    protected double getBalance() { return balance; }
    protected void adjust(double delta) {              // controlled mutation
        if (balance + delta < 0) throw new IllegalStateException();
        balance += delta;
    }
}
```

The second version keeps the invariant enforceable. A protected field is a
permanent commitment to every subclass, present and future.

> Key Takeaways
> - Implement concrete behaviour in terms of a small number of abstract
>   methods.
> - A `final` template method with overridable hooks fixes the algorithm while
>   allowing variation.
> - Skeletal implementations such as `AbstractList` let implementers write two
>   methods instead of twenty.
> - Leave a method abstract only when no sensible default exists.
> - Prefer protected accessors over protected fields so invariants stay
>   enforceable.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write an abstract class with one abstract method and three concrete
>    methods built on it.
> 2. Implement a custom read-only list by extending `AbstractList` and writing
>    only `get` and `size`.
> 3. Interview: What is a skeletal implementation, and what problem does it
>    solve? (Hint: count the methods in `List` versus the ones you must
>    actually write.)

#### Abstract Classes as Template Providers

The template method pattern deserves its own treatment because it is the single
most common reason to reach for an abstract class, and it demonstrates the
inversion of control that inheritance enables.

The idea: the superclass owns the *algorithm*, the subclass owns the *steps*.
Control flows from the superclass down, not the other way around.

```java
public abstract class DataImporter {

    // The template method: fixed sequence, cannot be changed by subclasses
    public final ImportResult importData(Path source) {
        validateSource(source);                    // fixed
        List<String> raw = readLines(source);      // varies
        List<Record> parsed = new ArrayList<>();

        for (String line : raw) {
            if (shouldSkip(line)) continue;        // hook with a default
            parsed.add(parseLine(line));           // varies
        }

        validate(parsed);                          // hook with a default
        int written = persist(parsed);             // varies
        afterImport(written);                      // hook, does nothing by default
        return new ImportResult(written);
    }

    // Required steps: each subclass must define these
    protected abstract List<String> readLines(Path source);
    protected abstract Record parseLine(String line);
    protected abstract int persist(List<Record> records);

    // Optional hooks: sensible defaults, may be overridden
    protected boolean shouldSkip(String line) { return line.isBlank(); }
    protected void validate(List<Record> records) { }
    protected void afterImport(int count) { }

    // Private: not an extension point
    private void validateSource(Path source) {
        if (!Files.exists(source)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("No such file");
    }
}
```

```java
public class CsvImporter extends DataImporter {
    @Override protected List<String> readLines(Path source) { ... }
    @Override protected Record parseLine(String line) {
        String[] parts = line.split(",");
        return new Record(parts[0], Integer.parseInt(parts[1]));
    }
    @Override protected int persist(List<Record> records) { ... }
    @Override protected boolean shouldSkip(String line) {
        return line.isBlank() || line.startsWith("#");     // extends the default
    }
}
```

```text
   CONTROL FLOW: the superclass calls down into the subclass

   caller ---> DataImporter.importData()      <- the algorithm lives here
                     |
                     +--> validateSource()    (private, fixed)
                     +--> readLines()         --> CsvImporter.readLines()
                     +--> shouldSkip()        --> CsvImporter.shouldSkip()
                     +--> parseLine()         --> CsvImporter.parseLine()
                     +--> persist()           --> CsvImporter.persist()

   This is the Hollywood Principle: "don't call us, we'll call you."
```

**Why `final` on the template method matters.** Without it, a subclass could
override `importData` and skip validation entirely, defeating the point:

```java
public final ImportResult importData(Path source) { ... }   // sequence guaranteed
```

**Three categories of method** in a well-designed template class:

| Category           | Access               | Purpose                          |
| ------------------ | -------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Template method    | `public final`       | The invariant algorithm          |
| Abstract steps     | `protected abstract` | Must be supplied by subclasses   |
| Hooks              | `protected` with a default | May be customised          |
| Internal helpers   | `private`            | Not extension points             |

The access modifiers document the design: a reader can tell at a glance what
they must implement, what they may implement, and what is off limits.

**Real examples in the JDK and common frameworks:**

```java
// java.io.InputStream: read(byte[], int, int) is built on the abstract read()
public abstract class InputStream {
    public abstract int read() throws IOException;
    public int read(byte[] b, int off, int len) throws IOException { ... }
}

// java.util.AbstractList, javax.servlet.http.HttpServlet.service(),
// Spring's JdbcTemplate.execute(), JUnit's test lifecycle
```

**When a lambda is better.** If there is exactly one varying step, an abstract
class is heavy machinery. A functional parameter does the same job without a
hierarchy:

```java
// Template method with one hook
public abstract class Processor {
    public final void run(List<String> items) {
        items.forEach(this::handle);
    }
    protected abstract void handle(String item);
}

// Equivalent with composition and a lambda -- no subclass needed
public class Processor {
    private final Consumer<String> handler;
    public Processor(Consumer<String> handler) { this.handler = handler; }
    public void run(List<String> items) { items.forEach(handler); }
}

new Processor(System.out::println).run(items);
```

The rule of thumb: several related varying steps that share state justify a
template class; one varying step is better as a function.

> Key Takeaways
> - The template method pattern puts the algorithm in the superclass and the
>   steps in subclasses.
> - Mark the template method `final` so the sequence cannot be bypassed.
> - Use `protected abstract` for required steps and `protected` with a default
>   for optional hooks.
> - Access modifiers document which methods are extension points.
> - A single varying step is usually better expressed as a functional
>   parameter than a subclass.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write an abstract `Game` class with a final `play()` template calling
>    `initialise()`, `takeTurn()`, and `announceWinner()`.
> 2. Add an optional hook with a default and override it in only one subclass.
> 3. Interview: Why should a template method be `final`? (Hint: what could a
>    subclass otherwise skip?)

#### Abstract versus Concrete Design Choices

Deciding whether a class should be abstract, concrete, or an interface is a
recurring design question. The answer follows from what the type is for.

**Make it abstract when** the type represents an incomplete concept that cannot
sensibly exist on its own, and when subclasses share state or implementation:

```java
public abstract class PaymentMethod {
    protected final String accountId;                  // shared state
    protected PaymentMethod(String accountId) { this.accountId = accountId; }

    public abstract PaymentResult charge(long amountCents);   // varies

    public final String maskedAccount() {              // shared implementation
        return "****" + accountId.substring(accountId.length() - 4);
    }
}
```

**Make it concrete when** instances of the type itself are meaningful, even if
subclasses exist:

```java
public class Employee { }                    // an employee is a real thing
public class Manager extends Employee { }    // and so is a manager
```

**Make it an interface when** you are describing a *capability* rather than a
kind of thing, or when implementers may already have a superclass:

```java
public interface Auditable { AuditRecord toAuditRecord(); }
public interface Comparable<T> { int compareTo(T other); }
```

Chapter 4 covers interfaces fully; the comparison table below is the summary
most often needed.

| Question                                   | Abstract class | Interface     |
| ------------------------------------------ | -------------- | ------------- |
| Can hold instance state                    | Yes            | No (constants only) |
| Can define constructors                    | Yes            | No            |
| How many can a class have                  | One            | Many          |
| Can have non-public members                | Yes            | `private` methods since Java 9 |
| Default implementations                    | Concrete methods | Default methods since Java 8 |
| Describes                                  | What something *is* | What something *can do* |
| Adding a method to it                      | Breaks nothing if concrete | Breaks implementers unless `default` |

**A worked decision.** Suppose you are modelling notifications sent by email,
SMS, and push.

```java
// They share state (recipient, retry count) and an algorithm (retry with backoff).
// The shared parts are substantial, so an abstract class fits.
public abstract class Notification {
    protected final String recipient;
    private int attempts;

    protected Notification(String recipient) { this.recipient = recipient; }

    public final boolean send() {                  // shared retry algorithm
        while (attempts < 3) {
            attempts++;
            if (doSend()) return true;
            sleepBackoff(attempts);
        }
        return false;
    }

    protected abstract boolean doSend();           // the only difference

    private void sleepBackoff(int attempt) { ... }
}
```

Now suppose some notifications must also be archived, and archiving applies to
unrelated types too. That is a capability, not a kind, so it becomes an
interface:

```java
public interface Archivable { void archive(); }

public class EmailNotification extends Notification implements Archivable { ... }
```

This combination — an abstract class for the shared implementation and
interfaces for orthogonal capabilities — is the standard modern shape.

**A caution against premature abstraction.** Creating an abstract base class
before you have two real implementations usually produces the wrong abstraction:

```java
// Written with one implementation in mind, before the second existed
public abstract class AbstractRepository {
    protected Connection connection;              // assumes SQL
    protected abstract String tableName();        // assumes tables
}
// The second implementation turns out to be a REST API. Nothing fits.
```

The common guidance is to write two or three concrete implementations first,
observe what is genuinely shared, and extract the abstraction afterwards.

> Key Takeaways
> - Abstract classes suit incomplete concepts with shared state and
>   implementation.
> - Interfaces suit capabilities and allow a class to have many of them.
> - Use both together: an abstract base for the shared algorithm, interfaces
>   for orthogonal capabilities.
> - Adding a method to an abstract class is safe; adding one to an interface
>   breaks implementers unless it is `default`.
> - Extract an abstraction after two or three concrete cases exist, not before.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Decide, with justification, whether each should be an abstract class,
>    concrete class, or interface: `Vehicle`, `Serializable`, `Order`,
>    `Comparable`, `DatabaseConnection`.
> 2. Design a notification hierarchy using an abstract class plus one
>    capability interface.
> 3. Interview: When would you choose an abstract class over an interface?
>    (Hint: what can one hold that the other cannot?)

<a id="35-the-object-superclass"></a>
### 3.5 The Object Superclass

Every class inherits from `Object`, so every object carries a small universal
API. Overriding those methods correctly is a routine but error-prone task.

#### Universal Methods Inherited from Object

`java.lang.Object` is the root of the class hierarchy. Its methods are available
on every reference, which is what makes generic containers, collections, and
reflection possible.

```java
public class Plain { }        // implicitly extends Object

Plain p = new Plain();
p.toString();   p.equals(other);   p.hashCode();   p.getClass();
```

**The eleven methods**, grouped by purpose:

| Method                        | Purpose                                | Commonly overridden |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| `toString()`                  | Human-readable representation          | Yes                 |
| `equals(Object)`              | Logical equality                       | Yes                 |
| `hashCode()`                  | Hash bucket value                      | Yes, with `equals`  |
| `clone()`                     | Field-by-field copy                    | Rarely              |
| `finalize()`                  | Pre-collection callback                | Never; deprecated   |
| `getClass()`                  | Runtime class object                   | Cannot: `final`     |
| `wait()`, `wait(long)`        | Release the monitor and pause          | Cannot: `final`     |
| `notify()`, `notifyAll()`     | Wake waiting threads                   | Cannot: `final`     |

The threading methods (`wait`, `notify`, `notifyAll`) exist on `Object` because
every object can act as a monitor lock; they are covered in chapter 10.

**The default implementations** are deliberately minimal and identity-based:

```java
public class Point {
    int x = 1, y = 2;
}

Point a = new Point();
Point b = new Point();

System.out.println(a);            // Point@1b6d3586  -- class name + hex hashCode
System.out.println(a.equals(b));  // false           -- identity comparison
System.out.println(a.hashCode()); // 460141958       -- derived from identity
System.out.println(a.getClass()); // class Point
```

`Object.toString()` is literally this:

```java
public String toString() {
    return getClass().getName() + "@" + Integer.toHexString(hashCode());
}
```

That output is useless in a log, which is why `toString` is the first method
most classes override.

**`getClass()` is `final`** and returns the runtime class, not the declared
type:

```java
Object o = "text";
System.out.println(o.getClass());                  // class java.lang.String
System.out.println(o.getClass().getSimpleName());  // String
System.out.println(o.getClass().getName());        // java.lang.String
```

**`finalize()` is deprecated** for removal and should never be used. It ran
before garbage collection, with no guarantee of when or whether, and it caused
unpredictable delays and resurrection bugs. Use `try`-with-resources and
`AutoCloseable` instead (chapter 5).

**Records and enums override some of these automatically:**

```java
public record Point(int x, int y) { }     // equals, hashCode, toString generated

Point a = new Point(1, 2);
Point b = new Point(1, 2);
System.out.println(a);            // Point[x=1, y=2]
System.out.println(a.equals(b));  // true
```

This is one of the strongest arguments for using records for pure data types:
the three methods that are tedious and error-prone to write by hand come for
free and are guaranteed consistent.

> Key Takeaways
> - Every class inherits `Object`'s methods, which is what makes collections
>   and reflection work.
> - `toString`, `equals`, and `hashCode` are the three intended for overriding.
> - The defaults are identity-based and rarely useful.
> - `getClass`, `wait`, `notify`, and `notifyAll` are `final` and cannot be
>   overridden.
> - `finalize` is deprecated; use `AutoCloseable` for cleanup.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Print a plain object and decode which part of the output is the class name
>    and which is the hash.
> 2. Compare `getClass().getName()` and `getSimpleName()` for a nested class and
>    an array type.
> 3. Interview: Why do `wait` and `notify` live on `Object` rather than on
>    `Thread`? (Hint: what can be used as a lock in Java?)

#### Overriding toString

`toString` produces a textual representation of an object. It is called
implicitly by string concatenation, `System.out.println`, and most logging
frameworks, so overriding it improves every diagnostic message in the program at
once.

```java
public class Point {
    private final int x, y;
    public Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "Point(" + x + ", " + y + ")";
    }
}

Point p = new Point(3, 4);
System.out.println(p);              // Point(3, 4)
System.out.println("at " + p);      // at Point(3, 4) -- implicit call
List.of(p, p).toString();           // [Point(3, 4), Point(3, 4)]
```

Without the override, the same three lines print `Point@1b6d3586`, which tells a
debugger nothing about the object's state.

**Where it is called implicitly:**

```java
String s = "" + object;                  // string concatenation
System.out.println(object);              // print methods
String.valueOf(object);                  // null-safe: returns "null"
logger.info("processing {}", object);    // logging frameworks
collection.toString();                   // collections call it on each element
String.format("%s", object);             // format specifiers
```

Note `String.valueOf(null)` returns `"null"` while `object.toString()` on a null
reference throws. Concatenation is null-safe for the same reason.

**What to include.** A good `toString` contains the fields a human debugging the
program would want, in a format that is easy to scan:

```java
// Poor: no context
@Override public String toString() { return name; }

// Poor: dumps everything, including a 10,000-element list
@Override public String toString() { return name + allTransactions; }

// Good: identifying fields, clearly labelled
@Override
public String toString() {
    return "Account[id=" + id + ", owner=" + owner + ", balance=" + balance + "]";
}
```

**The conventional format** used by the JDK and by IDE generators is
`ClassName[field=value, field=value]`:

```java
@Override
public String toString() {
    return getClass().getSimpleName()        // survives subclassing
            + "[id=" + id
            + ", name=" + name
            + ']';
}
```

Using `getClass().getSimpleName()` rather than a hard-coded literal means a
subclass inherits a correct representation automatically.

**Security and privacy.** `toString` output ends up in logs, which are often
retained and widely readable. Never include passwords, tokens, or personal data:

```java
@Override
public String toString() {
    return "User[email=" + email + ", passwordHash=" + passwordHash + "]";  // NO
}

@Override
public String toString() {
    return "User[id=" + id + ", email=" + maskEmail(email) + "]";           // better
}
```

**Performance.** `toString` is often called in logging statements that are
disabled at runtime. Building an expensive string that is then discarded is pure
waste, which is why parameterised logging exists:

```java
logger.debug("state: " + expensiveObject);        // toString ALWAYS runs
logger.debug("state: {}", expensiveObject);       // runs only if DEBUG is enabled
```

**Generating it.** Every IDE generates `toString`, and several libraries do it
reflectively. Records generate it automatically, which is the cleanest option
for data classes:

```java
public record Point(int x, int y) { }
System.out.println(new Point(3, 4));      // Point[x=3, y=4]
```

Unlike `equals` and `hashCode`, `toString` has no contract that code depends on
for correctness. Treat it as documentation for humans, and feel free to change
the format — unless someone has started parsing it, which is itself a design
error worth preventing by documenting that the format is not stable.

> Key Takeaways
> - `toString` is called implicitly by concatenation, printing, logging, and
>   collections.
> - The default prints a class name and a hash, which is useless for debugging.
> - Use the `ClassName[field=value]` convention and
>   `getClass().getSimpleName()` so subclasses inherit correct output.
> - Never include secrets or personal data; logs outlive the program.
> - Use parameterised logging so a disabled log statement does not build the
>   string.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add a `toString` to a class with four fields following the conventional
>    format.
> 2. Show that `System.out.println(obj)` and `"" + obj` both call it, while
>    `obj` being null behaves differently in each.
> 3. Compare a hand-written `toString` with the one a record generates for the
>    same fields.

#### The equals Contract

`equals` defines *logical* equality: whether two objects represent the same
value. `Object`'s default compares identity, which is almost never what you
want for value types.

```java
String a = new String("hello");
String b = new String("hello");
System.out.println(a == b);        // false -- different objects
System.out.println(a.equals(b));   // true  -- String overrides equals
```

**The contract.** A correct `equals` must satisfy five properties, stated in the
Javadoc of `Object.equals`:

| Property     | Requirement                                                     |
| ------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Reflexive    | `x.equals(x)` is true                                            |
| Symmetric    | `x.equals(y)` is true if and only if `y.equals(x)` is true       |
| Transitive   | If `x.equals(y)` and `y.equals(z)`, then `x.equals(z)`           |
| Consistent   | Repeated calls return the same result if nothing changes          |
| Null-safe    | `x.equals(null)` is false, never throws                          |

Violating any of these breaks collections in ways that are hard to diagnose,
because `HashMap`, `HashSet`, `List.contains`, and `List.remove` all rely on
them.

**The canonical implementation:**

```java
public final class Point {
    private final int x, y;

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;                 // 1. identity shortcut
        if (o == null || getClass() != o.getClass()) return false;  // 2. type check
        Point other = (Point) o;                    // 3. cast, now safe
        return x == other.x && y == other.y;        // 4. compare significant fields
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(x, y); }   // 5. always pair them
}
```

Modern form with pattern matching:

```java
@Override
public boolean equals(Object o) {
    return o instanceof Point p && x == p.x && y == p.y;
}
```

**Comparing fields correctly** depends on the type:

```java
@Override
public boolean equals(Object o) {
    if (!(o instanceof Item other)) return false;
    return count == other.count                          // primitives: ==
        && Objects.equals(name, other.name)              // objects: null-safe equals
        && Double.compare(price, other.price) == 0       // double: handles NaN and -0.0
        && Arrays.equals(tags, other.tags);              // arrays: Arrays.equals
}
```

`Double.compare` matters: `Double.NaN == Double.NaN` is false, so a raw `==`
would make an object containing `NaN` unequal to itself, violating reflexivity.

**The symmetry trap with inheritance.** Using `instanceof` across a hierarchy
breaks symmetry:

```java
public class Point {
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof Point p && x == p.x && y == p.y;
    }
}

public class ColourPoint extends Point {
    private final String colour;
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof ColourPoint c && super.equals(c) && colour.equals(c.colour);
    }
}

Point p = new Point(1, 2);
ColourPoint c = new ColourPoint(1, 2, "red");

System.out.println(p.equals(c));   // true  -- Point only checks x and y
System.out.println(c.equals(p));   // false -- p is not a ColourPoint
```

Symmetry is broken, and a `HashSet` containing both behaves differently
depending on insertion order. Two remedies exist:

1. Use `getClass() != o.getClass()`, which makes different classes never equal
   but also breaks substitutability for proxies and subclasses that add no
   state.
2. Favour composition over inheritance for value types, and make value classes
   `final`.

The second is the recommendation from *Effective Java*: there is no way to
extend an instantiable class and add a value component while preserving the
contract.

**Records handle all of this**, generating an `equals` that compares every
component and is automatically correct:

```java
public record Point(int x, int y) { }     // equals and hashCode generated
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `equals` must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, and false
>   for `null`.
> - The default implementation compares identity, not contents.
> - Compare primitives with `==`, objects with `Objects.equals`, doubles with
>   `Double.compare`, and arrays with `Arrays.equals`.
> - Extending an instantiable class and adding state cannot preserve symmetry.
> - Make value classes `final`, or use records, which generate a correct
>   implementation.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `equals` for a class with an `int`, a `String`, and a `double[]`
>    field.
> 2. Reproduce the `Point`/`ColourPoint` symmetry violation and demonstrate the
>    inconsistent `HashSet` behaviour.
> 3. Interview: Why must `equals` be symmetric? (Hint: think about what
>    `list.contains(x)` does internally and in which order.)

#### The hashCode Contract and equals Consistency

`hashCode` returns an `int` used by hash-based collections to choose a bucket.
It must be consistent with `equals`, and forgetting to override it alongside
`equals` is one of the most common bugs in Java.

**The contract:**

| Rule                                                      | Consequence if broken            |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Equal objects must have equal hash codes                  | Hash collections cannot find items |
| Unequal objects *may* share a hash code                   | Only a performance concern        |
| The hash must not change while the object is in a collection | Lookups silently fail          |

```java
// The bug: equals overridden, hashCode forgotten
public class Point {
    private final int x, y;
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof Point p && x == p.x && y == p.y;
    }
    // no hashCode: inherits Object's identity-based version
}

Set<Point> set = new HashSet<>();
set.add(new Point(1, 2));
System.out.println(set.contains(new Point(1, 2)));   // false!
System.out.println(set.add(new Point(1, 2)));        // true -- duplicate added
```

**Why it fails.** A `HashMap` locates an entry in two steps:

```text
   map.get(key)

   1. bucket = hash(key.hashCode()) % tableSize      <- finds the bucket
   2. within the bucket, compare with equals()       <- finds the entry

   If two equal objects produce different hash codes, step 1 looks in the
   wrong bucket and step 2 never runs.

   +--------+  +--------+  +--------+  +--------+
   | bucket |  | bucket |  | bucket |  | bucket |
   |   0    |  |   1    |  |   2    |  |   3    |
   +--------+  +--------+  +--------+  +--------+
        ^                       ^
        |                       |
   stored here            searched here    -> never found
```

**The correct implementation:**

```java
@Override
public int hashCode() {
    return Objects.hash(x, y);        // uses the same fields as equals
}
```

`Objects.hash` is convenient but allocates a varargs array. For a hot path,
the manual form avoids that:

```java
@Override
public int hashCode() {
    int result = Integer.hashCode(x);
    result = 31 * result + Integer.hashCode(y);
    result = 31 * result + Objects.hashCode(name);
    return result;
}
```

The multiplier 31 is conventional: it is odd and prime, and `31 * i` compiles to
a shift and subtract. The point of multiplying is that order matters, so that
`("a", "b")` and `("b", "a")` hash differently.

**Field-type specifics:**

```java
int      -> Integer.hashCode(f)  or just f
long     -> Long.hashCode(f)
double   -> Double.hashCode(f)
boolean  -> Boolean.hashCode(f)
Object   -> Objects.hashCode(f)        // null-safe, returns 0 for null
array    -> Arrays.hashCode(f)         // NOT f.hashCode(), which is identity-based
```

**Mutability is the other half of the problem.** If a field used in `hashCode`
changes while the object is in a hash collection, the object is stranded in the
wrong bucket:

```java
Set<MutablePoint> set = new HashSet<>();
MutablePoint p = new MutablePoint(1, 2);
set.add(p);
p.setX(99);                             // hash code changes

System.out.println(set.contains(p));    // false -- even for the SAME object
System.out.println(set.size());         // 1     -- it is still in there somewhere
```

This is the strongest practical argument for immutable keys, and it is why
`String` being immutable matters so much.

**Caching for expensive hashes.** Immutable objects can compute the hash once:

```java
public final class LongKey {
    private final String value;
    private int hash;                    // 0 means "not yet computed"

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        int h = hash;
        if (h == 0 && !value.isEmpty()) {
            h = value.hashCode();
            hash = h;                    // safe: the value never changes
        }
        return h;
    }
}
```

`String` itself uses exactly this technique.

**The rule to remember:** always override `equals` and `hashCode` together,
using the same fields. Every IDE generates both at once, and records generate
both automatically.

> Key Takeaways
> - Equal objects must have equal hash codes; unequal objects may collide.
> - Overriding `equals` without `hashCode` breaks `HashMap`, `HashSet`, and
>   every hash-based lookup.
> - Use `Objects.hash(...)` for convenience or the `31 * result` idiom for
>   performance.
> - Use `Arrays.hashCode` for array fields, never the array's own `hashCode`.
> - Mutating a field used in the hash while the object is in a collection
>   strands it; prefer immutable keys.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a class overriding `equals` but not `hashCode`, and show that a
>    `HashSet` fails to find an equal element.
> 2. Add a correct `hashCode` and verify the set now works.
> 3. Interview: Two objects have the same `hashCode` but are not equal. Is that
>    a bug? (Hint: read the contract in both directions.)

#### Object Cloning and the Cloneable Interface

`Object.clone()` produces a field-by-field copy of an object. The mechanism is
widely regarded as a design mistake, and understanding why is more useful than
learning to use it.

```java
public class Point implements Cloneable {          // marker interface required
    private int x, y;

    @Override
    public Point clone() {                         // covariant return type
        try {
            return (Point) super.clone();          // Object.clone does the copying
        } catch (CloneNotSupportedException e) {
            throw new AssertionError(e);           // unreachable: we are Cloneable
        }
    }
}
```

**Why the design is criticised:**

1. **`Cloneable` is a marker interface with no methods.** It does not declare
   `clone()`; it merely changes what `Object.clone()` does. Implementing an
   interface to alter a superclass method's behaviour is unlike anything else in
   Java.
2. **`Object.clone()` is `protected`**, so `Cloneable` alone does not make an
   object cloneable by callers. You must also override `clone()` as `public`.
3. **`CloneNotSupportedException` is checked**, forcing a try-catch for a
   condition that cannot occur if the class is `Cloneable`.
4. **The copy is shallow.** Nested mutable objects are shared between the
   original and the clone.
5. **It bypasses constructors**, so invariants enforced there are not applied,
   and `final` fields cannot be reassigned during cloning.

**The shallow-copy problem in practice:**

```java
public class Person implements Cloneable {
    private String name;                    // immutable: sharing is fine
    private List<String> hobbies;           // mutable: sharing is a bug

    @Override
    public Person clone() {
        try {
            return (Person) super.clone();  // hobbies is SHARED, not copied
        } catch (CloneNotSupportedException e) { throw new AssertionError(e); }
    }
}

Person original = new Person("Ada", new ArrayList<>(List.of("chess")));
Person copy = original.clone();
copy.getHobbies().add("cycling");
System.out.println(original.getHobbies());   // [chess, cycling] -- the original changed
```

The fix is to deep-copy the mutable components explicitly:

```java
@Override
public Person clone() {
    try {
        Person copy = (Person) super.clone();
        copy.hobbies = new ArrayList<>(this.hobbies);   // deep copy
        return copy;
    } catch (CloneNotSupportedException e) { throw new AssertionError(e); }
}
```

Note this cannot work if `hobbies` is `final`, because `clone` assigns after the
object exists. That restriction alone rules out `clone` for well-designed
immutable classes.

**The recommended alternatives:**

```java
// 1. A copy constructor -- explicit, works with final fields, no interface needed
public Person(Person other) {
    this.name = other.name;
    this.hobbies = new ArrayList<>(other.hobbies);
}

// 2. A static factory -- can return a subtype or a cached instance
public static Person copyOf(Person other) { return new Person(other); }

// 3. A record -- immutable, so copying is unnecessary; use a wither
public record Point(int x, int y) {
    public Point withX(int newX) { return new Point(newX, y); }
}

// 4. For collections, the library already provides copies
List<String> copy = new ArrayList<>(original);
List<String> snapshot = List.copyOf(original);
```

| Approach            | Deep copy control | Works with `final` | Type-safe | Verbose |
| ------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------ | --------- | ------- |
| `clone()`           | Manual, awkward   | No                 | With covariant return | Yes |
| Copy constructor    | Explicit          | Yes                | Yes       | No      |
| Static factory      | Explicit          | Yes                | Yes       | No      |
| Serialization round-trip | Deep, automatic | Yes             | Yes       | Slow    |

**Arrays are the one place `clone` is idiomatic**, because arrays have no other
copy syntax and their element type is known:

```java
int[] original = {1, 2, 3};
int[] copy = original.clone();       // conventional and safe for primitives

String[][] grid = {{"a"}, {"b"}};
String[][] shallow = grid.clone();   // still shallow: rows are shared
```

The guidance in *Effective Java* is blunt: provide a copy constructor or copy
factory instead of implementing `Cloneable`. New code should not use it.

> Key Takeaways
> - `Cloneable` is a marker interface that changes `Object.clone()`'s behaviour
>   rather than declaring a method.
> - `Object.clone()` performs a shallow copy and bypasses constructors.
> - Deep copying requires manual field fixes, which cannot work with `final`
>   fields.
> - Prefer a copy constructor or a static copy factory.
> - `array.clone()` is idiomatic for arrays, though still shallow for nested
>   arrays.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement `clone` on a class with a `List` field and demonstrate the
>    shared-state bug, then fix it.
> 2. Rewrite the same class using a copy constructor and compare the two.
> 3. Interview: Why is `Cloneable` considered a broken design? (Hint: name two
>    things it does not do that its name implies.)

#### getClass and Runtime Type Information

`getClass()` returns a `Class` object describing an object's runtime type. That
object is the entry point to reflection, and it also appears in ordinary code in
`equals` implementations and error messages.

```java
Object o = "text";
Class<?> c = o.getClass();

System.out.println(c.getName());          // java.lang.String
System.out.println(c.getSimpleName());    // String
System.out.println(c.getPackageName());   // java.lang
System.out.println(c.isInterface());      // false
System.out.println(c.getSuperclass());    // class java.lang.Object
```

**Three ways to obtain a `Class` object:**

```java
Class<?> a = "text".getClass();              // from an instance
Class<String> b = String.class;              // a class literal, compile-time
Class<?> d = Class.forName("java.lang.String");   // by name, at runtime
```

The class literal `String.class` is typed `Class<String>`, while `getClass()`
returns `Class<? extends X>` because of erasure. `Class.forName` throws
`ClassNotFoundException` and triggers class initialisation.

**Runtime type versus declared type**, which is the distinction that matters
most:

```java
Animal a = new Dog();
System.out.println(a.getClass().getSimpleName());   // Dog -- the ACTUAL class
```

The declared type is `Animal`, but `getClass()` always reports what the object
really is. This is the same information dynamic dispatch uses.

**Name formats differ by type**, which surprises people reading logs:

```java
System.out.println(int.class.getName());           // int
System.out.println(int[].class.getName());         // [I
System.out.println(String[].class.getName());      // [Ljava.lang.String;
System.out.println(new Outer.Inner().getClass().getName());   // Outer$Inner
System.out.println(new Runnable(){public void run(){}}.getClass().getName());
                                                   // Enclosing$1  (anonymous)
```

**Common uses in ordinary code:**

```java
// 1. Strict type checking in equals
@Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
    if (o == null || getClass() != o.getClass()) return false;
    ...
}

// 2. Informative error messages
throw new IllegalArgumentException(
        "Expected a Number but got " + value.getClass().getSimpleName());

// 3. Logger naming, the standard idiom
private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(MyService.class);

// 4. A subclass-aware toString
@Override public String toString() {
    return getClass().getSimpleName() + "[id=" + id + "]";
}
```

**`getClass()` versus `instanceof`**, restated because the choice is
consequential:

```java
Animal a = new Dog();
a instanceof Animal              // true  -- includes subtypes
a.getClass() == Animal.class     // false -- exact match only
a.getClass() == Dog.class        // true
Animal.class.isInstance(a)       // true  -- the reflective form of instanceof
```

For `equals`, the choice determines whether a subclass instance can ever equal a
superclass instance. `getClass()` says no, preserving symmetry at the cost of
substitutability; `instanceof` says maybe, which can break symmetry as shown
earlier.

**Reflection**, which `Class` unlocks, is covered in chapter 10. A brief taste:

```java
Class<?> c = obj.getClass();
for (Method m : c.getDeclaredMethods()) {
    System.out.println(m.getName());
}
Object instance = c.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance();
```

Reflection is how frameworks such as Spring, Jackson, and JUnit operate on
classes they have never seen. It is powerful, slow relative to direct calls, and
bypasses compile-time checking, so it belongs in framework code rather than
application logic.

**`getClass()` is `final`**, so no class can lie about its identity. That
guarantee is what makes it usable in security checks and in `equals`.

> Key Takeaways
> - `getClass()` returns the object's actual runtime class, not its declared
>   type.
> - A `Class` object can also be obtained from a class literal or by name with
>   `Class.forName`.
> - Array and nested class names use special formats such as `[I` and
>   `Outer$Inner`.
> - In `equals`, `getClass()` gives exact matching while `instanceof` accepts
>   subtypes.
> - `getClass()` is `final`, so its answer can be trusted; it is the gateway to
>   reflection.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Print `getName()` and `getSimpleName()` for a primitive, an array, a
>    nested class, and an anonymous class.
> 2. Write two `equals` implementations for one class, one using `getClass()`
>    and one using `instanceof`, and find an input where they disagree.
> 3. Interview: What is the difference between `String.class` and
>    `"x".getClass()` in terms of static type? (Hint: consider erasure.)

<a id="36-composition-and-design-choices"></a>
### 3.6 Composition and Design Choices

Inheritance is one way to reuse code and it is frequently the wrong one. This
section covers the alternative, the failure modes of inheritance, and how to
choose.

#### Has-A versus Is-A Relationships

Two classes can relate in two fundamentally different ways, and picking the
wrong one produces designs that resist every later change.

**Is-a** means the subclass is a specialised kind of the superclass, expressed
with `extends`. **Has-a** means one class contains another as a component,
expressed with a field.

```java
// IS-A: a Manager is a kind of Employee
public class Manager extends Employee {
    private String department;
}

// HAS-A: a Car has an Engine; it is not a kind of engine
public class Car {
    private final Engine engine;                 // composition
    public Car(Engine engine) { this.engine = engine; }
    public void start() { engine.ignite(); }     // delegation
}
```

```text
   IS-A (inheritance)              HAS-A (composition)

       Employee                        Car
           ^                            |
           |  extends                   |  field
       Manager                        Engine

   Manager inherits every             Car chooses which Engine
   Employee member                    capabilities to expose
```

**The substitution test.** Before writing `extends`, check whether the sentence
"every X is a Y" is true *for every use of Y in the program*:

```java
// Passes: every savings account is an account, everywhere
public class SavingsAccount extends Account { }

// Fails: a Stack is not a List -- a List allows insertion at any index,
// which would violate the stack discipline
public class Stack<E> extends ArrayList<E> { }     // Java's actual Stack does
                                                   // this, and it is a known mistake
Stack<Integer> s = new Stack<>();
s.push(1);
s.add(0, 99);        // inherited from List: inserts at the bottom. Nonsense.
```

Java's own `java.util.Stack` extends `Vector` for historical reasons, and the
JDK documentation now recommends `Deque` instead. It is a useful reminder that
the standard library contains inheritance mistakes too.

**The composition alternative:**

```java
public class Stack<E> {
    private final List<E> items = new ArrayList<>();    // HAS-A list

    public void push(E item) { items.add(item); }
    public E pop() {
        if (items.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
        return items.remove(items.size() - 1);
    }
    public boolean isEmpty() { return items.isEmpty(); }
    // No add(int, E). No get(int). The API is exactly the stack operations.
}
```

The composed version exposes only what a stack should support. The inherited
version exposes everything `List` has, including operations that break the
abstraction.

**A practical checklist:**

| Question                                             | Answer suggests |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
| Is every X genuinely a Y in all contexts?             | Inheritance     |
| Would X want to hide or forbid some of Y's methods?   | Composition     |
| Does X need to swap its Y at runtime?                 | Composition     |
| Does X need several Ys of different kinds?            | Composition     |
| Is the relationship "uses", "has", or "is made of"?   | Composition     |
| Is Y's author committed to supporting subclasses?     | Inheritance, cautiously |

**Both relationships can coexist:**

```java
public class ElectricCar extends Car {         // IS-A: a kind of car
    private final Battery battery;             // HAS-A: contains a battery
    private final List<Sensor> sensors;        // HAS-MANY
}
```

A third relationship, "implements", describes a capability and is covered in
chapter 4. `ElectricCar implements Chargeable` says what it can do rather than
what it is or has.

> Key Takeaways
> - `extends` expresses is-a; a field expresses has-a.
> - Use inheritance only when the substitution claim holds in every context.
> - Composition lets the containing class expose exactly the API it wants.
> - `java.util.Stack extends Vector` is a standard-library example of getting
>   this wrong.
> - A class commonly combines inheritance, composition, and interfaces.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Classify each pair as is-a or has-a: Dog/Animal, Car/Engine,
>    Square/Rectangle, Order/LineItem, Manager/Employee.
> 2. Implement a `Stack` twice, once extending `ArrayList` and once containing
>    one, then find an operation that breaks the first.
> 3. Interview: Why is `Stack extends Vector` considered a design mistake?
>    (Hint: what can you do to a Vector that makes no sense for a stack?)

#### Aggregation and Composition

"Has-a" subdivides into two relationships that differ in *lifetime ownership*.
The distinction comes from UML and affects how you construct and dispose of
objects.

**Aggregation** is a weak has-a: the contained object exists independently and
can outlive or be shared by the container.

```java
public class Department {
    private final List<Employee> employees = new ArrayList<>();

    public void add(Employee e) { employees.add(e); }    // received from outside
}

Employee ada = new Employee("Ada");
Department eng = new Department();
eng.add(ada);
// Deleting the department does not delete Ada; she may join another department.
```

**Composition** is a strong has-a: the container owns the part, creates it, and
the part cannot meaningfully exist without the whole.

```java
public class Order {
    private final List<LineItem> items = new ArrayList<>();

    public void addItem(String sku, int qty) {
        items.add(new LineItem(sku, qty));        // created and owned here
    }

    public List<LineItem> getItems() {
        return List.copyOf(items);                // never hand out the originals
    }
}
// A LineItem has no meaning outside its Order; deleting the Order deletes them.
```

```text
   AGGREGATION  (hollow diamond in UML)     COMPOSITION (filled diamond)

   Department <>---- Employee               Order <*>---- LineItem

   - Employee created elsewhere             - LineItem created by Order
   - may belong to several departments      - belongs to exactly one Order
   - survives the department                - dies with the Order
```

| Aspect             | Aggregation                | Composition                   |
| ------------------ | -------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Lifetime           | Independent                | Tied to the container         |
| Creation           | Passed in                  | Created by the container      |
| Sharing            | Can be shared              | Exclusively owned             |
| On container death | Part survives              | Part is destroyed             |
| Typical example    | Department and Employee    | Order and LineItem, House and Room |

**Why it matters in code.** The distinction drives three concrete decisions:

**1. Defensive copying.** Owned parts must not leak; shared parts are expected
to be shared:

```java
public class Order {                      // composition: protect the parts
    public List<LineItem> getItems() { return List.copyOf(items); }
}

public class Department {                 // aggregation: sharing is the point
    public List<Employee> getEmployees() { return Collections.unmodifiableList(employees); }
}
```

**2. Cascading operations.** Deleting an order should delete its line items;
deleting a department should not delete its employees. This maps directly onto
database cascade rules and ORM mappings:

```java
@OneToMany(cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)   // composition
private List<LineItem> items;

@ManyToMany                                                    // aggregation
private List<Employee> employees;
```

**3. Construction.** A composed part is created inside the container, so the
container controls its invariants. An aggregated part arrives already built.

```java
// Composition: the Order decides how a LineItem is made
public void addItem(String sku, int qty) {
    if (qty <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
    items.add(new LineItem(sku, qty));
}

// Aggregation: the Employee was validated by whoever created it
public void add(Employee e) {
    employees.add(Objects.requireNonNull(e));
}
```

**In practice the boundary blurs**, and many teams use "composition" loosely to
mean any has-a relationship, which is how the phrase "favour composition over
inheritance" is normally meant. The ownership distinction still matters whenever
lifecycle, copying, or persistence is involved.

> Key Takeaways
> - Aggregation is a weak has-a where the part exists independently.
> - Composition is a strong has-a where the container owns the part's lifetime.
> - Owned parts should be created internally and never leaked; shared parts are
>   passed in.
> - The distinction drives defensive copying, cascade rules, and construction
>   responsibility.
> - "Composition" is often used loosely to mean any has-a relationship.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Model a `House` with `Room` objects as composition and a `Library` with
>    `Book` objects as aggregation, and justify each choice.
> 2. Write a composed class that creates its parts internally and returns only
>    copies.
> 3. Interview: Should deleting an `Order` delete its `LineItem`s? What about
>    deleting a `Department` and its `Employee`s? (Hint: can the part exist
>    alone?)

#### Favoring Composition Over Inheritance

This is one of the most repeated pieces of object-oriented advice, and it rests
on a specific technical argument rather than mere taste: inheritance couples a
subclass to the *implementation* of its superclass, not just its interface.

**The problem, demonstrated.** A set that counts how many elements have been
added:

```java
public class CountingSet<E> extends HashSet<E> {
    private int addCount;

    @Override public boolean add(E e) {
        addCount++;
        return super.add(e);
    }

    @Override public boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) {
        addCount += c.size();
        return super.addAll(c);
    }

    public int getAddCount() { return addCount; }
}

CountingSet<String> set = new CountingSet<>();
set.addAll(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
System.out.println(set.getAddCount());     // 6, not 3
```

The count is doubled because `HashSet.addAll` internally calls `add` for each
element, and that call dispatches to the override. The subclass depends on an
undocumented implementation detail of its superclass — and that detail could
change in the next JDK release, silently changing the subclass's behaviour.

This is *self-use*, and it makes a superclass's internal call structure part of
its effective API.

**The composition solution.** Wrap rather than extend:

```java
public class CountingSet<E> implements Set<E> {
    private final Set<E> delegate;             // HAS-A set
    private int addCount;

    public CountingSet(Set<E> delegate) { this.delegate = delegate; }

    @Override public boolean add(E e) {
        addCount++;
        return delegate.add(e);                // no self-use: a different object
    }

    @Override public boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) {
        addCount += c.size();
        return delegate.addAll(c);             // delegate's internal calls stay internal
    }

    public int getAddCount() { return addCount; }

    // remaining Set methods delegate straightforwardly
    @Override public int size()               { return delegate.size(); }
    @Override public boolean contains(Object o){ return delegate.contains(o); }
    // ...
}

CountingSet<String> set = new CountingSet<>(new HashSet<>());
set.addAll(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
System.out.println(set.getAddCount());     // 3 -- correct
```

```text
   INHERITANCE                        COMPOSITION

   CountingSet                        CountingSet
     extends HashSet                    holds a Set
        |                                   |
   addAll() calls add()               addAll() calls delegate.addAll()
   which is OVERRIDDEN                delegate's internal add() is its own
        |                                   |
   double counting                     correct counting
```

**The additional benefits of composition:**

| Benefit                | Explanation                                            |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Works with any `Set`   | `new CountingSet<>(new TreeSet<>())` also works         |
| Survives library changes | No dependence on the delegate's internal call structure |
| Runtime flexibility    | The delegate can be swapped or decided by configuration |
| Narrower API           | Expose only the methods that make sense                 |
| Easier testing         | Inject a mock or stub delegate                          |

**The cost** is boilerplate: every interface method must be forwarded. Three
mitigations exist:

```java
// 1. A reusable forwarding class, then extend it (Effective Java's approach)
public class ForwardingSet<E> implements Set<E> {
    private final Set<E> s;
    public ForwardingSet(Set<E> s) { this.s = s; }
    public int size()                 { return s.size(); }
    public boolean add(E e)           { return s.add(e); }
    // ... all methods forwarded once, reusable by many wrappers
}

public class CountingSet<E> extends ForwardingSet<E> { ... }   // only the delta

// 2. IDE generation: "Generate delegate methods" writes them all
// 3. Project Lombok's @Delegate, if the project already uses Lombok
```

**When inheritance is still the right choice:**

- The superclass was explicitly designed and documented for extension, stating
  which methods are self-used.
- You control both classes and they live in the same package or module.
- The is-a relationship genuinely holds in every context.
- You need polymorphic substitution through the superclass type and the
  superclass is abstract.

```java
// Designed for inheritance: abstract, documents its self-use, and the
// extension points are clearly marked
public abstract class AbstractList<E> implements List<E> { ... }
```
