```java
staff.sort(ordering.reversed());                        // whole order flipped
```

| Factory or combinator               | Effect                                  |
| ----------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `Comparator.comparing(fn)`          | Order by an extracted `Comparable` key  |
| `comparingInt/Long/Double(fn)`      | Same, without boxing the key            |
| `thenComparing(fn)`                 | Tie-break with a second key             |
| `reversed()`                        | Invert the whole ordering               |
| `Comparator.naturalOrder()`         | Delegate to `compareTo`                 |
| `Comparator.reverseOrder()`         | Reverse of the natural ordering         |
| `nullsFirst(cmp)` / `nullsLast(cmp)`| Define where `null` elements sort       |

Null handling is a frequent source of `NullPointerException`, and the wrappers
solve it without writing branches:

```java
Comparator<String> safe = Comparator.nullsFirst(Comparator.naturalOrder());
List<String> values = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList("b", null, "a"));
values.sort(safe);                  // [null, a, b]
```

Anywhere a sorted structure is built, a comparator can be supplied in place of
the natural ordering:

```java
staff.sort(byName);                                       // List.sort
Collections.max(staff, bySalary);                         // single extreme
TreeSet<Employee> byPay = new TreeSet<>(bySalary);        // sorted set
TreeMap<Employee, String> map = new TreeMap<>(byName);    // sorted map
```

| Question                         | `Comparable`             | `Comparator`               |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------ | -------------------------- |
| Where does the logic live        | Inside the class         | Outside, in its own object |
| Method                           | `compareTo(T)`           | `compare(T, T)`            |
| How many orderings               | One                      | Unlimited                  |
| Can order classes you don't own  | No                       | Yes                        |
| Package                          | `java.lang`              | `java.util`                |
| Lambda-friendly                  | No, it needs `this`      | Yes, it is a SAM           |

> Key Takeaways
> - `Comparator` externalises ordering so one type can have many orderings.
> - It is a functional interface, so lambdas and method references work
>   directly.
> - `comparing(...).thenComparing(...).reversed()` composes multi-key
>   orderings readably.
> - Use `nullsFirst` or `nullsLast` rather than hand-writing null checks.
> - Prefer `Comparable` for the one obvious ordering and `Comparator` for
>   everything else.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Sort a list of `Book` by author, then by year descending, using
>    `Comparator` combinators.
> 2. Build a `TreeSet` of strings ordered by length then alphabetically.
> 3. Interview: When would you add `Comparable` to a class rather than always
>    passing a `Comparator`? (Hint: is there one ordering everyone would
>    expect?)

#### Iterable and Iterator

The enhanced `for` loop is not magic syntax reserved for arrays and library
collections. It is defined in terms of an interface, so any class that
implements `Iterable` can be used with it. Two interfaces work together:

```java
public interface Iterable<T> {
    Iterator<T> iterator();                    // hands out a fresh cursor
}

public interface Iterator<T> {
    boolean hasNext();                         // is there another element?
    T next();                                  // return it and advance
    default void remove() { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }
}
```

`Iterable` says "I can be traversed". `Iterator` is the cursor that does the
traversal and holds the position. Separating them means several independent
traversals of the same collection can run at once.

```java
public class Playlist implements Iterable<String> {
    private final String[] tracks;

    public Playlist(String... tracks) { this.tracks = tracks; }

    @Override
    public Iterator<String> iterator() {
        return new Iterator<>() {              // anonymous class, see 4.6
            private int index = 0;             // the cursor's own position

            @Override public boolean hasNext() { return index < tracks.length; }
            @Override public String next()     { return tracks[index++]; }
        };
    }
}
```

```java
Playlist playlist = new Playlist("Intro", "Verse", "Chorus");

for (String track : playlist) {        // works because Playlist is Iterable
    System.out.println(track);
}

playlist.forEach(System.out::println); // default method on Iterable
```

The compiler expands the enhanced `for` into exactly this:

```java
Iterator<String> it = playlist.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) {
    String track = it.next();
    System.out.println(track);
}
```

Knowing the expansion explains two things that puzzle beginners. First,
`next()` must throw `NoSuchElementException` when exhausted, and a correct
iterator checks. Second, removing from a collection inside an enhanced `for`
fails, because the loop's hidden iterator detects the structural change:

```java
List<String> items = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b", "c"));

// for (String s : items) { if (s.equals("b")) items.remove(s); }
//     -> ConcurrentModificationException

Iterator<String> it = items.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) {
    if (it.next().equals("b")) it.remove();    // the safe way
}

items.removeIf(s -> s.equals("b"));            // the modern way
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `Iterable` supplies an `Iterator`; the enhanced `for` loop works with any
>   `Iterable`.
> - `Iterator` holds the traversal position, so multiple cursors can coexist.
> - `next()` should throw `NoSuchElementException` past the end.
> - Removing during an enhanced `for` throws `ConcurrentModificationException`;
>   use `Iterator.remove()` or `removeIf`.
> - `Iterable.forEach` is a default method added in Java 8.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Make a `Range` class iterable over the integers from `start` to `end`.
> 2. Write an iterator that returns only the even elements of an array.
> 3. Interview: Why are `Iterable` and `Iterator` separate interfaces rather
>    than one? (Hint: what breaks if you nest two loops over the same object?)

#### AutoCloseable and Resource Contracts

Files, sockets, and database connections hold operating-system resources that
must be released. Releasing them in a `finally` block works but is verbose and
easy to get wrong, especially with several resources or an exception thrown
during cleanup. `AutoCloseable` lets the language do it.

```java
public interface AutoCloseable {
    void close() throws Exception;
}

public interface Closeable extends AutoCloseable {   // java.io
    @Override void close() throws IOException;       // narrower exception
}
```

Any class implementing `AutoCloseable` can be declared in a **try-with-resources
header**, and `close()` runs automatically when the block exits, whether
normally or by exception.

```java
public class Connection implements AutoCloseable {
    private final String name;

    public Connection(String name) {
        this.name = name;
        System.out.println("Opened " + name);
    }

    public void send(String data) { System.out.println(name + " <- " + data); }

    @Override
    public void close() {                 // narrowed: throws nothing at all
        System.out.println("Closed " + name);
    }
}
```

```java
try (Connection primary = new Connection("primary");     // both are closed
     Connection backup  = new Connection("backup")) {    // in REVERSE order
    primary.send("ping");
    throw new RuntimeException("boom");                  // close still runs
} catch (RuntimeException e) {
    System.out.println("Handled: " + e.getMessage());
}
```

Output:

```text
Opened primary
Opened backup
primary <- ping
Closed backup          <- reverse of declaration order
Closed primary
Handled: boom
```

The contract carries three obligations worth knowing:

- `close()` should be **idempotent**: calling it twice must be harmless.
- `close()` should not throw if it can avoid it, because an exception there can
  mask the real failure. Java records the masked one as a *suppressed*
  exception, reachable via `getSuppressed()`.
- Implementations are strongly encouraged to declare a narrower exception type
  than `Exception`, or none at all, so callers are not forced into broad
  `catch` clauses.

Resources declared in the header must be final or effectively final. Since Java
9 an existing effectively final variable can be named directly:

```java
Connection existing = new Connection("existing");
try (existing) {                     // Java 9+: no redundant new variable
    existing.send("data");
}
```

Chapter 5 covers try-with-resources, suppressed exceptions, and cleanup
ordering in full.

> Key Takeaways
> - `AutoCloseable` makes a class usable in try-with-resources, which closes it
>   automatically.
> - Resources close in reverse declaration order, even when the block throws.
> - `Closeable` extends `AutoCloseable` and narrows the exception to
>   `IOException`.
> - Implement `close()` to be idempotent and, ideally, non-throwing.
> - Exceptions thrown from `close()` are suppressed, not lost, and readable via
>   `getSuppressed()`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `Timer` class implementing `AutoCloseable` that prints the elapsed
>    time in `close()`, and use it in try-with-resources.
> 2. Open two of your resources in one header, throw inside the block, and
>    observe the closing order.
> 3. Interview: Why should `close()` avoid throwing? (Hint: two exceptions are
>    in flight at once; which one does the caller need to see?)

#### Serializable and Object Persistence

An object lives in heap memory as a graph of references. To save it to disk or
send it over a network, that graph must be flattened into a byte stream
(**serialisation**) and rebuilt later (**deserialisation**). Java's built-in
mechanism is driven by a marker interface.

```java
import java.io.Serializable;

public class Session implements Serializable {       // no methods to implement
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L; // explicit version stamp

    private String user;
    private int    requestCount;
    private transient String authToken;              // deliberately NOT saved
    private static String appName = "demo";          // static: never saved
}
```

```java
Session session = new Session();

try (ObjectOutputStream out =
             new ObjectOutputStream(new FileOutputStream("session.bin"))) {
    out.writeObject(session);                        // whole reachable graph
}

try (ObjectInputStream in =
             new ObjectInputStream(new FileInputStream("session.bin"))) {
    Session restored = (Session) in.readObject();    // cast: stream is untyped
}
```

Four rules explain most serialisation behaviour:

| Element                     | Serialised?                                   |
| --------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Instance field              | Yes, if its type is also serialisable         |
| `transient` field           | No; restored as `null`, `0`, or `false`       |
| `static` field              | No; it belongs to the class, not the instance |
| Referenced object           | Yes, recursively, the whole reachable graph   |

A field whose type is not serialisable throws `NotSerializableException` at
write time, which is why `transient` exists for caches, threads, streams, and
secrets.

**`serialVersionUID` is the compatibility stamp.** If you omit it, the compiler
derives one from the class structure, and any later edit, even adding a method,
changes it and makes old files unreadable with
`InvalidClassException`. Declaring it explicitly puts you in control.

**Deserialisation bypasses constructors.** The JVM allocates the object and
fills fields directly from the stream, so constructor validation never runs:

```java
public class Age implements Serializable {
    private final int value;

    public Age(int value) {
        if (value < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException();  // NOT run on read
        this.value = value;
    }

    private void readObject(ObjectInputStream in)             // the hook
            throws IOException, ClassNotFoundException {
        in.defaultReadObject();
        if (value < 0) throw new InvalidObjectException("negative age");
    }
}
```

This bypass is also a security concern: deserialising untrusted bytes can
instantiate arbitrary classes on the classpath and has produced serious
vulnerabilities. Modern guidance is to avoid Java serialisation for anything
crossing a trust boundary and to use JSON, Protocol Buffers, or another
explicit format instead. Chapter 10 revisits the mechanism, including
`writeObject`, `Externalizable`, and filtering.

> Key Takeaways
> - `Serializable` is a marker; the JVM supplies the read and write machinery.
> - `transient` and `static` fields are not written to the stream.
> - The entire reachable object graph is serialised, and every referenced type
>   must be serialisable.
> - Declare `serialVersionUID` explicitly or class changes will break existing
>   data.
> - Deserialisation skips constructors, so invariants need `readObject`
>   validation; never deserialise untrusted input.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Serialise an object with one `transient` field to a file, read it back,
>    and print the field's value.
> 2. Serialise a class, add a field, recompile without a `serialVersionUID`,
>    and try to read the old file.
> 3. Interview: Why is deserialising untrusted data dangerous? (Hint: what code
>    runs before you ever see the resulting object?)

<a id="45-enums-and-records"></a>
### 4.5 Enums and Records

Enums and records are specialised class forms that the compiler writes most of
for you: one fixes a type to a known set of instances, the other reduces a data
holder to a single line.

#### Enum Declaration and Constants

Before enums, a fixed set of options was encoded as integer or string
constants. Nothing stopped a caller passing a value outside the set, typos went
unnoticed until runtime, and error messages printed unhelpful numbers.

```java
// The old way: fragile.
public static final int STATUS_NEW = 0;
public static final int STATUS_PAID = 1;

process(7);         // compiles happily; means nothing
```

An `enum` makes the set a type. Only the declared constants exist, the compiler
rejects anything else, and each constant is a real object with a name.

```java
public enum Status {
    NEW, PAID, SHIPPED, CANCELLED       // the complete set of instances
}
```

```java
Status status = Status.PAID;
// Status bad = 7;                      // ERROR: incompatible types
System.out.println(status);             // PAID: toString gives the name
```

Every enum implicitly extends `java.lang.Enum`, which supplies these members:

| Member              | Returns                                          |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `name()`            | The constant's declared identifier as a `String` |
| `ordinal()`         | Its zero-based position in the declaration        |
| `values()`          | An array of all constants, in declaration order   |
| `valueOf(String)`   | The constant with that exact name, or throws      |
| `compareTo(E)`      | Comparison by ordinal (enums are `Comparable`)    |
| `equals` / `hashCode` | Identity-based, and final                       |

```java
for (Status s : Status.values()) {
    System.out.println(s.ordinal() + " -> " + s.name());
}
// 0 -> NEW, 1 -> PAID, 2 -> SHIPPED, 3 -> CANCELLED

Status parsed = Status.valueOf("PAID");        // exact match, case-sensitive
// Status.valueOf("paid");                     // IllegalArgumentException
```

Because the constants are singletons created by the JVM, comparison with `==`
is both safe and preferred; it is null-safe where `equals` is not:

```java
if (status == Status.PAID) { ... }             // idiomatic and null-safe
```

Enums work especially well in `switch`, where the constant names need no
qualification and the compiler can warn about unhandled cases:

```java
String message = switch (status) {             // arrow switch, Java 14+
    case NEW       -> "Awaiting payment";      // no Status. prefix needed
    case PAID      -> "Ready to ship";
    case SHIPPED   -> "On its way";
    case CANCELLED -> "Cancelled";
};                                             // exhaustive: no default needed
```

One caution: `ordinal()` is a position, not an identity. Reordering the
constants silently changes every ordinal, so never persist it or build logic on
it. Store `name()` instead, or an explicit code field as shown in the next
topic.

> Key Takeaways
> - An `enum` defines a fixed, compiler-checked set of named instances.
> - Every enum extends `java.lang.Enum` and gains `name`, `ordinal`, `values`,
>   and `valueOf`.
> - Constants are singletons, so compare them with `==`.
> - A switch over an enum can be exhaustive without a `default` branch.
> - Never persist or depend on `ordinal()`; it changes when constants are
>   reordered.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Define a `Direction` enum with four constants and print each one's name
>    and ordinal.
> 2. Write a switch expression over `Direction` that returns the opposite
>    direction.
> 3. Interview: Why is `==` preferred over `equals` for enum constants? (Hint:
>    how many instances of each constant can exist, and what happens if the
>    reference is null?)

#### Enums with Fields, Constructors, and Methods

An enum constant is a full object, so it can carry data. This turns an enum
from a list of names into a compact, type-safe lookup table: the constant, its
associated values, and the logic over them all live in one place.

```java
public enum Planet {
    // Each constant calls the constructor with its own arguments.
    MERCURY(3.303e+23, 2.4397e6),
    EARTH  (5.976e+24, 6.37814e6),
    MARS   (6.421e+23, 3.3972e6);          // semicolon required before members

    private static final double G = 6.67300E-11;

    private final double mass;             // fields should be final
    private final double radius;

    Planet(double mass, double radius) {   // implicitly private; cannot be public
        this.mass = mass;
        this.radius = radius;
    }

    public double surfaceGravity() {       // ordinary instance method
        return G * mass / (radius * radius);
    }

    public double weightOf(double earthKilos) {
        return earthKilos * surfaceGravity();
    }
}
```

```java
for (Planet p : Planet.values()) {
    System.out.printf("%s: %.2f m/s^2%n", p, p.surfaceGravity());
}
System.out.println(Planet.MARS.weightOf(75));
```

Four rules govern this form:

- The constant list comes first, and a semicolon separates it from the rest of
  the body.
- The constructor is implicitly `private`; declaring it `public` or `protected`
  is a compile error. You cannot write `new Planet(...)`.
- All constants are constructed eagerly, when the enum class is first loaded.
- A constructor cannot access static fields of the enum that are not compile-
  time constants, because those are initialised after the constants.

A very common pattern is an external code plus a reverse lookup map:

```java
public enum HttpStatus {
    OK(200), NOT_FOUND(404), SERVER_ERROR(500);

    private final int code;

    HttpStatus(int code) { this.code = code; }

    public int code() { return code; }

    // Built once, in a static initialiser that runs AFTER the constants.
    private static final Map<Integer, HttpStatus> BY_CODE = new HashMap<>();
    static {
        for (HttpStatus s : values()) BY_CODE.put(s.code, s);
    }

    public static HttpStatus fromCode(int code) {
        HttpStatus found = BY_CODE.get(code);
        if (found == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("code " + code);
        return found;
    }
}
```

```java
System.out.println(HttpStatus.fromCode(404));     // NOT_FOUND
System.out.println(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND.code());  // 404
```

Storing an explicit `code` rather than relying on `ordinal()` is what makes
this safe against reordering and safe to persist.

> Key Takeaways
> - Enum constants may carry fields supplied through constructor arguments.
> - The constant list ends with a semicolon before any fields or methods.
> - Enum constructors are implicitly private and run once per constant at class
>   load.
> - Static members initialise after the constants, so reverse-lookup maps go in
>   a `static` block.
> - Prefer an explicit code field over `ordinal()` for anything stored or
>   transmitted.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `Currency` enum with a symbol and a `format(double)` method.
> 2. Add a static `fromSymbol(String)` lookup backed by a map built in a static
>    initialiser.
> 3. Interview: Why can an enum constructor not be public? (Hint: how many
>    instances of a constant may ever exist?)

#### Constant-Specific Method Bodies

Sometimes each constant needs genuinely different behaviour, not just different
data. The naive approach switches on the constant inside a method, which works
but rots: adding a constant compiles fine and silently falls through to the
default, and the logic drifts away from the constant it belongs to.

```java
// Fragile: add a MODULO constant and this method quietly misbehaves.
public enum BadOperation {
    PLUS, MINUS, TIMES;

    public double apply(double x, double y) {
        switch (this) {
            case PLUS:  return x + y;
            case MINUS: return x - y;
            case TIMES: return x * y;
        }
        throw new AssertionError("unknown op " + this);
    }
}
```

A **constant-specific method body** attaches the implementation to the constant
itself. The enum declares the method `abstract`, and each constant supplies its
own body in braces. Now a new constant that forgets the method will not
compile.

```java
public enum Operation {
    PLUS("+")  { @Override public double apply(double x, double y) { return x + y; } },
    MINUS("-") { @Override public double apply(double x, double y) { return x - y; } },
    TIMES("*") { @Override public double apply(double x, double y) { return x * y; } },
    DIVIDE("/") {
        @Override
        public double apply(double x, double y) {
            if (y == 0) throw new ArithmeticException("divide by zero");
            return x / y;                       // per-constant validation
        }
    };

    private final String symbol;

    Operation(String symbol) { this.symbol = symbol; }

    public abstract double apply(double x, double y);   // every constant must

    @Override public String toString() { return symbol; }
}
```

```java
for (Operation op : Operation.values()) {
    System.out.printf("3 %s 4 = %.1f%n", op, op.apply(3, 4));
}
// 3 + 4 = 7.0, 3 - 4 = -1.0, 3 * 4 = 12.0, 3 / 4 = 0.8
```

Mechanically, each constant with a body becomes an anonymous subclass of the
enum. That explains two facts: an enum with constant bodies cannot be `final`
under the hood, and `getClass()` on such a constant returns something like
`Operation$1` rather than `Operation`.

Constants may also override a concrete method rather than implement an abstract
one, which gives a default plus exceptions:

```java
public enum Level {
    INFO, WARN,
    ERROR { @Override public boolean isFatal() { return true; } };

    public boolean isFatal() { return false; }   // default for INFO and WARN
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Constant-specific bodies attach behaviour to individual enum constants.
> - Declaring the method `abstract` forces every constant to implement it, so
>   new constants cannot be forgotten.
> - Each constant with a body compiles into an anonymous subclass of the enum.
> - Constants may override a concrete method to deviate from a shared default.
> - Prefer this to switching on `this` inside the enum.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `TrafficLight` enum where each constant returns the next light
>    from a constant-specific `next()` method.
> 2. Convert a switch-on-`this` enum method into constant-specific bodies.
> 3. Interview: What breaks if you add a constant to an enum whose method
>    switches on `this`, and how do constant-specific bodies prevent it? (Hint:
>    which error appears at compile time and which at runtime?)

#### Enums Implementing Interfaces

An enum cannot extend a class, because it already extends `java.lang.Enum`. It
can implement any number of interfaces, which is what lets enum constants be
passed wherever the interface is expected.

```java
public interface Calculable {
    double apply(double x, double y);
    default double applyTwice(double x) { return apply(apply(x, x), x); }
}

public enum MathOp implements Calculable {
    ADD { @Override public double apply(double x, double y) { return x + y; } },
    MUL { @Override public double apply(double x, double y) { return x * y; } };
}
```

```java
Calculable op = MathOp.ADD;            // an enum constant used as the interface
System.out.println(op.apply(2, 3));    // 5.0
System.out.println(op.applyTwice(2));  // inherits the interface default

List<Calculable> pipeline = List.of(MathOp.ADD, MathOp.MUL, (x, y) -> x - y);
```

That last line is the point: a lambda and an enum constant are interchangeable
behind the interface. The enum provides a fixed, named, exhaustively
enumerable set of implementations; a lambda provides an ad hoc one.

If the interface is functional, an enum constant can be passed to any API
expecting that function type:

```java
public enum Rounding implements java.util.function.DoubleUnaryOperator {
    FLOOR   { @Override public double applyAsDouble(double v) { return Math.floor(v); } },
    CEILING { @Override public double applyAsDouble(double v) { return Math.ceil(v); } },
    NEAREST { @Override public double applyAsDouble(double v) { return Math.round(v); } };
}

double result = Rounding.NEAREST.applyAsDouble(2.6);       // 3.0
```

This is also the standard way to write a singleton in Java. An enum with one
constant gives serialisation safety, reflection safety, and thread-safe lazy
class-loading initialisation for free:

```java
public enum ConfigRegistry implements Registry {
    INSTANCE;                                     // the single instance

    private final Map<String, String> values = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    @Override public String get(String key)         { return values.get(key); }
    @Override public void put(String key, String v) { values.put(key, v); }
}

ConfigRegistry.INSTANCE.put("env", "prod");
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Enums may implement interfaces but can never extend a class.
> - An interface plus an enum gives a closed, named set of implementations.
> - Enum constants are interchangeable with lambdas behind a functional
>   interface.
> - Interface default methods are inherited by every constant.
> - A single-constant enum is the safest Java singleton idiom.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Define a `Validator` interface and an enum of three named validation rules
>    implementing it.
> 2. Pass an enum constant to a method that takes `Predicate<String>`.
> 3. Interview: Why is a single-constant enum considered the best singleton
>    implementation? (Hint: think about what reflection and deserialisation can
>    do to a private constructor.)

#### EnumSet and EnumMap

`HashSet` and `HashMap` must work for any key type, so they hash, allocate
buckets, and box values. When the keys are enum constants the problem is far
simpler: the set of keys is known, finite, and numbered. `EnumSet` and
`EnumMap` exploit that, giving dramatically better performance and predictable
iteration order.

`EnumSet` represents membership as a **bit vector**. For an enum of 64 or fewer
constants the entire set is one `long`, so operations are single machine
instructions.

```java
public enum Day { MON, TUE, WED, THU, FRI, SAT, SUN }
```

```java
EnumSet<Day> weekend  = EnumSet.of(Day.SAT, Day.SUN);
EnumSet<Day> weekdays = EnumSet.complementOf(weekend);      // everything else
EnumSet<Day> midweek  = EnumSet.range(Day.TUE, Day.THU);    // declaration order
EnumSet<Day> none     = EnumSet.noneOf(Day.class);          // empty, typed
EnumSet<Day> all      = EnumSet.allOf(Day.class);

System.out.println(weekdays);      // [MON, TUE, WED, THU, FRI]
System.out.println(weekend.contains(Day.SAT));   // true, a bit test
```

Note that there is no public constructor; `EnumSet` is created only through its
static factories, which pick a 64-bit or larger implementation for you.

`EnumMap` stores values in a plain **array indexed by ordinal**. No hashing, no
collisions, no `Map.Entry` objects for lookup.

```java
EnumMap<Day, String> schedule = new EnumMap<>(Day.class);  // class is required
schedule.put(Day.WED, "Sprint review");
schedule.put(Day.MON, "Standup");

System.out.println(schedule);     // {MON=Standup, WED=Sprint review}
                                  // iteration follows declaration order
```

The `Day.class` argument is not optional: the map needs the constant list to
size its internal array, and generics are erased at runtime.

| Aspect            | `EnumSet` / `EnumMap`        | `HashSet` / `HashMap`     |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| Internal storage  | Bit vector / ordinal array   | Hash buckets              |
| Lookup cost       | Constant, no hashing         | Constant, with hashing    |
| Memory            | Very compact                 | Larger, per-entry objects |
| Iteration order   | Enum declaration order       | Unspecified               |
| Null keys         | Not permitted                | One null key allowed      |
| Keys accepted     | One enum type only           | Any type                  |

Use them as a flag set, the type-safe replacement for bitmask integers:

```java
public enum Permission { READ, WRITE, EXECUTE, DELETE }

EnumSet<Permission> granted = EnumSet.of(Permission.READ, Permission.WRITE);
granted.add(Permission.EXECUTE);
granted.removeIf(p -> p == Permission.WRITE);

if (granted.contains(Permission.EXECUTE)) { ... }
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `EnumSet` is a bit vector and `EnumMap` an ordinal-indexed array, both far
>   leaner than their hash-based counterparts.
> - Both iterate in enum declaration order.
> - `EnumSet` is created only through static factories such as `of`, `range`,
>   `allOf`, `noneOf`, and `complementOf`.
> - `EnumMap` requires the enum's `Class` object in its constructor.
> - Neither accepts null keys; prefer them to `HashSet` and `HashMap` whenever
>   the key is an enum.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build an `EnumSet<Permission>` for a user and test membership.
> 2. Use `EnumMap<Day, List<String>>` to store tasks per day and print it.
> 3. Interview: Why can `EnumSet` outperform `HashSet` so decisively? (Hint:
>    how many bits does it take to record membership of a 7-constant enum?)

#### Records as Transparent Data Carriers

Many classes exist only to carry a few values together. Written by hand, such a
class is a page of boilerplate: fields, a constructor, accessors, `equals`,
`hashCode`, and `toString`, all mechanically derived from the same list of
components and all of it a place for bugs to hide.

```java
// Roughly 40 lines by hand, all of it derivable.
public final class Point {
    private final int x;
    private final int y;
    public Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
    public int getX() { return x; }
    public int getY() { return y; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { /* ... */ }
    @Override public int hashCode() { /* ... */ }
    @Override public String toString() { /* ... */ }
}
```

A **record** (Java 16 onwards) declares the same thing in one line. The header
lists the components, and the compiler generates the rest.

```java
public record Point(int x, int y) { }
```

```java
Point p = new Point(3, 4);

System.out.println(p.x());                 // 3: accessor is x(), not getX()
System.out.println(p);                     // Point[x=3, y=4]
System.out.println(p.equals(new Point(3, 4)));   // true: value-based equals
```

What the compiler generates:

| Generated member          | Behaviour                                        |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `private final` field     | One per component                                |
| Canonical constructor     | Takes all components in declaration order        |
| Accessor per component    | Named exactly like the component, e.g. `x()`     |
| `equals`                  | Compares every component                         |
| `hashCode`                | Derived from every component                     |
| `toString`                | `Name[c1=v1, c2=v2]`                             |

Records are deliberately restricted, and the restrictions are the point:

- The class is implicitly `final`, so it cannot be extended.
- It cannot extend another class; it already extends `java.lang.Record`.
- It cannot declare additional *instance* fields, only static ones. All state
  is in the header.
- Components are final; a record is shallowly immutable.

Within those limits a record is an ordinary class. It may implement interfaces,
declare static members, add methods, and override the generated ones:

```java
public record Money(String currency, long cents) implements Comparable<Money> {

    public static final Money ZERO = new Money("EUR", 0);   // static is fine

    public Money plus(Money other) {                        // extra method
        if (!currency.equals(other.currency))
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency mismatch");
        return new Money(currency, cents + other.cents);    // returns a new one
    }

    @Override
    public int compareTo(Money other) { return Long.compare(cents, other.cents); }

    @Override
    public String toString() {                              // may be overridden
        return String.format("%.2f %s", cents / 100.0, currency);
    }
}
```

One caveat: immutability is **shallow**. A record holding a `List` still hands
out the same mutable list object, so defensive copying is on you.

```java
public record Team(String name, List<String> members) {
    public Team {                                  // compact constructor, below
        members = List.copyOf(members);            // defensive, unmodifiable
    }
}
```

Records also work with pattern matching, which makes them natural partners for
sealed hierarchies from chapter 3:

```java
Object shape = new Point(1, 2);
if (shape instanceof Point(int x, int y)) {        // record deconstruction
    System.out.println(x + y);                     // 3
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A record declares its state in its header and generates the constructor,
>   accessors, `equals`, `hashCode`, and `toString`.
> - Accessors are named after components, `x()` rather than `getX()`.
> - Records are implicitly final, cannot extend a class, and cannot add
>   instance fields.
> - They may implement interfaces, add methods, and override generated members.
> - Immutability is shallow; copy mutable components defensively.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Convert a hand-written immutable `Book` class into a record and confirm
>    `equals` and `toString` behave.
> 2. Add a derived method and a static factory to that record.
> 3. Interview: When is a record the wrong choice? (Hint: what does a record
>    forbid that an ordinary class allows, regarding state and inheritance?)

#### Compact Constructors and Record Validation

The generated canonical constructor simply assigns each component, which leaves
nowhere to validate or normalise. Rewriting the whole constructor works but
reintroduces the boilerplate a record was meant to remove. The **compact
constructor** solves this: it has no parameter list and no assignments, just
the checks.

```java
public record Fraction(int numerator, int denominator) {

    public Fraction {                         // compact: no parentheses content
        if (denominator == 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("denominator must not be zero");
        }
        int gcd = gcd(Math.abs(numerator), Math.abs(denominator));
        numerator   /= gcd;                   // reassigning the PARAMETER
        denominator /= gcd;                   // normalises the stored value
    }                                         // fields assigned implicitly here

    private static int gcd(int a, int b) { return b == 0 ? a : gcd(b, a % b); }
}
```

```java
Fraction half = new Fraction(2, 4);
System.out.println(half);                 // Fraction[numerator=1, denominator=2]
// new Fraction(1, 0);                    // IllegalArgumentException
```

The mechanism is worth stating precisely, because it is the part people get
wrong: inside a compact constructor you assign to the **parameters**, not the
fields. The compiler appends `this.numerator = numerator;` for every component
at the end of the block. Writing `this.numerator = ...` yourself is a compile
error in a compact constructor.

Null and defensive handling follow the same shape:

```java
public record Order(String id, List<String> items, Instant placedAt) {
    public Order {
        Objects.requireNonNull(id, "id");
        Objects.requireNonNull(placedAt, "placedAt");
        items = items == null ? List.of() : List.copyOf(items);   // normalise
    }
}
```

You may instead write the **canonical constructor** in full when you need
something the compact form cannot express, but then every assignment is yours:

```java
public record Range(int low, int high) {
    public Range(int low, int high) {          // explicit canonical form
        if (low > high) throw new IllegalArgumentException("low > high");
        this.low = low;                        // assignments are REQUIRED here
        this.high = high;
    }
}
```

Additional constructors must delegate to the canonical one, exactly as in an
ordinary class:

```java
public record Money(String currency, long cents) {
    public Money {
        if (cents < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative amount");
    }

    public Money(long cents) {                 // alternative constructor
        this("EUR", cents);                    // MUST delegate with this(...)
    }
}
```

| Form                  | Parameter list | Assignments      | Use when                       |
| --------------------- | -------------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Compact constructor   | Omitted        | Implicit, added by compiler | Validating or normalising |
| Canonical constructor | Full, matching components | Written by hand | Full control needed  |
| Alternative constructor | Any          | Must call `this(...)` | Convenient defaults     |

A closing note on deserialisation: unlike ordinary serialisable classes,
records are deserialised **through the canonical constructor**, so the
validation above does run. That makes records a safer carrier for data crossing
a boundary than a conventional serialisable class.

> Key Takeaways
> - A compact constructor has no parameter list and no field assignments, only
>   validation and normalisation.
> - Inside it you reassign the parameters; the compiler assigns the fields
>   afterwards.
> - Write the full canonical constructor only when the compact form is
>   insufficient, and then assign every field yourself.
> - Alternative constructors must delegate to the canonical one with
>   `this(...)`.
> - Record deserialisation runs the canonical constructor, so validation is not
>   bypassed.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add a compact constructor to a `Temperature` record rejecting values below
>    absolute zero.
> 2. Write a record holding a `List` and make it defensively copy in the
>    compact constructor; prove the original list can no longer affect it.
> 3. Interview: Why is a record safer to deserialise than an ordinary
>    `Serializable` class? (Hint: which code path is used to rebuild the
>    object?)

<a id="46-nested-and-anonymous-types"></a>
### 4.6 Nested and Anonymous Types

A class does not have to live in its own file; Java offers four ways to declare
one inside another, each with a different relationship to the enclosing code.

#### Inner Classes and Enclosing Instances

Some helper types make no sense on their own. A `Node` belongs to its
`LinkedList`; an `Entry` belongs to its `Map`. Putting them in separate
top-level files scatters one concept across the package and forces the helper's
fields to be visible more widely than they should be. Nesting keeps them
together.

Java has two kinds of nested class, and the distinction is entirely about
`static`:

```java
public class Outer {
    private int value = 42;

    static class StaticNested {              // NO link to an Outer instance
        void show() {
            // System.out.println(value);    // ERROR: needs an instance
            System.out.println("independent");
        }
    }

    class Inner {                            // holds a hidden Outer reference
        void show() {
            System.out.println(value);       // reaches Outer's private field
            System.out.println(Outer.this.value);   // the explicit form
        }
    }
}
```

The consequence shows up at creation time. A static nested class is created
like any other; an inner class needs an existing outer instance:

```java
Outer.StaticNested nested = new Outer.StaticNested();      // no Outer needed

Outer outer = new Outer();
Outer.Inner inner = outer.new Inner();                     // odd but correct
```

That `outer.new Inner()` syntax exists because each `Inner` object stores a
hidden reference to its `Outer`, which is what lets it read `value`. The hidden
reference is also the main hazard: an inner class instance keeps its entire
outer object alive in memory, so a long-lived inner instance, say a cached
listener, can pin a large object graph the garbage collector would otherwise
reclaim.

```java
public class LinkedStack<T> {
    private Node<T> top;                      // uses the nested type

    private static class Node<T> {            // static: no outer reference
        final T value;
        Node<T> next;
        Node(T value, Node<T> next) { this.value = value; this.next = next; }
    }

    public void push(T value) { top = new Node<>(value, top); }
}
```

| Aspect                        | Static nested        | Inner (non-static)     |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------- | ---------------------- |
| Reference to enclosing object | No                   | Yes, implicit          |
| Access outer instance fields  | No                   | Yes, including private |
| Instantiated with             | `new Outer.Nested()` | `outer.new Inner()`    |
| Can declare static members    | Yes                  | Yes, since Java 16     |
| Memory implication            | Independent          | Pins the outer object  |
| Default choice                | Yes                  | Only if it needs outer state |

The practical rule: **make a nested class `static` unless it genuinely needs
the enclosing instance.** Most do not, and the static form is cheaper and
safer.

> Key Takeaways
> - Nested classes keep a helper type next to the only code that uses it.
> - A static nested class is independent; an inner class carries a hidden
>   reference to its enclosing instance.
> - Inner classes are created with `outer.new Inner()` and can read the outer
>   object's private members.
> - The hidden reference can prevent garbage collection of the outer object.
> - Default to `static` and drop it only when outer state is required.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write an `Outer` class with both a static nested and an inner class, and
>    instantiate each correctly.
> 2. Access an outer private field from the inner class using `Outer.this`.
> 3. Interview: Why should a nested class usually be static? (Hint: think about
>    what the non-static version silently holds on to.)

#### Local Classes in Method Scope

Occasionally a helper type is needed by exactly one method. A nested class at
class level would advertise it to the whole class; a **local class**, declared
inside the method body, limits it to the block where it is used, just like a
local variable.

```java
public class Validation {

    public List<String> validate(List<String> inputs, int maxLength) {

        class Problem {                       // visible only inside validate
            final String input;
            final String reason;

            Problem(String input, String reason) {
                this.input = input;
                this.reason = reason;
            }

            String describe() {
                // captures maxLength from the enclosing method
                return input + ": " + reason + " (limit " + maxLength + ")";
            }
        }

        List<Problem> problems = new ArrayList<>();
        for (String input : inputs) {
            if (input.isBlank())               problems.add(new Problem(input, "blank"));
            else if (input.length() > maxLength) problems.add(new Problem(input, "too long"));
        }

        return problems.stream().map(Problem::describe).toList();
    }
}
// new Problem("a", "b");      // ERROR outside validate: Problem is out of scope
```

Local classes obey a short set of rules:

- Scope is the enclosing block; the type name is unusable outside it.
- They may not be `public`, `protected`, `private`, or `static`, because access
  modifiers are meaningless for something only one block can see.
- They can use the enclosing method's local variables, but only **effectively
  final** ones (the next topic).
- Declared inside an instance method, they can also reach the enclosing
  object's fields; inside a static method, they cannot.

```java
public class Counter {
    private int total;                        // instance field

    public Runnable makeIncrementer(int step) {
        class Incrementer implements Runnable {
            @Override public void run() {
                total += step;                // outer field + captured local
            }
        }
        return new Incrementer();
    }
}
```

In modern code a local class is comparatively rare: a lambda covers the
single-method case and a record covers the simple data-holder case. Reach for
a local class when the helper needs several methods, its own state, or a name
that makes the code clearer.

```java
// A local record, allowed since Java 16, often replaces a local class.
public List<String> validate(List<String> inputs, int maxLength) {
    record Problem(String input, String reason) { }      // one line
    ...
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A local class is declared inside a method and visible only within that
>   block.
> - It cannot carry access modifiers or be `static`.
> - It captures effectively final local variables and, in instance methods, the
>   enclosing object.
> - Lambdas and local records usually replace them in modern code.
> - Use one when the helper needs multiple methods, its own state, or a
>   descriptive name.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a method that defines a local class implementing `Comparator` and
>    uses it to sort a list.
> 2. Try to declare that local class `public static` and explain both errors.
> 3. Rewrite the same helper as a local record and compare the line counts.

#### Anonymous Inner Classes

When you need a one-off implementation of an interface or a one-off subclass,
naming it adds noise. An **anonymous inner class** declares the class and
creates its only instance in a single expression.

```java
Comparator<String> byLength = new Comparator<String>() {   // no class name
    @Override
    public int compare(String a, String b) {
        return Integer.compare(a.length(), b.length());
    }
};                                                         // semicolon: it is
                                                           // still an expression
```

Read the syntax as two things at once: `new Type(args)` names the supertype,
and the following braces are the body of an unnamed class that implements or
extends it. It works with an interface, where the argument list is always
empty, and with a class, where the arguments go to the superclass constructor.

```java
// From an interface: no constructor arguments possible.
Runnable task = new Runnable() {
    @Override public void run() { System.out.println("running"); }
};

// From a class: arguments are passed to the superclass constructor.
Thread worker = new Thread("worker-1") {       // Thread(String name)
    @Override public void run() { System.out.println(getName()); }
};
```

The most common use is passing behaviour to an API, which is exactly the role
lambdas took over in Java 8:

```java
button.addActionListener(new ActionListener() {              // pre-Java 8
    @Override public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) { save(); }
});

button.addActionListener(e -> save());                       // Java 8+
```

Lambdas do not make anonymous classes obsolete. A lambda only works for a
functional interface, has no state, and cannot be a subclass. An anonymous
class is still required when you need any of these:

| Situation                                    | Lambda | Anonymous class |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------ | --------------- |
| Interface with one abstract method            | Yes    | Yes             |
| Interface with several abstract methods       | No     | Yes             |
| Subclassing a concrete or abstract class      | No     | Yes             |
| Declaring fields to hold state                | No     | Yes             |
| Meaning of `this`                             | Enclosing object | The anonymous instance |

That last row causes real bugs, so it is worth a demonstration:

```java
public class Widget {
    private String name = "widget";

    public void demo() {
        Runnable anonymous = new Runnable() {
            private int runs = 0;                 // anonymous classes may have state
            @Override public void run() {
                runs++;
                // this.name;                     // ERROR: 'this' is the Runnable
                System.out.println(Widget.this.name + " " + runs);
            }
        };

        Runnable lambda = () -> System.out.println(this.name);   // 'this' is Widget
    }
}
```

Anonymous classes are also the mechanism behind two idioms you will encounter:
the iterator returned in 4.4, and the anonymous subclasses the compiler creates
for constant-specific enum bodies in 4.5.

> Key Takeaways
> - An anonymous inner class declares a type and instantiates it in one
>   expression.
> - It may implement an interface or extend a class, passing arguments to the
>   superclass constructor.
> - Unlike a lambda it can hold state, override several methods, and subclass a
>   class.
> - Inside an anonymous class `this` refers to the anonymous instance; inside a
>   lambda it refers to the enclosing object.
> - Prefer a lambda for functional interfaces and an anonymous class for
>   everything else.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Sort a list with an anonymous `Comparator`, then rewrite it as a lambda.
> 2. Create an anonymous subclass of an abstract class that overrides two
>    methods, and explain why a lambda cannot do this.
> 3. Interview: What does `this` refer to inside an anonymous class versus
>    inside a lambda? (Hint: one of them introduces a new scope for `this` and
>    the other does not.)

#### Effectively Final Variable Capture

A local class, anonymous class, or lambda can use local variables from the
method around it. This is called **capture**, and it comes with a restriction
that catches everyone once: the captured variable must be **final or
effectively final**, meaning it is never reassigned after initialisation.

```java
public Runnable make() {
    int count = 0;                 // effectively final: never reassigned
    Runnable r = () -> System.out.println(count);   // capture is allowed
    // count = 1;                  // adding this line breaks the lambda above:
                                   // "local variables referenced from a lambda
                                   //  expression must be final or effectively final"
    return r;
}
```

The reason is lifetime. A local variable lives on the method's stack frame,
which disappears when the method returns. The lambda may outlive it, so Java
does not share the variable; it **copies the value** into the object at
creation time. If the original could still change, the copy and the original
would diverge, and nobody could say which value the lambda should see. Java
avoids the question by forbidding reassignment.

```text
  make() stack frame                  heap
  +----------------+          +---------------------+
  | count = 0      | -- copy->| Runnable object     |
  +----------------+          |   captured count: 0 |
   frame destroyed on return  +---------------------+
                               object survives with its copy
```

Capturing *fields* is different and unrestricted, because a field lives in the
object on the heap and what is captured is the reference to that object:

```java
public class Counter {
    private int total = 0;                     // a FIELD, not a local

    public Runnable incrementer() {
        return () -> total++;                  // legal: fields may be reassigned
    }
}
```

The same loophole explains the standard workaround for needing mutable captured
state: put the value inside an object, and mutate the object rather than the
variable.

```java
// Does not compile:
// int sum = 0;
// list.forEach(n -> sum += n);

int[] sum = {0};                               // the array reference is final
list.forEach(n -> sum[0] += n);                // mutating the contents is fine

AtomicInteger safeSum = new AtomicInteger();   // the thread-safe version
list.forEach(safeSum::addAndGet);

int total = list.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum();  // usually better
```

One more trap: the loop variable of a classic `for` loop is reassigned each
iteration and therefore not effectively final, while the variable of an
enhanced `for` loop is a fresh variable per iteration and is capturable.

```java
List<Runnable> tasks = new ArrayList<>();

// for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) tasks.add(() -> System.out.println(i));  // ERROR

for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    int copy = i;                              // fresh effectively final local
    tasks.add(() -> System.out.println(copy)); // fine
}

for (String s : List.of("a", "b")) {
    tasks.add(() -> System.out.println(s));    // fine: s is effectively final
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Captured local variables must be final or effectively final, meaning never
>   reassigned.
> - The restriction exists because the value is copied when the lambda or inner
>   class is created, while the stack frame is temporary.
> - Instance and static fields can be captured and mutated freely; they live on
>   the heap.
> - Mutable captured state is emulated with a one-element array or an
>   `AtomicInteger`, though a stream reduction is usually cleaner.
> - A classic `for` loop variable is not effectively final; an enhanced `for`
>   variable is.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a lambda that captures a local variable, then reassign the variable
>    and read the error.
> 2. Accumulate a sum inside `forEach` using an `AtomicInteger`, then rewrite
>    it with a stream.
> 3. Interview: Why does Java require effectively final capture when other
>    languages allow full closures over mutable locals? (Hint: where does a
>    local variable live, and how long does it survive?)

#### Choosing Among Nested Type Forms

With five forms available, the choice is usually settled by two questions: how
much of the enclosing context the helper needs, and how widely it should be
visible.

| Form                  | Scope              | Access to enclosing        | Typical use                    |
| --------------------- | ------------------ | -------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Static nested class   | Enclosing class    | Static members only        | Helper types, builders, nodes  |
| Inner class           | Enclosing class    | Full outer instance        | Iterators, views over the outer |
| Local class           | One block          | Effectively final locals   | Multi-method helper for one method |
| Anonymous class       | One expression     | Effectively final locals   | One-off implementation with state |
| Lambda                | One expression     | Effectively final locals   | One-off functional interface   |

A decision sequence that resolves most cases:

```text
  Does it implement a functional interface with no extra state?
        yes -> LAMBDA
        no  v
  Is it needed only in one expression?
        yes -> ANONYMOUS CLASS
        no  v
  Is it needed only inside one method?
        yes -> LOCAL CLASS  (or a local record for pure data)
        no  v
  Does it need the enclosing object's instance state?
        yes -> INNER CLASS
        no  -> STATIC NESTED CLASS
```

Two further guidelines matter in practice. Any nested type that grows past
roughly fifty lines, or that is used by more than its enclosing class, belongs
in its own file: nesting is for helpers, not for hiding significant types.
And a nested type visible in the enclosing class's public API, such as a
returned `Map.Entry`, should be static and public rather than inner, so callers
are not forced to hold an enclosing instance.

```java
public class Grid {

    public record Cell(int row, int column) { }   // public static by default

    private static class Bucket { ... }           // private helper

    private class RowView implements Iterable<Cell> {   // needs Grid's state
        ...
    }

    public Iterable<Cell> row(int index) {
        return new RowView(index);
    }

    public void forEachCell(Consumer<Cell> action) {
        cells.forEach(action);                    // a lambda at the call site
    }
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Choose by context needed and scope wanted: lambda, anonymous, local, inner,
>   static nested, in that order of increasing weight.
> - A static nested class is the default; make it inner only when it needs the
>   outer instance.
> - Local and anonymous forms keep single-use helpers out of the class's
>   namespace.
> - Promote a nested type to its own file once it grows large or gains other
>   users.
> - Nested types appearing in a public API should be static so callers need no
>   enclosing instance.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Given a `Matrix` class needing a `Position` data holder and a row iterator,
>    pick a form for each and justify it.
> 2. Refactor an anonymous `Comparator` into a static nested class and say what
>    you gained and lost.
> 3. Interview: You see a 200-line inner class in a code review. What two
>    questions would you ask about it? (Hint: one is about size and one is
>    about that hidden reference.)

<a id="5-exception-handling-and-robustness"></a>
## 5. Exception Handling and Robustness

Every program meets conditions its normal logic cannot handle: a missing file,
a malformed input, a network that vanishes mid-request. This chapter covers
Java's mechanism for signalling and responding to those conditions, from the
`Throwable` hierarchy and the checked/unchecked divide through to
try-with-resources and the design decisions that separate an API people can
use safely from one that hides its failures. Exception handling is where
robustness is won or lost, because the difference between a program that fails
usefully and one that corrupts data is almost entirely a matter of these
choices.

<a id="51-exception-mechanics"></a>
### 5.1 Exception Mechanics

Before deciding how to handle failures, you need to know what an exception
actually is, what kinds exist, and what the JVM does when one is thrown.

#### Errors versus Exceptions

A method that cannot do its job has to tell its caller. Returning a special
value is the obvious idea, and it is what C does, but it fails in three ways:
the caller can ignore the value silently, a constructor has no return value to
use, and every layer in between must manually forward the failure.

```java
// The return-code approach: every caller must remember to check.
int result = parseAge("abc");
if (result == -1) { /* handle */ }     // nothing forces this line to exist
int doubled = result * 2;              // forgot to check: -2, silently wrong
```

Java uses a separate channel. When something goes wrong, the method **throws**
an object describing the failure, and normal execution stops until some caller
**catches** it. The failure cannot be ignored by accident, because ignoring it
terminates the thread with a printed trace.

Think of a return value as passing a note back to the person who called you,
and an exception as pulling a fire alarm: everyone in the building stops what
they are doing until someone trained to respond takes over.

Java divides these signals into two families with very different intent:

```java
// An Exception: the program did something wrong and could recover.
throw new IllegalArgumentException("age must not be negative");

// An Error: the environment is broken and the program cannot sensibly continue.
// OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError, NoClassDefFoundError
```

```java
public class Depth {
    static int recurse(int n) { return recurse(n + 1); }   // never terminates

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            recurse(0);
        } catch (StackOverflowError e) {        // catchable, but pointless
            System.out.println("caught, but the stack is still exhausted");
        }
    }
}
```

| Aspect             | `Error`                              | `Exception`                    |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------ |
| Signals            | A broken JVM or environment          | A problem in program logic or input |
| Expected to catch  | No                                   | Yes                            |
| Recovery realistic | Almost never                         | Usually                        |
| Typical examples   | `OutOfMemoryError`, `StackOverflowError` | `IOException`, `IllegalArgumentException` |
| Checked by compiler | No                                  | Depends on the subclass        |

`Error` is technically catchable, and that is exactly the trap. Catching
`OutOfMemoryError` gives you a handler that needs memory to run, and catching
`Throwable` at the top of a loop turns a fatal condition into an infinite
retry. The rule is simple: **catch `Exception` subtypes, let `Error` reach the
top.**

> Key Takeaways
> - Exceptions are a separate signalling channel, so failures cannot be ignored
>   by forgetting a return-value check.
> - `Error` means the environment is broken; `Exception` means the program or
>   its input is.
> - Errors are catchable but should not be caught, because the handler cannot
>   fix the condition.
> - `StackOverflowError` and `OutOfMemoryError` are the two you will actually
>   see, and both indicate a bug rather than bad input.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a method that recurses without a base case and observe the
>    `StackOverflowError` it produces.
> 2. Rewrite a method that returns `-1` on failure so it throws an exception
>    instead, and compare how a forgetful caller behaves in each version.
> 3. Interview: Why is catching `Error` almost always wrong? (Hint: ask what
>    resources your catch block itself needs in order to run.)

#### The Throwable Hierarchy

Every throwable thing in Java is an object, and all of them descend from one
class. Knowing the shape of that tree is what lets you predict which `catch`
clauses will fire and which exceptions the compiler will force you to declare.

```text
                          Object
                            |
                        Throwable                 <- the only throwable root
                        /        \
                   Error          Exception
                     |             /        \
        OutOfMemoryError     RuntimeException   IOException
        StackOverflowError        |             FileNotFoundException
        NoClassDefFoundError      |             SQLException
                                  |
                   NullPointerException
                   IllegalArgumentException
                   IndexOutOfBoundsException
                   ArithmeticException
                   ClassCastException

        UNCHECKED: Error + RuntimeException and their subclasses
        CHECKED:   everything else under Exception
```

Only a `Throwable` can appear after `throw` or in a `catch` clause. The
compiler enforces this:

```java
// throw new String("oops");        // ERROR: incompatible types
// catch (Integer e) { }            // ERROR: not a subclass of Throwable
```

`Throwable` itself provides the members every exception inherits:

| Member                       | Purpose                                            |
| ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `getMessage()`               | The human-readable detail text                      |
| `getLocalizedMessage()`      | A localised variant, overridable                    |
| `getCause()`                 | The underlying throwable, or `null`                 |
| `getStackTrace()`            | The call stack as an array of `StackTraceElement`   |
| `printStackTrace()`          | Dumps the trace to `System.err`                     |
| `getSuppressed()`            | Exceptions suppressed by try-with-resources         |
| `addSuppressed(Throwable)`   | Records a suppressed exception                      |

```java
try {
    Files.readString(Path.of("missing.txt"));
} catch (IOException e) {
    System.out.println(e.getClass().getName());   // java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException
    System.out.println(e.getMessage());           // missing.txt
    System.out.println(e.getCause());             // null: nothing underneath
}
```

Because `catch` matches by subtype, position in this tree decides everything. A
`catch (Exception e)` clause catches `IOException` and `NullPointerException`
alike, while `catch (IOException e)` catches neither `RuntimeException` nor
`Error`:

```java
Throwable t = new FileNotFoundException("x");
System.out.println(t instanceof IOException);     // true
System.out.println(t instanceof Exception);       // true
System.out.println(t instanceof RuntimeException);// false
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `Throwable` is the root; only its subclasses can be thrown or caught.
> - `Error` and `Exception` are its two branches, and `RuntimeException` is a
>   branch of `Exception`.
> - Unchecked means `Error`, `RuntimeException`, and their subclasses;
>   everything else under `Exception` is checked.
> - `catch` matches by subtype, so a clause catches the named type and all its
>   descendants.
> - `getMessage`, `getCause`, `getStackTrace`, and `getSuppressed` are
>   available on every throwable.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Print the full ancestry of `FileNotFoundException` by walking
>    `getSuperclass()` from its `Class` object.
> 2. Write `instanceof` checks proving that `ArithmeticException` is unchecked
>    and `SQLException` is checked.
> 3. Interview: Where exactly is the line between checked and unchecked drawn
>    in the hierarchy? (Hint: name the two subtrees that are unchecked.)

#### Checked versus Unchecked Exceptions

Java is unusual in making the compiler participate. For some exceptions it
demands that you either handle them or declare them; for others it says
nothing. The split is a design statement, not a technical one.

A **checked** exception represents a condition a correct program should
anticipate: the file might genuinely be missing, the network might genuinely be
down. The compiler insists the caller acknowledge it, which is the
**handle-or-declare** rule.

```java
// Will not compile: IOException is checked and neither handled nor declared.
public String readConfig(Path path) {
    return Files.readString(path);      // ERROR: unhandled exception IOException
}

// Option 1: handle it here.
public String readConfigOrDefault(Path path) {
    try {
        return Files.readString(path);
    } catch (IOException e) {
        return "";                      // a genuine recovery
    }
}

// Option 2: declare it and let the caller decide.
public String readConfig(Path path) throws IOException {
    return Files.readString(path);
}
```

An **unchecked** exception represents a programming mistake: a null reference,
a bad index, an argument that violates the method's documented contract. The
compiler stays silent because the correct fix is to change the code, not to add
a handler.

```java
public double divide(int a, int b) {
    return a / b;                      // ArithmeticException if b == 0
}                                      // no throws clause needed or wanted

int[] values = new int[3];
// values[5] = 1;                      // ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at runtime
```

| Question                        | Checked                       | Unchecked                     |
| ------------------------------- | ----------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Compiler enforcement            | Handle or declare             | None                          |
| Root types                      | `Exception`, not `RuntimeException` | `RuntimeException`, `Error` |
| Represents                      | An anticipated external failure | A bug in the code           |
| Caller can realistically recover | Usually yes                  | Usually no                    |
| Appears in `throws`             | Required                      | Optional, documentation only  |
| Examples                        | `IOException`, `SQLException`, `ClassNotFoundException` | `NullPointerException`, `IllegalArgumentException`, `IllegalStateException` |

The rule of thumb that has held up best: **if the caller can do something
useful about it, make it checked; if the only sensible response is to fix the
code, make it unchecked.** Section 5.4 returns to this as an API design
decision, including the criticism that checked exceptions do not compose well
with lambdas and streams.

One subtlety worth internalising now: overriding a method may narrow the
checked exceptions it declares, but never widen them, because callers of the
supertype were promised a limited set.

```java
class Base    { void run() throws IOException { } }
class Narrow  extends Base { @Override void run() throws FileNotFoundException { } }  // OK
class NoneAtAll extends Base { @Override void run() { } }                             // OK
// class Wider extends Base { @Override void run() throws Exception { } }             // ERROR
```

Unchecked exceptions are exempt from that rule and may be added freely by an
override.

> Key Takeaways
> - Checked exceptions must be handled or declared; unchecked ones need
>   neither.
> - `RuntimeException` and `Error` and their subclasses are unchecked;
>   everything else under `Exception` is checked.
> - Checked signals an anticipated external failure; unchecked signals a
>   programming bug.
> - An override may narrow or drop declared checked exceptions but never widen
>   them.
> - Unchecked exceptions may be thrown from anywhere without declaration.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a method calling `Files.readString` and make it compile in both
>    ways: once by catching, once by declaring.
> 2. Classify `NumberFormatException`, `InterruptedException`, and
>    `ClassCastException` as checked or unchecked, then verify against the
>    Javadoc.
> 3. Interview: Why can an overriding method not declare a broader checked
>    exception than the method it overrides? (Hint: think about a caller
>    holding a reference of the supertype.)

#### Stack Unwinding and Propagation

When a method throws, the JVM does not simply stop. It searches for a handler,
and the search is what gives exceptions their reach across the call stack.

Each method call pushes a **frame** onto the thread's stack. On a `throw`, the
JVM inspects the current frame for a matching `catch`. If there is none, it
discards that frame, which is called **unwinding**, and repeats with the
caller. This continues until a handler is found or the stack is empty.

```text
  main()                     main()                    main()
    -> process()               -> process()              (handler runs here)
         -> parse()  throws         [discarded]
              X                [discarded]
                            unwinding upward       handler found in process()
```

```java
public class Propagation {

    static int parse(String text) {
        return Integer.parseInt(text);      // throws NumberFormatException
    }

    static int process(String text) {       // no catch here: it just passes up
        System.out.println("before");
        int value = parse(text);
        System.out.println("after");        // NEVER runs when parse throws
        return value;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            process("abc");
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) { // found three frames up
            System.out.println("handled: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
// Output: before / handled: For input string: "abc"
```

Two consequences matter in practice. First, any code after the throwing call in
an unwound frame is skipped entirely, which is why cleanup belongs in `finally`
or try-with-resources rather than on the line after the risky call. Second, a
method need not mention an exception to propagate it; unchecked exceptions
travel upward through any number of frames silently.

If no frame handles it, the thread's default handler prints the trace and the
thread dies. In the `main` thread that ends the program with a non-zero exit
status:

```java
public static void main(String[] args) {
    Integer.parseInt("abc");       // nothing catches it
}
// Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "abc"
//     at java.base/java.lang.Integer.parseInt(Integer.java:652)
//     ...
// Process exits with status 1
```

Unwinding is per thread. An exception in one thread never propagates into
another, which is why an uncaught exception in a worker thread can kill that
worker while the rest of the program continues unaware:

```java
Thread worker = new Thread(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("worker died"); });
worker.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((t, e) ->       // install a handler, or the
        System.out.println(t.getName() + " failed: " + e.getMessage()));
worker.start();
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A throw causes the JVM to search each stack frame outward for a matching
>   `catch`, discarding frames as it goes.
> - Code after the throwing statement in an unwound frame never executes.
> - Exceptions propagate through methods that do not mention them, especially
>   unchecked ones.
> - An unhandled exception terminates the thread and prints a trace; in `main`
>   it ends the program.
> - Unwinding is confined to one thread; use an uncaught exception handler for
>   worker threads.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write three nested methods, throw from the innermost, catch in the
>    outermost, and print a line in each to trace what runs.
> 2. Add a statement after the throwing call in the middle method and confirm
>    it never executes.
> 3. Interview: A method calls something that throws an unchecked exception but
>    declares nothing. How does the caller find out? (Hint: what does the
>    compiler verify, and what does the JVM do at runtime?)

#### Reading and Interpreting Stack Traces

A stack trace is the single most useful diagnostic Java produces, and reading
it well is a learnable skill. It is a snapshot of the call stack at the moment
the exception was constructed, printed innermost first.

```text
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke
        "String.length()" because "name" is null
    at com.example.UserService.validate(UserService.java:42)   <- where it broke
    at com.example.UserService.register(UserService.java:28)   <- who called that
    at com.example.Main.main(Main.java:12)                     <- the entry point
Caused by: java.sql.SQLException: connection refused           <- the root cause
    at com.example.Repository.connect(Repository.java:55)
    ... 3 more                                                 <- repeated frames
```

Read it in four passes:

1. **The exception type** tells you the category of failure.
   `NullPointerException` is a bug; `SQLException` is an environment problem.
2. **The message** carries the specifics. Since Java 14, helpful
   `NullPointerException` messages name the exact expression that was null.
3. **The first frame mentioning your own package** is usually where to look.
   The top frames are often library internals that merely detected the problem.
4. **The last `Caused by` section** is the original failure. Everything above
   it is wrapping, so read a chained trace from the bottom up.

```java
public class TraceDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            level1();
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            e.printStackTrace();                    // the full trace to stderr
            System.out.println("top: " + e.getMessage());
            System.out.println("root: " + rootCause(e).getMessage());

            StackTraceElement origin = e.getStackTrace()[0];   // innermost frame
            System.out.println(origin.getClassName() + "." + origin.getMethodName()
                    + " line " + origin.getLineNumber());
        }
    }

    static Throwable rootCause(Throwable t) {
        while (t.getCause() != null) t = t.getCause();   // walk to the bottom
        return t;
    }

    static void level1() {
        try {
            level2();
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            throw new RuntimeException("level1 failed", e);   // wraps, keeps cause
        }
    }

    static void level2() { throw new IllegalStateException("original problem"); }
}
```

Two artefacts confuse newcomers. `... 23 more` means those frames are identical
to the ones already printed above, and were elided for brevity. And a trace
with no line numbers, showing `(Unknown Source)`, means the class was compiled
without debug information, so you cannot map it back to source lines.

Three habits make traces far more useful:

- Never call `printStackTrace()` in production code; log the throwable through
  your logging framework so it lands with context and a timestamp.
- Never throw away the cause when wrapping, or the bottom of the trace
  disappears.
- Never catch and rethrow a *new* exception without the original as its cause.

> Key Takeaways
> - A stack trace lists frames innermost first, with the failing line at the
>   top.
> - The first frame in your own package is usually the place to investigate.
> - `Caused by` sections read bottom-up: the last one is the original failure.
> - `... N more` means frames identical to those already shown were elided.
> - Log throwables through a logger rather than `printStackTrace`, and always
>   preserve the cause.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Produce a three-level nested exception with causes and read the trace from
>    the bottom up.
> 2. Write a `rootCause(Throwable)` helper and test it on a chained exception.
> 3. Interview: Given a 60-line trace whose top ten frames are all framework
>    classes, where do you start looking? (Hint: which frames did your team
>    actually write?)

<a id="52-handling-and-declaring"></a>
