### 5.2 Handling and Declaring

This subchapter covers the syntax you use every day: catching what you can
handle, declaring what you cannot, and raising exceptions of your own.

#### try, catch, and finally Blocks

The `try` statement marks a region where a failure is anticipated, and attaches
handlers to it. The shape is three-part, though only two parts are ever needed
at once.

```java
try {
    // guarded region: statements that might throw
} catch (SpecificException e) {
    // recovery: runs only if that exception type was thrown
} finally {
    // cleanup: runs no matter how the try block exits
}
```

A `try` needs at least one `catch` or a `finally`, or, since Java 7, a
resource list. A bare `try { }` does not compile.

```java
public static int readCount(Path path) {
    try {
        String text = Files.readString(path);      // may throw IOException
        return Integer.parseInt(text.trim());      // may throw NumberFormatException
    } catch (IOException e) {
        System.out.println("could not read: " + e.getMessage());
        return 0;                                  // a real recovery value
    } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
        System.out.println("not a number: " + e.getMessage());
        return 0;
    }
}
```

Scope matters more than beginners expect: a variable declared inside `try` is
invisible in `catch` and `finally`, because the compiler cannot prove it was
ever assigned.

```java
try {
    String text = Files.readString(path);
} catch (IOException e) {
    // System.out.println(text);      // ERROR: cannot find symbol
}

String text = null;                   // declare outside to share it
try {
    text = Files.readString(path);
} catch (IOException e) {
    System.out.println("value so far: " + text);
}
```

**`finally` always runs.** It executes after a normal exit, after a caught
exception, and even while an uncaught exception is unwinding through the frame.
It is the mechanism that guarantees cleanup:

```java
public static void demo() {
    try {
        System.out.println("try");
        throw new IllegalStateException("boom");
    } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
        System.out.println("catch");
        return;                        // finally still runs BEFORE returning
    } finally {
        System.out.println("finally");
    }
}
// Output: try / catch / finally
```

There are exactly two ways to escape it: `System.exit(...)`, which stops the
JVM outright, and the abrupt death of the thread or the JVM itself.

The dangerous interaction is a `return` or `throw` inside `finally`, which
**discards** whatever the `try` or `catch` was doing. This swallows exceptions
silently and is one of the classic Java bugs:

```java
public static int broken() {
    try {
        throw new IllegalStateException("real problem");
    } finally {
        return 42;              // the exception vanishes; caller sees 42
    }
}
```

Never return or throw from `finally`. Modern compilers and linters warn about
it, and try-with-resources removes most reasons to write a `finally` at all.

> Key Takeaways
> - `try` needs at least one `catch`, a `finally`, or a resource list.
> - Variables declared inside `try` are not visible in `catch` or `finally`.
> - `finally` runs on every exit path, including `return` and an exception
>   propagating through.
> - Only `System.exit` or JVM death skips a `finally` block.
> - Returning or throwing from `finally` discards the original outcome and
>   hides bugs.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a method whose `try` returns a value and whose `finally` prints a
>    line, and determine the order of execution.
> 2. Declare a variable inside `try` and try to read it in `catch`; fix the
>    error.
> 3. Interview: What does a method return if `try` returns 1 and `finally`
>    returns 2? (Hint: which one executes last, and what happens to the first
>    result?)

#### Multi-Catch Blocks

Before Java 7, handling several exception types the same way meant repeating
the handler body or catching something too broad. Both are bad: duplication
drifts, and an overbroad catch swallows unrelated failures.

```java
// The pre-Java 7 problem: identical bodies.
try {
    doWork();
} catch (IOException e) {
    log.error("work failed", e);
    notifyAdmin(e);
} catch (SQLException e) {
    log.error("work failed", e);      // exactly the same, duplicated
    notifyAdmin(e);
}
```

**Multi-catch** lists alternatives separated by `|`:

```java
try {
    doWork();
} catch (IOException | SQLException e) {      // one handler, two types
    log.error("work failed", e);
    notifyAdmin(e);
}
```

Three rules govern it:

- The listed types must not be in a subtype relationship with each other.
  Listing a type and its ancestor is redundant and rejected.
- The parameter is implicitly **final**, so it cannot be reassigned inside the
  block.
- The parameter's static type is the **least upper bound** of the alternatives,
  so only members common to all of them are accessible.

```java
// catch (IOException | FileNotFoundException e) { }
//     ERROR: FileNotFoundException is a subclass of IOException

try {
    doWork();
} catch (IOException | SQLException e) {
    // e = new IOException();          // ERROR: parameter is implicitly final
    System.out.println(e.getMessage());// fine: declared on Throwable
    // e.getSQLState();                // ERROR: only on SQLException
}
```

When the handlers genuinely differ, keep them separate. Multi-catch is for
shared responses, not for shortening code that should branch:

```java
try {
    processFile(path);
} catch (FileNotFoundException e) {
    createDefaultFile(path);                      // a specific recovery
} catch (IOException | SecurityException e) {     // both are unrecoverable here
    throw new ProcessingException("cannot process " + path, e);
}
```

If you need type-specific behaviour inside a multi-catch, the pattern-matching
`instanceof` from chapter 3 keeps it readable, though separate clauses are
usually clearer.

> Key Takeaways
> - Multi-catch handles several exception types with one block, written
>   `catch (A | B e)`.
> - The alternatives may not be related by inheritance.
> - The parameter is implicitly final and typed as the common supertype of the
>   alternatives.
> - Only members declared on that common supertype are accessible.
> - Use it only when the response is genuinely identical for every listed type.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Convert two identical catch blocks into a single multi-catch.
> 2. Try listing `Exception | IOException` in one clause and explain the error.
> 3. Inside a `catch (IOException | SQLException e)` block, attempt to call a
>    method that exists only on `SQLException` and explain why it fails.

#### Catch Ordering and Specificity

Multiple `catch` clauses are tested **top to bottom**, and the first one whose
type matches wins. That makes their order part of the program's meaning, not a
stylistic choice.

Because a clause matches the named type and all its subtypes, a broad clause
placed early absorbs everything below it. The compiler catches the obvious
version of this mistake:

```java
try {
    readFile();
} catch (Exception e) {                      // catches everything
    handle(e);
} catch (IOException e) {                    // ERROR: already caught above
    handleIo(e);                             //        unreachable code
}
```

Ordering must therefore run **most specific first**:

```java
try {
    readFile();
} catch (FileNotFoundException e) {          // most specific subtype
    createDefault();
} catch (IOException e) {                    // its parent
    log.warn("io failure", e);
} catch (Exception e) {                      // the broad safety net, last
    log.error("unexpected", e);
}
```

```text
  throw FileNotFoundException
        |
        v
  catch (FileNotFoundException)  -> MATCH, this block runs, search stops
  catch (IOException)            -> never consulted
  catch (Exception)              -> never consulted
```

Note that the compiler only rejects the unreachable case for *related* types.
Unrelated clauses can be written in any order and the compiler says nothing,
which is why the specificity habit matters even when it is not enforced:

```java
try {
    work();
} catch (SQLException e) {
    handleSql(e);                     // unrelated to IOException
} catch (IOException e) {
    handleIo(e);                      // order between these two is irrelevant
}
```

Two practical guidelines follow. A catch-all `catch (Exception e)` is
acceptable as a last clause at an application boundary, such as a request
handler or `main`, where the alternative is a crashed thread. It is a mistake
deep in business logic, where it hides bugs that should surface. And never
write `catch (Throwable t)` unless you intend to catch `OutOfMemoryError` too,
which you almost certainly do not.

> Key Takeaways
> - Catch clauses are evaluated in order, and the first matching type wins.
> - A clause matches the declared type and every subtype of it.
> - Placing a supertype before its subtype is a compile error for unreachable
>   code.
> - Order from most specific to most general.
> - Reserve `catch (Exception e)` for boundaries, and avoid
>   `catch (Throwable t)` entirely.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a try with three ordered catch clauses and trigger each one in turn.
> 2. Put `catch (Exception e)` first and read the compiler error for the clause
>    below it.
> 3. Interview: Why does the compiler reject one ordering but stay silent about
>    two unrelated clauses? (Hint: what can it prove about reachability in each
>    case?)

#### The throws Clause

Not every method should handle its own failures. A low-level file reader has no
idea whether a missing file means "use a default", "prompt the user", or "abort
the deployment". Only the caller knows. The `throws` clause is how a method
declines to decide and pushes the choice upward.

```java
public String readConfig(Path path) throws IOException {   // I might fail this way
    return Files.readString(path);                         // no try needed here
}
```

The clause becomes part of the method's published contract. Callers must then
handle or declare it themselves, so the obligation travels up the call chain
until someone takes responsibility.

```java
public void startup() throws IOException {     // passing it further up
    String config = readConfig(Path.of("app.conf"));
}

public static void main(String[] args) {       // main may declare it too
    try {
        new App().startup();
    } catch (IOException e) {                  // the buck stops here
        System.err.println("cannot start: " + e.getMessage());
        System.exit(1);
    }
}
```

A method may declare several exceptions, and may declare unchecked ones purely
as documentation:

```java
public void transfer(Account from, Account to, BigDecimal amount)
        throws InsufficientFundsException, AccountFrozenException {
    ...
}

/**
 * @throws IllegalArgumentException if amount is negative
 */
public void withdraw(BigDecimal amount) {      // unchecked: not in the clause
    if (amount.signum() < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative");
}
```

Declaring unchecked exceptions in `throws` is legal but unconventional; the
Javadoc `@throws` tag is the usual place for them.

| Element              | Keyword  | Where it appears        | Meaning                     |
| -------------------- | -------- | ----------------------- | --------------------------- |
| Declaration          | `throws` | Method signature        | This method may propagate it |
| Statement            | `throw`  | Method body             | Raise this exception now     |

That one-letter difference is a perennial source of confusion, and the table is
worth memorising.

Two design cautions. Declaring `throws Exception` is almost always wrong: it
tells the caller nothing and forces them into an overbroad catch. And a long
`throws` list often signals that a method is doing too much, or that the
exceptions should be translated into one meaningful type, which section 5.4
covers.

> Key Takeaways
> - `throws` declares that a method may propagate an exception instead of
>   handling it.
> - Checked exceptions must be declared; unchecked ones may be, for
>   documentation.
> - The obligation propagates to every caller until one handles it.
> - `throws` declares, `throw` raises; the two are different constructs.
> - Avoid `throws Exception`, which destroys the information the clause exists
>   to carry.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a three-method chain that declares `IOException` all the way up to
>    `main`, then handle it there.
> 2. Add an unchecked exception to a `throws` clause and confirm callers are
>    not forced to handle it.
> 3. Interview: What is wrong with `public void process() throws Exception`?
>    (Hint: what must every caller now write, and what have they learned about
>    the failure?)

#### Throwing Exceptions Explicitly

So far the exceptions came from the library. Your own code raises them with
`throw`, which takes a single `Throwable` instance and immediately begins
unwinding.

```java
throw new IllegalArgumentException("radius must be positive: " + radius);
//  ^      ^                        ^
//  |      |                        the detail message, for the trace
//  |      an instance: the exception object is created here
//  the statement: unwinding starts immediately
```

The overwhelmingly common case is **validating arguments and state** at the top
of a method, so a bad call fails at the boundary rather than corrupting data
deeper in:

```java
public class BankAccount {
    private BigDecimal balance;
    private boolean closed;

    public void withdraw(BigDecimal amount) {
        if (amount == null) {
            throw new NullPointerException("amount must not be null");
        }
        if (amount.signum() <= 0) {                      // bad ARGUMENT
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive: " + amount);
        }
        if (closed) {                                    // bad STATE
            throw new IllegalStateException("account is closed");
        }
        if (amount.compareTo(balance) > 0) {             // domain rule
            throw new InsufficientFundsException(balance, amount);
        }
        balance = balance.subtract(amount);              // only now, mutate
    }
}
```

Note the ordering: every check happens before any field is modified, so a
rejected call leaves the object exactly as it was. That property is called
**failure atomicity** and it is what makes exceptions safe to recover from.

Choosing the right standard type is most of the skill:

| Situation                                   | Throw                              |
| ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| An argument is invalid                      | `IllegalArgumentException`         |
| An argument is null and must not be         | `NullPointerException`             |
| The object is in the wrong state for this call | `IllegalStateException`         |
| An index is out of range                    | `IndexOutOfBoundsException`        |
| The operation is not supported at all       | `UnsupportedOperationException`    |
| A domain rule was violated                  | A custom exception (see 5.4)       |

The `java.util.Objects` helpers make null and range checks one-liners that
throw the right type with a sensible message:

```java
this.name = Objects.requireNonNull(name, "name");             // NPE with message
Objects.checkIndex(index, size);                              // IndexOutOfBounds
this.age  = Objects.requireNonNullElse(age, 0);               // with a fallback
```

Two habits separate useful exceptions from useless ones. Put the offending
**value** in the message, not just the rule: `"amount must be positive: -5"`
tells you what happened, `"invalid amount"` does not. And throw as early as
possible, because the stack trace then points at the caller who made the
mistake rather than at some distant consequence.

> Key Takeaways
> - `throw` raises an exception instance and starts unwinding immediately.
> - Validate arguments and state before mutating anything, preserving failure
>   atomicity.
> - Use `IllegalArgumentException` for bad arguments and `IllegalStateException`
>   for a bad receiver state.
> - Include the offending value in the message, not just the violated rule.
> - `Objects.requireNonNull` and `Objects.checkIndex` throw the conventional
>   types with good messages.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add argument validation to a `Rectangle` constructor that rejects
>    non-positive dimensions with informative messages.
> 2. Write a `Stack` class whose `pop()` throws `IllegalStateException` when
>    empty, and test both paths.
> 3. Interview: When would you choose `IllegalStateException` over
>    `IllegalArgumentException`? (Hint: is the problem with what was passed in,
>    or with the object being called?)

#### Rethrowing and Exception Chaining

A layer often needs to react to a failure without being the right place to
resolve it: log it, add context, convert it into the vocabulary of its own
abstraction, then pass it on. Java offers three ways to do that, and choosing
wrongly destroys diagnostic information.

**Rethrow the same exception** when you only wanted a side effect:

```java
try {
    repository.save(order);
} catch (SQLException e) {
    metrics.increment("save.failure");     // react
    throw e;                               // then let it continue upward
}
```

**Wrap it in a new exception** when the caller should not know about the lower
layer's types. The original must be passed as the **cause**, which is what
chaining means:

```java
try {
    repository.save(order);
} catch (SQLException e) {
    throw new OrderPersistenceException("could not save order " + order.id(), e);
    //                                                                       ^
    //            the cause: keeps the entire original trace attached
}
```

The two-argument constructor is the standard shape, inherited from
`Throwable(String, Throwable)`. Without it, the trace stops at your wrapper and
the real reason is gone forever:

```java
// Destroys the evidence. Never do this.
catch (SQLException e) {
    throw new OrderPersistenceException("could not save order");   // cause lost
}
```

A chained trace prints both halves, root cause last:

```text
OrderPersistenceException: could not save order 1042
    at com.example.OrderService.save(OrderService.java:31)
    at com.example.Api.handle(Api.java:18)
Caused by: java.sql.SQLException: connection refused
    at com.example.Repository.save(Repository.java:55)
    ... 2 more
```

For exceptions you write yourself, provide the chaining constructors so callers
can use them:

```java
public class OrderPersistenceException extends RuntimeException {
    public OrderPersistenceException(String message)                  { super(message); }
    public OrderPersistenceException(String message, Throwable cause) { super(message, cause); }
}
```

If a class was written without them, `initCause` retrofits the link once:

```java
SomeLegacyException e = new SomeLegacyException("failed");
e.initCause(original);        // allowed exactly once, and only if cause is null
throw e;
```

A final refinement: since Java 7, **precise rethrow** lets a broad catch
declare the narrow types actually possible, so the method signature stays
honest.

```java
public void run() throws IOException, SQLException {   // not "throws Exception"
    try {
        doWork();                     // declares IOException and SQLException
    } catch (Exception e) {           // broad catch...
        log.error("failed", e);
        throw e;                      // ...but the compiler knows the real set
    }
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Rethrow the same exception when you only needed a side effect such as
>   logging or metrics.
> - Wrap when the caller should not depend on a lower layer's exception types.
> - Always pass the original as the cause; a wrapper without a cause deletes
>   the real trace.
> - Give custom exceptions both a message constructor and a message-plus-cause
>   constructor.
> - Precise rethrow lets a `catch (Exception e)` block still declare only the
>   specific checked types possible.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Catch a `NumberFormatException` and rethrow it wrapped in a custom
>    exception with the cause attached; print the full trace.
> 2. Repeat without passing the cause and compare what the trace tells you.
> 3. Interview: Why is a wrapper exception without a cause considered harmful?
>    (Hint: what does the person debugging at 3am lose?)

<a id="53-resource-management"></a>
### 5.3 Resource Management

Exceptions interact badly with manual cleanup, so Java provides a construct
that closes resources automatically and correctly.

#### try-with-resources Syntax

A resource is anything holding an operating-system handle: a file, a socket, a
database connection. The operating system grants a limited number of these, so
failing to release one is a slow leak that eventually takes the process down.

Done by hand, correct cleanup is surprisingly hard. Here is the fully correct
pre-Java 7 version for a single resource:

```java
BufferedReader reader = null;
try {
    reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("data.txt"));
    return reader.readLine();
} finally {
    if (reader != null) {          // the constructor may have thrown
        try {
            reader.close();        // close itself throws IOException
        } catch (IOException ignored) {
            // and an exception here would mask the real one
        }
    }
}
```

Six lines of ceremony for one resource, and it gets worse with two. **try-with-
resources** reduces it to a declaration in the `try` header:

```java
try (BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("data.txt"))) {
    return reader.readLine();
}                                  // close() is called automatically, always
```

Any type implementing `AutoCloseable`, introduced in 4.4, may be declared
there. Several resources are separated by semicolons, and they close in
**reverse order**, which matches how dependencies are usually layered:

```java
try (FileInputStream in  = new FileInputStream("in.txt");
     FileOutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("out.txt")) {   // opened second
    in.transferTo(out);
}                                  // out closes FIRST, then in
```

The construct still accepts `catch` and `finally`, and the closing happens
**before** either runs, so a handler sees an already-released resource:

```java
try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection()) {
    conn.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = 0");
} catch (SQLException e) {         // conn is already closed by this point
    log.error("update failed", e);
} finally {
    log.info("attempt complete");
}
```

```text
  enter try  ->  open A  ->  open B  ->  run body
                                            |
                        +-------------------+------------------+
                        | normal exit                exception |
                        v                                      v
                    close B, close A                   close B, close A
                        |                                      |
                        v                                      v
                    finally                              catch, then finally
```

Resources must be final or effectively final. Since Java 9 an existing variable
can be listed directly, which is useful when the resource was created
elsewhere:

```java
BufferedReader reader = openReader();     // effectively final
try (reader) {                            // Java 9+: no redundant declaration
    process(reader);
}
```

One caveat: a resource that is `null` at the point of closing is skipped
silently, but a `null` in the header does not cause an error, so guard where
the value may legitimately be absent.

> Key Takeaways
> - try-with-resources closes every declared resource automatically, on both
>   normal and exceptional exit.
> - Resources must implement `AutoCloseable` and are declared in the `try`
>   header, separated by semicolons.
> - They close in reverse declaration order, before any `catch` or `finally`
>   runs.
> - A resource variable must be final or effectively final; Java 9 allows
>   naming an existing one.
> - It replaces the error-prone null-check-and-nested-try `finally` idiom
>   entirely.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Rewrite a manual `finally`-based file read as try-with-resources.
> 2. Open two resources in one header, throw inside the body, and print
>    messages proving the closing order.
> 3. Interview: Why does try-with-resources close resources before running the
>    `catch` block? (Hint: what state should the handler be able to assume?)

#### Implementing AutoCloseable

Your own classes can participate. Implementing `AutoCloseable` is what makes a
type usable in a try-with-resources header, and it is worth doing for anything
that acquires something needing release: a lock, a connection, a temporary
file, even a timer.

```java
public interface AutoCloseable {
    void close() throws Exception;      // the only method
}
```

The single method is all the compiler needs. Declaring a narrower exception, or
none at all, is a kindness to callers, since the `try` statement propagates
whatever `close` declares:

```java
public class ManagedConnection implements AutoCloseable {
    private final String endpoint;
    private boolean open = true;

    public ManagedConnection(String endpoint) {
        this.endpoint = endpoint;
        System.out.println("opened " + endpoint);
    }

    public void send(String data) {
        if (!open) throw new IllegalStateException("connection is closed");
        System.out.println(endpoint + " <- " + data);
    }

    @Override
    public void close() {               // narrowed: throws nothing at all
        if (!open) return;              // IDEMPOTENT: safe to call twice
        open = false;
        System.out.println("closed " + endpoint);
    }
}
```

```java
try (ManagedConnection conn = new ManagedConnection("db-1")) {
    conn.send("SELECT 1");
}
// opened db-1 / db-1 <- SELECT 1 / closed db-1
```

Three obligations come with the interface, and the first is the one most often
missed:

- **Be idempotent.** `close()` may be called more than once, so a second call
  must be harmless. The `open` guard above is the standard shape.
- **Avoid throwing.** An exception from `close` competes with whatever the body
  was already throwing. If cleanup can genuinely fail, consider logging instead
  of propagating.
- **Release everything, even on failure.** If `close` releases several things,
  a failure releasing the first must not skip the rest.

```java
@Override
public void close() {
    try {
        flushBuffers();
    } finally {
        releaseHandle();       // runs even if flushBuffers() threw
    }
}
```

`java.io.Closeable` is the older, narrower relative: it extends `AutoCloseable`
and restricts the exception to `IOException`. Implement `Closeable` for I/O
types and `AutoCloseable` for everything else.

| Interface       | Package     | `close()` throws | Idempotence           |
| --------------- | ----------- | ---------------- | --------------------- |
| `AutoCloseable` | `java.lang` | `Exception`      | Strongly recommended  |
| `Closeable`     | `java.io`   | `IOException`    | Required by contract  |

A pattern worth knowing is the **scoped action**, where `close` performs the
end of an operation rather than releasing a handle:

```java
public class Timed implements AutoCloseable {
    private final String label;
    private final long start = System.nanoTime();

    public Timed(String label) { this.label = label; }

    @Override
    public void close() {
        System.out.printf("%s took %.2f ms%n", label,
                          (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000.0);
    }
}

try (Timed t = new Timed("import")) {     // the timer stops automatically
    runImport();
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Implementing `AutoCloseable` makes any class usable in try-with-resources.
> - Make `close()` idempotent, because it may be invoked more than once.
> - Narrow or remove the declared exception so callers are not forced into
>   broad handling.
> - Release every held resource in `close`, using `finally` if the cleanup
>   itself can fail.
> - `Closeable` is the I/O-specific subtype restricted to `IOException`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `TempFile` class that deletes its file in `close()` and use it in
>    try-with-resources.
> 2. Call `close()` twice on your class directly and make sure nothing breaks.
> 3. Interview: Why should `close()` declare a narrower exception than
>    `Exception`? (Hint: what is every caller of your try block forced to write
>    otherwise?)

#### Suppressed Exceptions

Two failures can happen in one try statement: the body throws, and then
`close()` throws while cleaning up. Only one exception can propagate, so
something must give way. The question is which.

The hand-written `finally` idiom gets this exactly wrong. An exception from
`close` replaces the original, and the real failure disappears:

```java
BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("data.txt"));
try {
    throw new IllegalStateException("the REAL problem");
} finally {
    reader.close();          // if this throws, the IllegalStateException is LOST
}
```

try-with-resources inverts the priority. The **body's exception wins** and
propagates, while the exception from `close` is attached to it as a
**suppressed** exception rather than discarded:

```java
public class Failing implements AutoCloseable {
    @Override
    public void close() { throw new IllegalStateException("close failed"); }
}
```

```java
try (Failing f = new Failing()) {
    throw new RuntimeException("body failed");
} catch (RuntimeException e) {
    System.out.println("primary:    " + e.getMessage());        // body failed
    for (Throwable s : e.getSuppressed()) {                     // the others
        System.out.println("suppressed: " + s.getMessage());    // close failed
    }
}
```

Printed, the trace shows both:

```text
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.RuntimeException: body failed
    at com.example.Demo.main(Demo.java:5)
    Suppressed: java.lang.IllegalStateException: close failed
        at com.example.Failing.close(Failing.java:3)
        at com.example.Demo.main(Demo.java:4)
```

The priority ordering is worth stating plainly:

| Body throws | `close()` throws | Propagates      | Suppressed            |
| ----------- | ---------------- | --------------- | --------------------- |
| No          | No               | Nothing         | Nothing               |
| Yes         | No               | Body exception  | Nothing               |
| No          | Yes              | Close exception | Nothing               |
| Yes         | Yes              | Body exception  | The close exception   |

With several resources, every failing `close` is suppressed onto the same
primary exception, so `getSuppressed()` can return more than one element.

You can record a suppressed exception manually with `addSuppressed`, which is
occasionally useful when writing cleanup logic by hand:

```java
RuntimeException primary = new RuntimeException("primary failure");
primary.addSuppressed(new IllegalStateException("cleanup also failed"));
throw primary;
```

The practical lesson: when debugging, read the `Suppressed:` lines. They often
explain why the primary failure happened, particularly with connections and
transactions.

> Key Takeaways
> - When both the body and `close()` throw, the body's exception propagates.
> - The exception from `close` is attached as a suppressed exception, not
>   discarded.
> - Retrieve them with `getSuppressed()`, which returns an array because
>   several resources may fail.
> - A hand-written `finally` loses the original exception instead; this is the
>   main reason to prefer try-with-resources.
> - `addSuppressed` lets you record secondary failures in your own cleanup
>   code.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a resource whose `close()` throws, throw from the body too, and
>    print both the primary and the suppressed exception.
> 2. Do the same with two failing resources and count the suppressed entries.
> 3. Interview: Why does the body's exception take priority over the one from
>    `close()`? (Hint: which of the two tells you what the program was
>    actually trying to do?)

#### Resource Leaks and Cleanup Pitfalls

A resource leak is not dramatic. Nothing fails at the moment of the leak; the
program simply uses one more handle than it returns, and the failure appears
hours later as `Too many open files` or an exhausted connection pool, far from
the code responsible.

The pitfalls below cause most of them.

**Forgetting to close at all.** The oldest bug, and the reason
try-with-resources exists.

```java
// Leak: nothing closes this reader, especially if readLine() throws.
BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(path));
String line = reader.readLine();
```

**Closing inside `try` instead of `finally`.** If the body throws, the close
line is skipped by unwinding.

```java
// Leak on any exception before close().
Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection();
try {
    conn.execute(sql);       // if this throws...
    conn.close();            // ...this never runs
} catch (SQLException e) { log.error("failed", e); }
```

**Nested constructors in one resource declaration.** This one is subtle and
catches experienced developers. If the outer constructor throws, the inner
resource was already created and is now unreachable:

```java
// If the BufferedReader constructor fails, the FileReader leaks.
try (BufferedReader r = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(path))) { ... }

// Safe: each resource is declared separately, so each is tracked.
try (FileReader fr = new FileReader(path);
     BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(fr)) { ... }
```

In practice the wrapping case is low risk, because `BufferedReader`'s
constructor does little, but the separate-declaration form is free insurance
and is the habit worth having.

**Unclosed streams from the NIO API.** `Files.lines`, `Files.list`, and
`Files.walk` all return streams backed by an open file handle. Unlike most
streams, these must be closed.

```java
// Leak: the underlying file handle stays open.
Files.lines(path).forEach(System.out::println);

// Correct: the stream is a resource.
try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(path)) {
    lines.forEach(System.out::println);
}
```

**Loops that open without closing.** A leak inside a loop exhausts handles
quickly, so put the resource inside the loop body:

```java
for (Path path : paths) {
    try (BufferedReader reader = Files.newBufferedReader(path)) {   // per file
        process(reader);
    }
}
```

| Pitfall                            | Fix                                        |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| No cleanup at all                  | try-with-resources                         |
| `close()` inside the `try` body    | Move it to the resource header             |
| Nested constructors in one header  | Declare each resource separately           |
| `Files.lines` / `walk` / `list`    | Treat the returned stream as a resource    |
| Opening inside a loop              | Put the try-with-resources inside the loop |
| Returning an open resource         | Document it and make the caller close it   |

A last note on `finalize()`: it was the old escape hatch for forgotten cleanup,
it never ran reliably, and it is deprecated for removal. Never use it as a
safety net. If a class holds a resource, the contract is that the caller closes
it, and try-with-resources is how they do so.

> Key Takeaways
> - Leaks surface far from their cause, as exhausted file handles or connection
>   pools.
> - Any resource acquired outside a try-with-resources header is a leak waiting
>   for an exception.
> - Declare wrapped resources separately so each one is tracked independently.
> - Streams from `Files.lines`, `Files.list`, and `Files.walk` hold file
>   handles and must be closed.
> - Never rely on `finalize()`; it is unreliable and deprecated for removal.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Find the leak in a method that calls `close()` as the last statement of
>    its `try` block, and fix it.
> 2. Rewrite `Files.lines(path).count()` so the file handle is released.
> 3. Interview: Why is a resource leak harder to diagnose than a
>    `NullPointerException`? (Hint: compare where the symptom appears to where
>    the cause is.)

<a id="54-designing-exception-strategies"></a>
### 5.4 Designing Exception Strategies

Syntax is the easy half. This subchapter is about the decisions that make
exceptions useful to the people who call your code and to the people who debug
it later.

#### Creating Custom Exception Classes

The standard exceptions cover generic problems: a bad argument, a bad index, a
bad state. They say nothing about your domain. When a transfer fails because
the balance is too low, `IllegalArgumentException` loses the two facts a caller
needs, which are how much was available and how much was requested.

A custom exception is an ordinary class that extends an existing throwable,
carries domain-specific fields, and can be caught by name.

```java
public class InsufficientFundsException extends RuntimeException {

    private final BigDecimal available;          // domain data, not just a string
    private final BigDecimal requested;

    public InsufficientFundsException(BigDecimal available, BigDecimal requested) {
        super(String.format("insufficient funds: available %s, requested %s",
                            available, requested));   // a useful default message
        this.available = available;
        this.requested = requested;
    }

    public BigDecimal available()  { return available; }
    public BigDecimal requested()  { return requested; }
    public BigDecimal shortfall()  { return requested.subtract(available); }
}
```

The payoff is at the call site, where the handler can act on the data rather
than parse a message:

```java
try {
    account.withdraw(amount);
} catch (InsufficientFundsException e) {
    offerOverdraft(e.shortfall());              // precise, typed recovery
}
```

Choosing the parent class is the first decision. Extend `RuntimeException` for
unchecked and `Exception` for checked, following the guidance in the next
topic. Do not extend `Error`, and do not extend `Throwable` directly.

```java
public class ConfigurationException extends Exception {        // checked
    public ConfigurationException(String message)                  { super(message); }
    public ConfigurationException(String message, Throwable cause) { super(message, cause); }
}
```

Provide the conventional constructors. At minimum, a message constructor and a
message-plus-cause constructor, so callers can chain properly as described in
5.2:

| Constructor                       | Why it exists                          |
| --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `(String message)`                | The common case                        |
| `(String message, Throwable cause)` | Wrapping a lower-level failure       |
| `(Throwable cause)`               | Rare, when the cause's message suffices |
| Domain-specific parameters        | Carries structured data for handlers    |

A few conventions keep a codebase coherent:

- Name the class for the condition and end it with `Exception`:
  `OrderNotFoundException`, not `OrderError` or `BadOrder`.
- Make it `Serializable`-safe by keeping fields simple, and declare
  `serialVersionUID` if the class will cross a boundary.
- Consider a small hierarchy with a shared base, so callers can catch broadly
  or narrowly as they prefer.

```java
public abstract class BankingException extends RuntimeException { ... }
public class InsufficientFundsException extends BankingException { ... }
public class AccountFrozenException     extends BankingException { ... }

// Callers choose their granularity:
catch (InsufficientFundsException e) { ... }   // one specific case
catch (BankingException e)           { ... }   // anything from this domain
```

Do not create a custom exception where a standard one says exactly the same
thing. A class called `NullParameterException` adds nothing over
`NullPointerException` and forces every reader to look it up.

> Key Takeaways
> - Create a custom exception when the domain condition carries information the
>   standard types cannot express.
> - Extend `RuntimeException` for unchecked and `Exception` for checked; never
>   `Error` or `Throwable`.
> - Always supply message and message-plus-cause constructors.
> - Carry structured fields so handlers can act on data instead of parsing
>   messages.
> - A shared base class lets callers catch a whole domain or a single case.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write an `OrderNotFoundException` carrying the missing order id, and throw
>    it from a lookup method.
> 2. Give it both conventional constructors and wrap a `SQLException` in it.
> 3. Interview: When is a custom exception unnecessary? (Hint: compare it
>    against what `IllegalArgumentException` already communicates.)

#### Choosing Checked or Unchecked for an API

This is the most consequential exception decision you make, because it appears
in your method signatures and cannot be changed later without breaking every
caller.

The original design intent is clear enough. Checked means "a well-written
caller can and should recover"; unchecked means "this is a bug, fix the code".
Applied literally:

```java
// Checked: the caller can plausibly retry, use a default, or prompt.
public Config load(Path path) throws ConfigurationException { ... }

// Unchecked: passing null is a programming error, not a runtime condition.
public void register(User user) {
    Objects.requireNonNull(user, "user");
}
```

Experience has complicated this. Checked exceptions have three real costs:

- **They leak through abstractions.** Adding a checked exception to an
  interface method breaks every implementation and every caller.
- **They do not compose with lambdas.** None of the standard functional
  interfaces declare checked exceptions, so streams and checked exceptions mix
  badly.
- **They invite swallowing.** Faced with a forced `catch`, tired developers
  write an empty block, which is worse than no checking at all.

```java
// The lambda problem: this does not compile.
List<String> contents = paths.stream()
        .map(p -> Files.readString(p))     // ERROR: unhandled IOException
        .toList();

// The workaround everyone ends up writing:
List<String> contents = paths.stream()
        .map(p -> {
            try {
                return Files.readString(p);
            } catch (IOException e) {
                throw new UncheckedIOException(e);   // the JDK's own escape hatch
            }
        })
        .toList();
```

`UncheckedIOException` exists in the JDK precisely because the library authors
hit this wall themselves, which is a strong signal about how the trade-off has
aged.

A decision procedure that works in practice:

```text
  Can the caller do something OTHER than log and rethrow?
        no  -> UNCHECKED
        yes v
  Is the condition caused by a programming mistake?
        yes -> UNCHECKED
        no  v
  Will this method be used from a lambda or stream?
        yes -> UNCHECKED (or provide both variants)
        no  -> CHECKED is defensible
```

| Consideration                    | Favours checked | Favours unchecked |
| -------------------------------- | --------------- | ----------------- |
| Caller has a real recovery       | Yes             |                   |
| Condition is a programming bug   |                 | Yes               |
| Used from streams and lambdas    |                 | Yes               |
| Public library API               | Sometimes       | Sometimes         |
| Internal application code        |                 | Usually           |
| Failure is expected and frequent | Yes             |                   |

Modern practice has shifted noticeably toward unchecked. Spring, Hibernate, and
most contemporary frameworks expose unchecked exceptions almost exclusively,
translating the checked ones from lower layers. The JDK itself cannot change,
so `IOException` and `SQLException` remain checked and you will handle them
often.

Whichever you choose, **document it**. An unchecked exception is invisible in
the signature, so the Javadoc `@throws` tag is the only place a caller learns
about it:

```java
/**
 * Withdraws the given amount.
 *
 * @throws IllegalArgumentException if amount is not positive
 * @throws InsufficientFundsException if the balance is too low
 */
public void withdraw(BigDecimal amount) { ... }
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Checked means the caller has a realistic recovery; unchecked means the code
>   needs fixing.
> - Checked exceptions leak through abstraction layers and do not work with
>   lambdas or streams.
> - `UncheckedIOException` exists because the JDK hit this problem in its own
>   stream API.
> - Modern frameworks favour unchecked exceptions with translation at layer
>   boundaries.
> - Document unchecked exceptions with `@throws`, since the signature does not
>   reveal them.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write the same repository method twice, once throwing a checked exception
>    and once unchecked, and compare the caller code.
> 2. Try calling a method that throws `IOException` from inside a `stream.map`
>    and resolve the compiler error two different ways.
> 3. Interview: Why do modern frameworks prefer unchecked exceptions? (Hint:
>    consider what happens to an interface when one implementation needs a new
>    checked exception.)

#### Exception Translation Across Layers

A layered application has a persistence layer, a service layer, and a web
layer. If the web layer catches `SQLException`, the layering is a fiction: the
top of the application now depends on the database technology, and swapping to
a document store breaks code three layers away.

**Exception translation** is the discipline of converting an exception into the
vocabulary of the layer that is propagating it, keeping the original as the
cause.

```text
   Web layer          catches OrderNotFoundException -> HTTP 404
        ^
        | throws OrderNotFoundException  (domain vocabulary)
   Service layer      catches DataAccessException
        ^
        | throws DataAccessException     (persistence vocabulary)
   Repository layer   catches SQLException
        ^
        | throws SQLException            (JDBC vocabulary)
   JDBC driver
```

```java
// Repository: translates the technology exception into a persistence one.
public class JdbcOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
    @Override
    public Optional<Order> findById(long id) {
        try {
            return Optional.ofNullable(jdbc.queryForObject(SQL, mapper, id));
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            throw new DataAccessException("query failed for order " + id, e);
            //                                                            ^ cause
        }
    }
}

// Service: translates persistence failure into domain vocabulary.
public class OrderService {
    public Order require(long id) {
        return repository.findById(id)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new OrderNotFoundException(id));
    }
}

// Web: translates domain failure into a protocol response.
@ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFoundException.class)
public ResponseEntity<Problem> handle(OrderNotFoundException e) {
    return ResponseEntity.status(404).body(new Problem(e.getMessage()));
}
```

Each layer's callers now depend only on types they can reason about, and the
full chain of causes is still in the trace for whoever debugs it.

| Layer       | Speaks the language of | Typical exception            |
| ----------- | ---------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Driver      | The protocol           | `SQLException`, `IOException` |
| Repository  | Persistence            | `DataAccessException`        |
| Service     | The business domain    | `OrderNotFoundException`     |
| Web or UI   | The transport          | An HTTP status or error view |

Two refinements are worth knowing. **Exception translation is not always
wrapping.** Sometimes the right translation discards the original because it
carries no useful information, though this should be deliberate and rare, since
you lose the trace. And **do not translate at every single call**; translate at
the layer boundary, which is usually where an interface is defined.

The common mistake is translating without a cause, which produces a clean
architecture and an undebuggable one:

```java
catch (SQLException e) {
    throw new DataAccessException("query failed");   // cause dropped: don't
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Translate exceptions at layer boundaries so callers depend only on
>   vocabulary they understand.
> - Always pass the original exception as the cause to preserve the full trace.
> - Translation keeps persistence and transport details from leaking into
>   business logic.
> - Translate at interface boundaries, not at every call site.
> - Spring's `DataAccessException` hierarchy is a large-scale example of this
>   pattern.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a repository method that catches `SQLException` and rethrows a
>    domain exception with the cause attached.
> 2. Print the resulting trace and identify both the wrapper and the root
>    cause.
> 3. Interview: What breaks if a web controller catches `SQLException`
>    directly? (Hint: what happens when the team replaces the database?)

#### Fail-Fast Validation and Preconditions

A bug is cheapest to find at the moment it is introduced. A method that accepts
a bad argument and stores it will fail later, somewhere else, with a stack
trace pointing at innocent code. **Fail-fast** means detecting the problem at
the boundary and throwing immediately, so the trace names the actual culprit.

Compare the two:

```java
// Fails late: the null is stored and explodes somewhere unrelated.
public class Order {
    private Customer customer;
    public Order(Customer customer) { this.customer = customer; }
    public String label() { return customer.name(); }   // NPE here, hours later
}

// Fails fast: the trace points at whoever passed null.
public class Order {
    private final Customer customer;
    public Order(Customer customer) {
        this.customer = Objects.requireNonNull(customer, "customer");
    }
}
```

**Preconditions** are the conditions a caller must satisfy. Check them first,
before any state changes, which preserves the failure atomicity introduced in
5.2:

```java
public void schedule(Task task, Instant when, int priority) {
    Objects.requireNonNull(task, "task");
    Objects.requireNonNull(when, "when");
    if (when.isBefore(Instant.now())) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("when must be in the future: " + when);
    }
    if (priority < 1 || priority > 10) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("priority must be 1..10: " + priority);
    }
    if (shutdown) {
        throw new IllegalStateException("scheduler is shut down");
    }

    queue.add(new ScheduledTask(task, when, priority));   // only now, mutate
}
```

The `java.util.Objects` helpers cover the routine cases and throw the
conventional types:

```java
Objects.requireNonNull(value, "value");                  // NullPointerException
Objects.requireNonNullElse(value, fallback);             // substitute a default
Objects.checkIndex(index, length);                       // IndexOutOfBounds
Objects.checkFromToIndex(from, to, length);              // range checks
```

Validation belongs in constructors too, because an object that cannot be
created in an invalid state can never be found in one:

```java
public record Percentage(int value) {
    public Percentage {                                   // compact constructor
        if (value < 0 || value > 100) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("must be 0..100: " + value);
        }
    }
}
```

A word on `assert`. Java's `assert` statement is disabled at runtime unless the
JVM is started with `-ea`, so it is a development-time check for internal
invariants, never a substitute for validating public input:

```java
public void process(int[] sorted) {
    assert isSorted(sorted) : "input must be sorted";   // internal invariant only
}
```

| Check type               | Use                                  | Throws                      |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------ | --------------------------- |
| Public argument check    | Always, in public methods            | `IllegalArgumentException` / `NullPointerException` |
| Receiver state check     | Before operations needing a state    | `IllegalStateException`     |
| Internal invariant       | Private methods, development only    | `assert`                    |
| External input           | Parsing, deserialisation, requests   | A domain or validation exception |

> Key Takeaways
> - Validate at the boundary so the stack trace names the caller that made the
>   mistake.
> - Check every precondition before mutating any state, preserving failure
>   atomicity.
> - Use `Objects.requireNonNull` and `Objects.checkIndex` for the conventional
>   types and messages.
> - Validate in constructors so invalid objects cannot exist.
> - `assert` is for internal invariants only, because it is disabled by
>   default.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add fail-fast validation to a `DateRange` class rejecting an end before
>    its start.
> 2. Write a method that mutates a field before validating, then reorder it and
>    explain what improved.
> 3. Interview: Why is `assert` unsuitable for validating public method
>    arguments? (Hint: what does the JVM do with assertions by default?)

#### Anti-Patterns: Swallowing and Overbroad Catches

Most exception damage comes from a handful of habits that look harmless in a
code review and are devastating in production. Each one below removes
information that someone will later need.

**Swallowing.** An empty catch block discards the failure entirely. The program
continues in an unknown state, and the evidence is gone.

```java
try {
    saveToDatabase(order);
} catch (SQLException e) {
    // nothing here
}
// Execution continues as if the save succeeded. It did not.
```

If an exception really is expected and ignorable, say so explicitly, name the
variable `ignored`, and comment why:

```java
try {
    Thread.sleep(100);
} catch (InterruptedException ignored) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();    // restore the flag, then continue
}
```

**Logging and continuing.** Subtler than swallowing, and more common. The log
line makes it look handled, but the caller still proceeds on the assumption the
operation succeeded.

```java
try {
    saveToDatabase(order);
} catch (SQLException e) {
    log.error("save failed", e);           // logged, but the caller is not told
}                                          // -> rethrow, or return a result
```

**Logging and rethrowing.** This one produces duplicate stack traces, one per
layer, and makes logs unreadable. Log at the boundary where the exception is
finally handled, not on the way past.

```java
catch (SQLException e) {
    log.error("failed", e);                // logged here...
    throw new DataAccessException("failed", e);   // ...and again at the top
}
```

**Catching too broadly.** `catch (Exception e)` deep in business logic swallows
`NullPointerException` and every other bug along with the condition you meant
to handle.

```java
try {
    return Integer.parseInt(input);
} catch (Exception e) {            // also catches NPE, and anything else
    return 0;
}

try {
    return Integer.parseInt(input);
} catch (NumberFormatException e) { // only the condition you understand
    return 0;
}
```

**Using exceptions for control flow.** Exceptions are expensive to construct,
because filling in the stack trace walks the stack, and they obscure intent.

```java
// Abuse: an exception as a loop terminator.
try {
    int i = 0;
    while (true) { process(array[i++]); }
} catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) { /* done */ }

// Correct: a condition.
for (int value : array) { process(value); }
```

**Catching `NullPointerException`.** Almost always a sign that a null check
belongs somewhere earlier. Catching it hides the missing validation.

| Anti-pattern              | Why it hurts                          | Instead                          |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Empty catch               | The failure disappears entirely       | Handle, rethrow, or document why |
| Log and continue          | The caller acts on false success      | Rethrow or return a failure result |
| Log at every layer        | Duplicate traces, unreadable logs     | Log once, at the boundary        |
| `catch (Exception e)`     | Swallows unrelated bugs               | Catch the specific type          |
| `catch (Throwable t)`     | Catches `OutOfMemoryError` too        | Never do it                      |
| Exceptions as control flow | Slow and unclear                     | Use a conditional                |
| Catching `NullPointerException` | Hides a missing check           | Validate earlier                 |

> Key Takeaways
> - An empty catch block destroys the only evidence of a failure; never leave
>   one unexplained.
> - Logging without rethrowing lets the caller proceed as if the operation
>   succeeded.
> - Log an exception once, at the boundary where it is genuinely handled.
> - Catch the narrowest type you actually understand, and never `Throwable`.
> - Exceptions are for exceptional conditions, not for terminating loops or
>   branching.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Find and fix an empty catch block, choosing between handling, rethrowing,
>    and documenting.
> 2. Rewrite an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`-terminated loop as a normal
>    loop and measure the difference in a tight benchmark.
> 3. Interview: Why is logging and rethrowing at every layer a problem? (Hint:
>    count how many times one failure appears in the log file.)

#### Optional as an Alternative to Null Returns

Not every absence is exceptional. A lookup that finds nothing is an ordinary
outcome, and throwing for it is both slow and misleading. Yet returning `null`
pushes the problem to the caller, who has no reminder to check.

```java
// The caller cannot tell from the signature that null is possible.
public User findByEmail(String email) {
    return database.query(email);                 // may return null
}

User user = findByEmail("a@b.com");
System.out.println(user.name());                  // NullPointerException, eventually
```

`Optional<T>` makes the absence part of the **type**. A method returning
`Optional<User>` states in its signature that there may be no user, and the
caller cannot reach the value without acknowledging that.

```java
public Optional<User> findByEmail(String email) {
    return Optional.ofNullable(database.query(email));   // wraps a possible null
}
```

```java
Optional<User> found = findByEmail("a@b.com");

String name = found.map(User::name)                      // transform if present
                   .orElse("unknown");                   // otherwise a default

found.ifPresent(user -> sendWelcome(user));              // act only if present

User required = findByEmail("a@b.com")
        .orElseThrow(() -> new UserNotFoundException("a@b.com"));  // demand it
```

The core methods, which chapter 8 covers in full:

| Method                    | Behaviour                                        |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `Optional.of(value)`      | Wraps a non-null value; throws if null           |
| `Optional.ofNullable(v)`  | Wraps a value that may be null                   |
| `Optional.empty()`        | The explicitly empty instance                    |
| `isPresent()` / `isEmpty()` | Tests, though usually there is a better option |
| `orElse(default)`         | The value, or a fallback                         |
| `orElseGet(supplier)`     | The value, or a lazily computed fallback         |
| `orElseThrow(supplier)`   | The value, or throw the supplied exception       |
| `map` / `flatMap` / `filter` | Transform without unwrapping                  |
| `ifPresent(consumer)`     | Run an action only when present                  |

Choosing between the three strategies is the real lesson:

| Situation                                  | Return       |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------ |
| Absence is normal and the caller decides   | `Optional<T>` |
| Absence is a violated expectation          | Throw        |
| Absence has an obvious neutral value       | Empty list, empty string, zero |

Optional has clear boundaries, and misusing it is a common overcorrection:

```java
// Do NOT use Optional for fields: it is not Serializable and adds allocation.
private Optional<String> nickname;          // wrong

// Do NOT use it for parameters: callers must wrap, and null is still possible.
public void update(Optional<String> name);  // wrong

// Do NOT return Optional of a collection: return an empty collection instead.
public Optional<List<Order>> orders();      // wrong
public List<Order> orders();                // right, possibly empty

// Do NOT unwrap blindly: this is the NullPointerException you were avoiding.
String name = findByEmail(email).get();     // NoSuchElementException if empty
```

Optional is designed as a **return type**, and specifically for the case where
a caller must be reminded that nothing may come back.

> Key Takeaways
> - `Optional<T>` makes possible absence visible in the method signature.
> - Use it as a return type, not for fields, parameters, or collections.
> - Prefer `map`, `orElse`, `orElseGet`, and `ifPresent` to `isPresent` plus
>   `get`.
> - Return an empty collection rather than an `Optional` wrapping one.
> - Throw when absence violates an expectation, and return `Optional` when it
>   is a normal outcome.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Convert a lookup method returning `null` into one returning `Optional` and
>    update its callers.
> 2. Chain `map`, `filter`, and `orElse` to get a user's uppercase city name or
>    the string `"UNKNOWN"`.
> 3. Interview: Why should `Optional` not be used for method parameters?
>    (Hint: how many states can an `Optional` parameter be in, and how many did
>    you want?)

<a id="6-generics"></a>
## 6. Generics

Generics let a class or method be written once and used safely with many types,
with the compiler checking every use. This chapter covers how to declare and
consume generic types, how wildcards express "some unknown type" precisely
enough to be useful, and why type erasure, the compromise that let generics
ship without breaking existing code, produces the surprising restrictions you
will run into. Everything in the Collections Framework and the Stream API is
built on these rules, so this is the chapter that makes the next two readable.

<a id="61-generic-types"></a>
### 6.1 Generic Types

This subchapter covers declaring type parameters on classes and methods, and
constraining what may be substituted for them.

#### Motivation and Type Safety

Before Java 5 there was no way to tell a collection what it was supposed to
hold. Every container stored `Object`, so anything could go in, and everything
came out needing a cast.

```java
List names = new ArrayList();          // pre-generics: a list of Object
names.add("Ada");
names.add("Grace");
names.add(42);                         // nothing stops this: it is an Object too

String first = (String) names.get(0);  // cast required on every read
String third = (String) names.get(2);  // ClassCastException at RUNTIME
```

Two problems, and the second is the serious one. The casts are noise, but the
`ClassCastException` is a **runtime** failure caused by a mistake made much
earlier, possibly in a different file written by a different person. The
compiler had all the information needed to reject `names.add(42)` and was not
allowed to use it.

Generics give the container a **type parameter**, so the intent is part of the
type:

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();   // a list of String, and only String
names.add("Ada");
// names.add(42);                         // ERROR: caught at COMPILE time

String first = names.get(0);              // no cast: the compiler knows the type
```

The shift is from detecting errors late and expensively to detecting them
early and cheaply:

```text
  WITHOUT GENERICS                    WITH GENERICS
  write code                          write code
     |                                   |
  compile  (no complaint)             compile  -> ERROR here, at your desk
     |                                   
  ship                                
     |                                
  run  -> ClassCastException          
        in production, 3am            
```

A useful analogy: a pre-generics collection is an unlabelled cardboard box. You
can put anything in it, and when you take something out you have to guess what
it is and hope. A generic collection is a box stamped `STRING ONLY`, and the
loading dock refuses anything else.

Generics deliver three concrete benefits:

| Benefit               | What it means                                        |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| Compile-time checking | Type errors surface at build time, not in production |
| No casts              | The compiler knows the element type already           |
| Self-documenting APIs | `Map<String, List<Order>>` states its shape exactly   |

The cost is paid at compile time only. Generics are erased before the bytecode
runs, which is covered in 6.2, so there is no runtime performance penalty for
using them.

A closing warning about **raw types**, which is what a generic type looks like
with its parameters omitted. They still compile, for backwards compatibility,
but they switch the checking off:

```java
List<String> safe = new ArrayList<>();
List raw = safe;                       // legal, but warns: raw type
raw.add(42);                           // compiles! the checking is gone
String boom = safe.get(0);             // ClassCastException: 42 is not a String
```

Never write a raw type in new code. The compiler's unchecked warning is telling
you it has stopped protecting that reference.

> Key Takeaways
> - Without generics, collections held `Object`, requiring casts and deferring
>   type errors to runtime.
> - A type parameter moves those errors to compile time, where they are cheap
>   to fix.
> - Generic code needs no casts, because the compiler already knows the element
>   type.
> - Generic type declarations document an API's shape precisely.
> - Raw types disable all of this and should never appear in new code.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a raw `ArrayList`, add a `String` and an `Integer`, and trigger a
>    `ClassCastException` on read.
> 2. Rewrite the same code with `List<String>` and note at which stage the
>    error now appears.
> 3. Interview: Generics add no runtime cost. What does that tell you about
>    when the checking happens? (Hint: what is left in the bytecode after
>    compilation?)

#### Generic Classes and Type Parameters

A generic class is a class with one or more placeholders for types, filled in
by whoever uses it. The placeholder is declared in angle brackets after the
class name and can then be used anywhere a real type could be: as a field type,
a parameter, a return type, or a local variable.

Think of the class declaration as a template and the type argument as the
material: the same `Box` blueprint produces a box for strings and a box for
orders, with the compiler enforcing the difference.

```java
public class Box<T> {                 // T is the type PARAMETER
    private T contents;               // a field of the parameterised type

    public void put(T item)  { this.contents = item; }
    public T  get()          { return contents; }     // no cast needed
    public boolean isEmpty() { return contents == null; }
}
```

```java
Box<String> stringBox = new Box<>();     // String is the type ARGUMENT
stringBox.put("hello");
String value = stringBox.get();          // typed as String automatically
// stringBox.put(42);                    // ERROR: incompatible types

Box<Order> orderBox = new Box<>();       // same class, different material
```

The distinction between the two words matters and is a common exam question:

| Term                  | Where it appears        | Example                    |
| --------------------- | ----------------------- | -------------------------- |
| Type parameter        | The class declaration   | `class Box<T>`             |
| Type argument         | The use site            | `new Box<String>()`        |
| Parameterised type    | The resulting type      | `Box<String>`              |
| Raw type              | Parameters omitted      | `Box`                      |

A class may declare several parameters, separated by commas:

```java
public class Pair<K, V> {              // two independent parameters
    private final K key;
    private final V value;

    public Pair(K key, V value) {      // the constructor uses them...
        this.key = key;                // ...but is NOT written Pair<K, V>(...)
        this.value = value;
    }

    public K key()   { return key; }
    public V value() { return value; }

    public Pair<V, K> swapped() {      // reuses the parameters in a new order
        return new Pair<>(value, key);
    }
}

Pair<String, Integer> score = new Pair<>("Ada", 100);
Pair<Integer, String> flipped = score.swapped();
```

Note that the constructor is named `Pair`, not `Pair<K, V>`. The parameters are
already in scope from the class declaration.

Single-letter names are conventional and carry meaning:

| Letter | Conventional use          |
| ------ | ------------------------- |
| `T`    | Type, a general parameter |
| `E`    | Element, in a collection  |
| `K`    | Key, in a map             |
| `V`    | Value, in a map           |
| `R`    | Result, a return type     |
| `S`, `U` | Second and third types  |

Two limits to internalise now. A type argument must be a **reference type**, so
primitives are not allowed and you use their wrapper classes instead:

```java
// Box<int> intBox = new Box<>();      // ERROR: unexpected type
Box<Integer> intBox = new Box<>();     // the wrapper, with autoboxing
intBox.put(42);                        // autoboxed to Integer
```

And parameterised types are **invariant**: `Box<String>` is not a subtype of
`Box<Object>`, even though `String` is a subtype of `Object`. This surprises
everyone once, and wildcards in 6.2 exist to work around it.

```java
// Box<Object> any = new Box<String>();   // ERROR: incompatible types
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A generic class declares type parameters in angle brackets after its name.
> - A type parameter is the placeholder; a type argument is what you substitute
>   at the use site.
> - Constructors do not repeat the parameter list; it is already in scope.
> - Type arguments must be reference types, so use wrappers rather than
>   primitives.
> - `Box<String>` is not a subtype of `Box<Object>`; generic types are
>   invariant.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `Box<T>` with `put` and `get`, then instantiate it for `String`
>    and `Integer`.
> 2. Extend `Pair<K, V>` with a `toString` and a static factory, and use it to
>    return two values from a method.
> 3. Interview: Why can a type argument not be a primitive like `int`? (Hint:
>    what does the compiler substitute for `T` once generics are erased?)

#### Generic Methods and Type Inference

A class-level parameter is fixed for the whole object. Sometimes only a single
method needs to be generic, and often it is a `static` method with no instance
to take a parameter from. A **generic method** declares its own type parameter,
scoped to that one method.

The declaration goes between the modifiers and the return type, which is the
part that looks odd at first:

```java
public static <T> void printAll(List<T> items) {
//            ^^^ declares T for this method only
    for (T item : items) System.out.println(item);
}
```

```java
public class Utils {

    // Returns the first element, or a fallback if the list is empty.
    public static <T> T firstOr(List<T> items, T fallback) {
        return items.isEmpty() ? fallback : items.get(0);
    }

    // Two independent parameters, used for input and output.
    public static <T, R> List<R> mapAll(List<T> source, Function<T, R> mapper) {
        List<R> result = new ArrayList<>();
        for (T item : source) result.add(mapper.apply(item));
        return result;
    }

    // Swaps two elements in place; T ties the array and indices together.
    public static <T> void swap(T[] array, int i, int j) {
        T temp = array[i];
        array[i] = array[j];
        array[j] = temp;
    }
}
```

The payoff is **type inference**: you almost never write the type argument,
because the compiler works it out from the arguments you passed.

```java
List<String> names = List.of("Ada", "Grace");

String first = Utils.firstOr(names, "nobody");   // T inferred as String
List<Integer> lengths = Utils.mapAll(names, String::length);  // T=String, R=Integer

// The explicit form exists but is rarely needed:
String same = Utils.<String>firstOr(names, "nobody");
```

Inference occasionally needs help. When there is nothing to infer from, such as
an empty collection or a `null`, the compiler falls back to `Object` and you
supply the argument explicitly:

```java
List<String> empty = Collections.emptyList();          // inferred from the target
List<String> also  = Collections.<String>emptyList();  // explicit, when needed
```

A generic method on a generic class may introduce a *different* parameter, and
the two are unrelated:

```java
public class Box<T> {
    private T contents;

    public <U> Pair<T, U> pairedWith(U other) {   // U is new, T comes from the class
        return new Pair<>(contents, other);
    }
}

Box<String> box = new Box<>();
Pair<String, Integer> pair = box.pairedWith(42);   // T=String, U=Integer
```

| Form           | Parameter declared on | Scope           | Inferred from      |
| -------------- | --------------------- | --------------- | ------------------ |
| Generic class  | The class             | Every member    | The `new` expression |
| Generic method | The method            | That method     | The call's arguments |

The practical rule: **if only one method needs the parameter, put it on the
method, not the class.** A class-level parameter forces every user of the class
to commit to a type they may not care about.

> Key Takeaways
> - A generic method declares its own type parameter before the return type.
> - The parameter is scoped to that method and is independent of any class-level
>   parameter.
> - Type inference means the argument is almost never written explicitly.
> - Supply the type argument explicitly when there is nothing to infer from,
>   such as an empty collection.
> - Prefer a method-level parameter when only one method is generic.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a generic `<T> T last(List<T> list)` and call it on lists of two
>    different types.
> 2. Write `<K, V> Map<V, K> invert(Map<K, V> map)` and test it.
> 3. Interview: When does the compiler need you to write the type argument
>    explicitly? (Hint: what can it infer from a call with no useful
>    arguments?)

#### The Diamond Operator

Early generic code repeated itself. The type arguments appeared on both sides
of the assignment, and the right side never said anything the left side had not
already established.

```java
// Java 5 and 6: everything stated twice.
Map<String, List<Order>> byCustomer = new HashMap<String, List<Order>>();
```

Java 7 introduced the **diamond operator**, an empty `<>` that tells the
compiler to infer the arguments from the context:

```java
Map<String, List<Order>> byCustomer = new HashMap<>();   // inferred
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
Box<Pair<String, Integer>> nested = new Box<>();         // scales with nesting
```

The diamond is not the same as omitting the brackets. Leaving them off creates
a **raw type** and silently disables checking, which is the bug from the first
topic:

```java
List<String> a = new ArrayList<>();    // generic, inferred: correct
List<String> b = new ArrayList();      // RAW on the right: unchecked warning
```

That one-character difference is worth checking for in code review, because
both compile.

Inference comes from the **target type**, meaning whatever the expression is
assigned to or passed as:

```java
List<String> fromVariable = new ArrayList<>();          // from the variable type
process(new ArrayList<>());                             // from the parameter type

public static List<String> make() {
    return new ArrayList<>();                           // from the return type
}

// var reverses the direction, so the diamond has nothing to work from:
var list = new ArrayList<String>();      // must state it here
// var broken = new ArrayList<>();       // infers ArrayList<Object>: rarely wanted
```

That last case matters now that `var` is common. With `var`, the right side is
the only source of information, so write the type argument there.

Since Java 9 the diamond also works with **anonymous classes**, which was
previously forbidden:

```java
Comparator<String> byLength = new Comparator<>() {    // Java 9+: diamond allowed
    @Override
    public int compare(String a, String b) {
        return Integer.compare(a.length(), b.length());
    }
};
```

> Key Takeaways
> - The diamond `<>` infers type arguments from the target type.
> - Omitting the brackets entirely creates a raw type and disables checking.
> - Inference works from a variable type, a parameter type, or a return type.
> - With `var` there is no target type, so the arguments must be written on the
>   right.
> - Java 9 extended the diamond to anonymous classes.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Rewrite three verbose generic declarations using the diamond.
> 2. Write `List<String> x = new ArrayList();` and read the compiler's
>    unchecked warning.
> 3. Declare `var list = new ArrayList<>();` and inspect the inferred element
>    type; explain the result.

#### Bounded Type Parameters

An unbounded `<T>` accepts anything, which means the code inside can only use
the methods every object has. That is often too little. A method that sums
numbers needs `doubleValue()`; a method that sorts needs `compareTo`. Neither
is available on `Object`.

A **bound** constrains what may be substituted, and in exchange the compiler
lets you call that type's methods.

```java
// Without a bound: T could be anything, so nothing useful is available.
public static <T> double sumBroken(List<T> numbers) {
    double total = 0;
    for (T n : numbers) {
        // total += n.doubleValue();     // ERROR: Object has no doubleValue()
    }
    return total;
}

// With an upper bound: T is guaranteed to be a Number or a subtype.
public static <T extends Number> double sum(List<T> numbers) {
//              ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the bound
    double total = 0;
    for (T n : numbers) total += n.doubleValue();   // now allowed
    return total;
}
```

