```java
sum(List.of(1, 2, 3));            // Integer extends Number: fine
sum(List.of(1.5, 2.5));           // Double extends Number: fine
// sum(List.of("a", "b"));        // ERROR: String is not within bound Number
```

The keyword is always `extends`, whether the bound is a class or an interface.
There is no `implements` in a type bound, which trips people up:

```java
public static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(List<T> items) {
//                       ^^^^^^^^^^^^^ an interface, still written 'extends'
    T best = items.get(0);
    for (T item : items) {
        if (item.compareTo(best) > 0) best = item;   // available thanks to the bound
    }
    return best;
}

String longest = max(List.of("ab", "abcd", "abc"));   // String is Comparable
```

The bound serves two purposes at once, and it is worth separating them:

| Purpose            | Effect                                                 |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Restriction        | Rejects type arguments outside the bound, at compile time |
| Capability         | Grants access to the bound type's members inside the body |

Bounds work on classes as well as methods, and a bound may refer to another
parameter:

```java
public class NumberBox<T extends Number> {     // class-level bound
    private final List<T> values = new ArrayList<>();

    public void add(T value) { values.add(value); }

    public double average() {
        return values.stream().mapToDouble(Number::doubleValue).average().orElse(0);
    }
}

// A bound referring to another type parameter:
public static <T, C extends Collection<T>> C fill(C target, T value, int times) {
    for (int i = 0; i < times; i++) target.add(value);
    return target;      // returns the concrete collection type, not Collection
}
```

Note the difference between a bound and a wildcard, which 6.2 covers: a bound
constrains a parameter you **declared**, while a wildcard describes an unknown
type at a **use site**. `<T extends Number>` names the type so you can use it
consistently; `List<? extends Number>` does not.

> Key Takeaways
> - A bound restricts which types may be substituted and grants access to that
>   type's members.
> - Always written with `extends`, for both superclasses and interfaces.
> - Without a bound, only `Object` members are available inside the generic
>   code.
> - Bounds may be applied to classes as well as methods.
> - A bound may reference another type parameter, as in
>   `<T, C extends Collection<T>>`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `<T extends Number> double average(List<T> values)` and call it with
>    integers and doubles.
> 2. Write a `<T extends Comparable<T>> T min(List<T>)` method and test it on
>    strings.
> 3. Interview: Why is `implements` never used in a type bound? (Hint: does the
>    compiler need to distinguish a class bound from an interface bound here?)

#### Multiple Bounds

Sometimes one constraint is not enough. A method that both sorts its input and
serialises the result needs a type that is `Comparable` *and* `Serializable`.
Java allows a type parameter to carry several bounds, joined by `&`.

```java
public static <T extends Comparable<T> & Serializable> T maxSerializable(List<T> items) {
//                       ^^^^^^^^^^^^^   ^^^^^^^^^^^^ both required
    T best = items.get(0);
    for (T item : items) {
        if (item.compareTo(best) > 0) best = item;   // from Comparable
    }
    return best;                                     // guaranteed Serializable
}
```

Only a type satisfying **every** bound may be substituted:

```java
maxSerializable(List.of("a", "b"));   // String is Comparable and Serializable

class Plain implements Comparable<Plain> {
    @Override public int compareTo(Plain o) { return 0; }
}
// maxSerializable(List.of(new Plain()));   // ERROR: Plain is not Serializable
```

One ordering rule governs the syntax: **if a class is among the bounds, it must
be listed first**, and there may be at most one, since Java has single class
inheritance. Interfaces follow in any order.

```java
// Correct: class first, then interfaces.
public static <T extends Number & Comparable<T> & Serializable> void ok(T value) { }

// public static <T extends Comparable<T> & Number> void bad(T value) { }
//     ERROR: interface expected here  (Number is a class and must come first)
```

```text
  <T extends  Number  &  Comparable<T>  &  Serializable>
              ^^^^^^     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^     ^^^^^^^^^^^^
              class      interface         interface
              (at most one, and always first)
```

Inside the method, every member of every bound is available, as though the type
were a hypothetical class implementing all of them:

```java
public static <T extends Number & Comparable<T>> String describe(T value, T other) {
    double d = value.doubleValue();          // from Number
    int cmp  = value.compareTo(other);       // from Comparable
    return d + (cmp > 0 ? " is larger" : " is not larger");
}
```

Multiple bounds are uncommon in application code and more frequent in library
APIs, where an author wants precision. Two cautions keep them usable. Each
extra bound narrows the set of acceptable types, so three or four bounds often
means the design should use a single purpose-built interface instead. And the
**leftmost bound** determines the erasure, which matters for the binary
compatibility rules covered in the next subchapter.

> Key Takeaways
> - Multiple bounds are written with `&` and require the type to satisfy all of
>   them.
> - At most one bound may be a class, and it must be listed first.
> - Every member of every bound is available inside the generic code.
> - Heavily bounded parameters usually signal a missing interface.
> - The leftmost bound determines what the parameter erases to.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a method bounded by `Comparable<T> & Serializable` and call it with
>    `String`.
> 2. Put an interface before a class in a bound list and read the compiler
>    error.
> 3. Interview: Why may only one bound be a class, and why must it come first?
>    (Hint: connect it to a rule from the inheritance chapter.)

<a id="62-advanced-generics"></a>
### 6.2 Advanced Generics

Wildcards make generic APIs flexible enough to be usable, and erasure explains
every restriction the language imposes on them.

#### Wildcards and Unknown Types

Generic types are **invariant**, a rule introduced in 6.1 that becomes a real
obstacle here. `List<String>` is not a `List<Object>`, so a method written to
accept `List<Object>` rejects every other list:

```java
public static void printAll(List<Object> items) {
    for (Object item : items) System.out.println(item);
}

printAll(new ArrayList<Object>());        // fine
// printAll(new ArrayList<String>());     // ERROR: incompatible types
```

The restriction is not arbitrary. If `List<String>` were assignable to
`List<Object>`, this would compile and then corrupt the list:

```java
List<String> strings = new ArrayList<>();
// List<Object> objects = strings;        // suppose this were allowed...
// objects.add(42);                       // ...then an Integer is in a List<String>
// String boom = strings.get(0);          // ClassCastException, generics defeated
```

Arrays *are* covariant and do allow exactly that, which is why array stores are
checked at runtime:

```java
Object[] array = new String[2];      // legal: arrays are covariant
array[0] = 42;                       // compiles, then ArrayStoreException at runtime
```

Generics chose compile-time safety instead. The **wildcard** `?` is how you
recover the flexibility without losing it. It means "some specific type I do
not know":

```java
public static void printAll(List<?> items) {      // a list of SOMETHING
    for (Object item : items) System.out.println(item);
}

printAll(new ArrayList<String>());     // now all of these work
printAll(new ArrayList<Integer>());
printAll(List.of(1.5, 2.5));
```

Because the element type is unknown, the compiler blocks anything that would
require knowing it. You can **read** as `Object`, because every type is an
`Object`, but you cannot **write** anything:

```java
public static void inspect(List<?> items) {
    Object first = items.get(0);       // OK: whatever it is, it is an Object
    int size = items.size();           // OK: does not involve the element type
    items.clear();                     // OK: removes without naming the type

    // items.add("hello");             // ERROR: ? might not be String
    // items.add(new Object());        // ERROR: ? might be String
    items.add(null);                   // the single exception: null fits any type
}
```

```text
  List<?>  means "a List<X> for exactly one X, but I don't know which"

        could be List<String>   -> add(Integer) would be wrong
        could be List<Integer>  -> add(String)  would be wrong
        therefore: add(anything) is rejected, read as Object is safe
```

The distinction from a type parameter matters. `<T>` names the type, so it can
be used consistently in several places; `?` does not, so each `?` is
independent:

| Form                     | Names the type | Usable in several positions | Declared where |
| ------------------------ | -------------- | --------------------------- | -------------- |
| `<T> void f(List<T> a, List<T> b)` | Yes  | Yes, both lists share `T`   | Method signature |
| `void f(List<?> a, List<?> b)`     | No   | No, the two are unrelated   | Use site only  |

```java
// These two lists must have the SAME element type:
public static <T> void copy(List<T> from, List<T> to) { to.addAll(from); }

// These two may have DIFFERENT element types:
public static void compare(List<?> a, List<?> b) { ... }
```

One more form exists, the **unbounded wildcard versus the raw type**, and they
are not the same thing:

```java
List<?> wild = new ArrayList<String>();   // checked: add is rejected
List raw     = new ArrayList<String>();   // unchecked: add compiles, unsafely
```

Use `List<?>` when you genuinely do not care about the element type. Never use
the raw form.

> Key Takeaways
> - Generic types are invariant, so `List<String>` is not a `List<Object>`.
> - Invariance prevents the corruption that array covariance allows at runtime.
> - The wildcard `?` means one specific but unknown type.
> - You may read from a `List<?>` as `Object` but may not add anything except
>   `null`.
> - `List<?>` is type-checked; a raw `List` is not.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a method taking `List<?>` that prints every element, and call it
>    with three differently typed lists.
> 2. Try adding an element inside that method and explain the error.
> 3. Interview: Why are arrays covariant but generics invariant? (Hint: one
>    checks at runtime and one at compile time; what does each cost?)

#### Upper and Lower Bounded Wildcards

An unbounded `?` is safe but nearly useless: you can only read `Object` and
write nothing. Bounded wildcards restore precision by constraining the unknown
type from above or below.

An **upper bounded wildcard**, `? extends T`, means "some subtype of `T`". You
know every element is at least a `T`, so reading as `T` is safe:

```java
public static double sum(List<? extends Number> numbers) {
    double total = 0;
    for (Number n : numbers) total += n.doubleValue();   // safe: all are Numbers
    return total;
}

sum(List.of(1, 2, 3));            // List<Integer>: accepted
sum(List.of(1.5, 2.5));           // List<Double>:  accepted
sum(new ArrayList<Number>());     // List<Number>:  accepted
```

Writing is still forbidden, because the exact subtype is unknown:

```java
public static void broken(List<? extends Number> numbers) {
    Number first = numbers.get(0);    // OK: reading as Number is guaranteed
    // numbers.add(1);                // ERROR: the list might be List<Double>
    // numbers.add(1.5);              // ERROR: it might be List<Integer>
}
```

A **lower bounded wildcard**, `? super T`, is the mirror image: "some supertype
of `T`". You know the list accepts a `T`, because a `T` fits into any container
of its supertypes, so writing is safe:

```java
public static void addNumbers(List<? super Integer> target) {
    target.add(1);                    // OK: an Integer fits a List<Integer>,
    target.add(2);                    //     a List<Number>, or a List<Object>
    // Integer first = target.get(0); // ERROR: might be List<Object>
    Object any = target.get(0);       // only Object is guaranteed on read
}

addNumbers(new ArrayList<Integer>());   // accepted
addNumbers(new ArrayList<Number>());    // accepted
addNumbers(new ArrayList<Object>());    // accepted
// addNumbers(new ArrayList<Double>()); // ERROR: Double is not a supertype of Integer
```

```text
              Object            <- ? super Integer accepts these three
                |
              Number            <-
                |
              Integer           <- the pivot: T itself is in both ranges
                |
        (Integer's subtypes)    <- ? extends Number accepts Integer, Double, ...

   ? extends Number : read as Number,  cannot write
   ? super Integer  : write Integer,   read only as Object
```

The three forms compared:

| Wildcard            | Accepts                 | Safe to read as | Safe to write |
| ------------------- | ----------------------- | --------------- | ------------- |
| `List<Number>`      | Exactly `List<Number>`  | `Number`        | `Number` and subtypes |
| `List<? extends Number>` | `Number` and subtypes | `Number`      | Nothing but `null` |
| `List<? super Integer>`  | `Integer` and supertypes | `Object`  | `Integer` and subtypes |
| `List<?>`           | Any list                | `Object`        | Nothing but `null` |

Note the asymmetry that catches people: `? extends` gives you a useful **read**
type and no write; `? super` gives you a useful **write** type and no useful
read. You never get both, and that limitation is exactly what makes them safe.

A wildcard bound may name an interface, and unlike a type parameter bound it
cannot list multiple bounds with `&`:

```java
List<? extends Comparable<?>> items;      // interface bound: fine
// List<? extends Number & Comparable<?>> x;   // ERROR: not allowed on wildcards
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `? extends T` accepts `T` and its subtypes, allows reading as `T`, and
>   forbids writing.
> - `? super T` accepts `T` and its supertypes, allows writing a `T`, and
>   allows reading only as `Object`.
> - The restrictions follow from what the compiler can guarantee about the
>   unknown type.
> - You never get both safe reading and safe writing from one wildcard.
> - Wildcards take a single bound; `&` is only for type parameter bounds.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `double total(List<? extends Number>)` and call it with three
>    different numeric list types.
> 2. Write `void fill(List<? super String> target)` and call it with
>    `List<String>`, `List<CharSequence>`, and `List<Object>`.
> 3. Interview: Why can you not add to a `List<? extends Number>` even though
>    every element is a `Number`? (Hint: name two concrete lists the parameter
>    might refer to.)

#### The PECS Principle

Knowing what each wildcard permits is one thing; knowing which to reach for
when designing a method is another. The mnemonic that settles it is **PECS:
Producer Extends, Consumer Super**.

Ask what the parameter does from the method's point of view:

- If it **produces** values the method reads, use `? extends T`.
- If it **consumes** values the method writes, use `? super T`.
- If it does both, use a plain `T` with no wildcard.

The canonical example is a copy method, which has one of each:

```java
public static <T> void copy(List<? extends T> source,   // PRODUCER: we read from it
                            List<? super T>   target) { // CONSUMER: we write to it
    for (T item : source) {          // reading as T is safe: extends
        target.add(item);            // writing a T is safe: super
    }
}
```

That signature is far more flexible than the naive one. It accepts any pairing
where the source elements fit the target:

```java
List<Integer> integers = List.of(1, 2, 3);
List<Number>  numbers  = new ArrayList<>();
List<Object>  objects  = new ArrayList<>();

copy(integers, numbers);      // Integer -> Number: fine
copy(integers, objects);      // Integer -> Object: fine
copy(numbers,  objects);      // Number  -> Object: fine
// copy(numbers, integers);   // ERROR, correctly: a Number is not an Integer

// Compare with the rigid version:
// static <T> void copy(List<T> source, List<T> target)
// copy(integers, numbers);   // would FAIL: T cannot be both Integer and Number
```

The standard library follows PECS consistently, and recognising it makes the
Javadoc readable:

```java
// Collection: addAll consumes nothing from the argument except reads, so extends
boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c);

// Comparator is a consumer of the elements it compares, so super
void sort(Comparator<? super E> comparator);

// Stream: map produces R and consumes T
<R> Stream<R> map(Function<? super T, ? extends R> mapper);

// Collections.copy, the textbook case
public static <T> void copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src);
```

```text
             SOURCE                          TARGET
        List<? extends T>               List<? super T>
        "I produce T values"            "I consume T values"
                |                               ^
                +---------- copy ---------------+
                       reads T, writes T
```

Two refinements complete the picture. A **return type should not use a
wildcard**, because it forces every caller to deal with the wildcard too:

```java
// Poor: callers now hold a List<? extends Number> and cannot add to it.
public static List<? extends Number> parse(String input) { ... }

// Better: commit to a type.
public static List<Number> parse(String input) { ... }
```

And a parameter the method only inspects, never reading elements out by type
nor adding to, may simply use `List<?>`:

```java
public static int size(Collection<?> any) { return any.size(); }
```

| Parameter role                 | Use                   | Example                       |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Method reads elements from it  | `? extends T`         | `addAll(Collection<? extends E>)` |
| Method writes elements into it | `? super T`           | `sort(Comparator<? super E>)` |
| Method does both               | Plain `T`             | `List<T> swap(List<T>)`       |
| Method ignores the element type | `?`                  | `size(Collection<?>)`         |
| Return type                    | No wildcard           | `List<Number> parse(...)`     |

> Key Takeaways
> - PECS: use `extends` for parameters you read from and `super` for those you
>   write to.
> - A parameter doing both gets a plain type parameter with no wildcard.
> - PECS-typed parameters accept far more caller types than rigid ones.
> - The standard library applies PECS throughout, which is why its signatures
>   look the way they do.
> - Do not put wildcards in return types; they propagate the awkwardness to
>   callers.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `<T> void copy(List<? extends T> src, List<? super T> dst)` and
>    exercise it with three type pairings.
> 2. Explain, for `Collections.max(Collection<? extends T>, Comparator<? super T>)`,
>    why each wildcard is the one it is.
> 3. Interview: Why does `List.sort` take `Comparator<? super E>` rather than
>    `Comparator<E>`? (Hint: could a comparator written for `Object` sort a
>    `List<String>`?)

#### Type Erasure and Its Consequences

Generics arrived in Java 5, fifteen years into the language's life, with
millions of lines of existing code that had to keep working and keep
interoperating. The solution was **erasure**: generics are a compile-time
feature, and the compiler removes them once it has finished checking.

After erasure, every type parameter is replaced by its **leftmost bound**, or
by `Object` if it has none, and the compiler inserts the casts that the
programmer no longer writes.

```java
// What you write:
public class Box<T> {
    private T contents;
    public T get() { return contents; }
    public void put(T item) { contents = item; }
}

// What the bytecode effectively contains:
public class Box {
    private Object contents;                       // T erased to Object
    public Object get() { return contents; }
    public void put(Object item) { contents = item; }
}
```

```java
// With a bound, erasure uses the bound instead of Object:
public class NumberBox<T extends Number> { private T value; }
// becomes: private Number value;
```

At the call site the compiler inserts the cast it proved was safe:

```java
Box<String> box = new Box<>();
String s = box.get();
// compiles to: String s = (String) box.get();   <- a checked cast, inserted
```

The immediate consequence is that **generic type information does not exist at
runtime**. Two parameterisations of the same class are the same class:

```java
List<String>  strings = new ArrayList<>();
List<Integer> ints    = new ArrayList<>();

System.out.println(strings.getClass() == ints.getClass());   // true
System.out.println(strings.getClass().getName());            // java.util.ArrayList
```

Everything that follows from that is worth listing, because each one looks
arbitrary until you know the cause:

| You cannot                        | Because at runtime                    |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `new T()`                         | `T` is unknown; there is no class to instantiate |
| `new T[10]`                       | Same, and arrays need a real component type |
| `x instanceof List<String>`       | Only `List` exists; the argument is gone |
| Overload on `List<String>` vs `List<Integer>` | Both erase to the same signature |
| Catch a generic exception type    | The catch mechanism needs a real class |
| Use a primitive as a type argument | `Object` cannot hold an `int` directly |

```java
// public static void f(List<String> l) { }
// public static void f(List<Integer> l) { }
//     ERROR: both methods have the same erasure f(List)

List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
// if (list instanceof List<String>) { }    // ERROR: illegal generic type
if (list instanceof List<?>) { }            // legal: the only permitted form
```

Erasure also explains the **unchecked warning**. When the compiler cannot
verify a cast because the type is erased, it says so and shifts responsibility
to you:

```java
@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")              // only after proving it is safe
public static <T> T cast(Object value) {
    return (T) value;                       // unchecked: nothing verifies T here
}

String s = cast("hello");                   // fine
// Integer i = cast("hello");               // compiles! fails at the USE site
```

That last line shows the real hazard: an unchecked cast defers the
`ClassCastException` to wherever the value is finally used, which may be far
away. Suppress the warning only when you can prove safety by inspection, and
comment why.

Erasure is not all loss. It gave Java **migration compatibility**: pre-generics
code and generic code call each other freely, since they compile to the same
bytecode. C# chose reified generics and a cleaner runtime model, at the cost of
a breaking change to its runtime. Java chose not to break the world.

> Key Takeaways
> - Erasure removes type parameters after compile-time checking, replacing them
>   with their leftmost bound or `Object`.
> - The compiler inserts the casts you no longer write.
> - `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are the same class at runtime.
> - Every generic restriction in the language traces back to erasure.
> - Erasure bought interoperability with pre-generics code, which was the
>   design goal.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Print `getClass()` for `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` and explain the
>    result.
> 2. Write two overloads differing only in type argument and read the erasure
>    error.
> 3. Interview: Why did Java implement generics with erasure instead of
>    reifying them? (Hint: what already existed in 2004 that could not be
>    recompiled?)

#### Restrictions on Generic Arrays and Statics

Two restrictions cause more confusion than the rest combined, and both follow
directly from erasure.

**You cannot create a generic array.** `new T[10]` is rejected, and so is
`new List<String>[10]`:

```java
public class Stack<T> {
    // private T[] items = new T[10];          // ERROR: generic array creation
}

// List<String>[] lists = new List<String>[10];   // ERROR: generic array creation
```

The reason is that arrays are **reified**: an array knows its component type at
runtime and checks every store against it. A generic array would have nothing
to check, and the resulting hole is easy to demonstrate:

```java
// Suppose generic array creation were allowed:
// List<String>[] arrays = new List<String>[1];   // pretend this compiles
// Object[] objects = arrays;                     // arrays are covariant
// objects[0] = List.of(42);                      // stores a List<Integer>!
//                                                // the store check sees only List
// String s = arrays[0].get(0);                   // ClassCastException, silently
```

The store check would see `List` on both sides and allow it, defeating the
guarantee generics exist to provide. Two workarounds are standard:

```java
public class Stack<T> {
    private Object[] items = new Object[10];      // 1: store as Object[]
    private int size;

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public T pop() {
        return (T) items[--size];                 // cast on the way out
    }
}

public class Stack2<T> {
    private final T[] items;

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public Stack2(int capacity) {
        items = (T[]) new Object[capacity];       // 2: create Object[], cast once
    }
}

// 3: avoid arrays entirely, which is usually best
public class Stack3<T> {
    private final List<T> items = new ArrayList<>();
}
```

A reflective alternative exists when the caller can supply the class:

```java
public static <T> T[] newArray(Class<T> type, int size) {
    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    T[] array = (T[]) java.lang.reflect.Array.newInstance(type, size);
    return array;                                  // the type token supplies what
}                                                  // erasure removed
```

**You cannot use a class's type parameter in a static context.** Static members
belong to the class, not to any instance, and the type argument is supplied per
instance:

```java
public class Box<T> {
    // private static T shared;                    // ERROR: non-static T in static context
    // public static T create() { return null; }   // ERROR: same reason

    public static <U> Box<U> empty() {             // a static GENERIC method is fine
        return new Box<>();                        // U is declared by the method
    }
}
```

The logic: `Box<String>` and `Box<Integer>` share one static field after
erasure, so a static `T` would have to be `String` and `Integer` at once. A
static method may declare its own parameter, because that one is supplied per
call.

A few further restrictions round out the set:

```java
// public class BadException<T> extends Exception { }
//     ERROR: a generic class may not extend Throwable (catch needs a real type)

// try { } catch (T e) { }            // ERROR: cannot catch a type parameter

class Box<T> {
    // T t = new T();                 // ERROR: cannot instantiate a type parameter
}
```

The standard fix for the last one is a **factory** or a `Supplier`:

```java
public static <T> List<T> fill(int count, Supplier<T> factory) {
    List<T> result = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) result.add(factory.get());   // caller supplies
    return result;
}

List<StringBuilder> builders = fill(3, StringBuilder::new);
```

| Restriction                         | Standard workaround                  |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `new T()`                           | Pass a `Supplier<T>` or `Class<T>`   |
| `new T[n]`                          | `Object[]` plus a cast, or a `List`  |
| Static field of type `T`            | Make it a static generic method      |
| Generic subclass of `Throwable`     | Use a non-generic exception          |
| `instanceof List<String>`           | `instanceof List<?>`                 |

> Key Takeaways
> - Generic array creation is banned because arrays check stores at runtime and
>   generics are erased.
> - Use `Object[]` with a contained cast, or prefer a `List`, and suppress the
>   warning only when provably safe.
> - A class's type parameter cannot appear in a static field or static method.
> - Static methods may declare their own type parameters, which are supplied
>   per call.
> - A type parameter cannot be instantiated, caught, or used to extend
>   `Throwable`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement a generic `Stack<T>` backed by `Object[]` with a single
>    suppressed cast.
> 2. Try declaring `private static T cache;` in a generic class and explain the
>    error.
> 3. Write a `<T> List<T> fill(int, Supplier<T>)` and use it to create three
>    `ArrayList` instances.

#### Recursive Generic Bounds

Some contracts refer back to the type implementing them. `Comparable` is the
clearest case: a type is not comparable in general, it is comparable **to
itself**. Expressing that requires a bound that mentions the parameter being
declared, which looks circular and is not.

```java
public static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(List<T> items) {
//              ^                ^
//              the parameter    ...used in its own bound
    T best = items.get(0);
    for (T item : items) if (item.compareTo(best) > 0) best = item;
    return best;
}
```

Read it as a constraint, not a definition: "`T` is any type that can be
compared to `T`". The compiler simply checks that whatever you substitute
satisfies the condition.

```java
max(List.of("b", "a", "c"));      // String implements Comparable<String>: fine
max(List.of(3, 1, 2));            // Integer implements Comparable<Integer>: fine
```

The pattern has a name, the **curiously recurring generic pattern**, and its
main use is making a method return the *caller's own type* rather than a
supertype. Without it, fluent builders break under inheritance:

```java
// Without recursion: the superclass methods return the SUPERCLASS type.
public class Builder {
    public Builder name(String n)  { ...; return this; }
}
public class AdvancedBuilder extends Builder {
    public AdvancedBuilder extra(int x) { ...; return this; }
}

new AdvancedBuilder()
        .extra(1)
        .name("x")       // returns Builder...
        // .extra(2)     // ERROR: Builder has no extra()
        ;
```

The recursive bound fixes the chain by threading the concrete type through:

```java
public abstract class Builder<SELF extends Builder<SELF>> {
    protected String name;

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    protected SELF self() { return (SELF) this; }   // the one unchecked cast

    public SELF name(String name) {
        this.name = name;
        return self();                              // returns the SUBCLASS type
    }
}

public class AdvancedBuilder extends Builder<AdvancedBuilder> {
//                                           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ passes itself
    private int extra;

    public AdvancedBuilder extra(int extra) {
        this.extra = extra;
        return this;
    }
}
```

```java
new AdvancedBuilder()
        .extra(1)
        .name("x")       // now returns AdvancedBuilder
        .extra(2);       // so the chain continues
```

```text
  Builder<SELF extends Builder<SELF>>
              |
              | SELF = AdvancedBuilder
              v
  AdvancedBuilder extends Builder<AdvancedBuilder>

  name() declared to return SELF  ->  returns AdvancedBuilder
```

The same shape appears in `java.lang.Enum`, which is declared
`Enum<E extends Enum<E>>` precisely so that `compareTo` accepts only constants
of the same enum type:

```java
public abstract class Enum<E extends Enum<E>> implements Comparable<E> { ... }

// Consequence: you cannot compare constants of different enums.
// Day.MON.compareTo(Status.PAID);    // ERROR, and correctly so
```

Two honest cautions. The pattern does not *guarantee* correctness: a subclass
can pass the wrong type argument, as in
`class Wrong extends Builder<SomethingElse>`, and the compiler accepts it. And
the `self()` cast is unchecked by necessity. Use the pattern where the fluent
chain genuinely matters, and prefer simpler designs elsewhere, since the
declarations are hard to read.

> Key Takeaways
> - A recursive bound like `<T extends Comparable<T>>` constrains a type to
>   relate to itself.
> - It is a constraint the compiler checks, not a circular definition.
> - The self-referential form `<SELF extends Builder<SELF>>` lets inherited
>   methods return the subclass type.
> - `java.lang.Enum` uses it so comparisons stay within one enum type.
> - The pattern needs one unchecked `self()` cast and does not prevent a
>   subclass supplying the wrong argument.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `<T extends Comparable<T>> T min(List<T>)` and call it on strings
>    and integers.
> 2. Build a two-level fluent builder with `<SELF extends Builder<SELF>>` and
>    chain methods from both levels in any order.
> 3. Interview: Why is `Enum` declared as `Enum<E extends Enum<E>>`? (Hint:
>    what should happen if you compare a constant of one enum with a constant
>    of another?)

<a id="7-the-collections-framework"></a>
## 7. The Collections Framework

Almost every program has to hold a group of things, and an array is rarely the
right shape for the job: it cannot grow, it cannot answer "do you already
contain this?", and it has no notion of keys. The Collections Framework is the
standard library's answer, a small set of interfaces that describe *what* a
group of objects can do and a larger set of classes that implement them with
different performance trade-offs. This chapter covers the interfaces you should
declare against, the implementations you should instantiate, and the operations
that tie them together, all of it resting on the generics rules from chapter 6.

<a id="71-collection-interfaces"></a>
### 7.1 Collection Interfaces

This subchapter covers the contracts at the top of the framework: what each
interface promises, how they relate to one another, and how iteration works.

#### The Collection Hierarchy Overview

Suppose you write a method that prints every element of a group. If you declare
its parameter as `ArrayList<String>`, it will not accept a `HashSet<String>`, a
`LinkedList<String>`, or anything else, even though printing works identically
for all of them. The method has been welded to one particular storage strategy
for no reason.

The framework solves this by separating two questions that beginners tend to
merge:

- **What can this group do?** Answered by an **interface**: `List`, `Set`,
  `Queue`, `Map`.
- **How does it do it, and how fast?** Answered by an **implementation class**:
  `ArrayList`, `HashSet`, `ArrayDeque`, `HashMap`.

The practical rule that follows is *program to the interface*: declare
variables, parameters, and return types with the interface, and name a concrete
class only at the single point where you create the object.

```java
// Declare the CAPABILITY, instantiate the STRATEGY
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();

// This method now accepts ArrayList, LinkedList, List.of(...), anything
public static void printAll(Collection<String> items) {
    for (String item : items) {
        System.out.println(item);
    }
}
```

Swapping `new ArrayList<>()` for `new LinkedList<>()` later becomes a one-line
change instead of a refactor, because nothing downstream ever named the class.

The hierarchy itself has two roots that are often mistaken for one:

```text
                   Iterable<E>                        Map<K, V>
                        |                           (NOT a Collection)
                   Collection<E>                          |
         ___________|________|____________         _______|________
        |           |                     |       |       |        |
     List<E>      Set<E>               Queue<E>  HashMap LinkedHashMap
        |           |                     |              TreeMap
   ArrayList    HashSet              ArrayDeque          (SortedMap
   LinkedList   LinkedHashSet        PriorityQueue        -> NavigableMap)
   (Vector)     TreeSet                  |
                (SortedSet            Deque<E>
                 -> NavigableSet)      ArrayDeque
                                       LinkedList
```

`Map` is deliberately outside `Collection`. A `Collection` holds single
elements and `Map` holds *pairs*, so `add(E)` would be meaningless on it. Maps
are still part of the framework and expose their contents as collections
through `keySet()`, `values()`, and `entrySet()`.

`Iterable<E>` sits above everything and declares exactly one abstract method,
`iterator()`. That single method is what makes the enhanced `for` loop work,
and implementing it is all a custom class needs to be loopable.

`Collection<E>` adds the operations shared by every group of elements:

| Method                     | Meaning                                       |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `add(E e)`                 | Insert; returns whether the collection changed |
| `remove(Object o)`         | Remove one matching element, if present        |
| `contains(Object o)`       | Membership test, using `equals`                |
| `size()`, `isEmpty()`      | How many elements                              |
| `clear()`                  | Remove everything                              |
| `iterator()`               | Inherited from `Iterable`                      |
| `stream()`                 | Bridge to the Stream API of chapter 8          |

Note that `remove` and `contains` take `Object`, not `E`. That is a historical
wart kept for backwards compatibility, and it means `list.remove("typo")` on a
`List<Integer>` compiles silently and does nothing. It is worth remembering
when a removal mysteriously has no effect.

> Key Takeaways
> - Interfaces describe capability, implementation classes describe strategy
>   and performance.
> - Declare with the interface and instantiate the class only at the creation
>   site.
> - `Iterable` provides `iterator()`, which is what powers the enhanced `for`
>   loop.
> - `Collection` is the common parent of `List`, `Set`, and `Queue`.
> - `Map` is not a `Collection`, because it stores pairs rather than single
>   elements.
> - `contains` and `remove` accept `Object`, so a wrong-typed argument compiles
>   but never matches.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a method `int countNonNull(Collection<?> items)` and call it with an
>    `ArrayList`, a `HashSet`, and a `TreeSet`.
> 2. Declare a variable as `ArrayList<String>`, pass it to a method expecting
>    `List<String>`, then try the reverse and read the compiler error.
> 3. Interview: Why is `Map` not a subinterface of `Collection`? (Hint: what
>    would the single-argument `add(E)` method mean for a map?)

#### List, Set, and Queue Contracts

The three `Collection` subinterfaces differ in one thing each: what they
promise about order and duplicates. Choosing between them is a modelling
decision, not a performance one, and getting it right removes whole classes of
bug.

A **`List`** is an ordered sequence with integer positions. Duplicates are
allowed, insertion order is preserved, and every element has an index. Think of
a numbered shopping list: item 3 stays item 3, and "milk" may appear twice.

```java
List<String> tasks = new ArrayList<>();
tasks.add("write");
tasks.add("review");
tasks.add("write");              // duplicates are fine

System.out.println(tasks.get(1));      // "review": positional access
tasks.add(1, "plan");                  // insert AT an index, shifting the rest
System.out.println(tasks.indexOf("write"));  // 0: first occurrence only
System.out.println(tasks);             // [write, plan, review, write]
```

Methods unique to `List` are the index-based ones: `get(int)`, `set(int, E)`,
`add(int, E)`, `remove(int)`, `indexOf`, `subList`, and `sort`.

A **`Set`** is a collection with no duplicates. Adding an element that is
already present does nothing and returns `false`. There is no index, because
most sets have no meaningful position. Think of the set of tags on an article:
asking for "the third tag" is not a question the model supports.

```java
Set<String> tags = new HashSet<>();
System.out.println(tags.add("java"));   // true:  actually added
System.out.println(tags.add("java"));   // false: already present, no change
tags.add("collections");
System.out.println(tags.size());        // 2
// tags.get(0);                         // ERROR: no such method on Set
```

"Duplicate" here means *`equals` returned true*, which is why the hashing rules
later in this chapter matter so much for custom element types.

A **`Queue`** holds elements for processing in a defined order, normally
first-in-first-out. Its distinctive feature is that each operation comes in two
flavours: one that throws on failure and one that returns a special value. In
code that must not crash on an empty queue, the second family is the one you
want.

| Operation | Throws on failure | Returns special value |
| --------- | ----------------- | --------------------- |
| Insert    | `add(e)`          | `offer(e)` -> `false` |
| Remove    | `remove()`        | `poll()` -> `null`    |
| Examine   | `element()`       | `peek()` -> `null`    |

```java
Queue<String> jobs = new ArrayDeque<>();
jobs.offer("first");
jobs.offer("second");

System.out.println(jobs.peek());   // "first": look without removing
System.out.println(jobs.poll());   // "first": look AND remove
System.out.println(jobs.poll());   // "second"
System.out.println(jobs.poll());   // null: empty, but no exception
```

A **`Deque`** ("double-ended queue", pronounced "deck") extends `Queue` and
allows insertion and removal at both ends, which makes it usable as a queue and
as a stack at once:

```text
  addFirst / offerFirst            addLast / offerLast
          |                                |
          v                                v
        [ A ][ B ][ C ][ D ]
          ^                                ^
          |                                |
  removeFirst / pollFirst          removeLast / pollLast
```

Summarising the three contracts:

| Interface | Duplicates | Ordered            | Positional access |
| --------- | ---------- | ------------------ | ----------------- |
| `List`    | Yes        | By insertion index | Yes, `get(int)`   |
| `Set`     | No         | Implementation-dependent | No          |
| `Queue`   | Yes        | By processing order | No, ends only    |

> Key Takeaways
> - Pick the interface that matches the *meaning* of your data, then worry
>   about speed.
> - `List` keeps insertion order, permits duplicates, and supports indices.
> - `Set` rejects duplicates as defined by `equals`, and has no indices.
> - `Queue` offers a throwing family (`add`/`remove`/`element`) and a
>   returning family (`offer`/`poll`/`peek`).
> - `Deque` extends `Queue` with operations at both ends, serving as both
>   queue and stack.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add the same three strings to an `ArrayList` and a `HashSet`, print both
>    sizes, and explain the difference.
> 2. Use an `ArrayDeque` to reverse a sentence by pushing each word with
>    `addFirst` and then draining it.
> 3. Interview: When would `offer` return `false` rather than throwing? (Hint:
>    think about a queue created with a fixed capacity.)

#### The Map Interface Family

A `Map<K, V>` associates unique keys with values. It is the right model
whenever your data answers a lookup question: username to account, product code
to price, word to count. Scanning a list to find a matching element is a linear
search; a hash-based map answers the same question in effectively constant
time.

Keys form a set, so each key appears at most once. Values are unconstrained and
may repeat.

```text
   KEYS (unique)          VALUES (may repeat)
   +-----------+          +--------+
   | "alice"   | -------> | 30     |
   | "bob"     | -------> | 25     |
   | "carol"   | -------> | 30     |   <- same value, different key: fine
   +-----------+          +--------+
```

The core operations:

```java
Map<String, Integer> ages = new HashMap<>();

ages.put("alice", 30);
Integer previous = ages.put("alice", 31);  // REPLACES; returns the old value 30

System.out.println(ages.get("alice"));     // 31
System.out.println(ages.get("nobody"));    // null: absent, not an exception
System.out.println(ages.containsKey("bob"));   // false
System.out.println(ages.remove("alice"));  // 31: returns what was removed
```

Because `get` returns `null` for a missing key, a map holding `null` values is
ambiguous: you cannot tell "absent" from "present but null" without calling
`containsKey`. Avoid storing `null` values, and prefer the defaulting methods
below.

Those defaulting methods, added in Java 8, remove most of the boilerplate
around "check, then act":

```java
Map<String, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();

// Read with a fallback, without writing anything
int n = counts.getOrDefault("java", 0);

// Insert only if the key is currently absent
counts.putIfAbsent("java", 1);

// Compute a new value from the old one; the classic counter idiom
counts.merge("java", 1, Integer::sum);     // absent -> 1, present -> old + 1

// Build a value lazily, only when the key is missing
Map<String, List<String>> index = new HashMap<>();
index.computeIfAbsent("j", k -> new ArrayList<>()).add("java");
```

`merge` and `computeIfAbsent` are worth memorising: the first is the standard
way to count occurrences, the second the standard way to build a multi-valued
map without a null check on every insert.

A map exposes its contents as three collection **views**. A view is not a copy;
it is a window onto the same data, so changes flow both ways.

| View          | Type              | Contains                   |
| ------------- | ----------------- | -------------------------- |
| `keySet()`    | `Set<K>`          | Every key                  |
| `values()`    | `Collection<V>`   | Every value, duplicates ok |
| `entrySet()`  | `Set<Map.Entry<K, V>>` | Key-value pairs       |

Iterating a map should almost always go through `entrySet()`, because it yields
both halves in one pass rather than calling `get` for every key:

```java
for (Map.Entry<String, Integer> entry : ages.entrySet()) {
    System.out.println(entry.getKey() + " is " + entry.getValue());
}

// Equivalent and more compact when you need no control flow
ages.forEach((name, age) -> System.out.println(name + " is " + age));
```

`SortedMap` and its subinterface `NavigableMap` extend the contract with
ordering guarantees: `firstKey()`, `lastKey()`, `headMap`, `tailMap`, and the
neighbour lookups `floorKey`, `ceilingKey`, `higherKey`, `lowerKey`. `TreeMap`
implements them, and section 7.2 covers when that is worth the extra cost.

> Key Takeaways
> - A `Map` stores unique keys mapped to values, and is the right model for any
>   lookup.
> - `put` on an existing key replaces the value and returns the old one.
> - `get` returning `null` is ambiguous when null values are stored, so do not
>   store them.
> - `getOrDefault`, `putIfAbsent`, `merge`, and `computeIfAbsent` replace most
>   check-then-act code.
> - `keySet`, `values`, and `entrySet` are live views, not copies.
> - Iterate with `entrySet()` or `forEach` rather than looking up every key.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Count word frequencies in a sentence using `merge` with `Integer::sum`.
> 2. Build a `Map<Character, List<String>>` grouping words by first letter,
>    using `computeIfAbsent`.
> 3. Interview: What is the difference between `map.get(k) == null` and
>    `!map.containsKey(k)`? (Hint: consider a map that explicitly stores a null
>    value.)

#### Iteration and the Enhanced for Loop

Every collection needs to be walked, and Java offers several ways to do it.
They are not interchangeable, and the differences show up as soon as you try to
modify the collection mid-walk.

The **enhanced `for` loop** (also called the for-each loop) is the default
choice. It reads cleanly and works on any `Iterable` and on arrays:

```java
List<String> names = List.of("Ada", "Grace", "Alan");

for (String name : names) {      // read as: "for each name in names"
    System.out.println(name);
}
```

It is pure syntactic sugar. The compiler rewrites it into the underlying
iterator protocol, which is what `Iterable` and `Iterator` exist to provide:

```java
// What the compiler actually generates
for (Iterator<String> it = names.iterator(); it.hasNext(); ) {
    String name = it.next();
    System.out.println(name);
}
```

```text
  iterator()  ->  a cursor positioned BEFORE the first element

        [ Ada ][ Grace ][ Alan ]
       ^
    cursor        hasNext() -> true, next() -> "Ada", cursor advances
```

`Iterator<E>` has three methods:

| Method      | Purpose                                              |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `hasNext()` | Is there another element?                            |
| `next()`    | Return the next element and advance                  |
| `remove()`  | Remove the element last returned by `next()`         |

`remove()` is the reason to reach for an explicit iterator: it is the only safe
way to delete elements while iterating.

```java
List<String> words = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "bb", "c", "dd"));

Iterator<String> it = words.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) {
    if (it.next().length() > 1) {
        it.remove();          // safe: the iterator knows about this change
    }
}
System.out.println(words);    // [a, c]
```

Since Java 8 there is a shorter way to express exactly that, and it is
preferable when no other logic is involved:

```java
words.removeIf(w -> w.length() > 1);   // same result, one line
```

For read-only traversal, `forEach` takes a lambda and reads well when the body
is a single action:

```java
names.forEach(System.out::println);
```

Choosing between the options:

| Style             | Use when                                          |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Enhanced `for`    | Reading every element; the default                 |
| Explicit iterator | Removing elements during the walk                  |
| `removeIf`        | Removing by a condition, with no other logic       |
| Indexed `for`     | You need the index, or are walking backwards       |
| `forEach`         | One simple action per element                      |

One caution about the indexed loop: removing inside a forward indexed loop
skips elements, because the remaining elements shift left while the index keeps
moving right.

```java
// BUG: removes "b" but skips "c", which slid into index 1
for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++) {
    if (shouldRemove(list.get(i))) {
        list.remove(i);       // no i-- compensation
    }
}
```

`List` additionally offers a `ListIterator`, which can move backwards with
`hasPrevious()`/`previous()` and can insert with `add(E)` during the walk.

> Key Takeaways
> - The enhanced `for` loop compiles down to `iterator()`, `hasNext()`, and
>   `next()`.
> - Any class implementing `Iterable` can be used with it, including your own.
> - `Iterator.remove()` is the only safe removal during an explicit iteration.
> - `removeIf` expresses conditional removal in one line and should be
>   preferred.
> - A forward indexed loop that removes elements silently skips the next one.
> - `ListIterator` adds backwards traversal and insertion, for lists only.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Rewrite an enhanced `for` loop over a `List<Integer>` as an explicit
>    iterator loop, producing identical output.
> 2. Remove every negative number from an `ArrayList<Integer>` twice, once with
>    `Iterator.remove()` and once with `removeIf`.
> 3. Make a class `Deck` implement `Iterable<Card>` so it works with the
>    enhanced `for` loop.
> 4. Interview: Why does the enhanced `for` loop not expose an index? (Hint:
>    what would an index mean for a `HashSet`?)

#### Fail-Fast Iterators and ConcurrentModificationException

Sooner or later you will write a loop that modifies the collection it is
walking and be met with `ConcurrentModificationException`. It is one of the
most common runtime surprises in Java, and it is a feature rather than a bug.

The problem it guards against: an iterator holds a position inside a structure.
If the structure changes underneath it, that position may now point at the
wrong element, past the end, or at a node that no longer exists. Rather than
quietly producing wrong results, the collections detect the change and throw
immediately. That behaviour is called **fail-fast**.

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Ada", "Grace", "Alan"));

for (String name : names) {
    if (name.startsWith("G")) {
        names.remove(name);          // structural change behind the iterator
    }
}
// Exception in thread "main" java.util.ConcurrentModificationException
```

The mechanism is a counter. Each collection keeps a `modCount` field that is
incremented on every **structural modification**, meaning any change to the
number of elements. When an iterator is created it copies that value; on every
`next()` it compares the copy with the current value.

```text
  names.iterator()     modCount = 0      expectedModCount = 0   -> ok
  it.next()            modCount = 0  ==  expectedModCount = 0   -> ok
  names.remove(...)    modCount = 1                             (iterator unaware)
  it.next()            modCount = 1  !=  expectedModCount = 0   -> THROW
```

`Iterator.remove()` avoids the exception precisely because it updates both
counters, keeping them in step.

Two details catch people out. First, the name is misleading: no second thread
is needed. The example above is single-threaded. Second, the check happens on
the *next* call to `next()`, so removing the second-to-last element can slip
through undetected, because `hasNext()` returns `false` and the loop exits
before the comparison ever runs. Do not rely on that; it is an accident of the
implementation.

Only structural changes count. Replacing a value in place is fine:

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("ada", "grace"));
for (int i = 0; i < names.size(); i++) {
    names.set(i, names.get(i).toUpperCase());   // set() is NOT structural
}
```

The four safe ways to modify while traversing:

| Approach                       | Suitable for                          |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------- |
| `Iterator.remove()`            | Removing with extra logic in the loop |
| `removeIf(predicate)`          | Removing by a condition               |
| Collect first, modify after    | Adding, or complex multi-step edits   |
| A concurrent collection        | Genuine multi-threaded access         |

```java
// Adding during iteration is impossible: collect, then apply
List<String> toAdd = new ArrayList<>();
for (String name : names) {
    if (name.length() < 4) {
        toAdd.add(name + "-short");
    }
}
names.addAll(toAdd);          // safe: iteration has finished
```

For real concurrency, `java.util.concurrent` offers **weakly consistent**
iterators instead. `CopyOnWriteArrayList` iterates over a snapshot taken when
the iterator was created, and `ConcurrentHashMap` reflects some but not
necessarily all concurrent updates. Neither throws.

```java
List<String> shared = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b"));
for (String s : shared) {
    shared.add(s + "!");      // no exception; the loop sees the old snapshot
}
```

Note the trade-off: `CopyOnWriteArrayList` copies the whole backing array on
every write, so it suits read-heavy data that changes rarely, such as listener
lists, and is a poor choice for anything write-heavy.

> Key Takeaways
> - Fail-fast iterators throw `ConcurrentModificationException` on detecting a
>   structural change.
> - The check uses a `modCount` counter compared on each `next()` call.
> - No second thread is required; the usual cause is removing inside a
>   for-each loop.
> - Structural means the size changed; `set(i, v)` is not structural.
> - `Iterator.remove()` and `removeIf` are the safe in-loop removals.
> - Concurrent collections use weakly consistent iterators that never throw,
>   at a cost in memory or freshness.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Reproduce a `ConcurrentModificationException` by removing inside a
>    for-each loop, then fix it two different ways.
> 2. Show that removing the second-to-last element sometimes does not throw,
>    and explain why using `hasNext()`.
> 3. Replace an `ArrayList` with a `CopyOnWriteArrayList` in a loop that adds
>    elements, and print the size before and after.
> 4. Interview: Why is `ConcurrentModificationException` a `RuntimeException`
>    rather than a checked exception? (Hint: is it a condition a caller can
>    recover from, or a programming mistake?)

<a id="72-collection-implementations"></a>
### 7.2 Collection Implementations

This subchapter covers the concrete classes behind the interfaces, what data
structure each one uses, and how to choose between them.

#### ArrayList and LinkedList Trade-offs

Both implement `List`, so they are interchangeable from the outside. Inside
they are entirely different, and the difference decides which one is fast for
your access pattern.

An **`ArrayList`** stores elements in a contiguous array and remembers how many
slots are in use. Reaching element `i` is one address computation.

```text
  ArrayList: one block of memory, indexed directly

  index:     0      1      2      3      4      5      6
           +------+------+------+------+------+------+------+
           | Ada  |Grace | Alan |      |      |      |      |
           +------+------+------+------+------+------+------+
             size = 3                  capacity = 7
```

When the array fills, the list allocates a larger one (roughly 1.5x) and copies
everything across. That copy is occasional, so the *amortised* cost of `add` at
the end stays constant even though a single call can be expensive.

A **`LinkedList`** stores each element in its own node carrying references to
the previous and next node. There is no array, so there is no index arithmetic:
reaching element `i` means walking `i` links.

```text
  LinkedList: scattered nodes joined by references

   head                                              tail
    |                                                  |
    v                                                  v
  +------+     +------+     +------+
  | Ada  |<--->|Grace |<--->| Alan |
  +------+     +------+     +------+
   each node: prev | value | next
```

The costs that follow from those two shapes:

| Operation                  | `ArrayList`      | `LinkedList`          |
| -------------------------- | ---------------- | --------------------- |
| `get(i)` / `set(i, v)`     | O(1)             | O(n), walks the links |
| `add(e)` at the end        | O(1) amortised   | O(1)                  |
| `add(0, e)` at the front   | O(n), shifts all | O(1)                  |
| `remove(i)` in the middle  | O(n), shifts     | O(n) to find, O(1) to unlink |
| `contains(o)`              | O(n)             | O(n)                  |
| Memory per element         | One slot         | Node with two references |

Reading that table naively suggests `LinkedList` wins on front insertion, and
it does. In practice `ArrayList` still wins nearly every real benchmark,
because the table ignores hardware. An array is contiguous, so the CPU
prefetches the next elements into cache; linked nodes are scattered across the
heap, and each hop is a potential cache miss. Copying a few thousand array
slots is often faster than following a few hundred pointers.

There is also a memory cost. Each `LinkedList` node is a separate object with
its own header plus two references, commonly around 24 extra bytes per element
on a 64-bit JVM.

The classic trap is an indexed loop over a `LinkedList`:

```java
List<String> list = new LinkedList<>(/* 100_000 elements */);

// O(n^2): every get(i) restarts the walk from the nearest end
for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++) {
    process(list.get(i));
}

// O(n): the iterator keeps its position between steps
for (String s : list) {
    process(s);
}
```

Practical guidance:

- Default to `ArrayList`. It is the right answer for the large majority of
  lists.
- If you know the final size, presize it: `new ArrayList<>(10_000)` avoids
  every intermediate copy.
- Use `ArrayDeque`, not `LinkedList`, when you need fast insertion and removal
  at both ends. It is faster and uses less memory.
- `LinkedList` earns its place mainly when you hold a `ListIterator` and splice
  elements in and out at the current position.

`Vector` is a legacy synchronised `ArrayList` kept only for compatibility. Its
locking costs on every call even in single-threaded code. Use `ArrayList`, or
`Collections.synchronizedList` or `CopyOnWriteArrayList` when you genuinely
need thread safety.

> Key Takeaways
> - `ArrayList` is a growable array; `LinkedList` is a doubly linked list.
> - `ArrayList` gives O(1) indexed access, `LinkedList` gives O(n).
> - Big-O favours `LinkedList` for front insertion, but cache locality usually
>   favours `ArrayList` anyway.
> - `LinkedList` carries roughly 24 extra bytes of node overhead per element.
> - Never use an indexed loop over a `LinkedList`; it degrades to O(n^2).
> - Default to `ArrayList`, presize it when the size is known, and avoid
>   `Vector`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Time 100,000 `add(0, x)` calls on an `ArrayList` and a `LinkedList` and
>    compare.
> 2. Time an indexed loop against an enhanced `for` loop over a 100,000-element
>    `LinkedList`.
> 3. Presize an `ArrayList` to 1,000,000 and compare the fill time against the
>    default constructor.
> 4. Interview: `LinkedList.add(0, x)` is O(1) and `ArrayList.add(0, x)` is
>    O(n), yet `ArrayList` often wins. Why? (Hint: what does the CPU cache do
>    with contiguous memory?)

#### HashSet, LinkedHashSet, and TreeSet

All three implement `Set`, so all three reject duplicates. They differ in the
iteration order they promise and in what they demand of the elements you store.

A **`HashSet`** is backed by a `HashMap` whose keys are your elements. Adding
computes `hashCode()` to pick a bucket, then compares with `equals()` inside
that bucket. Both operations are effectively O(1), and iteration order is
unspecified: it depends on hash values and table size, and can change when the
set resizes.

```java
Set<String> set = new HashSet<>();
set.add("banana");
set.add("apple");
set.add("cherry");
System.out.println(set);      // [banana, cherry, apple] -- arbitrary order
```

A **`LinkedHashSet`** extends `HashSet` with a doubly linked list threaded
through the entries, recording insertion order. Lookups stay O(1); iteration
returns elements in the order they were first added. The cost is two extra
references per element.

```java
Set<String> set = new LinkedHashSet<>();
set.add("banana");
set.add("apple");
set.add("cherry");
set.add("banana");            // ignored; does NOT move it to the end
System.out.println(set);      // [banana, apple, cherry] -- insertion order
```

A **`TreeSet`** is a red-black tree, a self-balancing binary search tree. It
keeps elements in *sorted* order rather than insertion order, which costs
O(log n) per operation but enables range queries that a hash set cannot answer
at all.

```java
Set<String> set = new TreeSet<>();
set.add("banana");
set.add("apple");
set.add("cherry");
System.out.println(set);      // [apple, banana, cherry] -- sorted
```

```text
  HashSet             LinkedHashSet           TreeSet
  buckets             buckets + a chain       balanced BST

  [0] -> apple        apple -> banana         .     banana
  [1] ->                 ^        |          .      /    \
  [2] -> cherry          |        v         .    apple  cherry
  [3] -> banana       cherry <----+
        (arbitrary)   (insertion order)     (sorted order)
```

Side by side:

| Feature          | `HashSet`      | `LinkedHashSet`  | `TreeSet`            |
| ---------------- | -------------- | ---------------- | -------------------- |
| Backing structure| Hash table     | Hash table + list| Red-black tree       |
| `add`/`contains` | O(1)           | O(1)             | O(log n)             |
| Iteration order  | Unspecified    | Insertion order  | Sorted               |
| Requires         | `hashCode`/`equals` | `hashCode`/`equals` | `Comparable` or `Comparator` |
| Allows `null`    | One            | One              | No                   |
| Memory           | Lowest         | Medium           | Highest              |

Two practical consequences of the last two rows. `TreeSet` rejects `null` with
a `NullPointerException`, because it must compare every element against
existing ones. And a `TreeSet` decides duplicates by `compareTo` returning
zero, *not* by `equals`, which means a comparator that ignores case will treat
"Java" and "java" as the same element:

```java
Set<String> ci = new TreeSet<>(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER);
ci.add("Java");
ci.add("java");
System.out.println(ci.size());   // 1: compareTo returned 0
```

`TreeSet` also implements `NavigableSet`, which is the reason to choose it when
order matters:

```java
TreeSet<Integer> scores = new TreeSet<>(List.of(10, 20, 30, 40));

System.out.println(scores.first());          // 10
System.out.println(scores.last());           // 40
System.out.println(scores.floor(25));        // 20: greatest element <= 25
System.out.println(scores.ceiling(25));      // 30: least element >= 25
System.out.println(scores.headSet(30));      // [10, 20]: strictly below
System.out.println(scores.subSet(15, 35));   // [20, 30]
System.out.println(scores.descendingSet());  // [40, 30, 20, 10]
```

Choose `HashSet` by default, `LinkedHashSet` when reproducible iteration order
matters (tests, output stability), and `TreeSet` when you need sorting or range
queries.

> Key Takeaways
> - All three forbid duplicates; they differ in ordering and in element
>   requirements.
> - `HashSet` is O(1) with unspecified, unstable iteration order.
> - `LinkedHashSet` keeps insertion order at the cost of two references per
>   element; re-adding does not reorder.
> - `TreeSet` keeps sorted order at O(log n) and supports range and neighbour
>   queries.
> - `TreeSet` rejects `null` and defines duplicates by `compareTo`, not
>   `equals`.
> - Default to `HashSet`; upgrade only when you need the extra guarantee.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add the same five strings to each of the three sets and print each one,
>    noting the orders.
> 2. Use a `TreeSet<Integer>` to find the nearest value above and below a
>    target with `ceiling` and `floor`.
> 3. Build a `TreeSet` with `String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER`, add "ABC" and
>    "abc", and explain the resulting size.
> 4. Interview: Why does `TreeSet` reject `null` when `HashSet` allows one?
>    (Hint: what happens when you call `compareTo` on a null reference?)

#### HashMap, LinkedHashMap, and TreeMap

The three map implementations mirror the three set implementations exactly,
which is not a coincidence: `HashSet` is a `HashMap` with dummy values,
`LinkedHashSet` wraps a `LinkedHashMap`, and `TreeSet` wraps a `TreeMap`.
Learning the maps gives you the sets for free.

A **`HashMap`** is an array of buckets. `put` hashes the key, spreads the bits,
masks the result to a bucket index, and stores the entry there. Collisions, two
keys landing in the same bucket, are resolved by chaining the entries together.

```text
  key "alice" -> hashCode() -> spread -> index 3

  bucket:  0     1     2     3        4     5     6     7
         +---+ +---+ +---+ +-------+ +---+ +---+ +---+ +---+
         |   | |   | |   | | alice | |   | |   | |   | |   |
         +---+ +---+ +---+ +---|---+ +---+ +---+ +---+ +---+
                                v
                            +-------+
                            | bob   |   <- collision: same bucket, chained
                            +-------+
```

Since Java 8, a bucket whose chain exceeds eight entries converts to a balanced
tree, so pathological hashing degrades to O(log n) rather than O(n). That
matters for security as much as speed, because it defends against deliberately
crafted colliding keys.

Two parameters control the table. **Capacity** is the number of buckets, always
a power of two, defaulting to 16. **Load factor** defaults to 0.75; when
`size > capacity * loadFactor` the table doubles and every entry is rehashed.
Presizing avoids those rehashes:

```java
// Expecting ~1000 entries: 1000 / 0.75 = 1334, rounded up to 2048 buckets
Map<String, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>(2048);
```

A **`LinkedHashMap`** adds insertion-order iteration, and one feature the
linked set does not expose: **access order**. Constructed with the three-
argument constructor and `accessOrder = true`, every `get` moves the entry to
the end, which makes an LRU cache about ten lines of code.

```java
// A least-recently-used cache holding at most 3 entries
Map<String, String> lru = new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) {
    @Override
    protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<String, String> eldest) {
        return size() > 3;        // evict the front entry once we exceed 3
    }
};

lru.put("a", "1");
lru.put("b", "2");
lru.put("c", "3");
lru.get("a");                     // "a" is now the most recently used
lru.put("d", "4");                // evicts "b", the least recently used
System.out.println(lru.keySet()); // [c, a, d]
```

A **`TreeMap`** is a red-black tree keyed by sort order, implementing
`NavigableMap`. Every operation is O(log n), and it answers questions no hash
map can:

```java
TreeMap<Integer, String> grades = new TreeMap<>();
grades.put(60, "D");
grades.put(70, "C");
grades.put(80, "B");
grades.put(90, "A");

System.out.println(grades.firstKey());        // 60
System.out.println(grades.floorEntry(85));    // 80=B: the grade for a score 85
System.out.println(grades.headMap(80));       // {60=D, 70=C}
System.out.println(grades.descendingMap());   // {90=A, 80=B, 70=C, 60=D}
```

That `floorEntry` call is the idiomatic way to implement range lookups such as
tax brackets, shipping tiers, or grade boundaries.

| Feature         | `HashMap`   | `LinkedHashMap`   | `TreeMap`        |
| --------------- | ----------- | ----------------- | ---------------- |
| Structure       | Hash table  | Hash table + list | Red-black tree   |
| `get`/`put`     | O(1)        | O(1)              | O(log n)         |
| Key order       | Unspecified | Insertion or access | Sorted         |
| Null keys       | One allowed | One allowed       | Not allowed      |
| Null values     | Allowed     | Allowed           | Allowed          |
| Extra feature   | -           | LRU eviction      | Range queries    |

`Hashtable` is the legacy synchronised equivalent of `HashMap` and should not
be used. For concurrent access use `ConcurrentHashMap`, which locks only
individual bins rather than the whole table and scales far better.

> Key Takeaways
> - The three maps mirror the three sets, because the sets are implemented on
>   top of them.
> - `HashMap` uses buckets with chaining, converting long chains to trees after
>   eight entries.
> - Capacity 16 and load factor 0.75 are the defaults; presize to avoid
>   rehashing.
> - `LinkedHashMap` supports access order, giving an LRU cache via
>   `removeEldestEntry`.
> - `TreeMap` is sorted, O(log n), forbids null keys, and supports `floorEntry`
>   style range lookups.
> - Prefer `ConcurrentHashMap` over the legacy `Hashtable` for thread safety.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Insert ten entries into each map type and print `keySet()` for each,
>    noting the ordering.
> 2. Implement a fixed-size LRU cache with `LinkedHashMap` and verify the
>    eviction order.
> 3. Model tax brackets in a `TreeMap<Integer, Double>` and look up the rate
>    for an arbitrary income with `floorEntry`.
> 4. Interview: Why is `HashMap` capacity always a power of two? (Hint: how can
>    a modulo by a power of two be computed with a bitmask?)

#### ArrayDeque, Stack, and PriorityQueue

Three implementations for processing order rather than storage order. Each
answers a different question about which element comes next.

An **`ArrayDeque`** is a resizable circular array supporting insertion and
removal at both ends in O(1). It is the recommended implementation of both
`Queue` and `Deque`, and therefore also the recommended stack.

```text
  Circular array: head and tail move, elements never shift

   indices:   0     1     2     3     4     5
            +-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+
            |  D  |     |     |  A  |  B  |  C  |
            +-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+
                              ^                 wraps around to index 0
                            head        tail ---+
   logical order: A, B, C, D
```

Used as a FIFO queue:

```java
Deque<String> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
queue.offer("first");           // adds at the tail
queue.offer("second");
System.out.println(queue.poll());   // "first": removes from the head
```

Used as a LIFO stack:

```java
Deque<String> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
stack.push("first");            // push == addFirst
stack.push("second");
System.out.println(stack.pop());    // "second": pop == removeFirst
System.out.println(stack.peek());   // "first": top without removing
```

`ArrayDeque` rejects `null`, and that is intentional: `poll` and `peek` return
`null` to signal emptiness, so a stored `null` would be indistinguishable from
an empty deque.

**`Stack`** is a legacy class extending `Vector`. Avoid it in new code for two
reasons. It is synchronised, paying for locks you almost never need. More
confusingly, it inherits `Vector`'s list behaviour, so it exposes `get(int)`
and iterates *bottom to top*, the opposite of pop order.

```java
Stack<String> legacy = new Stack<>();
legacy.push("a");
legacy.push("b");
System.out.println(legacy);      // [a, b]: prints bottom-first, not pop order
System.out.println(legacy.get(0));  // "a": a stack should not have indices
```

A **`PriorityQueue`** returns the *smallest* element next rather than the
oldest. It is a binary heap stored in an array: the root is the minimum, and
each node is smaller than its children.

```text
  Binary min-heap, and its array layout

              1
            /   \
           3     2         array: [1, 3, 2, 7, 4]
          / \   /          parent of i = (i-1)/2
         7   4             children of i = 2i+1, 2i+2
```

```java
PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>();
pq.offer(5);
pq.offer(1);
pq.offer(3);

System.out.println(pq.poll());   // 1: always the smallest
System.out.println(pq.poll());   // 3
System.out.println(pq);          // [5]
```

A comparator flips or customises the ordering, which is how you build a
max-heap or prioritise by a field:

```java
// Max-heap
PriorityQueue<Integer> max = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());

// Highest-priority task first, breaking ties by name
PriorityQueue<Task> tasks =
    new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingInt(Task::priority).reversed()
                                  .thenComparing(Task::name));
```

The single most common mistake is expecting the whole queue to be sorted. It is
not. A heap only guarantees the *head*; printing it or iterating it yields heap
array order, which is partially sorted at best. Sorted output requires draining
it with repeated `poll()` calls.

| Implementation  | `offer`   | `poll`    | `peek` | Next element is     |
| --------------- | --------- | --------- | ------ | ------------------- |
| `ArrayDeque`    | O(1)      | O(1)      | O(1)   | Oldest, or newest   |
| `PriorityQueue` | O(log n)  | O(log n)  | O(1)   | Smallest by order   |
| `LinkedList`    | O(1)      | O(1)      | O(1)   | Oldest              |

> Key Takeaways
> - `ArrayDeque` is the default choice for both queues and stacks, at O(1) on
>   both ends.
> - It forbids `null` so that a `null` from `poll` unambiguously means empty.
> - The legacy `Stack` extends `Vector`, is synchronised, and iterates in the
>   wrong direction.
> - `PriorityQueue` is a binary heap returning the smallest element, O(log n)
>   per insert and remove.
> - A `PriorityQueue` is not sorted; only its head is guaranteed.
> - Pass a `Comparator` to build a max-heap or to order by a field.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Check whether a string of brackets is balanced using an `ArrayDeque` as a
>    stack.
> 2. Find the three largest numbers in a list using a size-bounded
>    `PriorityQueue`.
> 3. Print a `PriorityQueue` directly and then drain it with `poll`, and
>    explain why the two orders differ.
> 4. Interview: Why does `ArrayDeque` forbid null elements? (Hint: what would
>    `poll()` returning `null` then mean?)

#### Choosing an Implementation by Complexity

With roughly a dozen implementations available, the choice can feel arbitrary.
It is not. Two questions settle it almost every time, and only the second
involves performance.

**Question one: what shape is the data?**

```text
  Do you look things up by a key?
      |
      +-- YES --> Map
      |
      +-- NO --> Must duplicates be rejected?
                     |
                     +-- YES --> Set
                     |
                     +-- NO --> Do you take elements in a processing order?
                                    |
                                    +-- YES --> Queue / Deque
                                    |
                                    +-- NO --> List
```

**Question two: what guarantee do you need on order?** Within each family,
"no guarantee" is fastest, "insertion order" costs a little memory, and "sorted"
costs a logarithmic factor.

| Need                     | List        | Set             | Map             |
| ------------------------ | ----------- | --------------- | --------------- |
| Fastest, order irrelevant| `ArrayList` | `HashSet`       | `HashMap`       |
| Insertion order kept     | `ArrayList` | `LinkedHashSet` | `LinkedHashMap` |
| Sorted order             | sort a list | `TreeSet`       | `TreeMap`       |
| Both ends fast           | `ArrayDeque`| -               | -               |
| Thread-safe              | `CopyOnWriteArrayList` | `ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()` | `ConcurrentHashMap` |

The consolidated complexity table, worth committing to memory for interviews:

| Implementation  | Access by index | Search   | Insert         | Delete   |
| --------------- | --------------- | -------- | -------------- | -------- |
| `ArrayList`     | O(1)            | O(n)     | O(1) amortised at end | O(n) |
| `LinkedList`    | O(n)            | O(n)     | O(1) at ends   | O(1) at a known node |
| `ArrayDeque`    | -               | O(n)     | O(1) at ends   | O(1) at ends |
| `HashSet`       | -               | O(1)     | O(1)           | O(1)     |
| `LinkedHashSet` | -               | O(1)     | O(1)           | O(1)     |
| `TreeSet`       | -               | O(log n) | O(log n)       | O(log n) |
| `HashMap`       | -               | O(1)     | O(1)           | O(1)     |
