serialisable, and it does not prevent the field itself being null:

```java
public class User {
    private Optional<String> nickname;    // WRONG: wasteful and not serialisable
    private String nickname2;             // right: null means absent internally

    public Optional<String> getNickname() {
        return Optional.ofNullable(nickname2);   // wrap at the boundary
    }
}
```

**Do not use `Optional` as a method parameter.** It forces every caller to wrap
their argument, and the parameter can still be passed `null`:

```java
// WRONG: callers must write findUser(Optional.of(name))
public List<User> findUser(Optional<String> name) { ... }

// Right: overload, or accept null with a documented contract
public List<User> findUser(String name) { ... }
public List<User> findAllUsers() { ... }
```

**Never return a null `Optional`.** It is the worst of both worlds, since
callers reasonably assume a non-null container:

```java
public Optional<User> find(String id) {
    if (id == null) return null;          // WRONG
    return Optional.empty();              // right
}
```

**Do not use `Optional` for collections.** An empty collection already
expresses "nothing here", so an `Optional<List<T>>` gives callers two ways to
say the same thing:

```java
public Optional<List<User>> getUsers()  // WRONG: two empty states
public List<User> getUsers()            // right: return an empty list
```

**Do not wrap a value just to unwrap it immediately.** This adds allocation and
indirection for nothing:

```java
// WRONG
String result = Optional.ofNullable(value).orElse("default");
// Simpler and faster
String result2 = value != null ? value : "default";
```

The wrap is worth it only when a chain of transformations follows.

**Avoid `isPresent` followed by `get`**, which was covered earlier but is worth
repeating because it is the most common misuse of all:

```java
// WRONG: a null check with extra steps
if (opt.isPresent()) { process(opt.get()); }

// Right
opt.ifPresent(this::process);
```

**Avoid `Optional` in performance-critical inner loops.** Each one is a heap
allocation, so in a tight numeric loop the overhead is real. Use it at API
boundaries, not per iteration.

Summarised:

| Context                  | Use `Optional`? | Instead                       |
| ------------------------ | --------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Return type, may be absent | Yes           | -                             |
| Instance field           | No              | A nullable field, wrapped in the getter |
| Method parameter         | No              | Overloads, or a nullable parameter |
| Collection return type   | No              | An empty collection           |
| Returning null itself    | Never           | `Optional.empty()`            |
| Hot inner loop           | No              | Plain null checks             |
| Chained transformations  | Yes             | -                             |

Two final points. `Optional` is a **value-based class**, so never synchronise
on one and never compare with `==`; use `equals`, which compares the contained
values. And `Optional` does not remove the need for judgement about nulls
inside your own data structures. It documents a contract at a boundary; it is
not a null-safety system for the whole program.

```java
Optional<String> a = Optional.of("x");
Optional<String> b = Optional.of("x");
System.out.println(a == b);        // false, and not guaranteed either way
System.out.println(a.equals(b));   // true: compares the contents
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `Optional` was designed as a return type for methods that may have no
>   result.
> - Do not use it for fields; it wastes memory and is not serialisable.
> - Do not use it for parameters; use overloads instead.
> - Never return a null `Optional`; return `Optional.empty()`.
> - Return an empty collection rather than an `Optional` of a collection.
> - Wrapping only to call `orElse` immediately is worse than a ternary.
> - Replace `isPresent` plus `get` with `ifPresent`, `map`, or `orElseThrow`.
> - It is a value-based class, so compare with `equals` and never synchronise
>   on it.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Review a class with nullable fields and convert only the getters to return
>    `Optional`.
> 2. Rewrite a method taking `Optional<String>` as two overloads.
> 3. Find an `Optional.ofNullable(x).orElse(y)` in your code and simplify it.
> 4. Interview: Why is `Optional` discouraged as a field type? (Hint: consider
>    memory per instance, and what happens when the object is serialised.)

<a id="9-object-oriented-design-principles-and-patterns"></a>
## 9. Object-Oriented Design Principles and Patterns

Knowing the language is not the same as knowing how to arrange code so it can
be changed six months later by someone else. This chapter covers the vocabulary
of good design: the quality measures that tell you whether a class is well
shaped, the SOLID principles that turn those measures into rules, the classic
patterns that recur across every codebase, and the UML notation used to discuss
all of it on a whiteboard. None of it is Java-specific, but Java's type system
is what makes the patterns expressible, and interviews assume you know them.

<a id="91-design-quality-fundamentals"></a>
### 9.1 Design Quality Fundamentals

This subchapter covers the measures that distinguish maintainable code from
code that merely works, and the warning signs that a design is decaying.

#### Cohesion and Coupling

Every design discussion eventually reduces to two questions. Does this class do
one job? And how many other classes does it drag along with it? Those are
**cohesion** and **coupling**, and they are the foundation everything else in
this chapter builds on.

**Cohesion** measures how closely the parts of a class belong together. High
cohesion means every field and method serves one clear purpose. Low cohesion
means the class is a drawer where unrelated things were dropped because there
was nowhere else to put them.

```java
// LOW cohesion: three unrelated jobs in one class
public class UserManager {
    public void saveUser(User u) { /* database code */ }
    public void sendWelcomeEmail(User u) { /* SMTP code */ }
    public String formatUserAsHtml(User u) { /* rendering code */ }
    public boolean validatePassword(String p) { /* security rules */ }
}

// HIGH cohesion: each class has one reason to exist
public class UserRepository { public void save(User u) { } }
public class EmailService    { public void sendWelcome(User u) { } }
public class UserRenderer    { public String toHtml(User u) { } }
public class PasswordPolicy  { public boolean isValid(String p) { } }
```

A quick test: try to describe the class in one sentence without using "and" or
"or". If you cannot, cohesion is low.

**Coupling** measures how much one class depends on the internals of another.
Low coupling means a class can be understood, tested, and changed without
dragging half the codebase with it.

```java
// TIGHT coupling: OrderService creates and depends on a concrete class
public class OrderService {
    private final MySqlOrderRepository repo = new MySqlOrderRepository();
    // Cannot test without a real MySQL instance.
    // Cannot switch databases without editing this class.
}

// LOOSE coupling: depends on an interface, receives it from outside
public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repo;          // an interface

    public OrderService(OrderRepository repo) {  // injected by the caller
        this.repo = repo;
    }
}
```

```text
   TIGHT COUPLING                   LOOSE COUPLING

   OrderService                     OrderService
        |                                |
        | new MySqlOrderRepository()     | depends on
        v                                v
   MySqlOrderRepository             OrderRepository (interface)
                                         ^        ^
                                         |        |
                                    MySql...   InMemory... (for tests)
```

The two measures pull in the same direction, and the standard formulation is
**high cohesion, low coupling**. They are related: splitting a low-cohesion
class into focused pieces usually lowers coupling too, because each piece now
needs fewer collaborators.

Degrees of coupling, from worst to best:

| Level             | Description                                 | Example                        |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Content           | One class modifies another's internals      | Reaching into a public field   |
| Common            | Shared global mutable state                 | A mutable `static` singleton   |
| Control           | A flag argument tells the callee what to do | `process(data, true)`          |
| Stamp             | Passing a whole object when one field suffices | `calc(order)` needing only total |
| Data              | Passing exactly the needed values           | `calc(total, rate)`            |
| Interface-only    | Depending on an abstraction                 | Constructor-injected interface |

Some coupling is unavoidable and desirable. A class with zero dependencies does
nothing useful. The goal is to depend on **stable abstractions** rather than on
volatile implementations.

Practical signals of trouble:

- A method that uses fields of another object more than its own belongs on that
  object.
- A change to one class forces edits in five others.
- A unit test needs six mocks before it can run.
- A class name contains "Manager", "Processor", "Util", or "Helper", which
  often signals no single responsibility was ever identified.

> Key Takeaways
> - Cohesion measures whether a class's parts serve one purpose.
> - Coupling measures how much a class depends on other classes' internals.
> - The goal is high cohesion and low coupling; improving one usually improves
>   the other.
> - Depend on interfaces you own rather than on concrete implementations.
> - Describing a class without "and" is a quick cohesion test.
> - Names like Manager and Util often mark a class with no real
>   responsibility.
> - Zero coupling is not the aim; depending on stable abstractions is.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Find a class in your code with four or more unrelated methods and split
>    it.
> 2. Replace a `new ConcreteThing()` inside a class with a constructor
>    parameter typed as an interface.
> 3. Rate three of your classes on the coupling table above and justify each.
> 4. Interview: Can coupling ever be too low? (Hint: what happens to a system
>    made entirely of classes that know nothing about each other?)

#### Separation of Concerns

A **concern** is one area of responsibility: persistence, validation,
presentation, business rules, logging. Separation of concerns says each should
live in its own place, so a change to one does not require understanding the
others.

The motivation is human, not technical. A class mixing four concerns must be
read in full before any part of it can be safely changed, and four different
reasons to change it means four different people editing the same file.

Consider a method that mixes everything:

```java
public class OrderProcessor {
    public String process(String json) {
        // 1. Parsing (input format concern)
        Order order = new Gson().fromJson(json, Order.class);

        // 2. Validation (business rules concern)
        if (order.getItems().isEmpty()) return "<error>empty order</error>";

        // 3. Calculation (domain concern)
        double total = 0;
        for (Item i : order.getItems()) total += i.getPrice() * i.getQty();
        if (total > 100) total *= 0.9;

        // 4. Persistence (infrastructure concern)
        Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection("jdbc:...");
        // ... SQL ...

        // 5. Presentation (output format concern)
        return "<order><total>" + total + "</total></order>";
    }
}
```

Changing the output from XML to JSON means editing a class that also holds tax
rules and SQL. Testing the discount rule requires a live database.

Separated, each concern becomes independently testable:

```java
public class OrderParser    { public Order parse(String json) { } }
public class OrderValidator { public void validate(Order o) { } }
public class PricingService { public Money total(Order o) { } }   // pure logic
public class OrderRepository{ public void save(Order o) { } }
public class OrderRenderer  { public String render(Order o) { } }

// The coordinator does no work of its own; it only sequences the steps
public class OrderProcessor {
    private final OrderParser parser;
    private final OrderValidator validator;
    private final PricingService pricing;
    private final OrderRepository repository;
    private final OrderRenderer renderer;

    public String process(String json) {
        Order order = parser.parse(json);
        validator.validate(order);
        order.setTotal(pricing.total(order));
        repository.save(order);
        return renderer.render(order);
    }
}
```

The usual large-scale expression of this is **layering**:

```text
   +-------------------------------+
   |  Presentation (controllers)   |  HTTP, formatting
   +-------------------------------+
                 |  depends on
   +-------------------------------+
   |  Application (services)       |  use cases, orchestration
   +-------------------------------+
                 |  depends on
   +-------------------------------+
   |  Domain (entities, rules)     |  business logic, no frameworks
   +-------------------------------+
                 ^  implemented by
   +-------------------------------+
   |  Infrastructure (repositories)|  database, network, files
   +-------------------------------+
```

The key rule is that dependencies point **inward**. The domain layer knows
nothing about HTTP or SQL, which is what lets business rules be tested with
plain unit tests and reused behind a different interface.

Two cautions. First, separation has a cost: five classes are more files to
navigate than one, so split along real concern boundaries rather than
mechanically. Second, a coordinator that only delegates is fine and is not a
"useless" class; sequencing steps is itself a responsibility.

> Key Takeaways
> - A concern is one area of responsibility, such as persistence or
>   presentation.
> - Mixing concerns means every change requires understanding unrelated code.
> - Separated concerns can be tested independently, without databases or
>   frameworks.
> - Layering expresses the idea at architecture scale.
> - Dependencies should point inward, toward the domain, never outward.
> - A coordinating class that only sequences steps is legitimate.
> - Split along genuine boundaries; splitting for its own sake adds
>   navigation cost.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Take a method that parses, validates, and saves, and extract three
>    classes.
> 2. Write a unit test for extracted business logic with no database
>    involved.
> 3. Draw the layer diagram for a project you know and mark any inward-pointing
>    violations.
> 4. Interview: Why should the domain layer not import a database library?
>    (Hint: what happens to your business rules when the database is
>    replaced?)

#### Law of Demeter

The Law of Demeter, also called the principle of least knowledge, is a concrete
rule for limiting coupling: **talk only to your immediate friends**. An object
should call methods on itself, on its own fields, on its parameters, and on
objects it creates, but not on objects it reached through someone else.

The informal version is "one dot", and the symptom is a chain of calls:

```java
// Violation: reaching three objects deep
String city = order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCity().getName();
```

That single line couples the caller to `Order`, `Customer`, `Address`, and
`City`. Renaming a method on any of the four breaks it, and it cannot be
tested without constructing the whole graph.

```text
   VIOLATION: the caller knows the whole chain

   Caller ----> Order ----> Customer ----> Address ----> City
     |                                                     ^
     +-----------------------------------------------------+
            depends on all four types

   COMPLIANT: each object asks only its neighbour

   Caller ----> Order.getCityName()
                  |
                  +--> Customer.getCityName()
                          |
                          +--> Address.getCityName()
```

The fix is to push the behaviour down, so each object answers for its own part:

```java
public class Order {
    private final Customer customer;
    public String getCityName() { return customer.getCityName(); }  // delegate
}

public class Customer {
    private final Address address;
    public String getCityName() { return address.getCityName(); }
}

// The caller now knows only Order
String city = order.getCityName();
```

The deeper reformulation is **Tell, Don't Ask**. Rather than pulling data out
of an object to make a decision about it, tell the object to make the decision.

```java
// ASK: the caller extracts state and decides
if (account.getBalance() >= amount) {
    account.setBalance(account.getBalance() - amount);
}

// TELL: the account enforces its own invariant
account.withdraw(amount);     // throws or returns a result if insufficient
```

The second version keeps the rule inside the class that owns the data, which is
what encapsulation was for in the first place.

Formally, a method `m` of class `C` may call methods on:

| Allowed target              | Example                      |
| --------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `this`                      | `this.validate()`            |
| Fields of `C`               | `repository.save(x)`         |
| Parameters of `m`           | `order.total()`              |
| Objects created inside `m`  | `new Formatter().format(x)`  |
| Static/global objects       | `Logger.info(...)`           |

Two important exceptions, or the rule becomes absurd.

**Fluent interfaces and builders** chain deliberately, and each call returns
the same conceptual object:

```java
String s = new StringBuilder().append("a").append("b").toString();   // fine

Comparator<Person> c = Comparator.comparing(Person::getName)
                                 .thenComparing(Person::getAge);     // fine
```

**Streams** chain by design as well. The distinguishing question is whether
each dot navigates to a *different* object with its own identity, or continues
working with the same one. Navigation is the violation; fluent chaining is not.

**Data Transfer Objects** are the third exception. A structure whose entire
purpose is to carry fields, such as a JSON payload or a record, has no
behaviour to tell, so reading `dto.getUser().getName()` is acceptable.

The cost of the law is delegation methods, sometimes called "middle man"
methods. Applied without judgement it produces classes full of one-line
forwards. Apply it where a chain crosses a meaningful boundary, not
everywhere.

> Key Takeaways
> - Call methods only on yourself, your fields, your parameters, and objects
>   you create.
> - Long navigation chains couple the caller to every type in the chain.
> - Fix them by delegating, so each object answers for its own neighbour.
> - Tell, Don't Ask puts decisions inside the object that owns the data.
> - Fluent builders and streams are not violations, because they stay on one
>   conceptual object.
> - Data transfer objects are exempt, since they hold no behaviour.
> - Over-applying the law produces a layer of pointless forwarding methods.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Find a three-dot chain in your code and remove it by adding a delegating
>    method.
> 2. Rewrite an "ask then set" block as a single "tell" method on the object.
> 3. Explain why `list.stream().filter(...).count()` does not violate the law.
> 4. Interview: What is the cost of following the Law of Demeter strictly?
>    (Hint: count the methods you must add to each class in the chain.)

#### DRY, KISS, and YAGNI

Three slogans encode most of what experienced developers mean by "keep it
clean". They are simple to state and routinely misapplied, so the useful part
is knowing their limits.

**DRY**, Don't Repeat Yourself, is often quoted as "never copy and paste code".
The original formulation is more precise and more useful: *every piece of
knowledge should have a single authoritative representation in the system.*
The target is duplicated **knowledge**, not duplicated **text**.

```java
// Duplicated knowledge: the VAT rate lives in three places
public double invoiceTotal(double net)  { return net * 1.21; }
public double quoteTotal(double net)    { return net * 1.21; }
public double receiptTotal(double net)  { return net * 1.21; }

// Single source of truth: one place changes when the rate does
public final class Tax {
    public static final double VAT_RATE = 0.21;
    public static double withVat(double net) { return net * (1 + VAT_RATE); }
}
```

The misapplication is merging code that merely *looks* alike:

```java
// These two methods look alike but encode DIFFERENT rules
public double employeeDiscount(double p) { return p * 0.9; }   // staff policy
public double clearanceDiscount(double p) { return p * 0.9; }  // stock policy
```

Merging them couples two independent policies. When the staff discount changes
to 15 percent, you discover the coupling the hard way. The test is whether the
two would always change together, for the same reason. If not, the duplication
is coincidental and should stay.

**KISS**, Keep It Simple, favours the most obvious implementation that solves
the problem. Cleverness is a cost paid by every future reader:

```java
// Clever: hard to read, hard to modify
return items.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(i -> i.getType().name()
        .charAt(0), TreeMap::new, Collectors.mapping(Item::getName,
        Collectors.joining(","))));

// Simple: three named steps, each obvious
Map<Character, List<Item>> byInitial = groupByTypeInitial(items);
Map<Character, String> names = joinNames(byInitial);
return new TreeMap<>(names);
```

Simplicity is not the same as brevity. A one-liner that needs a comment to
explain it is less simple than three named lines that do not.

**YAGNI**, You Aren't Gonna Need It, says do not build for requirements you
only imagine. Speculative generality costs immediately and usually never pays
off:

```java
// Speculative: one implementation, a factory, and an interface,
// for a system that will only ever send email
public interface NotificationChannel { void send(Message m); }
public class NotificationChannelFactory { ... }
public class EmailChannel implements NotificationChannel { ... }

// YAGNI: start here. Extract the interface when the SECOND channel arrives.
public class EmailSender { public void send(Message m) { ... } }
```

The three interact, and sometimes conflict:

| Principle | Says                          | Overdone produces               |
| --------- | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| DRY       | One home per piece of knowledge | Wrong abstractions that couple unrelated code |
| KISS      | Prefer the obvious solution   | Under-engineering, copy-paste sprawl |
| YAGNI     | Build only what is needed now | Rewrites when a known requirement arrives |

DRY pushes toward abstraction; KISS and YAGNI push back. The resolution is the
**rule of three**: duplicate once without concern, and extract an abstraction
on the third occurrence, when you can actually see what varies. Abstracting
from a single example produces an abstraction shaped by a guess.

A useful counterweight, often attributed to Sandi Metz: duplication is far
cheaper than the wrong abstraction. Undoing a bad merge is harder than merging
two copies later.

> Key Takeaways
> - DRY targets duplicated knowledge, not duplicated characters.
> - Two similar methods encoding different rules should stay separate.
> - KISS prefers the obvious solution; simple is not the same as short.
> - YAGNI rejects building for imagined future requirements.
> - The principles conflict: DRY abstracts, KISS and YAGNI resist.
> - The rule of three delays extraction until the variation is visible.
> - The wrong abstraction costs more than the duplication it removed.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Find a magic number appearing in three places and give it one home.
> 2. Find two similar methods and argue whether they encode the same knowledge.
> 3. Identify an interface in your code with exactly one implementation and
>    decide whether it earns its place.
> 4. Interview: When is duplication better than abstraction? (Hint: what
>    happens when two merged rules later need to diverge?)

#### Programming to an Interface

"Program to an interface, not an implementation" is the oldest rule in the
patterns literature, and nearly every pattern in this chapter is an application
of it. The idea is to depend on *what* something does, never on *how* it does
it.

The problem it addresses is that concrete types leak decisions:

```java
public class ReportService {
    // Declares the exact class, so the whole method is welded to it
    public void generate(ArrayList<Sale> sales, MySqlConnection conn) { ... }
}
```

Callers holding a `LinkedList` cannot use this method, and a test cannot run
without MySQL, even though neither detail matters to report generation.

Declaring the abstraction instead removes both problems:

```java
public class ReportService {
    public void generate(List<Sale> sales, DataSource source) { ... }
}
```

```text
   CONCRETE DEPENDENCY              ABSTRACT DEPENDENCY

   ReportService                    ReportService
        |                                |
        v                                v
   MySqlConnection                  DataSource (interface)
                                      ^      ^       ^
                                      |      |       |
                                   MySql  Postgres  FakeForTests
```

The rule has three everyday applications.

**Declare variables, parameters, and return types with the most general type
that suffices:**

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();       // not ArrayList<String> names
Map<String, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();

public Collection<Order> findAll() { ... }    // free to change the container
public void process(Iterable<Order> orders) { ... }
```

**Inject dependencies rather than constructing them**, so the choice is made
by the caller and can differ in tests:

```java
public class OrderService {
    private final PaymentGateway gateway;       // an interface

    public OrderService(PaymentGateway gateway) { this.gateway = gateway; }
}

new OrderService(new StripeGateway());       // production
new OrderService(new FakeGateway());         // test, no network
```

**Return abstractions**, so a later change of implementation is invisible:

```java
// Returning ArrayList commits you forever; callers may depend on it
public ArrayList<Order> findAll() { ... }    // avoid

public List<Order> findAll() { ... }         // free to return List.of(...)
```

The limits are worth stating, because the rule is sometimes applied
mechanically.

An interface with exactly one implementation, created only because "interfaces
are good practice", is speculative generality and YAGNI applies. Extract the
interface when a second implementation appears, or when you need a test double
that cannot otherwise exist.

Sometimes the concrete type *is* the contract. If a method genuinely requires
the O(1) indexed access that `ArrayList` provides, or must return a modifiable
list, say so. Widening the type there would be dishonest.

And the most general type is not always the right one. Declaring a parameter as
`Object` because it is the most abstract choice is not programming to an
interface; it is discarding type information.

| Instead of declaring | Prefer         | Reason                       |
| -------------------- | -------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `ArrayList<T>`       | `List<T>`      | Free to change implementation |
| `HashMap<K, V>`      | `Map<K, V>`    | Same                          |
| `MySqlRepository`    | `Repository`   | Testable, swappable           |
| `FileInputStream`    | `InputStream`  | Works with any source         |
| `ArrayList<T>` param | `Collection<T>`| Accepts more callers          |

> Key Takeaways
> - Depend on what a type does, not on how it does it.
> - Declare variables, parameters, and return types with the general type.
> - Inject dependencies so callers and tests choose the implementation.
> - Returning a concrete collection type commits you to it permanently.
> - An interface with one implementation and no test need is speculative.
> - State the concrete type when its specific guarantees are genuinely
>   required.
> - Using `Object` everywhere is not abstraction; it is losing type
>   information.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Change three field declarations from concrete collection types to
>    interfaces.
> 2. Refactor a class that calls `new` on a dependency to receive it via the
>    constructor.
> 3. Write a fake implementation of a repository interface and test a service
>    with it.
> 4. Interview: When is depending on a concrete class the right choice? (Hint:
>    consider a method whose correctness relies on O(1) random access.)

#### Code Smells and Refactoring Triggers

A **code smell** is a surface symptom suggesting a deeper design problem. It is
not a bug: the code works. It is a signal that the structure will make the next
change expensive. Learning the catalogue gives you a vocabulary for saying what
is wrong in a review, rather than "this feels bad".

The most common smells, with their usual cure:

| Smell                   | Symptom                                    | Typical refactoring           |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------- |
| Long Method             | Cannot be seen on one screen               | Extract Method                |
| Large Class             | Dozens of fields, many responsibilities    | Extract Class                 |
| Long Parameter List     | Five or more parameters                    | Introduce Parameter Object    |
| Duplicated Code         | The same knowledge in several places       | Extract Method or Superclass  |
| Feature Envy            | A method uses another object's data more than its own | Move Method        |
| Data Clumps             | The same fields travel together everywhere | Extract Class                 |
| Primitive Obsession     | `String` and `int` where a type belongs    | Replace with a value type     |
| Switch on Type          | `switch` over a type code, repeated        | Replace with polymorphism     |
| Shotgun Surgery         | One change forces edits in many classes    | Move related behaviour together |
| Divergent Change        | One class changes for many reasons         | Extract Class                 |
| Message Chains          | `a.getB().getC().getD()`                   | Hide Delegate                 |
| Speculative Generality  | Abstractions with one user                 | Inline and delete             |
| Temporary Field         | A field set only during one operation      | Extract Method Object         |

Three worth seeing in code.

**Primitive obsession** uses built-in types where a domain concept belongs,
which loses validation and allows nonsense:

```java
// Anything can be passed; nothing is validated; order is easy to confuse
public void transfer(String fromIban, String toIban, double amount,
                     String currency) { }

transfer(to, from, -50, "euros");      // compiles, all four are wrong

// A value type validates once and makes misuse impossible
public record Iban(String value) {
    public Iban {
        if (!value.matches("[A-Z]{2}\\d{2}[A-Z0-9]+"))
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("invalid IBAN");
    }
}
public record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) { }

public void transfer(Iban from, Iban to, Money amount) { }
```

**Switch on type** duplicates the same branching in every new method, and every
added type requires finding all of them:

```java
// Every new shape means editing every switch in the codebase
public double area(Shape s) {
    switch (s.getType()) {
        case CIRCLE: return Math.PI * s.getRadius() * s.getRadius();
        case SQUARE: return s.getSide() * s.getSide();
    }
    throw new IllegalArgumentException();
}

// Polymorphism: a new shape is a new class, and nothing else changes
public interface Shape { double area(); }
public record Circle(double radius) implements Shape {
    public double area() { return Math.PI * radius * radius; }
}
```

**Feature envy** means the method is on the wrong class:

```java
// This method touches only Address fields: it belongs on Address
public class Invoice {
    public String formatAddress(Address a) {
        return a.getStreet() + ", " + a.getCity() + " " + a.getPostcode();
    }
}
```

Knowing when *not* to refactor matters as much. Useful triggers:

- You are about to change code and the smell is in your way.
- The same smell has caused a bug more than once.
- A new requirement does not fit the current structure.

Poor triggers are "it is not how I would have written it" and "this file is
old". Refactoring without tests is rewriting, and refactoring code nobody
touches spends effort for no return.

The discipline is: make the change easy, then make the easy change. Refactor
first so the feature becomes simple, rather than forcing a feature into a bad
structure and leaving it worse.

> Key Takeaways
> - A smell is a symptom of a design problem, not a bug.
> - The catalogue gives shared vocabulary for code review.
> - Primitive obsession loses validation that a small value type would
>   enforce.
> - Repeated switching on a type code should become polymorphism.
> - Feature envy means the method sits on the wrong class.
> - Refactor when a smell blocks a change you are making, not on sight.
> - Refactoring requires tests; without them it is an unverified rewrite.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Identify three smells in a file you did not write and name the refactoring
>    for each.
> 2. Replace a `String` parameter that has validation rules with a record value
>    type.
> 3. Convert a `switch` over an enum type code into polymorphic classes.
> 4. Interview: Why is Shotgun Surgery the opposite of Divergent Change?
>    (Hint: in each case, count the classes touched by one change and the
>    reasons one class changes.)

<a id="92-solid-principles"></a>
### 9.2 SOLID Principles

This subchapter covers the five principles that turn the vague goals of the
previous section into concrete rules for shaping classes and dependencies.

#### Single Responsibility Principle

The first principle is the most quoted and the most misunderstood. It is
usually stated as "a class should do one thing", which invites arguments about
what counts as one thing. Robert Martin's sharper formulation is:

> A class should have one, and only one, reason to change.

The shift from "one thing" to "one reason to change" makes it testable. A
reason to change corresponds to a **stakeholder** or an area of the business
that can issue a request. If the accounting department and the IT operations
team can each independently force an edit to the same class, that class has two
responsibilities.

```java
// Three stakeholders can force a change to this one class
public class Employee {
    public Money calculatePay() { }   // accounting changes the pay rules
    public void save() { }            // DBAs change the schema
    public String reportHours() { }   // HR changes the report format
}
```

The danger is not aesthetic. Two teams editing one class for unrelated reasons
produces merge conflicts, and a change made for accounting can break the HR
report because they share private helper methods.

Separated by stakeholder:

```java
public class Employee { }                                  // just the data
public class PayCalculator   { Money calculate(Employee e) { } }   // accounting
public class EmployeeRepository { void save(Employee e) { } }      // operations
public class HourReporter    { String report(Employee e) { } }     // HR
```

```text
   BEFORE                         AFTER

   Accounting ---+                Accounting ---> PayCalculator
   Operations ---+--> Employee    Operations ---> EmployeeRepository
   HR         ---+                HR         ---> HourReporter

   three reasons to change        one reason each
```

The usual objection is that this produces many small classes. It does, and that
is the trade. Small classes with clear names are easier to locate than large
ones with vague ones, and the total amount of code is roughly the same.

Applying it requires judgement about **granularity**. Taken to an extreme,
every method becomes its own class, which is its own design failure. Two useful
checks:

- Can you name the class without "and", "or", or a vague noun like Manager?
- Would a change requested by one team ever require this class to be edited by
  another?

Common Java applications of the principle:

| Mixed responsibility            | Split into                              |
| ------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Entity that saves itself        | Entity plus Repository                  |
| Service that also formats output| Service plus Renderer or DTO mapper     |
| Class that validates and persists| Validator plus Repository              |
| Controller with business logic  | Controller plus Service                 |

The principle also applies to methods. A method that both computes a value and
prints it has two reasons to change:

```java
// Two jobs: cannot test the calculation without capturing stdout
public void printTotal(Order o) {
    double total = o.items().stream().mapToDouble(Item::price).sum();
    System.out.println("Total: " + total);
}

// One job each: the calculation is now testable
public double total(Order o) { ... }
public void printTotal(Order o) { System.out.println("Total: " + total(o)); }
```

A final note on what SRP is not. It does not say a class may have only one
method, and it does not forbid a class from having several methods that serve
the same responsibility. A `PayCalculator` with six methods, all about pay, is
perfectly compliant.

> Key Takeaways
> - A class should have exactly one reason to change.
> - A reason to change maps to a stakeholder who can request it.
> - Mixing stakeholders in one class causes merge conflicts and accidental
>   breakage.
> - Entities that persist, validate, and render themselves violate the
>   principle.
> - It applies to methods too: computing and printing are two jobs.
> - Compliance produces more, smaller classes, which is the intended trade.
> - One responsibility does not mean one method.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. List every reason a class in your codebase might change and count the
>    stakeholders.
> 2. Split an entity that contains its own SQL into an entity and a repository.
> 3. Separate a method that calculates and prints into two methods.
> 4. Interview: Why is "one reason to change" better than "does one thing"?
>    (Hint: which of the two can two people disagree about indefinitely?)

#### Open-Closed Principle

Bertrand Meyer's principle states that software entities should be **open for
extension but closed for modification**. New behaviour should be added by
writing new code, not by editing code that already works.

The reason is risk. Editing a tested, deployed class can break every existing
caller, and each edit requires re-testing everything. Adding a new class risks
only the new path.

The violation is a conditional that grows with every requirement:

```java
public class DiscountCalculator {
    public double discount(Order order, String customerType) {
        if (customerType.equals("REGULAR"))  return 0;
        if (customerType.equals("PREMIUM"))  return order.total() * 0.1;
        if (customerType.equals("VIP"))      return order.total() * 0.2;
        // Every new customer type means editing and re-testing THIS method
        return 0;
    }
}
```

The fix is to make the varying part an abstraction, so new behaviour arrives as
a new implementation:

```java
public interface DiscountPolicy {
    double discount(Order order);
}

public class RegularDiscount implements DiscountPolicy {
    public double discount(Order o) { return 0; }
}
public class PremiumDiscount implements DiscountPolicy {
    public double discount(Order o) { return o.total() * 0.1; }
}
public class VipDiscount implements DiscountPolicy {
    public double discount(Order o) { return o.total() * 0.2; }
}

// This class is now CLOSED: it never changes again
public class DiscountCalculator {
    public double discount(Order order, DiscountPolicy policy) {
        return policy.discount(order);
    }
}

// A new tier is a NEW FILE, with no edits anywhere else
public class StudentDiscount implements DiscountPolicy {
    public double discount(Order o) { return o.total() * 0.15; }
}
```

```text
   OPEN FOR EXTENSION, CLOSED FOR MODIFICATION

   DiscountCalculator ------> DiscountPolicy  <-- abstraction is STABLE
        (never edited)              ^
                                    |
              +---------+-----------+-----------+
              |         |           |           |
          Regular   Premium       VIP      Student  <-- add freely
                                                        (new files only)
```

Java offers several mechanisms for the extension point:

| Mechanism             | Use when                                    |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Interface + implementations | Behaviour varies by type              |
| Abstract class with hooks   | Shared skeleton, varying steps        |
| Strategy passed as a lambda | The variation is a single function    |
| Enum with per-constant behaviour | The set of cases is genuinely fixed |

The lambda form is often the lightest option and needs no new files at all:

```java
public class DiscountCalculator {
    public double discount(Order o, Function<Order, Double> policy) {
        return policy.apply(o);
    }
}
calculator.discount(order, o -> o.total() * 0.15);
```

Two important qualifications.

First, you cannot be closed against *every* change. The principle is about
anticipating the axis along which a system varies, and abstracting that axis
only. Guessing wrong produces the speculative generality that YAGNI warns
about. In practice the sequence is: write the concrete version, and when the
second variation arrives, extract the abstraction then. The second occurrence
tells you where the seam belongs.

Second, an enum with per-constant behaviour is a legitimate implementation when
the set of cases is fixed by the domain and adding to it genuinely warrants a
review of all the code:

```java
public enum Planet {
    MERCURY(3.303e+23, 2.4397e6),
    VENUS(4.869e+24, 6.0518e6);

    private final double mass, radius;
    Planet(double mass, double radius) { this.mass = mass; this.radius = radius; }

    public double surfaceGravity() { return 6.67300E-11 * mass / (radius * radius); }
}
```

Sealed interfaces, from Java 17, make the opposite choice explicit: they
deliberately close the type hierarchy so the compiler can check exhaustiveness.
That is the right tool when you *want* every new case to force a review.

> Key Takeaways
> - Add behaviour by writing new code rather than editing working code.
> - A conditional that grows with each requirement is the classic violation.
> - Extract the varying behaviour behind an interface or a function.
> - The stable abstraction is what the rest of the system depends on.
> - Lambdas provide the same extension point without new files.
> - You cannot be closed against every change; abstract the axis that actually
>   varies.
> - Sealed types intentionally invert the principle when exhaustiveness
>   matters.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Replace an `if`/`else if` chain over a type string with polymorphic
>    classes.
> 2. Add a fourth variation and verify no existing file needed editing.
> 3. Rewrite the same design using a lambda instead of an interface hierarchy.
> 4. Interview: Can code be closed against all possible changes? (Hint: what
>    must you know in advance for the abstraction to be in the right place?)

#### Liskov Substitution Principle

Barbara Liskov's principle governs inheritance: **objects of a subtype must be
usable anywhere the supertype is expected, without the caller noticing.** If a
caller must check the actual type before using an object, inheritance has been
misused.

Java's compiler enforces the *syntax* of substitutability. It cannot enforce
the *semantics*, which is where violations hide.

The textbook example is a rectangle and a square. Mathematically a square is a
rectangle, so inheritance looks right:

```java
public class Rectangle {
    protected int width, height;
    public void setWidth(int w)  { this.width = w; }
    public void setHeight(int h) { this.height = h; }
    public int area() { return width * height; }
}

public class Square extends Rectangle {
    @Override public void setWidth(int w)  { this.width = w; this.height = w; }
    @Override public void setHeight(int h) { this.width = h; this.height = h; }
}
```

The override is necessary to keep a square square, and it breaks every caller
written against `Rectangle`:

```java
public void resize(Rectangle r) {
    r.setWidth(5);
    r.setHeight(4);
    assert r.area() == 20;      // holds for Rectangle, FAILS for Square (16)
}
```

The lesson is that an "is-a" relationship in the real world does not imply an
"is-substitutable-for" relationship in code. What matters is behaviour under
the supertype's contract, and `Rectangle`'s contract implicitly allows width
and height to vary independently.

Formally, a subtype may not:

| Rule                               | Violation looks like                      |
| ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Strengthen preconditions           | Rejecting inputs the parent accepted      |
| Weaken postconditions              | Returning less than the parent guaranteed |
| Throw new checked exceptions       | Adding a failure the caller cannot expect |
| Break invariants                   | Square's linked width and height          |
| Change expected behaviour          | `add` that silently does nothing          |

A precondition violation:

```java
public class Account {
    public void withdraw(double amount) { ... }        // any positive amount
}

public class SavingsAccount extends Account {
    @Override public void withdraw(double amount) {
        if (amount > 500) throw new IllegalArgumentException("limit 500");
        // STRENGTHENED precondition: code written for Account now fails
        super.withdraw(amount);
    }
}
```

The standard library has a well-known violation. `List.add` is specified to
append, but the fixed-size list from `Arrays.asList` throws:

```java
List<String> list = Arrays.asList("a", "b");
list.add("c");     // UnsupportedOperationException: not substitutable
```

The usual symptom in your own code is a caller forced to test the type:

```java
// If this appears, substitutability has already failed
if (shape instanceof Square) {
    // special handling
}
```

Three ways to fix a violation.

**Prefer composition.** If the subtype cannot honour the contract, it is not a
subtype:

```java
public class Square {
    private final Rectangle rect;              // HAS-A, not IS-A
    public Square(int side) { rect = new Rectangle(side, side); }
    public int area() { return rect.area(); }
    // no setWidth/setHeight to break
}
```

**Make the supertype immutable.** Without setters, the rectangle-square problem
disappears entirely, because there is no way to observe the inconsistency.

```java
public record Rectangle(int width, int height) {
    public int area() { return width * height; }
}
public record Square(int side) {
    public int area() { return side * side; }
}
```

**Restructure the hierarchy** so the common supertype holds only what both
genuinely share, such as a `Shape` interface with `area()`.

> Key Takeaways
> - A subtype must be usable wherever the supertype is, with no caller changes.
> - Java checks the syntax of substitutability but not the semantics.
> - A real-world "is-a" does not guarantee substitutability in code.
> - Subtypes must not strengthen preconditions or weaken postconditions.
> - A caller that checks `instanceof` is evidence of a violation.
> - `Arrays.asList` returning a list whose `add` throws is a standard-library
>   example.
> - Fix violations with composition, immutability, or a restructured
>   hierarchy.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write the rectangle-square example and make an assertion fail.
> 2. Rewrite it with composition so no assertion can fail.
> 3. Find an override in your code that throws where the parent did not.
> 4. Interview: Is a `Square` a `Rectangle`? (Hint: answer separately for
>    mutable and immutable versions, and say what changes.)

#### Interface Segregation Principle

The fourth principle says **no client should be forced to depend on methods it
does not use.** Many small, focused interfaces beat one large one.

The cost of a fat interface is that every implementer must supply every method,
even the meaningless ones, and every client recompiles when any method changes.

```java
// A fat interface: assumes every worker is human
public interface Worker {
    void work();
    void eat();
    void sleep();
}

public class Robot implements Worker {
    public void work()  { /* fine */ }
    public void eat()   { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }  // smell
    public void sleep() { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }
}
```

Those thrown exceptions are also a Liskov violation, which is typical: the
principles reinforce one another.

Segregated into roles:

```java
public interface Workable { void work(); }
public interface Eater    { void eat(); }
public interface Sleeper  { void sleep(); }

public class Human implements Workable, Eater, Sleeper { ... }
public class Robot implements Workable { ... }        // implements only what fits
```

```text
   FAT INTERFACE                    SEGREGATED

   Worker                           Workable   Eater   Sleeper
   +work()                              ^        ^       ^
   +eat()                               |        |       |
   +sleep()                          Human ------+-------+
     ^     ^                            |
     |     |                         Robot (Workable only)
   Human  Robot (must stub two)
```

The client's view matters as much as the implementer's. A class needing only
`work()` should depend on `Workable`, so it is unaffected when `Eater` changes:

```java
// Depends on three methods, uses one
public class Scheduler {
    public void schedule(Worker w) { w.work(); }
}

// Depends on exactly what it uses
public class Scheduler {
    public void schedule(Workable w) { w.work(); }
}
```

Recognising violations:

- An implementation throws `UnsupportedOperationException`.
- An implementation leaves methods empty.
- A client uses two methods out of fifteen.
- Adding a method forces edits to classes that do not care about it.

Java's standard library shows both sides. The single-method interfaces in
`java.util.function` are maximally segregated. `Collection` is deliberately
broad, which is why immutable implementations must throw from `add`, and it is
the compromise that motivated `default` methods.

`default` methods do reduce the burden, since an implementer can inherit a
reasonable body rather than stubbing one. They are not a licence to grow
interfaces without limit: a client still depends on the full type.

```java
public interface Repository<T> {
    Optional<T> findById(String id);
    // Not every store supports these; a default avoids forcing stubs
    default List<T> findAll() { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }
}
```

The counterweight is fragmentation. Splitting every interface to one method
produces dozens of types and obscures the concept they belong to. Segregate
along **client roles**: if two methods are always used by the same callers,
they belong together.

> Key Takeaways
> - Clients should not depend on methods they never call.
> - A fat interface forces implementers to stub or throw from irrelevant
>   methods.
> - Thrown `UnsupportedOperationException` signals both an ISP and a Liskov
>   violation.
> - Split interfaces along the roles that clients actually use.
> - Depend on the narrowest interface that covers your needs.
> - `default` methods ease the burden but do not justify unbounded interfaces.
> - Over-segregation fragments a coherent concept into unrelated types.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Find an interface with a method that some implementation stubs out, and
>    split it.
> 2. Narrow a method parameter from a broad interface to the narrowest one that
>    compiles.
> 3. Argue whether `java.util.List` violates ISP, given `List.of`.
> 4. Interview: How do `default` methods relate to this principle? (Hint: do
>    they reduce what the implementer must write, what the client depends on,
>    or both?)

#### Dependency Inversion Principle

The fifth principle has two clauses:

> High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend
> on abstractions. Abstractions should not depend on details; details should
> depend on abstractions.

The word *inversion* refers to reversing the direction of the conventional
dependency. Normally the important code calls the plumbing, so it depends on
it. Inversion makes the plumbing depend on an abstraction that the important
code owns.

Before inversion, the business logic is chained to infrastructure:

```java
// High-level policy depends directly on a low-level detail
public class OrderService {
    private final MySqlOrderRepository repo = new MySqlOrderRepository();
    private final SmtpEmailSender mailer = new SmtpEmailSender();

    public void place(Order o) {
        repo.insert(o);
        mailer.send(o.customerEmail(), "Order placed");
    }
}
```

Switching to Postgres, or testing without a mail server, means editing
`OrderService`, which holds the business rules that have nothing to do with
either.

After inversion, both sides depend on interfaces, and critically, the
interfaces are **defined by the high-level module** in its own package:

```java
// Owned by the domain, expressed in domain language
public interface OrderRepository { void save(Order o); }
public interface Notifier        { void notifyPlaced(Order o); }

public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repo;
    private final Notifier notifier;

    public OrderService(OrderRepository repo, Notifier notifier) {
        this.repo = repo;
        this.notifier = notifier;
    }

    public void place(Order o) { repo.save(o); notifier.notifyPlaced(o); }
}

// Infrastructure depends INWARD on the domain's interface
public class MySqlOrderRepository implements OrderRepository { ... }
public class SmtpNotifier implements Notifier { ... }
```

```text
   BEFORE: dependency flows outward      AFTER: it flows inward

   OrderService                          OrderService
        |                                     |
        v                                     v
   MySqlOrderRepository                 OrderRepository  <-- domain owns this
                                              ^
                                              | implements
                                        MySqlOrderRepository
```

The arrow from infrastructure now points *up* toward the policy. That is the
inversion, and it is what lets the domain be compiled and tested with no
database on the classpath at all.

Who owns the interface is the detail people miss. An interface placed in the
persistence package, and named after the database, has not inverted anything.
The interface belongs to the consumer and is named in the consumer's language.

**Dependency injection** is the mechanism that supplies the implementations.
Constructor injection is the default, since it makes dependencies explicit and
allows `final` fields:

```java
// Production wiring
var service = new OrderService(new MySqlOrderRepository(), new SmtpNotifier());

// Test wiring: no database, no mail server
var test = new OrderService(new InMemoryOrderRepository(), new FakeNotifier());
```

Note that dependency injection and dependency inversion are different things.
Injection is a technique for supplying collaborators; inversion is a rule about
which way dependencies point. You can inject a concrete class, which is
injection without inversion.

| Term                  | Means                                        |
| --------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| Dependency Inversion  | Depend on abstractions owned by the consumer  |
| Dependency Injection  | Receive collaborators from outside            |
| Inversion of Control  | The framework calls you, not the reverse      |
| IoC Container         | A tool that constructs and wires the graph    |

Chapter 13 covers how Spring automates the wiring. The principle stands
without any framework: a constructor parameter is enough.

The limit is the same as always. Not every dependency needs inverting.
Depending on `String`, `List`, or `LocalDate` is fine, because they are stable.
Invert where the dependency is **volatile**: things that touch the network, the
filesystem, the clock, randomness, or third-party services.

> Key Takeaways
> - High-level policy and low-level details should both depend on
>   abstractions.
> - The abstraction must be owned and named by the high-level module.
> - After inversion, infrastructure depends inward on the domain.
> - This is what lets business logic be tested without a database.
> - Dependency injection supplies collaborators; inversion decides the
>   direction.
> - Constructor injection is the default, since it permits `final` fields.
> - Invert volatile dependencies only; stable library types need no
>   abstraction.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Extract an interface for a repository and move it into the service's
>    package.
> 2. Write an in-memory implementation and test a service with no database.
> 3. Identify which of your dependencies are volatile and which are stable.
> 4. Interview: What is the difference between dependency injection and
>    dependency inversion? (Hint: one is a technique, the other a direction.
>    Can you have one without the other?)

#### Applying SOLID to Java Class Design

The five principles are usually taught separately and applied together. Working
one example from a violation to a clean design shows how they interact, and
where applying them all would be overkill.

Start with a class violating all five:

```java
public class ReportGenerator {
    public void generate(String type, List<Sale> sales) {
        double total = 0;
        for (Sale s : sales) total += s.amount();          // logic

        String output;
        if (type.equals("PDF"))       output = toPdf(total);    // OCP violation
        else if (type.equals("HTML")) output = toHtml(total);
        else                          output = String.valueOf(total);

        // SRP violation: also persists and emails
        new FileWriter("/reports/out.txt").write(output);   // DIP violation
        new SmtpClient().send("boss@corp.com", output);
    }
}
```

Apply the principles in order.

**SRP** splits the responsibilities by stakeholder:

```java
public class SalesTotaller { public Money total(List<Sale> sales) { ... } }
public interface ReportFormatter { String format(Money total); }
public interface ReportPublisher { void publish(String report); }
```

**OCP and ISP** make formats extensible without editing anything, each
interface holding exactly what its clients use:

```java
public class PdfFormatter  implements ReportFormatter { ... }
public class HtmlFormatter implements ReportFormatter { ... }
// A new format is a new class, nothing else changes
```

**DIP** has the high-level generator own the interfaces and receive
implementations:

```java
public class ReportGenerator {
    private final SalesTotaller totaller;
    private final ReportFormatter formatter;
    private final ReportPublisher publisher;

    public ReportGenerator(SalesTotaller t, ReportFormatter f, ReportPublisher p) {
        this.totaller = t; this.formatter = f; this.publisher = p;
    }

    public void generate(List<Sale> sales) {
        publisher.publish(formatter.format(totaller.total(sales)));
    }
}
```

**LSP** is satisfied by making every `ReportFormatter` genuinely
interchangeable: none throws where another returns, and none demands extra
setup.

The result is testable with no filesystem and no mail server:

```java
var generator = new ReportGenerator(new SalesTotaller(),
                                    new HtmlFormatter(),
                                    report -> captured = report);  // a lambda
```

Note the publisher supplied as a lambda. A single-method interface can be
satisfied by one, which keeps the test short and shows why ISP and functional
interfaces fit together.

How the principles relate:

| Principle | Governs          | Answers                              |
| --------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| SRP       | Class size       | What belongs in this class?          |
| OCP       | Extension        | How do I add behaviour safely?       |
| LSP       | Inheritance      | Is this really a subtype?            |
| ISP       | Interface size   | What should clients see?             |
| DIP       | Dependency direction | Which way do the arrows point?   |

A closing warning, because SOLID is frequently over-applied. Every abstraction
has a cost in indirection: more files, more jumps to follow a call, and harder
first-time comprehension. A three-line script does not need five interfaces.

Sensible defaults:

- Start concrete. Extract an abstraction when the second case appears.
- Invert dependencies on the network, the filesystem, the clock, and
  randomness. Leave the rest.
- Split a class when two teams edit it for unrelated reasons.
- Prefer composition to inheritance, which makes LSP mostly moot.
- Let tests drive it: code that is hard to test usually violates DIP or SRP.

> Key Takeaways
> - The principles are applied together and reinforce one another.
> - SRP decides class boundaries; ISP decides interface boundaries.
> - OCP adds behaviour by extension; LSP keeps substitutes honest.
> - DIP points dependencies at abstractions owned by the high-level module.
> - A single-method interface can be satisfied by a lambda, which shortens
>   tests.
> - Every abstraction costs indirection, so apply them where change actually
>   happens.
> - Difficulty writing a unit test is the most reliable signal of a violation.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Take a class that reads a file, computes, and prints, and apply all five
>    principles.
> 2. Write a test for the result using lambdas as the injected collaborators.
> 3. Find an abstraction in your code that has one implementation and no test
>    double, and justify removing it.
> 4. Interview: Which SOLID principle does a class that is hard to unit test
>    most often violate? (Hint: what makes a collaborator impossible to
>    replace in a test?)

<a id="93-creational-patterns"></a>
### 9.3 Creational Patterns

This subchapter covers the patterns that control how objects are created, so
that construction decisions do not spread through the code that uses them.

#### Singleton and Its Java Implementations

Some things should exist exactly once: a connection pool, a configuration
registry, a cache. **Singleton** guarantees one instance and provides a global
point of access to it.

The naive implementation has a concurrency bug:

```java
public class Config {
    private static Config instance;
    private Config() { }                       // private: blocks `new`

    public static Config getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) {                // two threads can BOTH see null
            instance = new Config();           // and both construct an instance
        }
        return instance;
    }
}
```

The standard fixes, in increasing order of quality.

**Eager initialisation** creates the instance when the class loads. The JVM
guarantees class initialisation is thread-safe, so this is correct and simple.
The cost is that the instance is built even if never used:

```java
public class Config {
    private static final Config INSTANCE = new Config();   // thread-safe by the JVM
    private Config() { }
    public static Config getInstance() { return INSTANCE; }
}
```

**Double-checked locking** defers creation but requires `volatile` to be
correct. Without it, another thread can observe a partially constructed object
through instruction reordering:

```java
public class Config {
    private static volatile Config instance;   // volatile is MANDATORY here
    private Config() { }

    public static Config getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) {                // fast path: no lock
            synchronized (Config.class) {
                if (instance == null) {        // re-check while holding the lock
                    instance = new Config();
                }
            }
        }
        return instance;
    }
}
```

**The holder idiom** gets laziness with no synchronisation at all. The nested
class is not loaded until first referenced, and class loading is already
thread-safe:

```java
public class Config {
    private Config() { }

    private static class Holder {              // loaded on first access only
        private static final Config INSTANCE = new Config();
    }

    public static Config getInstance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; }
}
```

**The enum singleton** is the form Joshua Bloch recommends. It is concise,
thread-safe, and the only version that resists both serialisation attacks and
reflection:

```java
public enum Config {
    INSTANCE;

    private final Properties props = load();
    public String get(String key) { return props.getProperty(key); }
}

Config.INSTANCE.get("db.url");
```

```text
   Eager       simple, always created
   DCL         lazy, needs volatile, easy to get wrong
   Holder      lazy, no locking, idiomatic
   Enum        lazy-ish, safest, resists reflection and serialisation
```

| Approach     | Thread-safe | Lazy | Reflection-proof | Verdict            |
| ------------ | ----------- | ---- | ---------------- | ------------------ |
| Naive        | No          | Yes  | No               | Broken             |
| Eager        | Yes         | No   | No               | Fine if cheap      |
| Synchronised method | Yes  | Yes  | No               | Slow on every call |
| Double-checked | Yes with `volatile` | Yes | No     | Works, error-prone |
| Holder       | Yes         | Yes  | No               | Recommended        |
| Enum         | Yes         | Yes  | Yes              | Best               |

Singleton is the most criticised pattern in the catalogue, and the criticism is
largely fair:

- It is **global mutable state**, so any code can change it and any bug can
  come from anywhere.
- It **hides dependencies**. A class calling `Config.getInstance()` has a
  dependency invisible in its constructor.
- It is **hard to test**, because the instance persists between tests and
  cannot be replaced with a fake.
- It **defeats DIP**, since callers depend on a concrete class by name.

The usual better answer is a single instance managed by a container or created
once in `main` and injected:

```java
// Not a singleton class, just one instance, injected where needed
var config = new Config(properties);
var service = new OrderService(config);
```

Spring beans are singleton-scoped by default and give the "one instance"
property without the global access point, which is why the pattern appears far
less often in modern Java.

> Key Takeaways
> - Singleton guarantees one instance with a global access point.
> - The naive lazy version is not thread-safe.
> - Double-checked locking requires `volatile` or it is broken.
> - The holder idiom gives lazy, lock-free initialisation.
> - The enum singleton is the safest and resists reflection and
>   serialisation.
> - Singletons are global state, hide dependencies, and complicate testing.
> - Prefer one injected instance over a class that enforces its own
>   singularity.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement the holder idiom and prove the instance is created on first
>    access.
> 2. Break the naive version by calling `getInstance` from many threads.
> 3. Convert a singleton in your code into an injected dependency.
> 4. Interview: Why is the enum singleton immune to reflection attacks? (Hint:
>    what does `Constructor.newInstance` do when the type is an enum?)

#### Factory Method

Direct use of `new` couples a class to the exact type it creates. **Factory
Method** defines an operation for creating an object and lets subclasses decide
which class to instantiate.

The problem, stated concretely: a class that both orchestrates a workflow and
picks the concrete type has two reasons to change, and a new type means editing
it.

```java
public class LogisticsPlanner {
    public void planDelivery() {
        Truck truck = new Truck();      // welded to Truck
        truck.deliver();
    }
}
```

The pattern moves creation into an overridable method:

```java
public abstract class Logistics {
    // The factory method: subclasses decide the concrete type
    protected abstract Transport createTransport();

    // The algorithm, written against the abstraction, never changes
    public void planDelivery() {
        Transport t = createTransport();
        t.deliver();
    }
}

public class RoadLogistics extends Logistics {
    @Override protected Transport createTransport() { return new Truck(); }
}

public class SeaLogistics extends Logistics {
    @Override protected Transport createTransport() { return new Ship(); }
}
```

```text
   Logistics                     Transport
   +planDelivery()   ---uses-->  +deliver()
   #createTransport()                ^
        ^        ^                   |
        |        |              +----+----+
   RoadLog.   SeaLog.           |         |
   creates    creates         Truck     Ship
      |          |              ^         ^
      +----------|--------------+         |
                 +------------------------+
```

The key structural point: `planDelivery` depends only on `Transport`, so adding
air freight means adding two classes and editing none. That is the Open-Closed
Principle expressed as a creation mechanism.

A lighter variant, sometimes called a **parameterised factory** or simple
factory, puts the decision in one static method rather than a hierarchy. It is
not the Gang of Four pattern, but it is far more common in practice:

```java
public class TransportFactory {
    public static Transport create(String mode) {
        return switch (mode) {
            case "road" -> new Truck();
            case "sea"  -> new Ship();
            default     -> throw new IllegalArgumentException(mode);
        };
    }
}
```

This centralises the `switch` in one place rather than scattering it, though
the switch itself still needs editing for each new type. A registry avoids even
that:

```java
public class TransportFactory {
    private static final Map<String, Supplier<Transport>> REGISTRY =
            new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public static void register(String key, Supplier<Transport> creator) {
        REGISTRY.put(key, creator);      // new types register themselves
    }

    public static Transport create(String key) {
        Supplier<Transport> s = REGISTRY.get(key);
        if (s == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException(key);
        return s.get();
    }
}

TransportFactory.register("air", Plane::new);    // no edit to the factory
```

Use Factory Method when:

- The class cannot know in advance which type it must create.
- Creation involves logic beyond a constructor call.
- You want subclasses to extend which products are produced.
- The creation decision should live in one place rather than at every call
  site.

In the standard library, `Calendar.getInstance()` and
`NumberFormat.getInstance(Locale)` are factory methods: the returned concrete
type depends on the locale and is not named by the caller.

The cost is a parallel hierarchy. Every product often gains a matching creator,
which is a lot of classes for a small gain. With lambdas, a `Supplier<T>`
frequently does the same job in one line, and that is the modern default for
simple cases.

> Key Takeaways
> - Factory Method delegates instantiation to a method that subclasses
>   override.
> - The calling algorithm depends only on the product abstraction.
> - Adding a product means adding classes, not editing existing ones.
> - The simple static factory centralises a `switch` but still needs editing.
> - A registry of suppliers removes even that edit.
> - `Calendar.getInstance` is a standard-library example.
> - The cost is a parallel creator hierarchy; a `Supplier` often suffices.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `Logistics` hierarchy with road and sea subclasses.
> 2. Add an air variant and verify no existing class needed changing.
> 3. Replace the hierarchy with a `Map<String, Supplier<Transport>>` registry.
> 4. Interview: How does Factory Method differ from a static factory method?
>    (Hint: which one involves inheritance, and which one is just a named
>    constructor?)

#### Abstract Factory

Factory Method creates one product. **Abstract Factory** creates **families of
related products** and guarantees the members of a family are used together.

The motivating problem is consistency. Imagine a user interface supporting two
themes. Mixing a dark button with a light checkbox produces a broken screen,
and nothing in the type system prevents it:

```java
Button button = new DarkButton();
Checkbox box = new LightCheckbox();     // compiles, but visually wrong
```

Abstract Factory makes the mismatch impossible by having one object produce the
whole family:

```java
// The abstract factory: one method per product in the family
public interface UiFactory {
    Button createButton();
    Checkbox createCheckbox();
}

public class DarkUiFactory implements UiFactory {
    public Button createButton()     { return new DarkButton(); }
    public Checkbox createCheckbox() { return new DarkCheckbox(); }
}

public class LightUiFactory implements UiFactory {
    public Button createButton()     { return new LightButton(); }
    public Checkbox createCheckbox() { return new LightCheckbox(); }
}

// Client code knows neither theme nor concrete widget types
public class Screen {
    private final Button button;
    private final Checkbox checkbox;

    public Screen(UiFactory factory) {
        this.button = factory.createButton();       // guaranteed to match
        this.checkbox = factory.createCheckbox();
    }
}

Screen screen = new Screen(userPrefersDark ? new DarkUiFactory()
                                           : new LightUiFactory());
```

```text
              UiFactory                  Button          Checkbox
           +createButton()                  ^                ^
           +createCheckbox()                |                |
                ^      ^              +-----+-----+    +-----+-----+
                |      |              |           |    |           |
          DarkUiF.  LightUiF.      Dark        Light  Dark       Light
             |  \      |  \        Button     Button  Checkbox  Checkbox
             |   \     |   +-----------------------------------> (creates)
             +----\----+----------------------> (creates)
```

The defining property is that the factory picks **one column** of the product
matrix, so every object created comes from the same family.

The classic Java example is JDBC. A `Connection` is an abstract factory
producing statements and metadata that all belong to the same database driver:

```java
Connection conn = DriverManager.getConnection(url);   // picks the family
Statement stmt = conn.createStatement();              // a matching product
PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql);    // another
```

`DocumentBuilderFactory` and `TransformerFactory` in the XML APIs follow the
same shape.

The distinction from Factory Method is a standard interview question:

| Aspect           | Factory Method              | Abstract Factory             |
| ---------------- | --------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Products created | One                         | A family of related products |
| Mechanism        | Inheritance, an overridden method | Composition, an object with several methods |
| Varies by        | Subclass                    | The factory instance passed in |
| Typical size     | One method                  | One method per product       |

The costs are real and explain why it appears less often than the simpler
patterns.

Adding a **new product type** to the family, a `Slider` for example, requires
editing the factory interface and every implementation. The pattern is open for
new *families* and closed against new *product types*, which is the opposite of
what people often assume.

It also multiplies classes quickly: with three families and four products, you
have twelve product classes plus four factory types.

Use it when a system must be configured with one of several families, when
products in a family are genuinely required to work together, and when the
family set changes more often than the product set. Otherwise a simple factory
or dependency injection is usually enough, since a DI container supplies
matched implementations by configuration without a bespoke factory hierarchy.

> Key Takeaways
> - Abstract Factory creates families of related products through one
>   interface.
> - It guarantees products used together come from the same family.
> - The client depends only on the abstract factory and abstract products.
> - JDBC's `Connection` producing statements is a standard-library example.
> - Factory Method uses inheritance for one product; Abstract Factory uses
>   composition for many.
> - Adding a family is easy; adding a product type forces edits everywhere.
> - Dependency injection often achieves the same result with less machinery.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a `UiFactory` with two themes and a client that cannot mix them.
> 2. Add a third theme and confirm no client code changed.
> 3. Add a `Slider` product and count the files you had to edit.
> 4. Interview: Why is Abstract Factory not open for extension in every
>    direction? (Hint: compare adding a new family with adding a new product
>    type.)

#### Builder for Complex Objects

Constructors handle a few parameters well. Beyond that they fail in two ways:
nobody can read the call site, and optional parameters require an explosion of
overloads.

```java
// What do these arguments mean? Which are optional? Are any swapped?
Pizza p = new Pizza(12, true, false, true, false, true, "thin");

// The telescoping alternative: one constructor per combination
public Pizza(int size) { ... }
public Pizza(int size, boolean cheese) { ... }
public Pizza(int size, boolean cheese, boolean pepperoni) { ... }
// ...and so on, unreadably
```

A JavaBeans-style approach with setters solves readability but creates two new
problems: the object is **temporarily inconsistent** between calls, and it
cannot be immutable.
