**Builder** separates construction from representation. A mutable builder
collects the parameters, then produces an immutable object in one step:

```java
public class Pizza {
    private final int size;                 // all final: immutable result
    private final boolean cheese;
    private final boolean pepperoni;
    private final String crust;

    private Pizza(Builder b) {              // private: only the builder constructs
        this.size = b.size;
        this.cheese = b.cheese;
        this.pepperoni = b.pepperoni;
        this.crust = b.crust;
    }

    public static Builder builder(int size) { return new Builder(size); }

    public static class Builder {
        private final int size;             // required: taken in the constructor
        private boolean cheese = false;     // optional: sensible defaults
        private boolean pepperoni = false;
        private String crust = "regular";

        public Builder(int size) { this.size = size; }

        // Each setter returns `this`, which is what enables chaining
        public Builder cheese()            { this.cheese = true; return this; }
        public Builder pepperoni()         { this.pepperoni = true; return this; }
        public Builder crust(String crust) { this.crust = crust; return this; }

        public Pizza build() {
            if (size < 6) throw new IllegalArgumentException("too small");
            return new Pizza(this);         // validate, then construct once
        }
    }
}
```

The call site now documents itself:

```java
Pizza pizza = Pizza.builder(12)
        .cheese()
        .pepperoni()
        .crust("thin")
        .build();          // the object exists only when fully specified
```

```text
   TELESCOPING                    BUILDER

   new Pizza(12,t,f,t,f,t,"thin") builder(12).cheese().crust("thin").build()
   unreadable, order-sensitive    named, order-independent, validated once
```

Builder's advantages over setters are worth stating precisely:

| Property                  | Setters | Builder |
| ------------------------- | ------- | ------- |
| Readable call site        | Yes     | Yes     |
| Immutable result          | No      | Yes     |
| Object never half-built   | No      | Yes     |
| Validation in one place   | No      | Yes     |
| Required parameters enforced | No   | Yes, via the builder's constructor |

Java's standard library uses the pattern widely:

```java
var client = HttpClient.newBuilder()
        .version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_2)
        .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
        .build();

Stream.Builder<String> sb = Stream.builder();
var calendar = new Calendar.Builder().setDate(2026, 0, 1).build();
```

Two Java-specific notes.

For a small number of fields, a **record** is usually better. It is immutable,
validated in the compact constructor, and needs no builder at all. Reach for a
builder when there are many optional fields or the construction is genuinely
multi-step.

```java
public record Pizza(int size, boolean cheese, String crust) {
    public Pizza {                                  // compact constructor
        if (size < 6) throw new IllegalArgumentException("too small");
    }
}
```

Libraries such as Lombok generate builders from an annotation, removing the
boilerplate that is the pattern's main cost:

```java
@Builder
public class Pizza { private final int size; private final String crust; }
```

The downsides: roughly twice the code for a hand-written builder, an extra
object per construction, and the fact that missing a required field is caught
at runtime in `build()` rather than at compile time, unless you take required
fields in the builder's constructor as above.

> Key Takeaways
> - Builder replaces telescoping constructors and setter-based construction.
> - A mutable builder produces an immutable, fully validated object.
> - Each builder method returns `this`, enabling a readable chain.
> - Required parameters belong in the builder's constructor.
> - Validation happens once, inside `build()`.
> - `HttpClient.newBuilder()` is a standard-library example.
> - Prefer a record for a few fields; use a builder for many optional ones.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Convert a class with a six-argument constructor into a builder.
> 2. Enforce a required field by taking it in the builder's constructor.
> 3. Add validation to `build()` and write a test that expects the exception.
> 4. Interview: Why does a builder produce a more robust object than a set of
>    setters? (Hint: at what moments can the object be observed in an invalid
>    state under each approach?)

#### Prototype and Object Copying

Sometimes creating an object from scratch is expensive: it required a database
query, a network call, or heavy parsing. **Prototype** creates new objects by
copying an existing configured instance rather than constructing one.

The pattern is simple in intent: keep a fully prepared exemplar, and clone it
whenever you need another.

```java
public interface Prototype<T> { T copy(); }

public class Document implements Prototype<Document> {
    private final String template;          // expensive to load
    private final List<String> sections;
    private String title;

    @Override
    public Document copy() {
        Document d = new Document(this.template);
        d.sections = new ArrayList<>(this.sections);   // copy, do not share
        d.title = this.title;
        return d;
    }
}

Document base = loadExpensiveTemplate();    // done once
Document invoice = base.copy();             // cheap
```

Java has a built-in mechanism, `Cloneable` and `Object.clone()`, which is
widely regarded as a design mistake. It is worth knowing because it appears in
older code:

```java
public class Point implements Cloneable {   // a marker interface, no methods
    private int x, y;

    @Override
    public Point clone() {
        try {
            return (Point) super.clone();   // native field-by-field copy
        } catch (CloneNotSupportedException e) {
            throw new AssertionError(e);    // unreachable: we are Cloneable
        }
    }
}
```

Its problems are substantial: `Cloneable` declares no `clone` method, so the
interface does not advertise the capability; `clone` is `protected` on
`Object`; it throws a checked exception that cannot happen; it bypasses
constructors, so `final` fields and invariants are not enforced; and the
default copy is shallow.

The **shallow versus deep** distinction is the part that causes real bugs. A
shallow copy duplicates the object but shares its referenced objects:

```text
   SHALLOW COPY                     DEEP COPY

   original ---> [ list ] <--- copy   original ---> [ list A ]
                                      copy     ---> [ list B ]

   mutating through either            fully independent
   reference affects both
```

```java
Order original = new Order(new ArrayList<>(List.of("item1")));
Order shallow = original.shallowCopy();
shallow.items().add("item2");
System.out.println(original.items());   // [item1, item2]: shared list!
```

Ways to copy properly in modern Java:

```java
// 1. A copy constructor: explicit, readable, no Cloneable
public Order(Order other) {
    this.id = other.id;
    this.items = new ArrayList<>(other.items);    // deep where it matters
}

// 2. A static factory, which reads better at the call site
public static Order copyOf(Order other) { return new Order(other); }

// 3. A record's wither-style method for one changed field
public record Config(String host, int port) {
    public Config withPort(int newPort) { return new Config(host, newPort); }
}

// 4. Serialisation round-trip: deep, but slow and fragile
```

Immutability removes the problem entirely. If an object cannot change, sharing
it is safe and copying is unnecessary:

```java
public record Point(int x, int y) { }       // no copy needed, ever
Point p2 = p1;                              // sharing is safe
```

Use Prototype when object creation is genuinely expensive, when you need many
objects differing slightly from a configured baseline, or when the concrete
class is decided at runtime and you hold an instance rather than a type.

| Approach          | Deep by default | Recommended |
| ----------------- | --------------- | ----------- |
| `Object.clone()`  | No              | No          |
| Copy constructor  | You decide      | Yes         |
| Static `copyOf`   | You decide      | Yes         |
| Record `with...`  | Not needed      | Yes         |
| Serialisation     | Yes             | Rarely      |

> Key Takeaways
> - Prototype creates objects by copying a configured instance.
> - It pays off when construction is expensive or the type is chosen at
>   runtime.
> - `Cloneable` and `clone()` are a flawed design and should be avoided.
> - `clone` bypasses constructors, so invariants and `final` fields are not
>   enforced.
> - A shallow copy shares referenced objects; mutations are visible through
>   both.
> - Prefer a copy constructor or a static `copyOf` factory.
> - Immutable objects need no copying at all.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a class with a `List` field and show a shallow copy sharing it.
> 2. Fix it with a copy constructor that duplicates the list.
> 3. Add a wither method to a record that changes one component.
> 4. Interview: Why is `Cloneable` considered a design mistake? (Hint: look at
>    which methods the interface actually declares.)

#### Static Factory Methods

A static factory method is a static method that returns an instance of its
class. It is not one of the Gang of Four patterns, but Joshua Bloch lists it as
Item 1 of *Effective Java*, and it is the creational technique you will use
most often.

The first advantage is that **methods have names** and constructors do not. A
class needing two constructors with the same parameter types cannot have them;
static factories can:

```java
// Impossible as constructors: same erasure, same parameter list
public static Complex fromCartesian(double re, double im) { ... }
public static Complex fromPolar(double r, double theta) { ... }
```

Names also make call sites self-documenting:

```java
BigInteger probablePrime = BigInteger.probablePrime(512, random);
// versus a constructor whose boolean flag means "prime"
```

The second advantage is that a factory is **not required to create a new
object**. It may return a cached instance, which a constructor can never do:

```java
Integer i = Integer.valueOf(127);    // returns a cached instance
Boolean b = Boolean.valueOf(true);   // always returns Boolean.TRUE
```

The third is that it may **return any subtype**, so the concrete class can stay
private and change without breaking callers:

```java
// The caller sees List; the implementation is an unexported class
List<String> l = List.of("a", "b");

// Collections returns different private implementations by size
Set<String> s = Collections.singleton("x");
```

The fourth is that the returned class **can vary by argument**:

```java
// EnumSet returns RegularEnumSet or JumboEnumSet depending on the enum size
EnumSet<Day> days = EnumSet.of(Day.MON, Day.TUE);
```

And the fifth is cleaner generics, though `var` and the diamond operator have
reduced this benefit:

```java
Map<String, List<Order>> m = HashMap.newHashMap(16);   // Java 19+
```

Widely used naming conventions, which are worth following because readers
expect them:

| Name           | Meaning                                       |
| -------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `of`           | Aggregates arguments: `List.of("a", "b")`     |
| `from`         | Converts one type to another: `Date.from(instant)` |
| `valueOf`      | A more verbose `from`: `Integer.valueOf("42")` |
| `getInstance`  | Returns an instance, possibly cached           |
| `newInstance`  | Guarantees a distinct new instance             |
| `copyOf`       | A copy of the argument: `List.copyOf(list)`    |
| `create`       | A new instance, no caching implied             |
| `getXxx` / `newXxx` | Factory on a different class, such as `Files.newInputStream` |

A worked example combining the benefits:

```java
public final class Temperature {
    private final double celsius;

    private Temperature(double celsius) { this.celsius = celsius; }  // no `new`

    public static Temperature ofCelsius(double c)    { return new Temperature(c); }
    public static Temperature ofFahrenheit(double f) {
        return new Temperature((f - 32) * 5 / 9);    // named, so no ambiguity
    }
    public static Temperature absoluteZero() { return ZERO; }   // cached constant

    private static final Temperature ZERO = new Temperature(-273.15);
}
```

The two limitations Bloch names:

- A class with only private constructors **cannot be subclassed**. That is
  often a benefit, since it forces composition, but it is a genuine
  restriction.
- Static factories are **harder to find** in documentation than constructors,
  which have their own section. Consistent naming is what mitigates this.

Static factories combine naturally with the other patterns here: a builder is
usually reached through one, and a singleton's accessor is one.

> Key Takeaways
> - A static factory method is a named alternative to a constructor.
> - Names distinguish factories that would otherwise have identical
>   signatures.
> - A factory may return a cached instance rather than always constructing.
> - It may return any subtype, keeping implementation classes private.
> - The returned class can vary by argument, as `EnumSet` does.
> - Follow the conventional names: `of`, `from`, `valueOf`, `copyOf`,
>   `getInstance`.
> - A class with only private constructors cannot be subclassed.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add `ofCelsius` and `ofFahrenheit` factories to a temperature class.
> 2. Cache and return a shared instance for a common value, and prove it with
>    `==`.
> 3. Rename three factory methods in your code to match the conventions.
> 4. Interview: Name two things a static factory can do that a constructor
>    cannot. (Hint: think about the returned object's identity and its exact
>    type.)

<a id="94-structural-patterns"></a>
### 9.4 Structural Patterns

This subchapter covers the patterns that compose classes and objects into
larger structures while keeping the pieces independently replaceable.

#### Adapter

Two pieces of code that should work together often have incompatible
interfaces: a third-party library, a legacy class, or a service whose API you
cannot change. **Adapter** wraps one interface in another so the client can use
it unchanged.

The analogy is the travel plug. The appliance and the socket both work; they
simply do not fit. The adapter changes the shape without changing either side.

Suppose your application is written against a `PaymentProcessor` interface, and
a third-party library offers something similar but different:

```java
// What your code expects
public interface PaymentProcessor {
    void pay(double amount, String currency);
}

// What the library provides: you cannot edit this
public class LegacyGateway {
    public void makePayment(int cents, int currencyCode) { ... }
}
```

The adapter implements your interface and translates:

```java
public class LegacyGatewayAdapter implements PaymentProcessor {
    private final LegacyGateway adaptee;          // the wrapped object

    public LegacyGatewayAdapter(LegacyGateway adaptee) { this.adaptee = adaptee; }

    @Override
    public void pay(double amount, String currency) {
        int cents = (int) Math.round(amount * 100);          // translate units
        int code = Currency.getInstance(currency).getNumericCode();  // and types
        adaptee.makePayment(cents, code);
    }
}

// The client never learns that LegacyGateway exists
PaymentProcessor processor = new LegacyGatewayAdapter(new LegacyGateway());
processor.pay(19.99, "EUR");
```

```text
   Client ---> PaymentProcessor (target)
                     ^
                     | implements
               LegacyGatewayAdapter
                     |
                     | wraps (composition)
                     v
               LegacyGateway (adaptee)
```

There are two forms. The **object adapter** above uses composition and is
almost always the right choice. The **class adapter** uses inheritance and is
limited in Java, since you can extend only one class:

```java
// Class adapter: only possible when the target is an interface
public class ClassAdapter extends LegacyGateway implements PaymentProcessor {
    @Override public void pay(double amount, String currency) {
        makePayment((int) (amount * 100), 978);     // inherited method
    }
}
```

| Form           | Mechanism   | Can adapt subclasses | Flexibility |
| -------------- | ----------- | -------------------- | ----------- |
| Object adapter | Composition | Yes, any instance    | High        |
| Class adapter  | Inheritance | No, one fixed class  | Low         |

The Java library is full of adapters:

```java
// Arrays.asList adapts an array to the List interface
List<String> list = Arrays.asList(array);

// InputStreamReader adapts a byte stream to a character stream
Reader reader = new InputStreamReader(inputStream, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);

// Collections.list adapts a legacy Enumeration to a List
List<String> l = Collections.list(enumeration);
```

`InputStreamReader` is the clearest example: bytes and characters are genuinely
different abstractions, and the adapter performs the decoding that bridges
them.

Adapter is also the natural partner of the Dependency Inversion Principle. Your
domain declares the interface it wants; the adapter sits in the infrastructure
layer and makes a third-party type satisfy it. That keeps vendor types out of
your business logic entirely, so replacing the vendor means writing one new
adapter.

Two cautions. An adapter that grows logic beyond translation has become a
service and should be renamed. And a chain of adapters, each adapting the
previous, is a sign the abstractions are wrong rather than that more adapters
are needed.

> Key Takeaways
> - Adapter converts one interface into another that clients already expect.
> - It lets incompatible code work together without modifying either side.
> - The object adapter uses composition and is preferred in Java.
> - The class adapter uses inheritance and is limited to one adaptee class.
> - `Arrays.asList` and `InputStreamReader` are standard-library adapters.
> - Adapter keeps third-party types out of the domain layer.
> - An adapter containing business logic has outgrown the pattern.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write an adapter that makes a third-party logging class satisfy your own
>    logging interface.
> 2. Adapt a class whose method returns an array into one returning a `List`.
> 3. Explain why `InputStreamReader` is an adapter rather than a decorator.
> 4. Interview: Why is the object adapter usually preferred over the class
>    adapter? (Hint: how many classes can a Java class extend?)

#### Decorator

Adding behaviour to a class by subclassing it does not scale. With three
optional features you need seven subclasses to cover every combination, and the
choice is fixed at compile time.

```text
   SUBCLASS EXPLOSION

   Coffee
     CoffeeWithMilk
     CoffeeWithSugar
     CoffeeWithMilkAndSugar
     CoffeeWithWhip
     CoffeeWithMilkAndWhip ...        2^n classes
```

**Decorator** attaches responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping
it. Each decorator implements the same interface as the thing it wraps, so
wrappers nest to any depth and the client cannot tell the difference.

```java
public interface Coffee {
    double cost();
    String description();
}

public class SimpleCoffee implements Coffee {
    public double cost() { return 2.00; }
    public String description() { return "coffee"; }
}

// The base decorator holds a reference to the wrapped component
public abstract class CoffeeDecorator implements Coffee {
    protected final Coffee wrapped;
    protected CoffeeDecorator(Coffee wrapped) { this.wrapped = wrapped; }
}

public class Milk extends CoffeeDecorator {
    public Milk(Coffee c) { super(c); }
    public double cost() { return wrapped.cost() + 0.50; }        // add to the inner
    public String description() { return wrapped.description() + " + milk"; }
}

public class Sugar extends CoffeeDecorator {
    public Sugar(Coffee c) { super(c); }
    public double cost() { return wrapped.cost() + 0.20; }
    public String description() { return wrapped.description() + " + sugar"; }
}
```

Combinations are now built at runtime, in any order and any number:

```java
Coffee order = new Sugar(new Milk(new SimpleCoffee()));
System.out.println(order.description());   // "coffee + milk + sugar"
System.out.println(order.cost());          // 2.70
```

```text
   NESTED WRAPPERS

   +-------------------------------+
   | Sugar                         |
   |  +-------------------------+  |
   |  | Milk                    |  |    cost() delegates inward,
   |  |  +-------------------+  |  |    then adds its own amount
   |  |  | SimpleCoffee 2.00 |  |  |
   |  |  +-------------------+  |  |
   |  |         + 0.50          |  |
   |  +-------------------------+  |
   |            + 0.20             |
   +-------------------------------+
```

Java's I/O library is the canonical example, and recognising it makes the whole
package easier to read:

```java
InputStream in = new GZIPInputStream(          // adds decompression
                     new BufferedInputStream(  // adds buffering
                         new FileInputStream("data.gz")));  // the component
```

Each wrapper adds one capability, and any order that makes sense is legal.
`Collections.unmodifiableList` is a decorator too: it wraps a list and adds the
behaviour of rejecting modification.

Decorator is easily confused with its neighbours:

| Pattern   | Interface of the wrapper | Purpose                       |
| --------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------------- |
| Decorator | Same as the component    | Add behaviour                 |
| Adapter   | Different                | Make an incompatible type fit |
| Proxy     | Same as the component    | Control access                |
| Facade    | New and simpler          | Hide a complex subsystem      |

The distinguishing test for Decorator is that the wrapper has the **same
interface** and **adds** something, whereas a Proxy has the same interface and
**controls** access without adding features.

The costs are genuine. A deeply wrapped object is hard to debug, since a stack
trace shows many near-identical frames. Identity is lost, so `equals` and `==`
on the outer object do not match the inner one. And many small classes can
obscure the overall behaviour.

In modern Java, a function chain often replaces a simple decorator:

```java
Function<String, String> pipeline = ((Function<String, String>) String::trim)
        .andThen(String::toLowerCase);
```

Use the class-based pattern when the decorated type has several methods or must
remain a domain type.

> Key Takeaways
> - Decorator adds behaviour by wrapping an object at runtime.
> - The wrapper implements the same interface, so wrappers nest freely.
> - It replaces an exponential number of subclasses with composable pieces.
> - Java's I/O streams are the canonical example.
> - `Collections.unmodifiableList` decorates a list with a restriction.
> - Decorator adds behaviour; Proxy controls access; Adapter changes the
>   interface.
> - Deep nesting complicates debugging and breaks object identity.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a coffee pricing example with three decorators and combine them.
> 2. Wrap a `FileInputStream` in a buffered and a compressed stream and explain
>    the order.
> 3. Write a decorator that logs every call before delegating.
> 4. Interview: How do you tell a Decorator from a Proxy when both wrap and
>    implement the same interface? (Hint: ask what the wrapper adds versus
>    what it withholds.)

#### Composite

Some structures are inherently recursive: a folder contains files and folders,
a menu contains items and submenus, a UI panel contains widgets and panels.
Writing client code that constantly checks "is this a leaf or a container?"
produces conditionals everywhere.

```java
// Without Composite: the client must know the difference
public long totalSize(Object node) {
    if (node instanceof File f) return f.size();
    if (node instanceof Folder d) {
        long sum = 0;
        for (Object child : d.children()) sum += totalSize(child);  // recursion
        return sum;
    }
    throw new IllegalArgumentException();
}
```

**Composite** composes objects into tree structures and lets clients treat
individual objects and compositions **uniformly**. Both leaf and container
implement one interface.

```java
public interface FileSystemNode {
    String name();
    long size();                        // both leaves and folders answer this
}

// Leaf: no children
public record FileNode(String name, long size) implements FileSystemNode { }

// Composite: holds children of the same interface type
public class FolderNode implements FileSystemNode {
    private final String name;
    private final List<FileSystemNode> children = new ArrayList<>();

    public FolderNode(String name) { this.name = name; }
    public String name() { return name; }

    public FolderNode add(FileSystemNode child) {
        children.add(child);            // accepts files AND folders
        return this;
    }

    @Override
    public long size() {
        return children.stream().mapToLong(FileSystemNode::size).sum();
        // recursion is implicit: each child answers for itself
    }
}
```

The client now has no conditionals at all:

```java
FileSystemNode root = new FolderNode("root")
        .add(new FileNode("a.txt", 100))
        .add(new FolderNode("sub")
                .add(new FileNode("b.txt", 250)));

System.out.println(root.size());     // 350: works the same for a file or folder
```

```text
                 FileSystemNode
                 +name() +size()
                    ^        ^
                    |        |
            FileNode          FolderNode
            (leaf)            children: List<FileSystemNode>
                                       |
                              +--------+--------+
                              |                 |
                          FileNode          FolderNode
                                                 |
                                             FileNode
```

The uniformity is the whole point: `size()` on a leaf returns a number, and on
a composite it aggregates its children, but the caller does not care.

The design question the pattern raises is where to put child-management
methods such as `add` and `remove`.

**Transparent** puts them on the shared interface, so every node has them. This
maximises uniformity but forces leaves to implement operations that make no
sense, which violates the Interface Segregation Principle.

**Safe** puts them only on the composite, as shown above. Leaves stay clean,
but a client holding a `FileSystemNode` must downcast to add a child.

| Variant     | `add` lives on   | Uniformity | Type safety |
| ----------- | ---------------- | ---------- | ----------- |
| Transparent | The interface    | High       | Low         |
| Safe        | The composite    | Lower      | High        |

Most modern Java code chooses the safe variant, because throwing
`UnsupportedOperationException` from a leaf is exactly the smell discussed
under ISP.

Standard-library and framework examples include the AWT and Swing component
hierarchy, where `Container` is both a `Component` and a holder of components,
and the composite structure of XML or JSON documents.

Sealed interfaces pair well with Composite when the set of node types is fixed,
because pattern matching then becomes exhaustive:

```java
public sealed interface Node permits FileNode, FolderNode { }

long size = switch (node) {
    case FileNode f -> f.size();
    case FolderNode d -> d.children().stream().mapToLong(this::size).sum();
};   // no default needed: the compiler knows the cases are complete
```

Two cautions: the shared interface tends to drift toward the lowest common
denominator, and deep trees risk stack overflow with naive recursion.

> Key Takeaways
> - Composite represents part-whole hierarchies as trees.
> - Leaves and containers implement the same interface, so clients need no
>   type checks.
> - A composite's operation delegates to its children, making recursion
>   implicit.
> - The transparent variant puts `add` on the interface and weakens leaves.
> - The safe variant keeps `add` on the composite and is usually preferred.
> - Swing's component hierarchy and document trees are real examples.
> - Watch for an interface diluted to the lowest common denominator.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Model a file system with files and folders and compute a total size.
> 2. Add a `print(int depth)` operation that renders the tree with
>    indentation.
> 3. Implement both the safe and transparent variants and compare their
>    drawbacks.
> 4. Interview: What does Composite let the client avoid writing? (Hint: what
>    kind of statement disappears from the traversal code?)

#### Facade

A subsystem with many classes is powerful but exhausting to use. Clients must
know which objects to create, in what order, and how they interrelate. Every
client repeats that knowledge, and every change to the subsystem breaks them
all.

**Facade** provides a single simplified interface to a complex subsystem.

```java
// The subsystem: four classes, a specific order, easy to get wrong
public class VideoFile { ... }
public class CodecFactory { public Codec extract(VideoFile f) { ... } }
public class BitrateReader {
    public byte[] read(VideoFile f, Codec c) { ... }
    public byte[] convert(byte[] buffer, Codec c) { ... }
}
public class AudioMixer { public byte[] fix(byte[] result) { ... } }
```

Without a facade, every caller carries the full procedure:

```java
VideoFile file = new VideoFile(name);
Codec source = CodecFactory.extract(file);
Codec dest = format.equals("mp4") ? new Mp4Codec() : new OggCodec();
byte[] buffer = BitrateReader.read(file, source);
byte[] result = BitrateReader.convert(buffer, dest);
result = new AudioMixer().fix(result);
```

The facade reduces that to one call:

```java
public class VideoConverter {
    public File convert(String fileName, String format) {
        VideoFile file = new VideoFile(fileName);
        Codec source = CodecFactory.extract(file);
        Codec dest = format.equals("mp4") ? new Mp4Codec() : new OggCodec();
        byte[] buffer = BitrateReader.read(file, source);
        byte[] result = BitrateReader.convert(buffer, dest);
        return save(new AudioMixer().fix(result));
    }
}

File mp4 = new VideoConverter().convert("holiday.ogg", "mp4");
```

```text
   WITHOUT FACADE                   WITH FACADE

   Client --+--> VideoFile          Client ---> VideoConverter
           +--> CodecFactory                        |
           +--> BitrateReader                       +--> VideoFile
           +--> AudioMixer                          +--> CodecFactory
                                                    +--> BitrateReader
   knows 4 classes and the order     knows 1 class  +--> AudioMixer
```

The defining characteristic is that a facade introduces a **new, simpler
interface** rather than reusing an existing one. That is what separates it from
Adapter, which converts to an interface the client already has.

An important property: a facade does not hide the subsystem. Clients with
unusual needs can still use the classes directly. A facade that forbids that,
by making everything package-private, becomes a bottleneck when someone needs
the twenty percent of functionality it does not expose.

Real examples:

```java
// javax.faces and java.net.URL both act as facades over layered subsystems
URL url = new URL("https://example.com");
InputStream in = url.openStream();     // hides sockets, protocols, and streams

// SLF4J is a facade over multiple logging implementations
Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(MyClass.class);

// A service class is usually a facade over repositories and domain objects
public class CheckoutService {
    public Receipt checkout(Cart cart) {
        validator.validate(cart);
        Payment p = gateway.charge(cart.total());
        inventory.reserve(cart.items());
        return receipts.create(cart, p);
    }
}
```

That last one is worth noticing: most well-written application service classes
are facades, whether or not anyone calls them that.

| Pattern   | Interface           | Intent                          |
| --------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Facade    | New and simpler     | Hide subsystem complexity       |
| Adapter   | An existing one     | Convert an incompatible type    |
| Mediator  | New                 | Coordinate peers that would otherwise talk directly |

The risk is the **god facade**. As features accumulate, a facade can grow into
a class that does everything and violates SRP. If it exceeds a few cohesive
operations, split it by use case.

> Key Takeaways
> - Facade offers one simplified entry point to a complex subsystem.
> - It removes knowledge of subsystem classes and their call order from
>   clients.
> - It defines a new interface, unlike Adapter which conforms to an existing
>   one.
> - The subsystem should remain accessible for advanced clients.
> - `java.net.URL` and SLF4J's `LoggerFactory` are real examples.
> - Most application service classes are facades over repositories and domain
>   logic.
> - Facades tend to grow; split them when they stop being cohesive.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a facade over three classes that must be called in a fixed order.
> 2. Show that a client can still bypass the facade when it needs to.
> 3. Identify a facade in a framework you use and list what it hides.
> 4. Interview: How does a Facade differ from an Adapter? (Hint: does the
>    client interface already exist, or is it newly invented?)

#### Proxy

A **Proxy** is a stand-in that implements the same interface as a real object
and controls access to it. The client cannot tell the difference, which is
exactly what lets the proxy add laziness, access checks, caching, logging, or
remote communication.

The shape is identical to Decorator. The difference is intent: a decorator
**adds behaviour**, a proxy **manages access** to something that may be
expensive, remote, or restricted.

The most common variant is the **virtual proxy**, which defers creating an
expensive object until it is genuinely needed:

```java
public interface Image { void display(); }

public class RealImage implements Image {
    private final String filename;
    public RealImage(String filename) {
        this.filename = filename;
        loadFromDisk();                   // expensive, happens in the constructor
    }
    private void loadFromDisk() { System.out.println("loading " + filename); }
    public void display() { System.out.println("displaying " + filename); }
}

public class ImageProxy implements Image {
    private final String filename;
    private RealImage real;               // created only on first use

    public ImageProxy(String filename) { this.filename = filename; }

    @Override
    public void display() {
        if (real == null) {
            real = new RealImage(filename);   // lazy initialisation
        }
        real.display();
    }
}

Image image = new ImageProxy("photo.jpg");   // nothing loaded yet
image.display();                             // loads, then displays
image.display();                             // reuses the loaded image
```

```text
   Client ---> Image (interface)
                 ^        ^
                 |        |
            ImageProxy   RealImage
                 |            ^
                 +------------+  holds and controls access
```

The recognised variants:

| Variant            | Controls                                       |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Virtual proxy      | Creation cost, by deferring it                 |
| Protection proxy   | Access, by checking permissions                |
| Remote proxy       | Location, by hiding network communication      |
| Caching proxy      | Repetition, by storing previous results        |
| Smart reference    | Lifecycle, by counting references or locking   |

A protection proxy:

```java
public class SecureDocumentProxy implements Document {
    private final Document real;
    private final User user;

    public String read() {
        if (!user.hasRole("READER")) throw new AccessDeniedException();
        return real.read();               // delegate only if permitted
    }
}
```

Java has first-class support through **dynamic proxies**, which generate a
proxy class at runtime for any set of interfaces:

```java
Document proxy = (Document) Proxy.newProxyInstance(
        Document.class.getClassLoader(),
        new Class<?>[]{ Document.class },
        (p, method, args) -> {                    // an InvocationHandler
            System.out.println("calling " + method.getName());
            return method.invoke(realDocument, args);   // delegate
        });
```

This is the mechanism behind a great deal of framework behaviour. Spring's
`@Transactional` works by wrapping your bean in a proxy that opens a
transaction, calls your method, and commits or rolls back. Its well-known
limitation follows directly: a call from one method of a class to another
method of the same class bypasses the proxy, so the annotation has no effect.

```java
@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Transactional public void outer() { inner(); }   // bypasses the proxy
    @Transactional public void inner() { ... }        // NOT transactional here
}
```

Hibernate uses the same technique for lazy loading, which is why accessing an
uninitialised association outside a session throws `LazyInitializationException`.

The costs: an extra indirection on every call, more complex stack traces, and
the subtlety that a proxy's identity differs from the real object's, so `==`
and sometimes `equals` behave unexpectedly.

> Key Takeaways
> - Proxy implements the same interface as the real object and controls access
>   to it.
> - Decorator adds behaviour; Proxy manages access, cost, or location.
> - Virtual proxies defer expensive creation until first use.
> - Protection proxies enforce permissions before delegating.
> - `java.lang.reflect.Proxy` generates proxies at runtime from interfaces.
> - Spring's `@Transactional` and Hibernate's lazy loading are proxy-based.
> - Self-invocation bypasses a proxy, which is why internal calls skip the
>   annotation.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a virtual proxy that defers loading and prove the load happens
>    once.
> 2. Write a protection proxy that rejects calls from an unauthorised user.
> 3. Use `Proxy.newProxyInstance` to log every method call on an interface.
> 4. Interview: Why does calling one `@Transactional` method from another in
>    the same class not start a transaction? (Hint: which object is the caller
>    actually invoking the method on?)

#### Bridge

Sometimes a hierarchy varies along two independent dimensions at once.
Modelling both with inheritance multiplies classes, because every combination
needs its own subclass.

```text
   INHERITANCE EXPLOSION: shape x rendering

   Shape
     Circle           CircleVector    CircleRaster
     Square     ->    SquareVector    SquareRaster
     Triangle         TriangleVector  TriangleRaster

   m shapes x n renderers = m*n classes
```

**Bridge** separates an abstraction from its implementation so the two can vary
independently. Rather than one inheriting from the other, the abstraction
**holds a reference** to the implementation.

```java
// The implementation side: how drawing happens
public interface Renderer {
    void renderCircle(double x, double y, double r);
    void renderSquare(double x, double y, double side);
}

public class VectorRenderer implements Renderer {
    public void renderCircle(double x, double y, double r) {
        System.out.println("vector circle r=" + r);
    }
    public void renderSquare(double x, double y, double s) { ... }
}

public class RasterRenderer implements Renderer {
    public void renderCircle(double x, double y, double r) {
        System.out.println("raster pixels for circle r=" + r);
    }
    public void renderSquare(double x, double y, double s) { ... }
}

// The abstraction side: what is being drawn
public abstract class Shape {
    protected final Renderer renderer;          // the BRIDGE to the other axis

    protected Shape(Renderer renderer) { this.renderer = renderer; }
    public abstract void draw();
}

public class Circle extends Shape {
    private final double x, y, radius;

    public Circle(Renderer renderer, double x, double y, double radius) {
        super(renderer);
        this.x = x; this.y = y; this.radius = radius;
    }

    @Override public void draw() { renderer.renderCircle(x, y, radius); }
}
```

Either axis now grows independently:

```java
Shape c1 = new Circle(new VectorRenderer(), 0, 0, 5);
Shape c2 = new Circle(new RasterRenderer(), 0, 0, 5);   // same shape, new renderer
c1.draw();
c2.draw();
```

```text
   BRIDGE: m + n classes, not m * n

   Shape  (abstraction)  <>------------> Renderer (implementor)
     ^                                       ^
     |                                       |
   +-+----+-------+                   +------+------+
   |      |       |                   |             |
 Circle Square Triangle          VectorRenderer  RasterRenderer
```

The pattern is frequently confused with Adapter and Strategy. The distinctions:

| Pattern  | When applied     | Purpose                               |
| -------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| Bridge   | Designed upfront | Let two dimensions vary independently |
| Adapter  | Applied after    | Make incompatible types work together |
| Strategy | Either           | Swap one algorithm at runtime         |

Structurally Bridge and Strategy look nearly identical, since both hold a
reference to an interface. The difference is scope and intent: Strategy varies
a single algorithm, while Bridge separates an entire hierarchy from an entire
implementation hierarchy, and is usually planned from the start.

The classic real example is JDBC. The `java.sql` interfaces are the
abstraction; each vendor's driver is an implementation. Your code varies
queries and connections freely, while the driver varies independently:

```java
// Same abstraction, different implementations, no client changes
Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection("jdbc:mysql://...");
Connection p = DriverManager.getConnection("jdbc:postgresql://...");
```

The same shape appears in SLF4J, where the logging API is the abstraction and
Logback or Log4j the implementation, and in AWT's peer architecture, where
components bridge to platform-specific widgets.

The costs: an extra level of indirection, and the need to identify the two
dimensions correctly upfront. Applying Bridge where only one dimension actually
varies adds complexity for nothing, so wait until the second axis is real.

> Key Takeaways
> - Bridge separates an abstraction from its implementation so both can vary.
> - It replaces an m by n class explosion with m plus n classes.
> - The abstraction holds a reference to the implementor instead of
>   inheriting.
> - Bridge is usually designed upfront; Adapter is applied to existing code.
> - Bridge and Strategy look alike; Bridge separates whole hierarchies.
> - JDBC and SLF4J are large-scale examples of the pattern.
> - Do not apply it until a genuine second dimension of variation exists.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement shapes and renderers as a bridge and combine them freely.
> 2. Add a third renderer and confirm no shape class changed.
> 3. Count the classes needed with and without the pattern for four shapes and
>    three renderers.
> 4. Interview: How does Bridge differ from Strategy when the code looks the
>    same? (Hint: compare what varies on each side, one algorithm or a whole
>    hierarchy.)

<a id="95-behavioral-patterns"></a>
### 9.5 Behavioral Patterns

This subchapter covers the patterns that govern how objects communicate and
how responsibility for an algorithm is distributed between them.

#### Strategy

A method that selects between several algorithms with a conditional has to be
edited every time a new algorithm appears, and the algorithms cannot be tested
or reused independently.

```java
public class Sorter {
    public void sort(int[] data, String algorithm) {
        if (algorithm.equals("quick"))      { /* 30 lines */ }
        else if (algorithm.equals("merge")) { /* 30 lines */ }
        else if (algorithm.equals("bubble")){ /* 20 lines */ }
        // one class, three algorithms, one enormous method
    }
}
```

**Strategy** defines a family of interchangeable algorithms, encapsulates each
one, and makes them swappable at runtime. The context holds a strategy and
delegates to it.

```java
public interface SortStrategy {
    void sort(int[] data);
}

public class QuickSort implements SortStrategy {
    public void sort(int[] data) { /* ... */ }
}
public class MergeSort implements SortStrategy {
    public void sort(int[] data) { /* ... */ }
}

// The context: knows nothing about any specific algorithm
public class Sorter {
    private SortStrategy strategy;

    public Sorter(SortStrategy strategy) { this.strategy = strategy; }
    public void setStrategy(SortStrategy s) { this.strategy = s; }   // swap at runtime

    public void sort(int[] data) { strategy.sort(data); }
}

Sorter sorter = new Sorter(new QuickSort());
sorter.sort(data);
sorter.setStrategy(new MergeSort());     // changed without touching Sorter
```

```text
   Sorter (context) <>------> SortStrategy
                                  ^
                     +------------+------------+
                     |            |            |
                 QuickSort    MergeSort    BubbleSort
```

Strategy is the purest expression of the Open-Closed Principle: the context is
closed for modification, and the family of algorithms is open for extension.

In modern Java a single-method strategy is usually a lambda, and no interface
hierarchy is needed at all:

```java
public class Sorter {
    public void sort(int[] data, IntBinaryOperator comparator) { ... }
}

// Strategy as a lambda
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("bob", "alice"));
names.sort(Comparator.comparing(String::length));     // a strategy
names.sort((a, b) -> b.compareTo(a));                 // a different one
```

`Comparator` is the standard library's canonical Strategy: `Collections.sort`
delegates the comparison decision entirely to the object you pass. Other
examples include `ThreadPoolExecutor`'s `RejectedExecutionHandler` and the
`Predicate` passed to `removeIf`.

A practical example where the class form still earns its place, because each
strategy needs its own state and configuration:

```java
public interface ShippingStrategy {
    Money cost(Order order);
}

public class StandardShipping implements ShippingStrategy {
    public Money cost(Order o) { return Money.of(5.00); }
}
public class ExpressShipping implements ShippingStrategy {
    private final double surcharge;                    // per-strategy state
    public ExpressShipping(double surcharge) { this.surcharge = surcharge; }
    public Money cost(Order o) { return Money.of(15.00 + surcharge); }
}

public class Checkout {
    public Money total(Order order, ShippingStrategy shipping) {
        return order.subtotal().plus(shipping.cost(order));
    }
}
```

Strategy is often confused with State and with Template Method:

| Pattern        | Who chooses     | What varies                  |
| -------------- | --------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Strategy       | The client      | A whole algorithm            |
| State          | The object itself | Behaviour as state changes |
| Template Method| The subclass    | Steps within a fixed skeleton|

The distinction from State is the useful one: with Strategy the client picks
and the strategies do not know about each other; with State the object
transitions between states itself.

The costs are that clients must know the strategies exist in order to choose
one, and that trivial strategies add classes for little benefit. Use a lambda
when the strategy is one function with no state, and a class when it carries
configuration, needs a name, or must be tested on its own.

> Key Takeaways
> - Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind one interface.
> - The context delegates and never changes when a new algorithm is added.
> - It is the clearest application of the Open-Closed Principle.
> - A single-method strategy is usually better expressed as a lambda.
> - `Comparator` is the standard library's canonical Strategy.
> - Use a class when the strategy holds state or configuration.
> - The client must know enough about the strategies to choose one.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a payment processor with card, bank transfer, and wallet
>    strategies.
> 2. Swap the strategy at runtime and confirm the context was not modified.
> 3. Rewrite a single-method strategy as a lambda and compare readability.
> 4. Interview: How is Strategy different from State? (Hint: who decides which
>    implementation is active, and do the implementations know about each
>    other?)

#### Observer

When one object changes, several others may need to react. Hard-coding the
notifications couples the source to every consumer and requires editing it
whenever a consumer is added.

```java
public class Stock {
    private final EmailAlerter email;        // knows every consumer by name
    private final Dashboard dashboard;
    private final AuditLog log;

    public void setPrice(double p) {
        this.price = p;
        email.send(p);                       // a new consumer means editing here
        dashboard.update(p);
        log.record(p);
    }
}
```

**Observer** defines a one-to-many dependency so that when one object changes
state, all its dependents are notified automatically. The subject knows only
that observers exist, not who they are.

```java
public interface PriceObserver {
    void onPriceChange(String symbol, double price);
}

public class Stock {
    private final List<PriceObserver> observers = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
    private double price;

    public void subscribe(PriceObserver o)   { observers.add(o); }
    public void unsubscribe(PriceObserver o) { observers.remove(o); }

    public void setPrice(double price) {
        this.price = price;
        notifyObservers();                    // push the change outward
    }

    private void notifyObservers() {
        for (PriceObserver o : observers) {
            o.onPriceChange(symbol, price);   // the subject knows only the interface
        }
    }
}

// Observers register themselves; Stock never mentions them
stock.subscribe((sym, p) -> System.out.println(sym + " now " + p));
stock.subscribe(new AuditLog()::record);
```

```text
                      Stock (subject)
                    observers: List<PriceObserver>
                             |
             notifies        |         (subject knows only the interface)
        +--------------+-----+------+--------------+
        v              v            v              v
   EmailAlerter   Dashboard    AuditLog      (added later, no edit)
```

Note the `CopyOnWriteArrayList`. Observers frequently unsubscribe from inside a
notification, which would throw `ConcurrentModificationException` with an
`ArrayList`. This is a real bug, not a theoretical one.

Two delivery models:

| Model | The subject sends        | Trade-off                            |
| ----- | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------ |
| Push  | The changed data         | Simple; may send more than needed    |
| Pull  | Only "something changed" | Observers query; more round trips    |

Java's original `java.util.Observable` and `Observer` were **deprecated in Java
9** and should not be used. `Observable` is a class, so it consumes the single
inheritance slot, it is not thread-safe, and the notification order is
unspecified. Modern options:

```java
// 1. A hand-rolled listener list, as above: clear and dependency-free

// 2. PropertyChangeSupport from java.beans
private final PropertyChangeSupport support = new PropertyChangeSupport(this);
support.addPropertyChangeListener(evt -> System.out.println(evt.getNewValue()));
support.firePropertyChange("price", oldPrice, newPrice);

// 3. Flow API (Java 9), reactive streams with backpressure
SubmissionPublisher<Double> publisher = new SubmissionPublisher<>();
publisher.subscribe(new Flow.Subscriber<>() { ... });

// 4. Framework events, such as Spring's ApplicationEventPublisher
```

The pattern underpins a great deal of familiar code: Swing's
`addActionListener`, JavaFX properties and bindings, the DOM's
`addEventListener`, and every message bus.

Three hazards worth knowing.

**Memory leaks.** A subject holds strong references to observers, so an
observer that never unsubscribes cannot be collected. Long-lived subjects with
short-lived observers are the usual leak source.

**Notification storms.** An observer that updates state which triggers another
notification can cascade or loop. Guard against re-entrancy.

**Unpredictable order and failure.** Observers are notified in an unspecified
order, and an exception from one can prevent the rest from running unless you
catch per observer.

```java
for (PriceObserver o : observers) {
    try { o.onPriceChange(symbol, price); }
    catch (RuntimeException e) { log.warn("observer failed", e); }  // isolate
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Observer notifies many dependents automatically when a subject changes.
> - The subject depends only on an interface, so observers can be added
>   freely.
> - Use a `CopyOnWriteArrayList` so observers may unsubscribe during
>   notification.
> - Push sends the data; pull sends only a signal and lets observers query.
> - `java.util.Observable` is deprecated; use listeners, `Flow`, or framework
>   events.
> - Observers that never unsubscribe cause memory leaks.
> - Isolate observer exceptions so one failure does not block the rest.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a stock price subject with two lambda observers.
> 2. Unsubscribe an observer from inside its own callback and handle the
>    result.
> 3. Add exception isolation and prove a failing observer does not block
>    others.
> 4. Interview: How can Observer cause a memory leak? (Hint: who holds a
>    reference to whom, and what happens if nobody calls unsubscribe?)

#### Template Method

Several algorithms often share the same overall shape while differing in a few
steps. Copying the skeleton into each variant duplicates the sequence, and a
change to the order must then be made everywhere.

**Template Method** defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class and
lets subclasses override specific steps without changing the structure.

```java
public abstract class DataImporter {

    // The TEMPLATE METHOD: final, so the sequence cannot be altered
    public final void importData(Path file) {
        String raw = readFile(file);          // shared step
        List<Record> records = parse(raw);    // varies: abstract
        validate(records);                    // shared, but overridable hook
        save(records);                        // varies: abstract
        onComplete(records.size());           // optional hook, empty by default
    }

    // Shared implementation
    private String readFile(Path file) { ... }

    // Steps subclasses MUST supply
    protected abstract List<Record> parse(String raw);
    protected abstract void save(List<Record> records);

    // Hooks: subclasses MAY override
    protected void validate(List<Record> records) { /* default: nothing */ }
    protected void onComplete(int count) { }
}

public class CsvImporter extends DataImporter {
    @Override protected List<Record> parse(String raw) { /* split on commas */ }
    @Override protected void save(List<Record> r) { /* insert into SQL */ }
}

public class JsonImporter extends DataImporter {
    @Override protected List<Record> parse(String raw) { /* Jackson */ }
    @Override protected void save(List<Record> r) { /* write to Mongo */ }
    @Override protected void validate(List<Record> r) { /* extra checks */ }
}
```

```text
   DataImporter.importData()  <-- fixed sequence, declared final
        |
        +-- readFile()     shared
        +-- parse()        abstract  ---> CsvImporter / JsonImporter supply
        +-- validate()     hook      ---> optional override
        +-- save()         abstract  ---> subclasses supply
        +-- onComplete()   hook      ---> optional override
```

Three details make the pattern work correctly.

The template method should be **`final`**, so subclasses cannot change the
sequence. That is the invariant the pattern exists to protect.

Steps should be **`protected`**, not public. They are extension points for
subclasses, not part of the class's public interface.

**Hooks** with empty default bodies let subclasses opt in without forcing every
one to implement them, which keeps the abstract surface small.

This is an application of the **Hollywood Principle**: "don't call us, we'll
call you". The framework owns the flow and calls into your code, rather than
your code calling the framework. That inversion is what distinguishes a
framework from a library.

Standard-library and framework examples:

```java
// AbstractList implements the algorithms; you supply get() and size()
public class Range extends AbstractList<Integer> {
    private final int n;
    public Range(int n) { this.n = n; }
    @Override public Integer get(int i) { return i; }     // the varying step
    @Override public int size() { return n; }
    // indexOf, contains, iterator, subList all work from these two
}
```

`AbstractList`, `AbstractMap`, `InputStream`, JUnit's `setUp` and `tearDown`,
and Spring's `JdbcTemplate` all use the pattern.

The comparison with Strategy is the usual interview question:

| Aspect          | Template Method          | Strategy                |
| --------------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------- |
| Mechanism       | Inheritance              | Composition             |
| Binding time    | Compile time             | Runtime                 |
| Varies          | Steps inside a skeleton  | The whole algorithm     |
| Coupling        | Subclass to superclass   | Context to interface    |
| Changeable later| No, fixed at compile time| Yes, swappable          |

Template Method's weakness is inheritance itself: a subclass depends on the
protected structure of its parent, so changing the base class can break every
subclass, and you get only one inheritance slot.

The composition-based alternative passes the varying steps as functions,
which is often preferable in modern Java:

```java
public final class DataImporter {
    public void importData(Path file,
                           Function<String, List<Record>> parser,
                           Consumer<List<Record>> saver) {
        saver.accept(parser.apply(readFile(file)));
    }
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Template Method fixes an algorithm's skeleton and defers steps to
>   subclasses.
> - Declare the template method `final` so the sequence cannot be changed.
> - Abstract steps are mandatory; hooks with empty bodies are optional.
> - Extension points should be `protected`, not public.
> - It embodies the Hollywood Principle, where the framework calls your code.
> - `AbstractList` and JUnit lifecycle methods are real examples.
> - Template Method binds at compile time via inheritance; Strategy binds at
>   runtime via composition.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write an abstract report generator with a fixed sequence and two
>    subclasses.
> 2. Add an optional hook and override it in only one subclass.
> 3. Rewrite the same design using functions passed as parameters.
> 4. Interview: Why should the template method be declared `final`? (Hint:
>    what guarantee does the base class lose if a subclass overrides it?)

#### Command

Calling a method directly means the call happens immediately, once, and cannot
be recorded, queued, or undone. **Command** turns a request into an object, so
it can be passed around, stored, scheduled, logged, and reversed.

The analogy is a restaurant order slip. The waiter writes the request down; the
slip can be queued, re-read, handed to a different cook, or cancelled. The
customer and the cook never interact directly.

```java
public interface Command {
    void execute();
    void undo();                    // what makes undo/redo possible
}

// The receiver: the object that does the real work
public class Document {
    private final StringBuilder text = new StringBuilder();
    public void append(String s) { text.append(s); }
    public void deleteLast(int n) { text.delete(text.length() - n, text.length()); }
    public String content() { return text.toString(); }
}

// A concrete command captures the receiver AND the parameters
public class AppendCommand implements Command {
    private final Document doc;
    private final String textToAdd;

    public AppendCommand(Document doc, String textToAdd) {
        this.doc = doc;
        this.textToAdd = textToAdd;
    }

    @Override public void execute() { doc.append(textToAdd); }
    @Override public void undo()    { doc.deleteLast(textToAdd.length()); }
}
```

The invoker stores commands, which is what enables history:

```java
public class Editor {
    private final Deque<Command> history = new ArrayDeque<>();

    public void run(Command c) {
        c.execute();
        history.push(c);              // remember it for undo
    }

    public void undo() {
        if (!history.isEmpty()) history.pop().undo();
    }
}

Editor editor = new Editor();
Document doc = new Document();
editor.run(new AppendCommand(doc, "Hello"));
editor.run(new AppendCommand(doc, " world"));
editor.undo();                        // "Hello"
```

```text
   Client ---creates---> Command (interface)
                             ^
   Invoker ---stores--------+|
   (history)                 |
                        AppendCommand ---calls---> Document (receiver)
```

The four roles are worth naming, because interviews ask for them: the
**client** creates commands, the **invoker** triggers them, the **command**
encapsulates the request, and the **receiver** performs the work.

What Command buys you:

| Capability   | How the pattern provides it                    |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Undo/redo    | Each command knows how to reverse itself        |
| Queuing      | Commands are objects, so they can wait in a list |
| Logging      | Serialise commands to replay after a crash      |
| Scheduling   | Execute later, or on another thread             |
| Macros       | A composite command holding a list of commands   |
| Decoupling   | The invoker never learns what the command does   |

A macro command is Composite applied to Command:

```java
public class MacroCommand implements Command {
    private final List<Command> commands;
    public void execute() { commands.forEach(Command::execute); }
    public void undo() {
        // Reverse order matters: undo the last action first
        for (int i = commands.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) commands.get(i).undo();
    }
}
```

In Java the interface is functional in spirit, and `Runnable` is effectively a
command without undo. That is exactly how executors use it:

```java
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);
pool.submit(() -> processOrder(id));      // a command, queued and run later
```

Other examples include Swing's `Action`, which bundles a command with its label
and icon, and the request objects in messaging systems.

The costs: a class per operation, which is why undo-less commands are usually
lambdas, and the fact that correct `undo` is genuinely hard. A command must
capture enough state to reverse itself, and for operations that lose
information, such as overwriting text, it must store the old value.

> Key Takeaways
> - Command turns a request into an object with its own lifetime.
> - The four roles are client, invoker, command, and receiver.
> - Storing executed commands in a stack gives undo and redo.
> - Commands can be queued, logged, replayed, and scheduled.
> - A macro command composes several commands, undoing them in reverse order.
> - `Runnable` submitted to an executor is a command without undo.
> - Implementing `undo` correctly requires capturing the state being
>   replaced.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a text editor with append commands and a working undo stack.
> 2. Add a macro command that groups three operations into one undo step.
> 3. Implement a command that overwrites a value and correctly restores it.
> 4. Interview: What must a command store to support undo? (Hint: consider an
>    operation that replaces a value rather than adding one.)

#### State

An object whose behaviour depends on its internal state usually accumulates
conditionals in every method, and the legal transitions are scattered and
implicit.

```java
public class Order {
    private String state = "NEW";

    public void pay() {
        if (state.equals("NEW"))            state = "PAID";
        else if (state.equals("PAID"))      throw new IllegalStateException();
        else if (state.equals("SHIPPED"))   throw new IllegalStateException();
    }
    public void ship() {
        if (state.equals("PAID"))           state = "SHIPPED";
        else                                throw new IllegalStateException();
    }
    // every method repeats the same branching
}
```

**State** allows an object to alter its behaviour when its internal state
changes, by moving each state's behaviour into its own class. The object
appears to change class.

```java
public interface OrderState {
    OrderState pay(Order order);        // returns the NEXT state
    OrderState ship(Order order);
    OrderState cancel(Order order);
}

public class NewState implements OrderState {
    public OrderState pay(Order o)    { o.chargeCard(); return new PaidState(); }
    public OrderState ship(Order o)   { throw new IllegalStateException("unpaid"); }
    public OrderState cancel(Order o) { return new CancelledState(); }
}

public class PaidState implements OrderState {
    public OrderState pay(Order o)    { throw new IllegalStateException("paid"); }
    public OrderState ship(Order o)   { o.dispatch(); return new ShippedState(); }
    public OrderState cancel(Order o) { o.refund(); return new CancelledState(); }
}

public class ShippedState implements OrderState {
    public OrderState pay(Order o)    { throw new IllegalStateException(); }
    public OrderState ship(Order o)   { throw new IllegalStateException(); }
    public OrderState cancel(Order o) { throw new IllegalStateException("in transit"); }
}

// The context delegates everything and holds only the current state
public class Order {
    private OrderState state = new NewState();

    public void pay()    { state = state.pay(this); }     // no conditionals left
    public void ship()   { state = state.ship(this); }
    public void cancel() { state = state.cancel(this); }
}
```

```text
   STATE MACHINE made explicit

        pay()          ship()
   NEW --------> PAID --------> SHIPPED
    |              |
    | cancel()     | cancel() (refund)
    v              v
   CANCELLED <-----+
```

The gain is that each state class holds the complete rules for one state, and
the legal transitions are visible in the return types rather than buried in
conditionals. Adding a state means adding a class.

Java's enums make a compact alternative when states carry no extra data, and
this is the form most Java codebases use:

```java
public enum OrderState {
    NEW {
        @Override public OrderState pay() { return PAID; }
    },
    PAID {
        @Override public OrderState ship() { return SHIPPED; }
    },
    SHIPPED;

    // Defaults reject everything; each constant permits only what it allows
    public OrderState pay()  { throw new IllegalStateException(name()); }
    public OrderState ship() { throw new IllegalStateException(name()); }
}
```

The enum version gives exhaustive switch support, serialisation, and a natural
place to define the full set of states, at the cost of not allowing per-state
fields of different types.

State is structurally identical to Strategy, and the difference is worth
stating precisely:

| Aspect             | Strategy                  | State                      |
| ------------------ | ------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| Who selects it     | The client                | The object, internally     |
| Implementations know each other | No           | Yes, they name successors  |
| Changes over time  | Only if the client swaps it | Continuously, by transition |
| Models             | An algorithm choice       | A lifecycle                |

Where to put the transition logic is the pattern's main design decision.
Returning the next state from the state object, as above, keeps each state's
rules together. The alternative has the context decide, which centralises the
machine but reintroduces conditionals.

The cost is a class per state, so for two or three states a simple enum with a
switch is usually clearer. The pattern pays off when there are many states,
many operations, or complex transition rules.

> Key Takeaways
> - State moves behaviour that depends on a mode into one class per mode.
> - The context delegates and holds only the current state object.
> - Conditionals disappear because each state implements only its own rules.
> - Transitions become explicit, typically by returning the next state.
> - Java enums with per-constant bodies are a compact alternative.
> - State and Strategy look identical; State transitions itself, Strategy is
>   chosen by the client.
> - For two or three simple states, an enum and a switch are clearer.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Model a vending machine with idle, has-coin, and dispensing states.
> 2. Implement the same machine as an enum with per-constant transitions.
> 3. Make an illegal transition throw and write a test proving it.
> 4. Interview: Why do State implementations know about each other when
>    Strategy implementations do not? (Hint: who is responsible for deciding
>    what comes next?)

#### Iterator and Visitor

The last two patterns both concern traversal, and they answer opposite
questions. Iterator asks how to walk a structure without exposing it. Visitor
asks how to add operations to a structure without editing it.

**Iterator** provides sequential access to the elements of an aggregate without
revealing how it is stored. It was covered mechanically in chapter 7; here it
matters as a design decision.

Exposing the internal collection leaks the representation and lets callers
mutate it:

```java
public class Playlist {
    private final List<Song> songs = new ArrayList<>();
    public List<Song> getSongs() { return songs; }   // leaks; callers can clear it
}
```

Implementing `Iterable` gives traversal without exposure:

```java
public class Playlist implements Iterable<Song> {
    private final List<Song> songs = new ArrayList<>();

    @Override
    public Iterator<Song> iterator() {
        return Collections.unmodifiableList(songs).iterator();   // read-only walk
    }
}

for (Song s : playlist) { ... }     // works because of Iterable
```

A custom iterator can also traverse something that is not a collection at all,
which is where the pattern earns its place:

```java
public class Fibonacci implements Iterable<Long> {
    private final int count;
    public Fibonacci(int count) { this.count = count; }

    @Override
    public Iterator<Long> iterator() {
        return new Iterator<>() {
            private long a = 0, b = 1;
            private int emitted = 0;

            @Override public boolean hasNext() { return emitted < count; }
            @Override public Long next() {
                if (!hasNext()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
                long result = a;
                long next = a + b; a = b; b = next;   // advance the state
                emitted++;
                return result;
            }
        };
    }
}

for (long f : new Fibonacci(8)) System.out.print(f + " ");   // 0 1 1 2 3 5 8 13
```

**Visitor** separates an algorithm from the object structure it operates on.
The motivation is the "expression problem": with ordinary polymorphism, adding
a new *type* is easy and adding a new *operation* means editing every class.
Visitor reverses that trade.

```java
public interface Visitor {
    void visit(Circle c);
    void visit(Square s);
}

public interface Shape {
    void accept(Visitor v);        // double dispatch: the shape calls back
}

public record Circle(double radius) implements Shape {
    public void accept(Visitor v) { v.visit(this); }    // picks visit(Circle)
}
public record Square(double side) implements Shape {
    public void accept(Visitor v) { v.visit(this); }
}

// A new OPERATION is a new class; no shape is edited
public class AreaVisitor implements Visitor {
    private double total;
    public void visit(Circle c) { total += Math.PI * c.radius() * c.radius(); }
    public void visit(Square s) { total += s.side() * s.side(); }
    public double total() { return total; }
}

AreaVisitor area = new AreaVisitor();
shapes.forEach(s -> s.accept(area));
```

The `accept` call is **double dispatch**: the first dispatch selects the shape's
`accept`, and the second selects the visitor's overload. Java resolves overloads
at compile time, so this round trip is what makes the right method run.

```text
   shape.accept(visitor)
        |
        | dispatch 1: which Shape?     -> Circle.accept
        v
   visitor.visit(this)
        |
        | dispatch 2: which overload?  -> visit(Circle)
        v
   the correct operation
```

The trade-off, stated plainly:

| Change             | Ordinary polymorphism | Visitor            |
| ------------------ | --------------------- | ------------------ |
| Add a new type     | Easy, one new class   | Hard, edit every visitor |
| Add a new operation| Hard, edit every class| Easy, one new visitor |

So Visitor suits a **stable set of types** with a **growing set of
operations**, such as compiler passes over a fixed abstract syntax tree.

Modern Java offers a lighter alternative. Sealed interfaces with pattern
matching give the same "add an operation without editing the types" property,
with compiler-checked exhaustiveness and no `accept` boilerplate:

```java
public sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square { }

double area = switch (shape) {
    case Circle c -> Math.PI * c.radius() * c.radius();
    case Square s -> s.side() * s.side();
};   // exhaustive: adding a permitted type breaks this switch at compile time
```

For new code this is usually the better choice. Classic Visitor remains
relevant in older codebases and in libraries that must work across Java
versions.

> Key Takeaways
> - Iterator gives sequential access without exposing the underlying
>   structure.
> - Implementing `Iterable` enables the enhanced `for` loop over your own
>   types.
> - A custom iterator can traverse computed sequences, not just collections.
> - Visitor separates operations from the structure they act on.
> - It uses double dispatch through `accept` to select the right overload.
> - Visitor makes new operations easy and new types hard, reversing the usual
>   trade.
> - Sealed interfaces with pattern matching achieve the same goal with
>   compiler-checked exhaustiveness.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Make a custom class implement `Iterable` and use it in a for-each loop.
> 2. Write an iterator over a computed sequence such as primes.
> 3. Implement area and perimeter visitors over a shape hierarchy.
> 4. Rewrite the same operations with a sealed interface and a switch.
> 5. Interview: Why does Visitor need double dispatch? (Hint: when does Java
>    decide which overload of `visit` to call, and what does it know at that
>    moment?)

<a id="96-uml-and-modeling"></a>
### 9.6 UML and Modeling

This subchapter covers the diagram notation used to discuss designs, and the
process of turning a written requirement into a class model.

#### Class Diagram Notation

Design discussions happen on whiteboards, and UML is the shared notation for
them. You rarely need the full specification; a small subset covers almost
every real conversation, and interviews expect you to read and draw it.

A **class** is a box with three compartments: name, attributes, operations.

```text
   +---------------------------+
   |         Account           |   <- class name (italic if abstract)
   +---------------------------+
   | - balance: BigDecimal     |   <- attributes: visibility name: type
   | - owner: String           |
   | + MAX_LIMIT: int {static} |
   +---------------------------+
   | + deposit(amount: Money)  |   <- operations
   | + withdraw(amount: Money) |
   | - validate(): boolean     |
   +---------------------------+
```

Visibility markers map directly onto Java's access modifiers:

| Symbol | UML visibility | Java equivalent     |
| ------ | -------------- | ------------------- |
| `+`    | public         | `public`            |
| `-`    | private        | `private`           |
| `#`    | protected      | `protected`         |
| `~`    | package        | package-private     |

Notation conventions worth knowing:

- Types follow the name after a colon: `balance: BigDecimal`. This reads
  backwards from Java and trips people up.
- `{static}` or underlining marks static members.
- *Italics* mark abstract classes and abstract methods.
- A **stereotype** in guillemets labels the kind of element:
  `<<interface>>`, `<<abstract>>`, `<<enumeration>>`, `<<record>>`.

```text
   +---------------------------+
   |     <<interface>>         |
   |      Repository           |
   +---------------------------+
   | + save(entity: T): void   |
   | + findById(id: ID): T     |
   +---------------------------+
```

The Java that corresponds to the account box above:

```java
public class Account {
    public static final int MAX_LIMIT = 10_000;   // + and {static}
    private BigDecimal balance;                    // -
    private String owner;                          // -

    public void deposit(Money amount) { }          // +
    public void withdraw(Money amount) { }         // +
    private boolean validate() { return true; }    // -
}
```

Diagrams should be **partial on purpose**. Showing every field and getter
produces a picture nobody reads. Include only what the conversation needs: for
a discussion about dependencies, class names and relationships are often
enough, with both other compartments left empty.

```text
   Minimal but useful for an architecture discussion

   +----------------+      +-------------------+      +--------------+
   | OrderService   |----->| OrderRepository   |<|----| JpaOrderRepo |
   +----------------+      |   <<interface>>   |      +--------------+
                           +-------------------+
```

Other elements that appear regularly:

- A **note** is a dog-eared box attached by a dashed line, used for
  constraints or explanations.
- A **package** is a tabbed folder shape grouping related classes.
- A **constraint** in braces states a rule: `{balance >= 0}`.

Tools such as PlantUML let you keep diagrams in version control as text, which
