is worth preferring over images that drift from the code:

```text
@startuml
interface Repository {
  +save(entity: T)
}
class JpaRepository
Repository <|.. JpaRepository
@enduml
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A class box has three compartments: name, attributes, and operations.
> - Visibility uses `+`, `-`, `#`, and `~` for public, private, protected, and
>   package.
> - Types follow the member name after a colon, the reverse of Java.
> - Italics mark abstract classes and methods; `{static}` or underlining marks
>   static.
> - Stereotypes in guillemets label interfaces, enums, and records.
> - Leave out detail that the discussion does not need.
> - Text-based tools keep diagrams versioned alongside the code.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Draw a class box for a `Book` class with three fields and two methods.
> 2. Translate a given UML box into compiling Java, including visibility.
> 3. Draw an interface box with a stereotype and one operation.
> 4. Interview: What does an italic class name mean in UML? (Hint: what cannot
>    be instantiated?)

#### Modeling Associations and Multiplicity

Boxes alone say nothing. The lines between them carry most of a diagram's
information: who knows about whom, how many, and who owns whose lifetime.

An **association** is a plain line meaning one class holds a reference to
another. An arrowhead makes it one-directional.

```text
   +---------+              +---------+
   | Student |------------->| Course  |     Student knows Course
   +---------+              +---------+     (a unidirectional association)
```

```java
public class Student {
    private List<Course> courses;      // the reference the line represents
}
```

**Multiplicity** labels each end with how many instances participate:

| Notation | Meaning              |
| -------- | -------------------- |
| `1`      | Exactly one          |
| `0..1`   | Zero or one          |
| `*`      | Zero or more         |
| `1..*`   | One or more          |
| `0..*`   | Same as `*`          |
| `2..5`   | A specific range     |

```text
   +---------+ 1        0..* +---------+
   | Order   |---------------| OrderLine|
   +---------+               +---------+

   Read: one Order has zero or more OrderLines,
         each OrderLine belongs to exactly one Order.
```

```java
public class Order {
    private final List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();   // 0..*
}
public class OrderLine {
    private final Order order;        // 1
}
```

Two special associations express **ownership**, and the distinction matters
because it tells you about object lifetimes.

**Aggregation**, a hollow diamond, is a "has-a" where the part can outlive the
whole. A department has employees, but deleting the department does not delete
the people.

**Composition**, a filled diamond, is a "part-of" where the part cannot exist
without the whole. Delete the order and its lines go with it.

```text
   AGGREGATION (hollow diamond): parts survive independently

   +------------+ 1      0..* +----------+
   | Department |<>-----------| Employee |
   +------------+             +----------+

   COMPOSITION (filled diamond): parts die with the whole

   +---------+ 1        1..* +-----------+
   | Order   |<#>------------| OrderLine |
   +---------+               +-----------+
   (a filled diamond is drawn solid; shown here as <#>)
```

```java
// Aggregation: the employees exist before and after
public class Department {
    private final List<Employee> members;
    public Department(List<Employee> members) { this.members = members; }
}

// Composition: the order creates and owns its lines
public class Order {
    private final List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();
    public void addLine(Product p, int qty) {
        lines.add(new OrderLine(this, p, qty));   // created here, owned here
    }
}
```

A **dependency** is a dashed arrow meaning "uses temporarily", typically a
method parameter, a local variable, or a return type rather than a field:

```text
   +---------------+          +-----------+
   | OrderService  |- - - - ->| Validator |    uses, but does not hold
   +---------------+          +-----------+
```

```java
public class OrderService {
    public void place(Order o, Validator v) { v.validate(o); }  // a parameter
}
```

The full set of line types, which is the vocabulary most interviews check:

| Relationship | Line              | Meaning                    | In Java             |
| ------------ | ----------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------- |
| Association  | Solid line        | Holds a reference          | A field             |
| Aggregation  | Hollow diamond    | Has-a, parts independent   | A field, injected   |
| Composition  | Filled diamond    | Part-of, shared lifetime   | A field, created inside |
| Dependency   | Dashed arrow      | Uses temporarily           | Parameter or local  |
| Inheritance  | Hollow triangle, solid line | Extends      | `extends`           |
| Realization  | Hollow triangle, dashed line| Implements   | `implements`        |

The diamond is drawn on the side of the **whole**, not the part, which is the
detail most often reversed on a whiteboard.

A last note: the aggregation-versus-composition distinction is frequently
debated and rarely changes code. If a diagram's audience does not need it, a
plain association with multiplicity communicates nearly as much.

> Key Takeaways
> - A solid line is an association, meaning one class holds a reference.
> - Multiplicity at each end states how many instances participate.
> - Aggregation, a hollow diamond, means the part can outlive the whole.
> - Composition, a filled diamond, means the part dies with the whole.
> - The diamond is drawn on the side of the containing whole.
> - A dashed arrow is a dependency: a parameter or local, not a field.
> - Multiplicity usually conveys more than the aggregation distinction.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Draw `Library`, `Book`, and `Member` with correct multiplicities.
> 2. Decide whether `House` and `Room` is aggregation or composition, and
>    justify it.
> 3. Translate a composition relationship into Java that enforces the
>    lifetime.
> 4. Interview: What is the practical difference between aggregation and
>    composition in code? (Hint: who calls `new`, and what happens on
>    deletion?)

#### Representing Inheritance and Realization

Two relationships express type hierarchies, and UML distinguishes them by line
style. Both use a hollow triangle pointing at the more general type.

**Generalization**, drawn with a **solid** line, is class inheritance:

```text
   +----------------+
   |   *Shape*      |       italic name = abstract
   +----------------+
   | # name: String |
   +----------------+
   | + area(): double {abstract} |
   +----------------+
            /_\                 hollow triangle points at the PARENT
             |
      +------+------+
      |             |
   +--------+   +--------+
   | Circle |   | Square |
   +--------+   +--------+
```

```java
public abstract class Shape {
    protected String name;
    public abstract double area();
}
public class Circle extends Shape {
    @Override public double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; }
}
```

**Realization**, drawn with a **dashed** line and the same hollow triangle, is
interface implementation:

```text
   +---------------------+
   |   <<interface>>     |
   |     Drawable        |
   +---------------------+
   | + draw(): void      |
   +---------------------+
            /_\
             :                  dashed line = realization
             :
        +---------+
        | Circle  |
        +---------+
```

```java
public interface Drawable { void draw(); }
public class Circle implements Drawable {
    @Override public void draw() { }
}
```

The mnemonic: **solid line for `extends`, dashed line for `implements`**. Both
triangles point toward the abstraction.

A class doing both, which is the common case:

```text
        +---------+              +----------------+
        | *Shape* |              |  <<interface>> |
        +---------+              |    Drawable    |
            /_\                  +----------------+
             |                          /_\
             |                           :
             +------------+--------------+
                          |
                     +---------+
                     | Circle  |
                     +---------+
```

```java
public class Circle extends Shape implements Drawable, Comparable<Circle> { }
```

Java's single inheritance and multiple interface implementation show directly
in the diagram: at most one solid triangle leaves a class, but any number of
dashed ones may.

Interface **extension** uses a dashed or solid line depending on the
convention, but since one interface extending another is genuinely
generalization, a solid line is correct:

```text
   <<interface>> Collection
            /_\
             |  (solid: interface generalization)
   <<interface>> List
```

```java
public interface List<E> extends Collection<E> { }
```

Two further notations complete the picture.

A **default method** is shown as a normal operation on the interface, sometimes
marked with a note, since it is not abstract:

```text
   +------------------------------+
   |       <<interface>>          |
   |         Comparator           |
   +------------------------------+
   | + compare(a, b): int         |
   | + reversed(): Comparator {default} |
   +------------------------------+
```

A **sealed** hierarchy is annotated with a constraint listing the permitted
subtypes:

```text
   +--------------------+
   |  <<sealed>> Shape  |
   |  {permits Circle,  |
   |   Square}          |
   +--------------------+
```

```java
public sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square { }
```

A design caution that belongs with the notation: a diagram showing deep
inheritance chains, four or five levels, is usually showing a design problem.
Favour shallow hierarchies and composition, which appear as diamonds and plain
associations rather than long triangle chains.

| Relationship            | Line   | Triangle | Java          |
| ----------------------- | ------ | -------- | ------------- |
| Class generalization    | Solid  | Hollow   | `extends` a class |
| Interface realization   | Dashed | Hollow   | `implements`  |
| Interface generalization| Solid  | Hollow   | `extends` an interface |

> Key Takeaways
> - Generalization uses a solid line with a hollow triangle for `extends`.
> - Realization uses a dashed line with a hollow triangle for `implements`.
> - Both triangles point toward the more abstract type.
> - A class shows at most one solid triangle but many dashed ones.
> - One interface extending another is generalization, so the line is solid.
> - Sealed hierarchies are annotated with their permitted subtypes.
> - Deep triangle chains in a diagram usually signal overused inheritance.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Draw a hierarchy where `Circle` extends `Shape` and implements
>    `Drawable`.
> 2. Diagram part of the Java collections hierarchy with correct line styles.
> 3. Translate a diagram containing both relationships into a class
>    declaration.
> 4. Interview: Why can a UML class have only one solid inheritance triangle
>    in Java? (Hint: what does Java permit only once per class?)

#### Sequence Diagrams for Object Interaction

A class diagram shows structure: which types exist and how they relate. It says
nothing about **order**. A sequence diagram shows how objects collaborate over
time to satisfy one scenario, which is what you draw when explaining a flow.

The layout is objects across the top, time flowing downward:

```text
   :Client        :OrderService     :PaymentGateway    :OrderRepository
      |                 |                  |                  |
      |  place(order)   |                  |                  |
      |---------------->|                  |                  |
      |                 |   charge(total)  |                  |
      |                 |----------------->|                  |
      |                 |                  |                  |
      |                 |<- - - - - - - - -|  receipt         |
      |                 |                  |                  |
      |                 |         save(order)                 |
      |                 |------------------------------------>|
      |                 |                                     |
      |<- - - - - - - - |  confirmation                       |
      |                 |                  |                  |
```

The elements:

| Element             | Notation                          | Meaning                  |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| Participant         | Box at the top, named `:Type`     | An object, not a class   |
| Lifeline            | Dashed vertical line              | The object's existence   |
| Activation bar      | Narrow rectangle on the lifeline  | The object is executing  |
| Synchronous message | Solid line, filled arrowhead      | A normal method call     |
| Return              | Dashed line, open arrowhead       | The value coming back    |
| Asynchronous message| Solid line, open arrowhead        | Fire and forget          |
| Self-message        | An arrow looping back             | A call on itself         |
| Object creation     | Arrow to a box drawn lower down   | `new`                    |
| Destruction         | An X at the end of a lifeline     | The object is discarded  |

The colon prefix matters: `:OrderService` means "an unnamed instance of
OrderService", while `order:Order` names the instance. Sequence diagrams show
objects, not classes.

The Java that the diagram above describes:

```java
public class OrderService {
    public Confirmation place(Order order) {
        Receipt receipt = gateway.charge(order.total());   // second message
        repository.save(order);                             // third message
        return new Confirmation(order.id(), receipt);       // the return
    }
}
```

Control structures are drawn as **combined fragments**, labelled boxes drawn
around a region:

```text
   alt  = alternatives (if/else)
   opt  = optional (if with no else)
   loop = repetition
   par  = parallel execution

   :Service          :Repository
      |                   |
   +--+-------------------+------------------+
   | alt [found]          |                  |
   |  |---- update() ---->|                  |
   |--+-------------------+------------------|
   | [else]               |                  |
   |  |---- insert() ---->|                  |
   +--+-------------------+------------------+
      |                   |
```

```java
if (repository.exists(id)) {
    repository.update(order);      // the [found] branch
} else {
    repository.insert(order);      // the [else] branch
}
```

Sequence diagrams are most useful for a small number of specific jobs:

- Explaining a non-obvious flow to someone new to the code.
- Designing an interaction before writing it, to find missing calls.
- Documenting a protocol between services, including the failure paths.
- Showing where a pattern's indirection actually goes, such as a proxy or an
  observer notification.

They are poor at showing branching-heavy logic. Once a diagram needs four
nested fragments, prose or code is clearer. Keep one diagram to one scenario,
including the error scenario as its own diagram rather than cramming both in.

A practical note: like class diagrams, sequence diagrams drift from the code
quickly. Draw them for the design conversation and for genuinely stable
protocols, and prefer text-based tools so they can live in the repository.

> Key Takeaways
> - A sequence diagram shows the order of interactions in one scenario.
> - Participants are objects, written `:Type`, with time flowing downward.
> - A solid arrow is a call; a dashed arrow is the return.
> - Activation bars show when an object is executing.
> - Combined fragments labelled alt, opt, loop, and par express control flow.
> - One diagram should cover one scenario, with errors drawn separately.
> - They suit protocols and unfamiliar flows, not branch-heavy logic.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Draw the sequence for a user login that checks a cache, then a database.
> 2. Add an `alt` fragment for the invalid-password path.
> 3. Diagram an observer notification reaching three subscribers.
> 4. Interview: When is a sequence diagram more useful than a class diagram?
>    (Hint: which one can express the order in which things happen?)

#### From Requirements to Class Model

The final skill is turning prose into a design. It is the core of most
object-oriented design interviews, and the process is mechanical enough to
practise.

Take a requirement:

> A library lends books to members. Each member can borrow up to five books at
> a time for fourteen days. Late returns incur a fine of 0.50 per day. Members
> can reserve a book that is currently out.

**Step one: find the nouns.** They are candidate classes.

```text
   library, book, member, loan, fine, reservation, day
```

Filter them. Discard nouns that are attributes rather than types, duplicates,
or things outside the system's responsibility. `day` is a unit, not a class.
`library` may be the system itself rather than an object.

Remaining candidates: `Book`, `Member`, `Loan`, `Fine`, `Reservation`.

**Step two: find the verbs.** They are candidate operations.

```text
   lends, borrow, return, incur, reserve
```

**Step three: assign responsibilities.** Put each operation on the class that
owns the data it needs. This is where the Law of Demeter and cohesion pay off.

| Operation           | Belongs on | Because                              |
| ------------------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `canBorrow()`       | `Member`   | It knows how many loans it holds      |
| `isOverdue()`       | `Loan`     | It knows the due date                 |
| `calculateFine()`   | `Loan`     | It knows how many days are late       |
| `reserve(member)`   | `Book`     | It knows its availability             |

**Step four: distinguish entities from value objects.** An entity has identity
and a lifecycle; a value object is defined entirely by its contents and should
be immutable.

```java
// Value objects: immutable, compared by value
public record Isbn(String value) {
    public Isbn { if (!value.matches("\\d{13}")) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); }
}
public record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) { }

// Entities: identity matters, state changes over time
public class Member {
    private final MemberId id;                       // identity
    private final List<Loan> activeLoans = new ArrayList<>();

    public boolean canBorrow() { return activeLoans.size() < MAX_LOANS; }
}

public class Loan {
    private final Book book;
    private final Member member;
    private final LocalDate dueDate;
    private LocalDate returnedOn;                    // state changes

    public boolean isOverdue(LocalDate today) {
        return returnedOn == null && today.isAfter(dueDate);
    }

    public Money calculateFine(LocalDate today) {
        long daysLate = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(dueDate, today);
        return daysLate <= 0 ? Money.ZERO
                             : Money.of(BigDecimal.valueOf(daysLate * 0.50));
    }
}
```

**Step five: decide the relationships and multiplicities.**

```text
   +--------+ 1      0..5 +--------+ 1        1 +--------+
   | Member |<>-----------| Loan   |------------| Book   |
   +--------+             +--------+            +--------+
                                                     ^ 1
                                                     |
                                                0..* |
                                             +-------------+
                                             | Reservation |
                                             +-------------+
```

Encode the constraint, rather than leaving it in the diagram:

```java
public class Member {
    private static final int MAX_LOANS = 5;

    public Loan borrow(Book book, LocalDate today) {
        if (!canBorrow()) throw new BorrowLimitExceededException(id);
        Loan loan = new Loan(book, this, today.plusDays(14));
        activeLoans.add(loan);
        return loan;
    }
}
```

**Step six: apply the principles.** Check the model against the earlier
sections. Does each class have one reason to change? Are volatile dependencies,
such as persistence, inverted behind an interface the domain owns? Is a rule
that will vary, like the fine calculation, behind a strategy?

```java
public interface FinePolicy { Money fineFor(long daysLate); }
// Now the rate can change without editing Loan
```

Common mistakes in interviews, worth avoiding deliberately:

- Making everything a class, including `Day` and `Fine`, when a `LocalDate` and
  a `Money` value object suffice.
- Anemic classes: data holders with getters and setters, and all behaviour in a
  `LibraryService`. Put behaviour with the data it uses.
- Starting with the database schema. Model the domain first; persistence is a
  detail that should be inverted behind an interface.
- Designing for requirements nobody stated, which YAGNI rejects.
- Using `String` and `double` for identifiers and money, which loses validation
  and, for money, precision.

> Key Takeaways
> - Nouns suggest classes, verbs suggest operations, but both lists need
>   filtering.
> - Put each operation on the class that owns the data it needs.
> - Entities have identity and lifecycle; value objects are immutable and
>   compared by content.
> - Encode constraints such as a borrow limit in code, not only in the
>   diagram.
> - Invert persistence behind an interface the domain owns.
> - Put a rule likely to change behind a strategy interface.
> - Avoid anemic classes, and never model money as a `double`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Model a parking garage with levels, spots, vehicles, and tickets.
> 2. Identify which of your classes are entities and which are value objects.
> 3. Draw the class diagram with multiplicities, then write the skeleton code.
> 4. Add a pricing rule behind a strategy interface and a second
>    implementation.
> 5. Interview: Given "a customer places orders containing products", name the
>    classes and the multiplicities. (Hint: consider whether the price on an
>    order line should come from the product or be copied at purchase time.)

<a id="10-advanced-runtime-and-language-features"></a>
## 10. Advanced Runtime and Language Features

Everything so far has assumed the compiler knows your types. This chapter
covers the two features that let code work with types it has never seen:
reflection, which reads and manipulates classes at runtime, and annotations,
which attach machine-readable metadata to your declarations. Together they are
the engine behind JUnit, Spring, Jackson, Hibernate, and almost every framework
you will use, so understanding them turns "framework magic" into ordinary code.

<a id="101-reflection"></a>
### 10.1 Reflection

This subchapter covers how the JVM exposes its own type information to running
code, how to read and manipulate members that the compiler would never let you
touch, and when the power is worth its considerable cost.

#### The Class Object and Runtime Introspection

Normally you write `new ArrayList<>()` because you knew at compile time that
you wanted an `ArrayList`. But consider the problem JUnit has: it must find and
run your test methods without anyone ever writing a line of code that names
them. Or the problem Jackson has: it must turn arbitrary JSON into an instance
of a class that did not exist when Jackson was compiled. Neither problem can be
solved with ordinary method calls, because the types involved are unknown until
the program is already running.

**Reflection** is the JVM's answer. It is the ability of a program to examine
and modify its own structure at runtime. The word comes from the image of code
looking at itself in a mirror.

The mechanism rests on one idea: when a class loader loads a class, the JVM
builds a permanent in-memory description of it and hands you a handle to that
description. The handle is an object of type `java.lang.Class`. Think of it as
the blueprint kept in the building's lobby. The building is the running object;
the blueprint tells you what rooms it has, without you having to walk through
them.

```text
   Employee.java  --javac-->  Employee.class  --ClassLoader-->  Class object
   (source)                   (bytecode)                        (in metaspace)
                                                                     |
        +--------------------+--------------------+-----------------+
        |                    |                    |                 |
   getDeclaredFields()  getDeclaredMethods()  getSuperclass()  getInterfaces()
        |                    |                    |                 |
     Field[]              Method[]             Class<?>         Class<?>[]
```

There is exactly one `Class` object per type per class loader, so identity
comparison with `==` is safe and is the idiomatic way to test types
reflectively.

There are three ways to obtain one, and the difference between them matters.

```java
public class ClassObjectDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // 1. Class literal: resolved by the compiler, needs the type by name.
        //    Does NOT trigger static initializers.
        Class<String> fromLiteral = String.class;

        // 2. From an instance: gives the DYNAMIC type, not the declared one.
        Object o = "hello";                 // declared type is Object
        Class<?> fromInstance = o.getClass();   // but this is String

        // 3. From a String: the entry point every framework uses, because the
        //    name can come from a config file. DOES initialize the class.
        Class<?> fromName = Class.forName("java.util.ArrayList");

        System.out.println(fromLiteral == fromInstance);   // true: one per type
        System.out.println(fromName.getName());            // java.util.ArrayList
        System.out.println(fromName.getSimpleName());      // ArrayList
    }
}
```

`Class.forName` throws a checked `ClassNotFoundException`, which is exactly the
right design: the name was a string, so it might be wrong.

The naming methods differ in ways that surprise people, especially for arrays
and nested types.

| Expression                     | `getName()`              | `getSimpleName()` |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------ | ----------------- |
| `String.class`                 | `java.lang.String`       | `String`          |
| `int.class`                    | `int`                    | `int`             |
| `int[].class`                  | `[I`                     | `int[]`           |
| `String[].class`               | `[Ljava.lang.String;`    | `String[]`        |
| `Map.Entry.class`              | `java.util.Map$Entry`    | `Entry`           |

Use `getCanonicalName()` when you want the form a programmer would type
(`java.util.Map.Entry`), and `getName()` when you need the form a class loader
accepts.

Beyond names, a `Class` object answers structural questions:

```java
Class<?> c = java.util.ArrayList.class;

c.getSuperclass();          // class java.util.AbstractList
c.getInterfaces();          // [List, RandomAccess, Cloneable, Serializable]
c.getPackageName();         // java.util
c.isInterface();            // false
c.isEnum();                 // false
c.isArray();                // false
c.isRecord();               // false  (Java 16+)
Modifier.toString(c.getModifiers());   // "public"

// Runtime type tests, the reflective equivalents of instanceof and a cast
Object value = new java.util.ArrayList<String>();
List.class.isInstance(value);        // true, like (value instanceof List)
List.class.isAssignableFrom(c);      // true, like "an ArrayList IS-A List"
List<?> narrowed = List.class.cast(value);   // checked cast, no unchecked warning
```

Two limits are worth internalizing now.

**Generics are erased.** There is no `List<String>.class`, and
`new ArrayList<String>().getClass()` is just `ArrayList`. Generic type
arguments survive only where they were written into the class file as
declarations, such as a field's or method's signature, which is why the next
topic can still recover them.

**Class literals do not initialize.** Touching `Config.class` does not run
`Config`'s static block; `Class.forName("Config")` does. If you need the handle
without the side effects, use the three-argument form:

```java
// Load and link, but do NOT run static initializers
Class<?> c = Class.forName("com.example.Config", false,
                           ClassObjectDemo.class.getClassLoader());
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Reflection lets running code inspect and manipulate types that were unknown
>   at compile time.
> - Every loaded type has exactly one `Class` object per class loader, so `==`
>   is a valid comparison.
> - Get it three ways: `Type.class`, `instance.getClass()`, and
>   `Class.forName(String)`.
> - `getClass()` returns the dynamic type, which is why it ignores the declared
>   variable type.
> - `Class.forName` initializes the class; a class literal does not.
> - `getName`, `getSimpleName`, and `getCanonicalName` differ for arrays and
>   nested classes.
> - `isInstance` and `isAssignableFrom` are the reflective forms of `instanceof`
>   and assignment compatibility.
> - Generic type arguments are erased from objects, so `List<String>.class` does
>   not exist.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a method `describe(Object o)` that prints the object's class name,
>    its superclass chain up to `Object`, and every interface it implements.
> 2. Add a `static { System.out.println("init"); }` block to a class, then show
>    that a class literal does not print it but `Class.forName` does.
> 3. Write a method that takes a `String` class name from the command line and
>    prints whether it is an interface, an enum, a record, or a plain class.
> 4. Interview: Why does `getClass()` on a variable declared as `Object` return
>    `String`? (Hint: which of the two types exists at runtime?)

#### Inspecting Fields, Methods, and Constructors

A `Class` object is a directory. The entries in it live in `java.lang.reflect`
and come in three flavours that mirror what you can declare in a class body:
`Field`, `Method`, and `Constructor`. `Method` and `Constructor` share a parent,
`Executable`, because both take parameters and can throw.

The first thing to learn is the pair of prefixes, because choosing wrong is the
single most common reflection bug.

| Method                    | Access levels returned | Inherited members? |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------ |
| `getFields()`             | `public` only          | Yes                |
| `getDeclaredFields()`     | All, including private | No                 |
| `getMethods()`            | `public` only          | Yes                |
| `getDeclaredMethods()`    | All, including private | No                 |
| `getConstructors()`       | `public` only          | Not applicable     |
| `getDeclaredConstructors()` | All                  | Not applicable     |

Read it as: **`getDeclared*` means "written in this exact class, whatever its
visibility"; the plain form means "publicly usable on this type, wherever it
came from"**. Neither one alone gives you "every field including inherited
private ones", so frameworks walk the superclass chain themselves.

```java
import java.lang.reflect.*;
import java.util.Arrays;

class Employee {
    private String name;
    protected int age;
    public double salary;
    private static final String COMPANY = "Acme";

    public Employee() { }
    private Employee(String name) { this.name = name; }

    public String getName() { return name; }
    private void raise(double percent) { salary *= 1 + percent / 100; }
}

public class Inspect {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Class<?> c = Employee.class;

        // Every field declared here, at any access level
        for (Field f : c.getDeclaredFields()) {
            System.out.printf("%-20s %-8s %s%n",
                Modifier.toString(f.getModifiers()),  // "private static final"
                f.getType().getSimpleName(),          // String, int, double
                f.getName());
        }

        // Only public fields, but inherited ones too
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(c.getFields()));  // [public double Employee.salary]

        // Look up one member by name and parameter types
        Method raise = c.getDeclaredMethod("raise", double.class);
        System.out.println(raise.getReturnType());        // void
        System.out.println(raise.getParameterCount());    // 1

        Constructor<?> ctor = c.getDeclaredConstructor(String.class);
        System.out.println(ctor.getParameterTypes()[0]);  // class java.lang.String
    }
}
```

Lookup by name uses the exact signature. `getDeclaredMethod("raise",
double.class)` finds nothing if the parameter is `Double`, because boxing does
not apply to reflective lookup. A missing member raises
`NoSuchMethodException` or `NoSuchFieldException`.

Modifiers arrive as an `int` bitmask, decoded through `Modifier`:

```java
int mods = field.getModifiers();
Modifier.isPrivate(mods);    // true
Modifier.isStatic(mods);     // true
Modifier.isFinal(mods);      // true
Modifier.isTransient(mods);  // false
Modifier.toString(mods);     // "private static final"
```

**Recovering generic types.** Erasure removes generics from objects, but not
from declarations. Field, method, and superclass signatures keep theirs in the
class file, so reflection can read them through the `getGeneric*` methods, which
return `java.lang.reflect.Type` rather than `Class`.

```java
class Repository {
    Map<String, List<Integer>> index;
}

Field f = Repository.class.getDeclaredField("index");

System.out.println(f.getType());          // interface java.util.Map  (erased)

// The generic view keeps the type arguments
ParameterizedType pt = (ParameterizedType) f.getGenericType();
System.out.println(pt.getActualTypeArguments()[0]);  // class java.lang.String
System.out.println(pt.getActualTypeArguments()[1]);  // java.util.List<java.lang.Integer>
```

This is precisely how Jackson knows to deserialize into
`Map<String, List<Integer>>` rather than a raw `Map`.

**Parameter names** are erased by default. `Parameter.getName()` returns
`arg0`, `arg1`, and so on unless the class was compiled with `javac
-parameters`. Frameworks that bind by parameter name, including Spring MVC,
either require that flag or fall back to an annotation that states the name
explicitly.

**Breaking encapsulation.** Reading a `private` field's metadata is always
allowed; reading its value is not, until you ask:

```java
Employee e = new Employee();
Field name = Employee.class.getDeclaredField("name");

name.setAccessible(true);     // suppress the access check
name.set(e, "Ada");           // now legal despite being private
System.out.println(name.get(e));  // Ada
```

`setAccessible(true)` is the line that makes reflection feel like cheating, and
since Java 9 the module system limits it. Inside a named module, a package must
be explicitly opened for this to work:

```java
// module-info.java
module com.example.app {
    opens com.example.model;              // to everyone, for reflection
    opens com.example.entity to org.hibernate.orm.core;   // to one module
}
```

Reflecting into JDK internals such as `java.lang` has been denied by default
since Java 16 and throws `InaccessibleObjectException`. The escape hatch is a
launch flag, and needing it is a sign you are relying on something you should
not:

```bash
java --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED -jar app.jar
```

Your own classes on the classpath live in the unnamed module, which is open by
default, so ordinary application reflection keeps working.

Two more rules that bite in practice. `final` fields can be set reflectively
only when they are instance fields and the field is made accessible; `static
final` fields, especially ones the compiler inlined as constants, cannot be
changed meaningfully. And records are shallowly immutable by design: their
fields reject reflective writes outright.

> Key Takeaways
> - `Field`, `Method`, and `Constructor` in `java.lang.reflect` mirror what a
>   class body can declare.
> - `getDeclaredX` means "declared here, any visibility"; `getX` means "public,
>   including inherited".
> - Neither prefix returns inherited private members, so walk the superclass
>   chain yourself.
> - Reflective lookup matches exact parameter types, with no boxing or widening.
> - Decode `getModifiers()` with the `Modifier` helper methods.
> - `getGenericType` recovers type arguments from declarations, which erasure
>   leaves in the class file.
> - Parameter names need `javac -parameters` to survive compilation.
> - `setAccessible(true)` bypasses access control, subject to module `opens`
>   rules since Java 9.
> - Record fields and `static final` constants resist reflective mutation.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `printAllFields(Class<?> c)` that lists fields of a class and of
>    every superclass, marking which class each came from.
> 2. Given a class with a `List<String>` field and a `Map<Integer, String>`
>    field, print the actual type arguments of each without hard-coding them.
> 3. Write a method that finds every `private` method in a class whose name
>    starts with `validate` and prints its parameter types.
> 4. Interview: Your framework needs to read a private field of a class in a
>    named module and gets `InaccessibleObjectException`. What are the two
>    proper fixes? (Hint: one belongs to the module being read, the other to the
>    command line.)

#### Dynamic Instantiation and Invocation

Inspection is read-only. The second half of reflection is acting: creating
objects and calling methods chosen at runtime. This is what turns introspection
into a framework.

Creation goes through `Constructor`, not through the deprecated
`Class.newInstance()`. The old method was removed from favour because it
propagated the constructor's checked exceptions without declaring them, which
defeats the compiler's exception checking.

```java
import java.lang.reflect.*;

public class Dynamic {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Class<?> c = Class.forName("Employee");

        // Public no-arg constructor: the common framework case
        Object emp = c.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance();

        // A private constructor, with an argument
        Constructor<?> ctor = c.getDeclaredConstructor(String.class);
        ctor.setAccessible(true);
        Object ada = ctor.newInstance("Ada");

        // Call a private instance method
        Method raise = c.getDeclaredMethod("raise", double.class);
        raise.setAccessible(true);
        raise.invoke(ada, 10.0);          // first arg is the receiver

        // Call a static method: receiver is null
        Method valueOf = Integer.class.getMethod("valueOf", String.class);
        Object boxed = valueOf.invoke(null, "42");
        System.out.println(boxed);        // 42

        // Read and write a field
        Field salary = c.getDeclaredField("salary");
        salary.setAccessible(true);
        salary.setDouble(ada, 50_000);
        System.out.println(salary.getDouble(ada));   // 50000.0
    }
}
```

`invoke` and `newInstance` erase the return type to `Object`, so every result
needs a cast, and a wrong cast fails only at runtime. That loss of type safety
is the real price of reflection, more than the speed cost.

**Exception wrapping is the detail everyone trips on.** If the invoked method
throws, reflection does not let that exception escape directly. It wraps it:

```java
try {
    method.invoke(target, args);
} catch (InvocationTargetException e) {
    // e is the wrapper; e.getCause() is what the method ACTUALLY threw
    Throwable actual = e.getCause();
    throw new IllegalStateException("call failed: " + method.getName(), actual);
} catch (IllegalAccessException e) {
    // The member was not accessible; setAccessible was needed
    throw new IllegalStateException(e);
}
```

Forgetting `getCause()` produces the notorious stack trace that says only
`InvocationTargetException` and hides the real `NullPointerException` three
frames down.

Here is the whole toolkit in one small but genuinely useful piece of code: a
mapper that builds an object out of a string-keyed map, which is the core of
every CSV and form binder you have used.

```java
import java.lang.reflect.*;
import java.util.*;

public final class SimpleMapper {

    public static <T> T fromMap(Class<T> type, Map<String, String> data) {
        try {
            // Requires a no-arg constructor, possibly non-public
            Constructor<T> ctor = type.getDeclaredConstructor();
            ctor.setAccessible(true);
            T instance = ctor.newInstance();

            for (Field f : type.getDeclaredFields()) {
                if (Modifier.isStatic(f.getModifiers())) continue;  // skip constants
                String raw = data.get(f.getName());
                if (raw == null) continue;                          // absent key
                f.setAccessible(true);
                f.set(instance, convert(f.getType(), raw));
            }
            return instance;
        } catch (ReflectiveOperationException e) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("cannot map to " + type.getName(), e);
        }
    }

    // Reflective set() needs the boxed form for primitives; the JVM unboxes it
    private static Object convert(Class<?> target, String raw) {
        if (target == String.class)                          return raw;
        if (target == int.class    || target == Integer.class) return Integer.valueOf(raw);
        if (target == double.class || target == Double.class)  return Double.valueOf(raw);
        if (target == boolean.class|| target == Boolean.class) return Boolean.valueOf(raw);
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("unsupported type " + target);
    }
}
```

Note `ReflectiveOperationException`: it is the common supertype of
`ClassNotFoundException`, `NoSuchMethodException`, `NoSuchFieldException`,
`IllegalAccessException`, and `InstantiationException`, and catching it once is
much cleaner than five catch blocks.

**Cost.** Reflection is slower than a direct call, but the numbers are widely
exaggerated. What actually costs is the lookup, not the call.

| Operation                                | Rough relative cost |
| ---------------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| Direct method call (JIT-inlined)         | 1                   |
| Cached `Method.invoke` with accessibility set | 2 to 5          |
| `getDeclaredMethod` on every call        | 50 to 100           |
| `Class.forName` on every call            | 100 and up          |

The rule follows directly: **resolve reflectively once, cache the `Method` or
`Field`, then reuse it.** Every serious framework builds a
`Map<Class<?>, Metadata>` at startup for exactly this reason.

For hot paths where even cached `invoke` is too slow, `java.lang.invoke` offers
method handles, which the JIT can inline like ordinary calls:

```java
import java.lang.invoke.*;

MethodHandles.Lookup lookup = MethodHandles.lookup();
MethodType signature = MethodType.methodType(String.class);   // returns String
MethodHandle getName = lookup.findVirtual(Employee.class, "getName", signature);

Employee emp = new Employee();            // note the DECLARED type, see below
String n = (String) getName.invokeExact(emp);   // strongly typed, JIT-friendly
```

Method handles are harder to use, and `invokeExact` is the reason: it compares
the handle's type against the **static** types at the call site, not the runtime
types. Declaring the receiver as `Object`, the way `newInstance` returns it,
throws `WrongMethodTypeException` even though the object really is an
`Employee`:

```java
Object loose = new Employee();
String bad = (String) getName.invokeExact(loose);   // WrongMethodTypeException
String ok  = (String) getName.invoke(loose);       // invoke adapts the types
```

Use `invokeExact` when you control the static types and want maximum speed, and
`invoke` when you need the looser conversion behaviour. Either way, method
handles are the right tool when reflection sits inside a loop that runs millions
of times.

**When not to reflect.** Reflection defeats the compiler, breaks refactoring
tools, hides dependencies from readers, and can be blocked by the module system
or a security policy. Reach for it only when the type genuinely is not known
until runtime. The alternatives, in order of preference:

| Need                                  | Prefer                              |
| ------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Call one of several known behaviours  | An interface plus polymorphism       |
| Plug in implementations by config     | `ServiceLoader` or a factory map     |
| Generate boilerplate from annotations | An annotation processor at compile time |
| Invoke unknown members in a hot loop  | `MethodHandle` / `VarHandle`         |
| Truly arbitrary user-supplied types   | Reflection, with cached lookups      |

> Key Takeaways
> - Create objects with `getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance()`, not the
>   deprecated `Class.newInstance()`.
> - `Method.invoke(receiver, args)` takes `null` as the receiver for static
>   methods.
> - Exceptions thrown by the target are wrapped in `InvocationTargetException`;
>   always unwrap with `getCause()`.
> - Catch `ReflectiveOperationException` to cover the whole family in one block.
> - Reflective results are typed `Object`, so you trade compile-time safety for
>   flexibility.
> - Lookup dominates the cost, so cache `Method` and `Field` objects instead of
>   re-resolving them.
> - `MethodHandle` from `java.lang.invoke` is the fast alternative for hot
>   paths.
> - Prefer interfaces, `ServiceLoader`, or annotation processing whenever the
>   type is actually known.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Extend `SimpleMapper` with a `toMap(Object)` method that produces a
>    `Map<String, String>` from any object's non-static fields.
> 2. Write a method that invokes a method named on the command line, and prints
>    the real exception message when the target throws. Verify that without
>    `getCause()` the message is useless.
> 3. Benchmark one million calls to a getter three ways: directly, through a
>    cached `Method`, and through a `Method` looked up each iteration. Report
>    the ratios.
> 4. Interview: A colleague uses reflection to call a method whose name is a
>    compile-time constant. What should you suggest instead, and what does the
>    codebase gain? (Hint: think about what a rename refactor does to each
>    version.)

<a id="102-annotations"></a>
### 10.2 Annotations

This subchapter covers metadata: how to attach it to declarations, how to decide
who is allowed to see it, and how to write the runtime code that acts on it.

#### Built-In Annotations

Some information about code is not code. "This method replaces one in the
superclass." "Do not use this any more." "Yes, I know this cast is unchecked,
and I have checked it myself." Before annotations existed, that information went
into comments, naming conventions, or separate XML files, where nothing could
verify it and nothing kept it in sync.

An **annotation** is metadata attached to a declaration in a form the compiler
and the runtime can read. The analogy is a luggage tag. It is not part of the
suitcase and it does not change what is inside, but the handling system reads it
and behaves differently because of it.

Annotations do not, by themselves, do anything. Something must read them: the
compiler, an annotation processor at build time, or reflective code at runtime.
An annotation nobody reads is an expensive comment.

Java ships a handful in `java.lang`, and all of them are read by the compiler.

| Annotation             | Applies to            | What the compiler does                |
| ---------------------- | --------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `@Override`            | Methods               | Errors if nothing is being overridden |
| `@Deprecated`          | Any declaration       | Warns at each use site                |
| `@SuppressWarnings`    | Any declaration       | Silences the named warnings           |
| `@FunctionalInterface` | Interfaces            | Errors unless exactly one abstract method |
| `@SafeVarargs`         | Certain methods, constructors | Silences generic varargs warnings |

**`@Override`** is the one you will use most. It is optional, and that is
exactly why it is valuable: it converts a silent mistake into a compile error.

```java
class Animal {
    public void speak() { }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    public void speak() { }        // fine

    @Override
    public void speek() { }        // COMPILE ERROR: typo caught immediately
    // Without @Override this would silently become a new, never-called method.
}
```

It also works for implementing an interface method, and using it there is good
practice for the same reason.

**`@Deprecated`** marks something that still works but should not be used in new
code. Since Java 9 it carries two elements that turn a vague warning into
actionable information.

```java
public class LegacyApi {
    /**
     * @deprecated Use {@link #fetch(Query)} instead; this form cannot paginate.
     */
    @Deprecated(since = "2.4", forRemoval = true)   // forRemoval escalates the warning
    public List<Row> fetch(String sql) { return List.of(); }
}
```

Note the pair: the `@Deprecated` annotation tells the compiler, and the
`@deprecated` Javadoc tag tells the human what to use instead. Write both.
`forRemoval = true` produces a stronger "removal" warning rather than an
ordinary deprecation warning.

**`@SuppressWarnings`** is a promise, not a fix. You are telling the compiler
you have verified something it cannot verify.

```java
public class Warnings {
    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")      // I verified the list really holds Strings
    public List<String> readList(Object source) {
        return (List<String>) source;   // unavoidable unchecked cast
    }

    @SuppressWarnings({"unchecked", "rawtypes"})  // several at once
    public void legacyBridge(List raw) { }
}
```

Common values are `unchecked`, `deprecation`, `rawtypes`, `serial`, and
`unused`. The discipline that matters: **apply it to the narrowest possible
declaration**, ideally a single local variable, never a whole class. A
class-level suppression hides the warnings you wanted to see next month.

**`@FunctionalInterface`** documents intent and enforces it, which protects your
lambdas from a future maintainer.

```java
@FunctionalInterface
public interface Validator<T> {
    boolean test(T value);          // the single abstract method

    // Allowed: default and static methods do not count against the limit
    default Validator<T> negate() { return v -> !test(v); }
}
```

Add a second abstract method and the interface itself fails to compile, rather
than breaking every lambda that used it.

**`@SafeVarargs`** addresses a narrow but real problem: a varargs parameter of a
generic type creates an array of a generic type, which is unsound in general, so
the compiler warns at the declaration. If your method only reads the array and
never leaks it, the warning is noise.

```java
@SafeVarargs                                   // allowed on static, final, or private
public static <T> List<T> listOf(T... items) { // and on constructors
    return new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(items));   // only reads items
}
```

It is restricted to methods that cannot be overridden, because a subclass could
otherwise break the promise.

Beyond these, `java.lang.annotation` holds the meta-annotations covered later,
and the ecosystem supplies thousands more: `@Test` and `@BeforeEach` from JUnit,
`@Entity` and `@Column` from Jakarta Persistence, `@Component` and
`@Autowired` from Spring. They are all ordinary annotations plus ordinary code
that reads them, which is what the rest of this subchapter builds.

> Key Takeaways
> - An annotation is machine-readable metadata on a declaration; it changes
>   nothing by itself.
> - Something must read it: the compiler, a build-time processor, or reflection.
> - `@Override` turns a misspelled override into a compile error, so use it
>   always.
> - `@Deprecated(since, forRemoval)` pairs with the `@deprecated` Javadoc tag
>   naming the replacement.
> - `@SuppressWarnings` is a claim you verified something; scope it as narrowly
>   as possible.
> - `@FunctionalInterface` enforces exactly one abstract method, protecting
>   existing lambdas.
> - `@SafeVarargs` only applies where the method cannot be overridden.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a subclass that misspells an overridden method name, compile it
>    without `@Override`, then add the annotation and compare the outcomes.
> 2. Deprecate a method with `since` and `forRemoval = true`, call it from
>    another class, and record the exact compiler warning text.
> 3. Take a class with a class-level `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")` and push
>    the suppression down to the smallest declarations that need it.
> 4. Interview: Why is `@Override` optional when the compiler could infer
>    everything it checks? (Hint: what does overloading look like next to
>    overriding?)

#### Defining Custom Annotations

Once you see that annotations plus a reader equal a framework, writing your own
becomes routine. The declaration looks like an interface with an `@` in front,
because that is literally what it is: `@interface` declares an interface that
extends `java.lang.annotation.Annotation`.

```java
public @interface Author {
    String name();                       // required: no default given
    String date() default "unknown";     // optional
    int revision() default 1;
    String[] reviewers() default {};     // an array element, empty by default
}
```

The members look like methods but behave like named fields with defaults. That
is why they are called **elements**, and why the reader gets their values by
calling them.

```java
@Author(name = "Ada Lovelace", date = "1843-10-01", reviewers = {"Babbage"})
public class AnalyticalEngine { }

// revision was omitted, so it is 1
```

Three pieces of syntax sugar are worth knowing, because published annotations
use them constantly.

```java
// 1. A single element named exactly "value" can be written without its name
public @interface Retry { int value(); }

@Retry(3)                    // shorthand for @Retry(value = 3)
void flakyCall() { }

// 2. A single-element array can drop the braces
public @interface Roles { String[] value(); }

@Roles("ADMIN")              // same as @Roles({"ADMIN"})
@Roles({"ADMIN", "AUDITOR"}) // several still need braces
void deleteAccount() { }

// 3. No elements at all makes a MARKER annotation, and parentheses are optional
public @interface Experimental { }

@Experimental
class NewParser { }
```

Element types are restricted, because the values must be storable in a class
file as constants. The permitted set is:

| Allowed                        | Example element declaration             |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------- |
| Primitives                     | `int max();`                            |
| `String`                       | `String message();`                     |
| `Class` or `Class<?>`          | `Class<?> handler();`                   |
| Enum types                     | `Level level();`                        |
| Another annotation type        | `Validation check();`                   |
| One-dimensional arrays of the above | `String[] tags();`                 |

Notably absent: `null` as a default, arbitrary objects, and nested arrays. The
standard workaround for "no value" is a sentinel such as `""`, `-1`, or a
dedicated enum constant.

```java
import java.lang.annotation.*;

public enum Severity { LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH }

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface Issue {
    String id();
    Severity severity() default Severity.MEDIUM;   // enum element
    Class<? extends Throwable> expected() default Throwable.class;  // Class element
    String owner() default "";                     // "" stands in for absent
}

@Issue(id = "JAVA-118", severity = Severity.HIGH, expected = TimeoutException.class)
class RetryingClient { }
```

**Repeating annotations.** By default a declaration may carry each annotation
once. To allow several, mark the annotation `@Repeatable` and supply a container
annotation whose `value()` is an array of it.

```java
import java.lang.annotation.*;

@Repeatable(Schedules.class)              // points at its container
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
public @interface Schedule {
    String cron();
}

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)       // the container needs matching
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)               // retention and targets
public @interface Schedules {
    Schedule[] value();                   // must be named value
}

public class Jobs {
    @Schedule(cron = "0 0 * * *")
    @Schedule(cron = "0 12 * * *")        // legal only because of @Repeatable
    public void reconcile() { }
}
```

The compiler quietly rewrites the two `@Schedule` annotations into one
`@Schedules`. That detail leaks into the reader, which must use
`getAnnotationsByType(Schedule.class)` rather than `getAnnotation`, as the last
topic shows.

**Inheritance.** Annotations are not inherited unless you say so, and even then
only in one narrow case, covered next.

> Key Takeaways
> - Declare an annotation with `@interface`; it is an interface extending
>   `Annotation`.
> - Members are elements: they look like methods, and `default` makes them
>   optional.
> - An element named `value` can be written without its name.
> - A single-element array can omit its braces.
> - No elements at all makes a marker annotation.
> - Element types are limited to primitives, `String`, `Class`, enums,
>   annotations, and one-dimensional arrays of those.
> - `null` cannot be a default, so use a sentinel such as `""` or `-1`.
> - `@Repeatable` needs a container annotation whose `value()` is an array of
>   the repeatable type.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Define `@Benchmark` with elements `iterations` (default 100) and `warmup`
>    (default 10), then annotate three methods using all three call styles:
>    defaults only, one element, both.
> 2. Define `@Column` with `name`, a `boolean nullable` defaulting to `true`,
>    and a `Class<?> converter` defaulting to a no-op converter class.
> 3. Make a `@Tag` annotation repeatable, annotate one class with three tags,
>    and confirm it compiles.
> 4. Interview: Why can an annotation element not have a `null` default, and
>    what do real libraries do instead? (Hint: where are element values stored?)

#### Retention Policies and Targets

An annotation without meta-annotations is nearly useless, and the reason is
specific: **by default an annotation is discarded before your program can read
it.** Understanding why requires following an annotation through the build.

Java code passes through three stages, and an annotation can be visible in any
prefix of them. `@Retention` chooses how far it travels.

```text
   stage:      SOURCE (.java)     CLASS FILE (.class)     RUNTIME (in the JVM)
               --------------     -------------------     -------------------
   SOURCE      visible        ->  DISCARDED by javac  ->  absent
   CLASS       visible        ->  stored              ->  not readable reflectively
   RUNTIME     visible        ->  stored              ->  readable via reflection

   default when @Retention is omitted:  CLASS
```

| Policy    | Survives to    | Who reads it                          | Example            |
| --------- | -------------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------------ |
| `SOURCE`  | Compilation only | The compiler, annotation processors, linters | `@Override`, `@SuppressWarnings`, Lombok's `@Data` |
| `CLASS`   | The class file | Bytecode tools, not reflection        | Nullability annotations read by static analysers |
| `RUNTIME` | The running JVM | Reflection, therefore frameworks     | `@Test`, `@Entity`, `@Autowired` |

The practical rule is short: **if reflective code must see it, it needs
`@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)`.** The default of `CLASS` is the single
most common cause of "my annotation processing code finds nothing", because
`getAnnotation` returns `null` without any error.

```java
import java.lang.annotation.*;

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)     // REQUIRED for the runtime reader below
public @interface Audited { }

class Ledger {
    @Audited void post() { }
}

// Ledger.class.getDeclaredMethod("post").isAnnotationPresent(Audited.class)
//   true with RUNTIME, false with CLASS or SOURCE
```

**`@Target`** restricts where the annotation may legally appear. Omitting it
allows almost every declaration, which invites misuse; stating it turns a
misplaced annotation into a compile error.

```java
@Target({ElementType.METHOD, ElementType.CONSTRUCTOR})
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface Transactional { }

class Service {
    @Transactional void save() { }    // fine

    @Transactional String name;       // COMPILE ERROR: FIELD is not a target
}
```

The full set of `ElementType` constants:

| Constant          | Legal position                                        |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| `TYPE`            | Class, interface, enum, record, annotation type        |
| `FIELD`           | Instance and static fields, enum constants            |
| `METHOD`          | Method declarations                                   |
| `PARAMETER`       | Method and constructor parameters                     |
| `CONSTRUCTOR`     | Constructor declarations                              |
| `LOCAL_VARIABLE`  | Local variables                                       |
| `ANNOTATION_TYPE` | Other annotation declarations, making it a meta-annotation |
| `PACKAGE`         | A `package-info.java` declaration                     |
| `TYPE_PARAMETER`  | A generic parameter, as in `<@Nullable T>`             |
| `TYPE_USE`        | Any use of a type, including casts and `new`           |
| `MODULE`          | A `module-info.java` declaration                       |

`TYPE_USE` is the widest and enables annotations in positions that look unusual
at first:

```java
@Target(ElementType.TYPE_USE)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@interface NonNull { }

// All of these become legal with TYPE_USE
@NonNull String name = "Ada";
List<@NonNull String> names = new ArrayList<>();
String s = (@NonNull String) value;
```

Two smaller meta-annotations complete the set.

**`@Inherited`** makes an annotation visible on subclasses through
`getAnnotation`. Its scope is narrower than the name suggests: it applies only
to class inheritance. Annotations on interfaces are never inherited by
implementing classes, and annotations on methods are never inherited by
overriding methods.

```java
@Inherited
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
@interface Monitored { }

@Monitored class BaseJob { }
class NightlyJob extends BaseJob { }

// NightlyJob.class.isAnnotationPresent(Monitored.class)
//   true with @Inherited, false without it
// Note: getDeclaredAnnotations() on NightlyJob is empty either way
```

**`@Documented`** includes the annotation in the generated Javadoc of anything
it is applied to. It costs nothing and should be on any annotation that forms
part of your public API.

A complete, production-shaped annotation declaration therefore stacks four
meta-annotations:

```java
import java.lang.annotation.*;

@Documented                              // show up in Javadoc
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)      // readable by our reflective reader
@Target({ElementType.TYPE, ElementType.METHOD})   // classes and methods only
@Inherited                               // subclasses of an annotated class count
public @interface Cacheable {
    String region() default "default";
    long ttlSeconds() default 300;
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `@Retention` decides whether an annotation survives to the class file and to
>   runtime.
> - The default is `CLASS`, which reflection cannot read, so runtime annotations
>   must say `RUNTIME` explicitly.
> - A missing `RUNTIME` retention fails silently: `getAnnotation` just returns
>   `null`.
> - `SOURCE` retention suits compiler checks, linters, and annotation
>   processors.
> - `@Target` restricts legal positions and converts misuse into a compile
>   error.
> - `TYPE_USE` allows annotations on any appearance of a type, including generic
>   arguments and casts.
> - `@Inherited` works only down a class hierarchy, never from interfaces or
>   onto overriding methods.
> - `@Documented` puts the annotation in the Javadoc of what it annotates.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Define the same annotation twice with `CLASS` and `RUNTIME` retention, then
>    show that only one is found by `isAnnotationPresent`.
> 2. Give an annotation `@Target(ElementType.METHOD)` and deliberately place it
>    on a field; record the compiler error.
> 3. Build a three-level hierarchy where the top class carries an `@Inherited`
>    annotation, and print what `getAnnotations()` and
>    `getDeclaredAnnotations()` each return at every level.
> 4. Interview: Your custom annotation compiles and reads well, but your
>    reflective scanner never finds it. What is the first thing you check?
>    (Hint: what is the default retention?)

#### Processing Annotations at Runtime

This topic joins the two halves of the chapter. Reflection can see declarations;
annotations mark which declarations matter. Put them together and you have
written a framework.

The reading API lives on every reflective element, because `Class`, `Field`,
`Method`, `Constructor`, `Parameter`, and `Package` all implement
`AnnotatedElement`.

| Method                              | Returns                                            |
| ----------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `isAnnotationPresent(X.class)`      | `boolean`, the cheap filter                        |
| `getAnnotation(X.class)`            | The instance, or `null`                            |
| `getAnnotations()`                  | All present, including `@Inherited` ones           |
| `getDeclaredAnnotations()`          | Only those written on this element itself          |
| `getAnnotationsByType(X.class)`     | An array, and the only correct call for `@Repeatable` |

The returned object is a proxy implementing your annotation interface, so you
read element values as method calls:

```java
Method m = Jobs.class.getDeclaredMethod("reconcile");

if (m.isAnnotationPresent(Cacheable.class)) {
    Cacheable c = m.getAnnotation(Cacheable.class);
    System.out.println(c.region() + " for " + c.ttlSeconds() + "s");  // element access
}

// Repeatable: getAnnotation would return null, because the compiler wrapped them
for (Schedule s : m.getAnnotationsByType(Schedule.class)) {
    System.out.println(s.cron());
}
```

**A complete example: a validation framework.** Two annotations and one reader,
which is the whole of Jakarta Bean Validation in miniature.

```java
import java.lang.annotation.*;
import java.lang.reflect.*;
import java.util.*;

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.FIELD)
@interface NotBlank {
    String message() default "must not be blank";
}

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.FIELD)
@interface Range {
    int min();
    int max();
    String message() default "out of range";
}

class User {
    @NotBlank(message = "username is required")
    private String username;

    @Range(min = 18, max = 120)
    private int age;

    User(String username, int age) { this.username = username; this.age = age; }
}

public final class Validator {

    public static List<String> validate(Object target) {
        List<String> errors = new ArrayList<>();
        Class<?> type = target.getClass();

        // Walk the hierarchy so inherited private fields are covered too
        for (Class<?> c = type; c != null && c != Object.class; c = c.getSuperclass()) {
            for (Field f : c.getDeclaredFields()) {
                f.setAccessible(true);
                try {
                    checkField(f, f.get(target), errors);
                } catch (IllegalAccessException e) {
                    throw new IllegalStateException("cannot read " + f.getName(), e);
                }
            }
        }
        return errors;
    }

    private static void checkField(Field f, Object value, List<String> errors) {
        NotBlank notBlank = f.getAnnotation(NotBlank.class);
        if (notBlank != null) {
            if (!(value instanceof String s) || s.isBlank()) {   // pattern matching
                errors.add(f.getName() + ": " + notBlank.message());
            }
        }

        Range range = f.getAnnotation(Range.class);
        if (range != null && value instanceof Integer n) {
            if (n < range.min() || n > range.max()) {
                errors.add(f.getName() + ": " + range.message()
                           + " [" + range.min() + ".." + range.max() + "]");
            }
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(validate(new User("  ", 9)));
        // [username: username is required, age: out of range [18..120]]
        System.out.println(validate(new User("ada", 36)));   // []
    }
}
```

Nothing in `User` calls the validator, and nothing in the validator names
`User`. That decoupling is the entire point of annotation-driven design.

**A second example: a test runner**, which is JUnit reduced to forty lines and
shows the invocation side.

```java
import java.lang.annotation.*;
import java.lang.reflect.*;

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
@interface Test {
    Class<? extends Throwable> expected() default None.class;

    // A sentinel class, since annotations cannot default to null
    final class None extends Throwable { private None() { } }
}

public final class MiniRunner {

    public static void run(Class<?> testClass) throws Exception {
        Object suite = testClass.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance();
        int passed = 0, failed = 0;

        for (Method m : testClass.getDeclaredMethods()) {
            Test t = m.getAnnotation(Test.class);
            if (t == null) continue;                  // not a test method

            m.setAccessible(true);
            try {
                m.invoke(suite);
                if (t.expected() != Test.None.class) {
                    System.out.println("FAIL " + m.getName()
                                       + ": expected " + t.expected().getSimpleName());
                    failed++;
                } else {
                    passed++;
                }
            } catch (InvocationTargetException e) {
                Throwable actual = e.getCause();     // the REAL failure
                if (t.expected().isInstance(actual)) {
                    passed++;                        // the expected exception
                } else {
                    System.out.println("FAIL " + m.getName() + ": " + actual);
                    failed++;
                }
            }
        }
        System.out.printf("%d passed, %d failed%n", passed, failed);
    }
}
```

Note the two details that come straight from earlier topics: the sentinel
`None` class standing in for a `null` default, and `getCause()` unwrapping
`InvocationTargetException` so an expected exception can be matched.

**Practical cautions.**

- **Scan once, at startup.** Walking every field of every class on every request
  is the classic annotation-framework performance bug. Build a
  `Map<Class<?>, List<FieldRule>>` when the application boots and reuse it.
- **Reflection sees only loaded classes.** Finding all annotated classes in a
  package requires scanning the classpath, which the JDK does not offer. Real
  frameworks use Spring's `ClassPathScanningCandidateComponentProvider`,
  Reflections, or ClassGraph, or they generate an index at build time.
- **Respect the module system.** Reading annotations is always allowed, but
  reading private field values needs the package `opens`.
- **Do not put behaviour in annotations.** An annotation holds constants. The
  policy belongs in the reader, which is what makes the same annotation usable
  by a validator, a documentation generator, and a schema exporter.

**Runtime reflection is not the only option**, and for many jobs it is the worst
one. Compare the three places annotation-driven work can happen:

| Approach                      | When it runs | Cost at runtime | Errors surface | Typical use          |
| ----------------------------- | ------------ | --------------- | -------------- | -------------------- |
| Reflection                    | Every run    | Highest         | At runtime     | Spring, Jackson, JUnit |
| Annotation processor (`javax.annotation.processing`) | At compile time | None | At compile time | Lombok, Dagger, MapStruct, immutables |
| Bytecode generation or weaving | Build or load time | Near zero  | Build time     | AspectJ, mocking libraries |

An **annotation processor** reads `SOURCE`-retention annotations during
compilation and generates real source files, so the output is ordinary code the
compiler checks. That is why Dagger can do dependency injection with no runtime
reflection at all, and why native-image builds prefer it. The trade is
flexibility: the processor cannot see anything decided after the build.

Choose runtime reflection when the configuration genuinely varies per
deployment, and compile-time processing when it does not.

> Key Takeaways
> - `Class`, `Field`, `Method`, `Constructor`, and `Parameter` all implement
>   `AnnotatedElement`, which is where the reading API lives.
> - Use `isAnnotationPresent` to filter cheaply, then `getAnnotation` to read
>   element values as method calls.
> - `getAnnotationsByType` is mandatory for `@Repeatable` annotations, because
>   the compiler wraps them in a container.
> - Annotation instances are proxies; element values are constants fixed at
>   compile time.
> - Walk the superclass chain to reach inherited private fields.
> - Cache the result of annotation scanning at startup rather than rescanning
>   per call.
> - The JDK cannot enumerate annotated classes in a package; that needs a
>   classpath scanner or a build-time index.
> - Keep policy in the reader, not the annotation, so several readers can share
>   one annotation.
> - Annotation processors do the same work at compile time with no runtime cost
>   and earlier errors.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add a `@MaxLength(int value)` rule to the validator above, including a
>    default message, and verify it reports the field name.
> 2. Extend `MiniRunner` to honour `@BeforeEach` and `@AfterEach` annotations,
>    running the marked method around every test.
> 3. Rewrite the validator so it builds its rules into a
>    `Map<Class<?>, List<Field>>` on first use and reuses them on later calls.
>    Measure the difference over ten thousand validations.
> 4. Write an `@Inject` annotation and a tiny container that instantiates a
>    class by reflection and fills every `@Inject` field from a
>    `Map<Class<?>, Object>` registry.
> 5. Interview: Spring can inject dependencies at runtime and Dagger does it at
>    compile time, both driven by annotations. What does each approach buy, and
>    what does it cost? (Hint: think about startup time, error timing, and
>    configuration that is only known after deployment.)

<a id="11-memory-model-and-object-lifecycle"></a>
## 11. Memory Model and Object Lifecycle

Java's headline promise is that you never free memory by hand, but that promise
is kept by machinery you can starve, confuse, and defeat. This chapter covers
where objects actually live, what the JVM does between `new` and the moment
memory is reclaimed, how garbage collection decides what is garbage, and the
reference types that let you influence that decision. Understanding it is the
difference between reading a heap dump and guessing.

<a id="111-memory-layout-and-object-allocation"></a>
### 11.1 Memory Layout and Object Allocation

This subchapter covers the regions the JVM divides memory into, what happens in
the moments around a `new` expression, and how the just-in-time compiler
sometimes makes an allocation disappear entirely.

#### Stack versus Heap Allocation

A running program needs memory for two jobs with very different lifetimes. One
job is bookkeeping for a method call: the parameters, the local variables, and
where to return to. That memory is needed for exactly as long as the call lasts,
and calls nest perfectly, so the last one started is always the first one
finished. The other job is holding data that outlives the method that created
it, which can be shared, and whose lifetime nobody can predict.

Those two shapes call for two different structures, and the JVM provides both.

The **stack** handles the first job. It is a stack in the data-structure sense:
frames are pushed on call and popped on return. Because the discipline is strict
last-in-first-out, allocation is nothing more than moving a pointer, and
deallocation is moving it back. There is no bookkeeping and no garbage
collection. Crucially, **each thread has its own stack**, so nothing on a stack
is shared and nothing on it needs locking.

The **heap** handles the second job. It is a large shared region with no
ordering: objects are created in any order and die in any order. That
flexibility is what garbage collection pays for.

```text
+------------------------------ JVM PROCESS --------------------------------+
|                                                                           |
|  PER THREAD  (created and destroyed with the thread)                      |
|  +---------------------+   +---------------------+                        |
|  | Thread 1            |   | Thread 2            |                        |
|  |   stack frames      |   |   stack frames      |  <- locals, references,|
|  |   program counter   |   |   program counter   |     return addresses   |
|  +---------------------+   +---------------------+                        |
|                                                                           |
|  SHARED BY ALL THREADS                                                    |
|  +---------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
|  | HEAP        every object and array; garbage collected               |  |
|  +---------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
|  | METASPACE   class metadata; native memory, NOT part of the heap     |  |
|  +---------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
|  | CODE CACHE  machine code produced by the JIT compiler               |  |
|  +---------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

The rule for where a value lives has one subtlety that trips up almost everyone.
**Every object lives on the heap. What can live on the stack is a primitive
value or a reference.**

```java
public class Where {
```
