```java
    private int instanceCount;          // on the HEAP, inside the Where object
    private static int total;           // in the class's storage, a GC root

    void run() {
        int count = 3;                  // primitive LOCAL: on the stack
        Point p = new Point(1, 2);      // the REFERENCE p is on the stack,
                                        // the Point OBJECT is on the heap
        int[] data = new int[100];      // same split: reference on the stack,
                                        // the 100-element array on the heap
        Integer boxed = 42;             // boxed: reference on stack, object on heap
    }
}
```

Drawn out, the split looks like this:

```text
        STACK (thread 1, private)             HEAP (shared)
    +----------------------------+        +---------------------+
    | frame: run()               |        |  Point object       |
    |   count = 3     <- a value |        |    x = 1            |
    |   p     = 0x7f3a ----------|------->|    y = 2            |
    |   data  = 0x7f52 ----------|---+    +---------------------+
    +----------------------------+   |    +---------------------+
    | frame: main()              |   +--->|  int[100] array     |
    |   args  = 0x7f10 ----------|--...   +---------------------+
    +----------------------------+
```

Notice that `int count = 3` stores the number itself, while `Point p = ...`
stores an address. That single difference is the whole of "primitives have value
semantics, objects have reference semantics". A field, in contrast, lives
wherever its owner lives: an `int` field sits inside the heap object that
declares it, not on any stack.

The two regions also fail differently, and the two errors tell you different
things.

| Region     | Exhausted by                          | Error thrown                     | Sized by |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- | -------- |
| Stack      | Deep or infinite recursion            | `StackOverflowError`             | `-Xss`   |
| Heap       | Too many live objects                 | `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` | `-Xmx` |
| Metaspace  | Too many loaded classes               | `OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace`    | `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize` |

```java
public class Overflow {
    // Each call pushes a frame; nothing ever pops. Typical depth is
    // 10,000 to 20,000 frames with a default 512 KB to 1 MB stack.
    static int depth(int n) { return depth(n + 1); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            depth(0);
        } catch (StackOverflowError e) {     // an Error, not an Exception
            System.out.println("stack exhausted");
        }
    }
}
```

Note that these are `Error` subclasses, not exceptions. Catching
`StackOverflowError` to print a message in a demo is fine; catching it to
continue working is not, because you have no idea what was half-finished.

Two practical notes on sizing. Stack size is **per thread**, so a server with
four thousand threads at 1 MB each reserves four gigabytes of stack before
touching the heap. And since Java 10 the JVM reads container memory limits, so
inside Docker prefer a percentage over a fixed figure:

```bash
# Fixed sizing: same minimum and maximum avoids resize pauses
java -Xms2g -Xmx2g -Xss512k -jar app.jar

# Container-friendly: take 75% of whatever the cgroup allows
java -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 -jar app.jar
```

One clarification about a phrase you will hear: "the Java memory model". That
term does not mean this layout. The Java Memory Model is the specification of
when one thread is guaranteed to see another thread's writes, and it belongs to
the concurrency chapter. This topic is about memory *regions*, which is a
different subject with a confusingly similar name.

> Key Takeaways
> - The stack holds per-call bookkeeping with strict last-in-first-out
>   lifetimes; the heap holds data with unpredictable lifetimes.
> - Every thread gets a private stack, so stack data needs no synchronization.
> - All objects and arrays live on the heap; only primitives and references can
>   live on the stack.
> - A field lives inside its owning object, wherever that object lives.
> - Storing a value versus storing an address is the whole of value versus
>   reference semantics.
> - Metaspace holds class metadata in native memory and is not part of the heap.
> - Deep recursion gives `StackOverflowError`; too much live data gives
>   `OutOfMemoryError`, and both are `Error`, not `Exception`.
> - Stack size is per thread, so thread count multiplies it.
> - "The Java Memory Model" means thread visibility rules, not this layout.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a recursive method and print a counter before each call to measure
>    how deep your JVM goes before `StackOverflowError`. Re-run with
>    `-Xss256k` and `-Xss4m` and compare.
> 2. For a method containing a `long`, a `String` reference, a `new int[10]`,
>    and a `static` counter, draw which region each one occupies.
> 3. Write a program that fills an `ArrayList` until it throws
>    `OutOfMemoryError` under `-Xmx64m`, and print how many elements it managed.
> 4. Interview: An object has an `int` field. Is that `int` on the stack or the
>    heap, and does the answer change if the object is a local variable?
>    (Hint: ask where the object is, then ask where its fields must therefore
>    be.)

#### Object Creation and Reachability

`new Point(1, 2)` looks like one operation. It is closer to seven, and knowing
them explains initialization bugs that otherwise look like magic.

When the JVM evaluates a `new` expression:

1. **Resolve and initialize the class.** If this is the first active use of
   `Point`, it is loaded, linked, and its static initializers run. Exactly once.
2. **Allocate memory** for the header and all instance fields, including
   inherited ones.
3. **Zero the memory.** Every field takes its default: `0`, `0.0`, `false`,
   `'\u0000'`, or `null`. This happens before any of your code runs, which is
   why Java has no uninitialized-field reads.
4. **Write the object header**, which carries identity, locking, and GC state
   plus a pointer to the class metadata.
5. **Run the superclass constructor**, recursively up to `Object`.
6. **Run instance field initializers and instance initializer blocks**, in
   source order.
7. **Run the constructor body.**

Steps 5, 6, and 7 in that order are the part worth memorizing: **the superclass
constructor finishes before your field initializers run.** That single fact
explains the classic trap below.

```java
class Base {
    Base() {
        System.out.println("Base constructor");
        describe();                   // calls the OVERRIDE, on a half-built object
    }
    void describe() { System.out.println("Base.describe"); }
}

class Derived extends Base {
    private String label = "ready";   // field initializer: runs AFTER Base()

    Derived() {
        super();                      // implicit; runs first
        System.out.println("Derived constructor, label=" + label);
    }

    @Override
    void describe() {
        // label is still null here: step 5 has not reached step 6 yet
        System.out.println("Derived.describe, label=" + label);
    }
}
```

Running `new Derived()` prints:

```text
Base constructor
Derived.describe, label=null        <- the trap: the field is not assigned yet
Derived constructor, label=ready
```

The lesson is a hard rule: **never call an overridable method from a
constructor.** The subclass's fields do not exist yet, and no amount of care in
the subclass can fix it.

Static and instance initialization interleave in a fixed order too:

```java
class Order {
    static { System.out.println("1. static block"); }      // once, at class init
    private int a = init("3. field initializer");
    { System.out.println("4. instance block"); }           // instance initializer
    Order() { System.out.println("5. constructor body"); }

    private int init(String msg) { System.out.println(msg); return 0; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("2. before new");
        new Order();
    }
}
```

**Reachability** is the other half of the lifecycle. Java does not track when
you are "done" with an object, because you never say so. Instead the collector
asks a structural question: **starting from a fixed set of roots, can this
object be reached by following references?** If yes it is live. If no it is
garbage, and the collector may reclaim it.

The **GC roots** are the places a live reference can originate:

- Local variables and parameters in every frame of every live thread
- Static fields of loaded classes
- Active thread objects themselves
- JNI (native code) local and global references
- Objects held by the JVM internally, such as interned strings and class objects
- Monitors currently used for synchronization

```text
   GC ROOTS
   +--------------------+
   | local variables    |----> A ----> B ----> C       reachable: KEPT
   | static fields      |----> D ----> B                (B has two paths in)
   | live threads       |
   | JNI references     |          E <---> F           unreachable CYCLE:
   +--------------------+                              still COLLECTED
```

That diagram makes the most important property visible. Java uses **tracing**,
not reference counting, so a cycle of objects that reference each other but
which no root can reach is collected without special handling. Languages that
count references need weak pointers to break such cycles; Java does not.

Making an object unreachable is just breaking the last path to it:

```java
public class Reach {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        StringBuilder a = new StringBuilder("first");
        StringBuilder b = new StringBuilder("second");

        a = b;             // the "first" object now has NO reference: garbage
        b = null;          // the "second" object is still reachable through a

        // Cycles are not a problem for a tracing collector
        Node x = new Node();
        Node y = new Node();
        x.next = y;
        y.next = x;        // they reference each other
        x = null;
        y = null;          // the pair is now unreachable, and will be collected
    }

    static class Node { Node next; }
}
```

Note the honest wording: garbage is *eligible* for collection, not collected at
a known moment. Nothing in Java guarantees when, or that it happens at all
before the program exits.

That is why **`finalize()` must not be used.** It was deprecated in Java 9,
deprecated for removal in Java 18, and its problems were fatal: no guarantee it
ever runs, unpredictable timing, it can resurrect the object, an exception in it
is swallowed, and it delays reclamation by an extra GC cycle. Use
`AutoCloseable` with try-with-resources for anything that must be released
promptly, and `java.lang.ref.Cleaner` only as a safety net for native memory.

The full lifecycle, then:

```text
  created        reachable          unreachable        finalized*     reclaimed
  (new)   --->   (in use)   --->   (no root path) ---> (Cleaner, ---> (memory
                     ^                    |            if any)         reused)
                     |                    |
                     +--- reachable again |    * optional, and never guaranteed
                          (a root gets a  |      to run at a particular time
                           reference)  <--+
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `new` resolves and initializes the class, allocates, zeroes the memory,
>   writes the header, then runs constructors.
> - Fields are zeroed to defaults before any user code runs, so there are no
>   uninitialized reads.
> - The superclass constructor completes before subclass field initializers, so
>   never call an overridable method from a constructor.
> - Static initializers run once at class initialization; instance initializers
>   run per object, before the constructor body.
> - An object is live if it is reachable from a GC root by following references.
> - GC roots are stack frames, static fields, live threads, JNI references, and
>   some JVM internals.
> - Java traces references rather than counting them, so unreachable cycles are
>   collected normally.
> - Unreachable means eligible for collection, never collected at a known time.
> - `finalize()` is deprecated for removal; use `AutoCloseable`, and `Cleaner`
>   only as a backstop.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run the `Order` class above and predict the output before you see it. Then
>    add a superclass with its own static block and field initializer, and
>    predict again.
> 2. Write a class whose constructor calls an overridable method, and a subclass
>    that overrides it and reads a subclass field. Demonstrate the `null`.
> 3. Draw the object graph for a `Map` held in a static field whose values hold
>    references back to their keys, and mark what is reachable after the local
>    variable pointing at the map goes out of scope.
> 4. Interview: Two objects reference each other and nothing else references
>    either. Are they collected, and would your answer change in a
>    reference-counted language such as CPython? (Hint: what question does a
>    tracing collector actually ask?)

#### Escape Analysis and Object Scope

Heap allocation in HotSpot is remarkably cheap. Each thread gets a private slab
of Eden called a **thread-local allocation buffer** (TLAB), and allocating in it
is one pointer bump with no locking, perhaps ten instructions. But cheap is not
free: the object still consumes space, still must be zeroed, and still has to be
traced and eventually reclaimed.

So the JIT compiler asks a question about every allocation it compiles: **can a
reference to this object be observed from outside the method that created it?**
That analysis is called **escape analysis**, and it classifies each allocation
into one of three outcomes.

| Result            | Meaning                                                | Optimizations unlocked |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------- |
| `NoEscape`        | The reference never leaves the method                  | Scalar replacement, lock elision |
| `ArgEscape`       | Passed to a method, but does not reach the heap or another thread | Lock elision |
| `GlobalEscape`    | Stored in a field, returned, or reachable by another thread | None                 |

An object escapes when it is returned, assigned to a field or static, added to a
collection, thrown, or published to another thread. If none of that happens, the
object is provably invisible to anyone else, and the compiler can rewrite the
code as if it never existed.

```java
public class Escape {

    // NoEscape: the Point is created, read, and abandoned inside this method
    double distance(double x, double y) {
        Point p = new Point(x, y);      // the JIT can delete this allocation
        return Math.sqrt(p.x() * p.x() + p.y() * p.y());
    }

    // GlobalEscape: the reference is handed to the caller
    Point origin() {
        return new Point(0, 0);         // must be a real heap object
    }

    private Point cached;

    // GlobalEscape: stored in a field, so it outlives the call
    void remember(double x, double y) {
        this.cached = new Point(x, y);
    }

    record Point(double x, double y) { }
}
```

The main payoff is not what people usually claim. HotSpot does not generally
"allocate the object on the stack". It does something better called **scalar
replacement**: it dissolves the object and keeps its fields in registers or
stack slots as if you had written the primitives by hand.

```text
   SOURCE                            AFTER SCALAR REPLACEMENT
   ------------------------------    -----------------------------------
   Point p = new Point(x, y);        (no object at all)
   return sqrt(p.x()*p.x()           double px = x;   // in a register
             + p.y()*p.y());         double py = y;   // in a register
                                     return sqrt(px*px + py*py);
```

The second payoff is **lock elision**. A lock on an object that cannot escape
can be removed entirely, because no other thread could ever contend for it.

```java
// Every StringBuilder method is unsynchronized, but the classic example is
// a StringBuffer that never escapes: its locks are provably pointless.
String join(String a, String b) {
    StringBuffer sb = new StringBuffer();   // NoEscape
    sb.append(a);                           // synchronized method ...
    sb.append(b);                           // ... but the lock can be elided
    return sb.toString();                   // the String escapes, the buffer does not
}
```

Escape analysis is a JIT optimization, which has three consequences that matter
in practice.

- **It only applies to hot code.** The interpreter and the first compilation
  tier do not do it, so a method that runs ten times allocates normally.
- **It is fragile.** Inlining is a prerequisite, so a method too large to
  inline, a megamorphic call site, or a `synchronized` block in the wrong place
  can silently disable it.
- **You cannot rely on it.** It is an optimization, not a guarantee, and it is
  absent in the specification.

You can observe its effect by turning it off and measuring the difference:

```bash
# Compare a benchmark with and without the optimization
java -XX:+DoEscapeAnalysis  -jar bench.jar     # the default
java -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis  -jar bench.jar     # forces real allocations

# Show which allocations were eliminated (fastdebug JVM builds only)
java -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintEliminateAllocations -jar bench.jar
```

The practical advice is deliberately boring. **Do not hand-optimize for escape
analysis.** Write small, focused methods with short-lived local objects, which
is what you should do for readability anyway, and the compiler will take the
opportunities it finds. What you *can* usefully avoid is defeating it: do not
stash objects in fields, static caches, or collections that outlive the work,
because that turns a free allocation into a traced, promoted, long-lived one.

This connects back to design. An object that never escapes costs close to
nothing, so "avoid creating objects" is bad advice. **"Avoid *publishing*
objects"** is the useful version, and it improves thread safety and
encapsulation at the same time.

> Key Takeaways
> - Allocation is a pointer bump in a thread-local buffer, so it is cheap but
>   not free.
> - Escape analysis asks whether a reference can be observed outside the method
>   that created it.
> - The three outcomes are `NoEscape`, `ArgEscape`, and `GlobalEscape`.
> - Objects escape by being returned, stored in a field, added to a collection,
>   thrown, or shared with another thread.
> - The main optimization is scalar replacement, which dissolves the object into
>   registers, not literal stack allocation.
> - Lock elision removes synchronization on objects that cannot escape.
> - It runs only in JIT-compiled hot code, depends on inlining, and is never
>   guaranteed.
> - Write small methods with short-lived locals rather than optimizing for it
>   directly; the real cost is publishing objects, not creating them.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Label each allocation in a class of your own as `NoEscape`, `ArgEscape`, or
>    `GlobalEscape`, and justify each label in one sentence.
> 2. Write a loop that creates ten million short-lived objects in a method that
>    returns only a `double`. Time it with `-XX:+DoEscapeAnalysis` and
>    `-XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis` and report the ratio.
> 3. Take a method whose local object does not escape, then add a line that
>    stores it in a field. Explain precisely which optimizations you just
>    disabled.
> 4. Interview: A colleague replaces a small local object with four loose
>    primitive variables "for performance". When is that justified, and what
>    would you measure first? (Hint: consider which tier of compilation the code
>    actually reaches.)

<a id="112-garbage-collection-and-reference-types"></a>
### 11.2 Garbage Collection and Reference Types

This subchapter covers how the collector finds and reclaims garbage, the four
reference strengths that let you tell it how badly you want an object kept, and
the retention bugs that survive all of it.

#### Garbage Collection Fundamentals

In a language with manual memory management, every allocation creates an
obligation to free it exactly once, at a moment when nothing else still needs
it. Getting that wrong produces the two worst bug classes in systems
programming: free too early and you have a dangling pointer that corrupts
unrelated data; free twice or never and you have a crash or a leak. Worse, the
obligation cannot be discharged locally, because whether an object is still
needed is a property of the whole program.

**Garbage collection** removes the obligation by answering the question the
programmer cannot: it computes reachability directly. The previous topic
established the criterion. This one covers the mechanics.

Every collector is built from three primitive operations.

**Mark-sweep** traces from the roots, marking everything it reaches, then sweeps
the heap and frees anything unmarked. Simple, and it leaves the heap fragmented.

```text
   BEFORE   [A][B][ ][C][ ][D][E][ ]      B and D unreachable
   MARK     [A*][B][ ][C*][ ][D][E*][ ]   * = reached from a root
   SWEEP    [A][ ][ ][C][ ][ ][E][ ]      free space, but in scattered holes
```

**Mark-compact** adds a third phase that slides the survivors together, which
removes fragmentation and makes future allocation a pointer bump, at the cost of
moving objects and updating every reference to them.

```text
   COMPACT  [A][C][E][                 ]  one contiguous free region
```

**Copying** collection divides the space in two and copies live objects from one
half to the other, then declares the source half entirely free. Its cost is
proportional to the *surviving* data, not to the heap size, which makes it
almost free when nearly everything is garbage.

That last property is decisive, because of an empirical observation that holds
across nearly all programs, called the **generational hypothesis**:

> Most objects die young. The overwhelming majority of allocations become
> unreachable almost immediately, and objects that have already survived a while
> tend to keep surviving.

Think of a restaurant kitchen. Nearly everything on the prep counter is scraps
cleared within minutes, while the stockpot at the back stays for days. It would
be absurd to inspect the stockpot every time you wipe the counter.

So the heap is split by age, and the two halves are collected with different
algorithms at different frequencies.

```text
                                 HEAP
  +--------------------------------------+----------------------------+
  |           YOUNG GENERATION           |      OLD GENERATION        |
  |  +----------+  +------+  +------+    |                            |
  |  |   Eden   |  |  S0  |  |  S1  |    |   long-lived objects       |
  |  +----------+  +------+  +------+    |                            |
  +--------------------------------------+----------------------------+
       ^                ^                          ^
       | new objects    | survivors copied         | promoted after surviving
       | allocated here | back and forth           | enough young collections
       | (TLAB bump)    | (one is always empty)    |
```

A **minor GC** (young collection) runs often and is fast: it copies the live
objects out of Eden and the occupied survivor space into the other survivor
space, bumping each object's age, and promotes anything old enough to the old
generation. Eden is then entirely free. Because typically 90 to 98 percent of
Eden is garbage, the copy is small.

A **major** or **full GC** touches the old generation, is much more expensive,
and is what people mean when they complain about GC pauses.

| Event      | Region collected       | Typical duration | Frequency |
| ---------- | ---------------------- | ---------------- | --------- |
| Minor GC   | Young generation only  | Under 10 ms      | Often     |
| Major GC   | Old generation         | Tens to hundreds of ms | Rarely |
| Full GC    | Entire heap, plus metaspace | 100 ms to seconds | Should be very rare |

One detail makes generational collection possible at all. To collect the young
generation without tracing the old one, the JVM must know about old-to-young
references. It tracks them with a **write barrier**, a few instructions injected
after every reference field write, which records the change in a **card table**
or **remembered set**. That is why a reference assignment is slightly more
expensive than a primitive one.

Collection also generally requires the heap to stop changing while it is
inspected, which is a **stop-the-world** pause. All application threads are
suspended at a safepoint. Modern collectors work hard to do most of their work
concurrently and keep only short pauses, but no production collector eliminates
pauses entirely.

Which collector you get matters more than any other tuning decision.

| Collector   | Flag                        | Optimized for              | Use when |
| ----------- | --------------------------- | -------------------------- | -------- |
| Serial      | `-XX:+UseSerialGC`          | Small footprint, one thread | Tiny heaps, containers with one CPU |
| Parallel    | `-XX:+UseParallelGC`        | Throughput                 | Batch jobs where pauses do not matter |
| G1          | `-XX:+UseG1GC`              | Balance, pause targets     | The default since Java 9; most server apps |
| ZGC         | `-XX:+UseZGC`               | Very low pauses, huge heaps | Latency-sensitive services, multi-terabyte heaps |
| Shenandoah  | `-XX:+UseShenandoahGC`      | Low pauses                 | Similar niche to ZGC |
| Epsilon     | `-XX:+UseEpsilonGC`         | Doing nothing at all       | Benchmarking and allocation testing only |

**G1**, the default, is worth understanding because you are almost certainly
using it. It divides the heap into a few thousand equal-sized regions, each
tagged at any moment as Eden, survivor, old, or humongous, rather than using
fixed contiguous generations. It then collects the regions with the most garbage
first, which is where "garbage first" comes from, choosing how many to include
in order to meet a pause-time target you set.

**ZGC** is the modern low-latency option: pauses stay in the sub-millisecond
range essentially independent of heap size, and since Java 21 it is generational
by default.

The flags worth knowing are few:

```bash
# Sizing and collector choice
java -Xms4g -Xmx4g -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100 -jar app.jar

# Observability: always turn GC logging on in production, it is nearly free
java -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime:filecount=5,filesize=10M -jar app.jar

# Get a heap dump automatically when the heap is exhausted
java -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/log/app.hprof -jar app.jar
```

Two last points that come up constantly.

**Do not call `System.gc()`.** It is a *suggestion*, it typically triggers a
full stop-the-world collection, and if it appears to fix a problem, the real
problem is retention that is still there. Production JVMs are often launched
with `-XX:+DisableExplicitGC` precisely to neutralize library code that calls
it.

**`OutOfMemoryError` is not always a leak.** Read the message, because each
variant points somewhere different.

| Message                                   | Actual cause                                       |
| ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `Java heap space`                         | Genuinely too much live data, or a retention leak   |
| `GC overhead limit exceeded`              | Over 98% of time in GC reclaiming under 2%: near-full heap |
| `Metaspace`                               | Too many loaded classes, often a class loader leak  |
| `unable to create native thread`          | OS thread or memory limit, not the Java heap        |
| `Requested array size exceeds VM limit`   | An array larger than roughly `Integer.MAX_VALUE`    |
| `Cannot reserve ... direct buffer memory` | `ByteBuffer.allocateDirect` off-heap, bounded by `MaxDirectMemorySize` |

> Key Takeaways
> - Garbage collection replaces a non-local correctness obligation with a
>   computed reachability answer.
> - The three primitives are mark-sweep, mark-compact, and copying.
> - Copying costs scale with surviving data, not heap size, which makes young
>   collection cheap.
> - The generational hypothesis says most objects die young, which is why the
>   heap is split by age.
> - Minor GC collects only the young generation and is frequent and fast; full
>   GC is rare and expensive.
> - A write barrier and card table record old-to-young references so the young
>   generation can be collected alone.
> - Collection requires stop-the-world pauses at safepoints, which modern
>   collectors shorten rather than eliminate.
> - G1 is the default and collects the emptiest regions first against a pause
>   target; ZGC targets sub-millisecond pauses.
> - `System.gc()` is only a suggestion and usually hides the real problem.
> - Read the `OutOfMemoryError` message, because metaspace, native threads, and
>   direct buffers are not heap problems.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run any allocation-heavy program with
>    `-Xlog:gc` and count the minor collections against the major ones.
> 2. Run the same benchmark under `-XX:+UseSerialGC`, `-XX:+UseParallelGC`, and
>    `-XX:+UseG1GC` with a fixed heap, and record total time and worst pause.
> 3. Trigger each of `Java heap space` and `GC overhead limit exceeded`
>    deliberately, and explain what differs between the two situations.
> 4. Interview: Your service has a 99th-percentile latency spike every few
>    minutes that matches a full GC. Name three things you would check before
>    changing any GC flag. (Hint: whether the heap is too small and whether
>    something is retaining objects are different diagnoses.)

#### Strong, Soft, Weak, and Phantom References

Reachability as described so far is binary, and that turns out to be too blunt
for two common designs.

Consider a cache. You want entries kept while memory is plentiful and dropped
when it is not. An ordinary `Map` cannot express that: every entry is reachable,
so nothing is ever evicted, and the cache grows until the heap is gone.

Now consider metadata keyed by object. You want to attach extra information to
objects someone else owns, for exactly as long as those objects live. An
ordinary `Map` keeps every key alive forever, so your bookkeeping table stops
the very objects it describes from being collected.

Both problems need the same thing: a reference that **does not, by itself, keep
its target alive**. The `java.lang.ref` package provides three of them, giving
four strengths in total.

| Type                | Cleared by the collector when                    | Survives an OOM? | Typical use |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | ---------------- | ----------- |
| Strong (ordinary)   | Never; retention is guaranteed                   | Heap fills first | Everything normal |
| `SoftReference`     | The JVM needs memory                             | No, cleared first | Memory-sensitive caches |
| `WeakReference`     | No strong reference remains, at the next GC      | No               | Canonical maps, listener registries |
| `PhantomReference`  | Already unreachable; enqueued before reclamation | No               | Post-mortem resource cleanup |

The ordering is a promise about collection order: **soft references are cleared
only when memory is tight, weak references are cleared at the first collection
that notices them, and phantom references are enqueued after the object is
already unreachable.**

```text
   STRENGTH                  WILL THE OBJECT SURVIVE?
   ---------------------     ---------------------------------------
   strong    o-----> obj     always, until the reference goes away
   soft      o- - -> obj     yes, until memory pressure
   weak      o . . > obj     no, cleared at the next GC
   phantom   o ~ ~ > obj     no, and get() always returns null
```

The basic mechanics are the same for all three: wrap the target, and call
`get()` to attempt to retrieve it.

```java
import java.lang.ref.*;

public class Weakly {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Object target = new Object();
        WeakReference<Object> weak = new WeakReference<>(target);

        System.out.println(weak.get() != null);   // true: a strong ref exists

        target = null;          // drop the ONLY strong reference
        System.gc();            // a hint; adequate for a demonstration only
        Thread.sleep(100);

        System.out.println(weak.get() == null);   // true: the weak ref was cleared
    }
}
```

The critical discipline with `get()`: it can return `null` at any moment, so
**assign it to a local variable once and check that, rather than calling `get()`
twice.**

```java
// WRONG: the object can be collected between the two calls
if (ref.get() != null) {
    ref.get().doWork();          // may throw NullPointerException
}

// RIGHT: one call creates a strong reference for the duration of the block
Widget w = ref.get();
if (w != null) {
    w.doWork();                  // w keeps it alive here
}
```

**`WeakHashMap`** packages the weak-key pattern. Its entries vanish once nothing
else references the key, which is exactly the metadata case.

```java
import java.util.*;

public class Metadata {
    // Keys are held weakly: an entry disappears when its key becomes garbage
    private final Map<Session, Stats> stats = new WeakHashMap<>();

    void record(Session s, long millis) {
        stats.computeIfAbsent(s, k -> new Stats()).add(millis);
    }
}
```

There is a trap here that catches everyone once. **If the value references the
key, the entry is immortal**, because the value is held strongly by the map, and
through it the key stays strongly reachable.

```java
// BROKEN: Stats holds its Session, so the weak key can never be cleared
class Stats { Session owner; }

// FIX: hold the back-reference weakly, or do not hold it at all
class Stats { WeakReference<Session> owner; }
```

**`SoftReference`** suits caches whose entries are expensive to rebuild but
always rebuildable.

```java
import java.lang.ref.SoftReference;
import java.util.*;

public class ImageCache {
    private final Map<String, SoftReference<byte[]>> cache = new HashMap<>();

    public byte[] get(String path) {
        SoftReference<byte[]> ref = cache.get(path);
        byte[] data = (ref == null) ? null : ref.get();   // may have been cleared

        if (data == null) {                  // miss, or cleared under pressure
            data = load(path);               // rebuild
            cache.put(path, new SoftReference<>(data));
        }
        return data;
    }

    private byte[] load(String path) { return new byte[1024]; }
}
```

Be honest about soft references, though: the JVM's clearing policy is opaque and
tied to `-XX:SoftRefLRUPolicyMSPerMB`, they tend to be cleared all at once under
pressure, and they can make a full GC worse. For real caching, a library such as
Caffeine with an explicit size and time policy is almost always the better
answer. Note also that the map above accumulates dead `SoftReference` wrappers
forever, which the next mechanism solves.

**`ReferenceQueue`** is how you find out that clearing happened. Register a
queue when you create the reference, and the collector enqueues the reference
object after clearing its target.

```java
import java.lang.ref.*;
import java.util.*;

public class QueueDemo {
    // Subclass so the enqueued reference still tells us which key to remove
    static class KeyedRef extends WeakReference<Object> {
        final String key;
        KeyedRef(String key, Object value, ReferenceQueue<Object> q) {
            super(value, q);          // register with the queue
            this.key = key;
        }
    }

    private final Map<String, KeyedRef> map = new HashMap<>();
    private final ReferenceQueue<Object> queue = new ReferenceQueue<>();

    void purge() {
        KeyedRef ref;
        while ((ref = (KeyedRef) queue.poll()) != null) {   // non-blocking drain
            map.remove(ref.key);                            // remove the dead entry
        }
    }
}
```

**`PhantomReference`** exists for cleanup that must happen *after* the object is
gone. Its `get()` always returns `null` by design, so you cannot resurrect the
object the way `finalize()` could. In modern code you almost never use it
directly, because `java.lang.ref.Cleaner` wraps it correctly.

```java
import java.lang.ref.Cleaner;

public class NativeBuffer implements AutoCloseable {
    private static final Cleaner CLEANER = Cleaner.create();

    // MUST be a static class holding no reference to NativeBuffer. An inner
    // class would capture the outer instance, which would then never become
    // unreachable, and the cleanup would never run.
    private static class State implements Runnable {
        private long handle;
        State(long handle) { this.handle = handle; }

        @Override public void run() {
            if (handle != 0) {
                // free(handle) via native code
                handle = 0;                  // idempotent: safe to run twice
            }
        }
    }

    private final State state;
    private final Cleaner.Cleanable cleanable;

    public NativeBuffer(long handle) {
        this.state = new State(handle);
        this.cleanable = CLEANER.register(this, state);   // the safety net
    }

    @Override
    public void close() {
        cleanable.clean();       // the PRIMARY path: prompt and deterministic
    }
}
```

That class shows the correct pattern in full: `close()` is how cleanup is
supposed to happen, and the `Cleaner` only covers the case where a caller
forgot. The `static` nested state holder is not a style choice but a
requirement.

The summary rule: **use ordinary strong references unless you can state exactly
which of these two problems you have.** Weak for "do not let my bookkeeping
extend a lifetime", soft for "cheap to lose, expensive to rebuild", and
`Cleaner` for "native memory must eventually be freed".

> Key Takeaways
> - Ordinary references are strong and guarantee retention; `java.lang.ref`
>   supplies three weaker strengths.
> - Soft references are cleared only under memory pressure; weak ones at the
>   next collection that notices them.
> - Phantom references are enqueued after the object is unreachable, and their
>   `get()` always returns `null`.
> - Call `get()` once into a local variable, then null-check that, because the
>   target can vanish between calls.
> - `WeakHashMap` holds keys weakly, which fits per-object metadata.
> - A `WeakHashMap` value that references its own key makes the entry immortal.
> - A `ReferenceQueue` notifies you after clearing, so you can purge dead
>   wrappers.
> - Prefer a real cache library over `SoftReference` when you need eviction
>   policy.
> - `Cleaner` replaces `finalize()`, and its state holder must be a static class
>   that does not reference the owner.
> - `close()` through `AutoCloseable` is the primary cleanup path; `Cleaner` is
>   only a backstop.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create a `WeakReference` to an object, drop the strong reference, force a
>    collection, and confirm `get()` returns `null`. Then repeat with a
>    `SoftReference` and explain why the result differs.
> 2. Build a `WeakHashMap` of one thousand keys, drop half the key references,
>    force a collection, and print the resulting size.
> 3. Write the broken `WeakHashMap` case where the value references the key,
>    demonstrate that the map never shrinks, then fix it.
> 4. Implement `NativeBuffer` above with a counter instead of a native handle,
>    and prove that `close()` runs the cleanup once and that a second `close()`
>    is harmless.
> 5. Interview: You are asked to build a cache and reach for `SoftReference`.
>    What would a reviewer object to, and what would they suggest? (Hint: who
>    decides the eviction policy, and can you predict it?)

#### Memory Leaks in Object Graphs

Java cannot leak in the C sense, because nothing is ever forgotten by the
allocator. Yet Java programs run out of memory constantly, and the reason is
subtler and harder to spot.

**A Java memory leak is unintentional retention: an object you are finished with
is still reachable from a GC root.** The collector is working perfectly. It is
correctly concluding that an object you forgot about is still needed, because
you left a path to it.

The analogy is a library with a flawless catalogue. Nothing is ever lost, but if
readers keep signing books out and never return them, the shelves still empty.
The catalogue is not broken; the borrowing is.

Leaks cluster into a small number of recurring shapes, and recognizing them is
most of the skill.

**1. Unbounded static collections.** A `static` field is a GC root, so anything
it holds lives as long as the class loader. This is the single most common
cause.

```java
public class Registry {
    // A GC root that only ever grows. Nothing here is ever collected.
    private static final List<Session> ALL = new ArrayList<>();

    public static void register(Session s) { ALL.add(s); }
    // ... and no remove() anywhere in the codebase
}
```

**2. Stale references in your own data structures.** The classic from *Effective
Java*: a hand-written stack that decrements its size without clearing the slot.

```java
public class Stack {
    private Object[] elements = new Object[16];
    private int size;

    public void push(Object e) { elements[size++] = e; }

    // LEAK: the slot still holds the reference, so the object stays reachable
    public Object popLeaky() {
        return elements[--size];
    }

    // FIXED: clear the obsolete slot
    public Object pop() {
        Object result = elements[--size];
        elements[size] = null;          // let the collector have it
        return result;
    }
}
```

The amount retained is worth being precise about, because it explains why this
leak hides so well. The array keeps stale references in every slot below its
**high-water mark**, so the waste equals the largest the stack ever got, not the
total number of objects pushed. A stack that stays around ten elements leaks
almost nothing. A stack that once held fifty thousand and is now empty retains
all fifty thousand, indefinitely.

```text
   after pushing 5000, then popping all 5000 with popLeaky()

   size = 0            <- logically empty
   elements = [ref][ref][ref][ref] ... [ref]  [null][null] ...
               \________ 5000 stale references still reachable ______/
                        the collector cannot touch any of them
```

That also makes it reproducible. With a 96 MB heap, pushing 5000 arrays of
10 KB, popping them all, and then asking for another 50 MB throws
`OutOfMemoryError` with `popLeaky` and succeeds with `pop`.

This is worth internalizing because it generalizes: whenever *you* manage the
storage, you own the job of nulling out obsolete references. Inside `ArrayList`
and friends this is already done for you, which is a good reason to prefer them.

**3. Listeners and callbacks that are never unregistered.** Registration creates
a reference from the long-lived publisher to the short-lived subscriber.

```java
public class Widget {
    public Widget(EventBus bus) {
        bus.subscribe(this::onEvent);   // the bus now holds this Widget forever
    }
    private void onEvent(Event e) { }
    // No unsubscribe, so every Widget ever created is retained by the bus.
}
```

The fix is symmetry: whatever registers must also deregister, usually in a
`close()` method, or the registry must hold subscribers weakly.

**4. `ThreadLocal` in a pooled thread.** Thread-pool threads are never
discarded, so their thread-local map is never discarded either.

```java
public class Context {
    private static final ThreadLocal<UserSession> CURRENT = new ThreadLocal<>();

    public static void set(UserSession s) { CURRENT.set(s); }

    // MANDATORY in any pooled environment, and belongs in a finally block
    public static void clear() { CURRENT.remove(); }
}
```

Every servlet filter and request interceptor that sets a thread-local must
remove it in `finally`. Forgetting this leaks one session per pool thread, and
in an application server it also pins the web application's class loader.

**5. Non-static inner classes and lambdas capturing `this`.** A non-static
nested class holds an implicit reference to its enclosing instance, so a
long-lived inner object keeps a large outer object alive.

```java
public class Report {
    private final byte[] hugeData = new byte[100_000_000];

    // Non-static: every Row silently retains the whole Report, including hugeData
    class Row { }

    // Static: retains nothing extra
    static class BetterRow { }

    // A method reference to an instance method also captures this
    Runnable leaky()      { return this::render; }      // retains the Report
    Runnable notLeaky()   { return () -> System.out.println("ok"); }  // captures nothing

    private void render() { }
}
```

**6. Caches with no eviction.** A `HashMap` used as a cache is an unbounded
collection with a friendly name. Use a real cache with a maximum size or a time
policy.

**7. Unclosed resources.** An open stream, connection, or channel holds buffers
and often native memory. Try-with-resources exists for this.

**8. Class loader leaks.** In an application server, a single strong reference
from container code into a redeployed application, very often a thread-local or
a JDBC driver registration, retains that application's entire class loader and
therefore every class it loaded. This is what usually produces
`OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace` after several redeployments.

Here is the general shape of all eight:

```text
   GC ROOT                                      what you think you have
   (static field,  ------> COLLECTION ------>    (nothing)
    pooled thread,           |
    event bus,               +--> entry --> object --> object --> object
    class loader)                           ^
                                            |
                              what you actually still have: all of it,
                              retained by ONE reference you forgot
```

**Diagnosing a suspected leak** follows a fixed sequence, and the order matters
because each step rules something out.

```bash
# 1. Confirm it is growth, not just a small heap. Live set should be flat after
#    a full GC; a leak makes the post-GC floor climb steadily over hours.
java -Xlog:gc* -jar app.jar

# 2. List processes, then watch class histograms while the heap grows
jcmd -l
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram | head -20

# 3. Capture a heap dump. Do this twice, minutes apart, and compare.
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/app-1.hprof

# 4. Inspect it in Eclipse MAT or VisualVM
```

The one concept you need in order to read a heap dump is the difference between
two sizes:

| Term          | Meaning                                                          |
| ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Shallow size  | The object's own bytes, excluding what it references              |
| Retained size | Everything that would be freed if this object became unreachable  |
| Dominator     | The object through which all paths to a subgraph pass             |

**Sort by retained size, not shallow size.** A `HashMap` with a shallow size of
48 bytes can retain two gigabytes. Then use the "path to GC roots" view on the
biggest retainer, which names the exact field that is holding on. That single
view answers "who is keeping this alive", which is the only question that
matters.

The comparison of two dumps is the most reliable signal: whatever class grew by
hundreds of thousands of instances between them is your leak.

Finally, the fixes, mapped to the causes:

| Symptom found in the dump                  | Usual fix                                  |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------ |
| Huge `static` collection                   | Bound it, or remove entries on completion   |
| Growing listener list                      | Unregister in `close()`, or hold weakly     |
| `ThreadLocal` entries on pool threads      | `remove()` in a `finally` block             |
| Map used as a cache                        | A real cache with size and time eviction    |
| Many inner-class instances retaining outers | Make the nested class `static`              |
| Your own array or buffer holding old slots | Null out obsolete elements                  |
| Class loaders retained after redeploy      | Remove container-side references, deregister drivers |

> Key Takeaways
> - A Java leak is unintentional retention, not lost memory; the collector is
>   behaving correctly.
> - `static` fields are GC roots, so unbounded static collections are the most
>   common leak.
> - When you manage storage yourself, you must null out obsolete references.
> - Registration without deregistration leaks one object per registration.
> - `ThreadLocal` must be removed in a `finally` block on pooled threads.
> - Non-static inner classes and `this`-capturing lambdas retain their enclosing
>   instance.
> - A `HashMap` used as a cache is an unbounded collection; use eviction.
> - Confirm growth in the post-GC live set before capturing dumps.
> - Compare two heap dumps taken minutes apart to see what is growing.
> - Sort by retained size, not shallow size, then follow the path to GC roots to
>   name the culprit.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write the leaky `Stack` above. Under `-Xmx96m`, push 5000 arrays of
>    `new byte[10_000]`, pop them all, then allocate another 50 MB. Show that
>    `popLeaky` throws `OutOfMemoryError` and the one-line fix does not.
> 2. Build an event bus that retains subscribers, then rewrite it with
>    `WeakReference` subscribers and demonstrate the difference in retained
>    count.
> 3. Create a non-static inner class inside a class holding a large array, keep
>    ten thousand inner instances, and measure the heap. Make the nested class
>    `static` and measure again.
> 4. Capture two heap dumps of a deliberately leaking program a minute apart and
>    identify the growing class by retained size in VisualVM or Eclipse MAT.
> 5. Interview: A service restarts with `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`
>    every few days. Walk through how you would distinguish a genuine leak from
>    an undersized heap. (Hint: what should the live set look like immediately
>    after a full GC in each case?)

<a id="12-concurrency-and-parallelism"></a>
## 12. Concurrency & Parallelism

Every previous chapter assumed one thread executing your code in the order you
wrote it. Drop that assumption and almost everything becomes harder: a counter
loses increments, a field never shows its new value, two correct methods combine
into a broken one. This chapter covers why concurrency is necessary anyway, the
rules the Java Memory Model actually guarantees, the tools for enforcing
correctness, and the high-level utilities that let you avoid most of the danger.

<a id="121-concurrency-foundations"></a>
### 12.1 Concurrency Foundations

This subchapter covers the distinction between doing many things at once and
merely managing many things at once, and the mechanics of getting a second
thread running.

#### Concurrency versus Parallelism

Two completely different pressures push programs toward multiple threads, and
conflating them causes bad design decisions.

The first pressure is **waiting**. A program that fetches a web page spends
almost all its time doing nothing, blocked on the network. A single-threaded
server handling one request at a time would leave the processor idle while
serving nobody. The problem here is not a shortage of computing power; it is
that work is *blocked*.

The second pressure is **capacity**. A machine has sixteen cores, and a
single-threaded program uses one of them. Summing a billion numbers takes
sixteen times longer than it needs to. Here nothing is blocked; there is simply
more computing power available than one thread can use.

These two pressures have different names.

**Concurrency** is a property of the *structure* of a program: it is composed of
tasks that can make progress independently, in overlapping time periods.
**Parallelism** is a property of the *execution*: multiple operations physically
happen at the same instant, which requires multiple processors.

The clearest way to hold the distinction is that concurrency is about *dealing
with* many things at once, while parallelism is about *doing* many things at
once. Concurrency is a way of structuring a solution; parallelism is a way of
executing one.

A kitchen makes it concrete. One cook juggling three dishes, stirring one while
another simmers, is concurrent but not parallel. Three cooks each making one
dish are parallel. Three cooks each juggling three dishes are both.

```text
   CONCURRENT, NOT PARALLEL (one core, interleaved)
   core 1: [A--][B--][A--][C--][B--][A--][C--]     tasks take turns
           time ------------------------------->

   PARALLEL (three cores, simultaneous)
   core 1: [A------------------------]
   core 2: [B------------------------]
   core 3: [C------------------------]
           time ------------------------------->

   SEQUENTIAL (neither)
   core 1: [A--------][B--------][C--------]
```

Crucially, **concurrency does not require multiple cores**, and a correct
concurrent program is correct on one core or sixty-four. Parallelism is an
optimization that concurrency makes possible.

The distinction maps directly onto what kind of work you have.

| Aspect            | I/O-bound work                       | CPU-bound work                     |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------- |
| Time spent        | Waiting on network, disk, database   | Executing instructions             |
| Bottleneck        | Latency of external systems          | Number of cores                    |
| Useful thread count | Far more than cores, sometimes thousands | Roughly the number of cores    |
| Goal              | Throughput and responsiveness        | Reducing wall-clock time           |
| Best tool         | Virtual threads, async I/O           | Fixed pool sized to cores, parallel streams |

That last row matters. Running four hundred threads for CPU-bound work is
actively harmful, because context switching adds overhead without adding
capacity. Running four hundred threads for I/O-bound work is often exactly
right, because they are all blocked anyway.

Parallelism also has a hard ceiling, given by **Amdahl's law**. If a fraction
`p` of a program can be parallelized and the rest is inherently serial, the best
possible speedup on `n` processors is:

```text
                   1
   speedup = ---------------
              (1 - p) + p/n

   With p = 0.95 (95% parallelizable):
     n = 2    ->  1.9x
     n = 8    ->  6.0x
     n = 32   -> 15.4x
     n = inf  -> 20.0x     <- the hard ceiling from the 5% serial part
```

The lesson is that the serial fraction, which includes every lock you hold and
every point where threads must coordinate, sets the limit. Doubling the cores
does not double the throughput, and beyond a point it adds nothing.

Java offers two kinds of thread, and since Java 21 the choice is a real design
decision.

| Kind             | Mapped to                  | Cost each      | Good for |
| ---------------- | -------------------------- | -------------- | -------- |
| Platform thread  | One operating-system thread | About 1 MB of stack, expensive to create | CPU-bound work, and bounded pools |
| Virtual thread   | Many multiplexed onto few OS threads | A few hundred bytes, cheap to create | I/O-bound work, millions of concurrent tasks |

A platform thread that blocks holds an OS thread hostage. A virtual thread that
blocks is unmounted from its carrier, which continues with other work. That is
why virtual threads make the simple blocking style viable at a scale that
previously demanded callbacks or reactive frameworks.

```java
// Platform thread: expensive, backed by the OS scheduler
Thread platform = Thread.ofPlatform().name("worker-1").start(() -> work());

// Virtual thread: cheap enough to create one per task, even a million of them
Thread virtual = Thread.ofVirtual().name("task-1").start(() -> work());
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Two different pressures motivate threads: work that blocks, and processing
>   capacity that sits unused.
> - Concurrency is a structural property, meaning tasks that can progress
>   independently; parallelism is simultaneous execution.
> - Concurrency is about dealing with many things at once, parallelism about
>   doing many at once.
> - Concurrency needs no extra cores, and a correct concurrent program is
>   correct on one core.
> - I/O-bound work benefits from many more threads than cores; CPU-bound work
>   does not.
> - Amdahl's law caps speedup by the serial fraction, which includes all
>   coordination and locking.
> - Platform threads map one-to-one onto OS threads and cost roughly a megabyte
>   each.
> - Virtual threads are cheap and unmount when they block, making blocking code
>   scale.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Classify each as concurrent, parallel, both, or neither: a single-core
>    server handling ten requests, a parallel stream summing an array, a
>    cooperative event loop, a plain `for` loop.
> 2. Compute the maximum speedup from Amdahl's law for `p = 0.9` at 4, 16, and
>    infinite processors. State what limits the third answer.
> 3. Write a program that sums a large array in one thread and then in four, and
>    report the speedup. Explain any gap between your result and 4x.
> 4. Interview: A service handles requests that each wait 200 ms on a database.
>    How many threads would you configure, and how does your answer change if
>    each request instead burns 200 ms of processor time? (Hint: ask what the
>    thread is doing during those 200 ms.)

#### Creating Threads: Thread versus Runnable

A thread needs two separate things: a *task*, meaning the code to run, and an
*execution mechanism*, meaning something to run it. Java's API offers two ways
to combine them, and they differ in whether they keep those concerns separate.

The first way is to **extend `Thread`** and override `run()`. This bundles task
and mechanism into one class.

```java
public class DownloadThread extends Thread {   // IS-A thread
    private final String url;

    public DownloadThread(String url) { this.url = url; }

    @Override
    public void run() { System.out.println("downloading " + url); }
}

new DownloadThread("https://example.com").start();
```

The second way is to **implement `Runnable`** and hand it to a thread. Here the
task is just a task, and something else decides how to run it.

```java
public class DownloadTask implements Runnable {   // HAS-A job to do
    private final String url;

    public DownloadTask(String url) { this.url = url; }

    @Override
    public void run() { System.out.println("downloading " + url); }
}

new Thread(new DownloadTask("https://example.com")).start();

// Runnable is a functional interface, so a lambda is usually enough
new Thread(() -> System.out.println("inline task")).start();
```

**Prefer `Runnable`**, for reasons that are mostly the composition-over-
inheritance argument from the design chapter.

| Consideration        | `extends Thread`                       | `implements Runnable`               |
| -------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Inheritance slot     | Used up; you cannot extend anything else | Free                              |
| Separation of concerns | Task and execution mechanism fused    | Task is independent of how it runs   |
| Reusability          | Tied to one thread, single use          | Submit to a pool, reuse, wrap, test  |
| Works with executors | Awkward                                 | Directly, which is how real code runs |
| Lambda-friendly      | No                                      | Yes                                 |
| Testability          | Needs a thread to test                  | Call `run()` directly in a unit test |

The most common beginner error is calling `run()` instead of `start()`.

```java
Runnable task = () -> System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName());

new Thread(task).run();     // WRONG: runs on the CALLER's thread, prints "main"
new Thread(task).start();   // RIGHT: creates a new thread, prints "Thread-1"
```

The second line prints `Thread-1` rather than `Thread-0` because the first
`Thread` object was still constructed, and constructing one consumes a name even
if it is never started.

`start()` asks the JVM to create a thread and invoke `run()` on it. Calling
`run()` directly is an ordinary method call with no concurrency at all. A thread
can also be started only once; a second `start()` throws
`IllegalThreadStateException`.

Every thread moves through a fixed set of states, which `Thread.getState()`
reports.

```text
                         start()
      +-------+   ------------------>   +----------+
      |  NEW  |                        | RUNNABLE |  <-- may or may not be
      +-------+                        +----------+      on a core right now
                                    /      |      \
                    waiting for a  /       |       \  wait(), join(),
                    monitor lock  /        |        \ park()
                                 v         |         v
                          +---------+      |    +---------+
                          | BLOCKED |      |    | WAITING |
                          +---------+      |    +---------+
                                           |    | TIMED_  |  sleep(n), wait(n),
                                           |    | WAITING |  join(n)
                                           |    +---------+
                                           v
                                    +------------+
                                    | TERMINATED |   run() returned or threw
                                    +------------+
```

| State           | Meaning                                                    |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `NEW`           | Created but `start()` not yet called                        |
| `RUNNABLE`      | Eligible to run; may be executing or waiting for a core     |
| `BLOCKED`       | Waiting to acquire a monitor lock                           |
| `WAITING`       | Waiting indefinitely for another thread, via `wait()` or `join()` |
| `TIMED_WAITING` | Same, but with a deadline, via `sleep(n)` or `wait(n)`       |
| `TERMINATED`    | `run()` has completed or thrown                              |

Note that `RUNNABLE` does not mean "running". Java does not distinguish a thread
holding a core from one queued for one, and a thread blocked on ordinary file
I/O also reports `RUNNABLE`.

The essential control methods:

```java
public class Controls {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread worker = new Thread(() -> {
            try {
                Thread.sleep(1000);                 // TIMED_WAITING, keeps no lock
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                // Interrupted while sleeping: the flag was CLEARED by the throw,
                // so restore it and let the thread finish
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                return;
            }
        }, "worker");                                // naming aids every stack trace

        worker.setDaemon(true);   // JVM will not wait for this thread to finish
        worker.start();

        worker.join(2000);        // wait up to 2 s for worker to terminate
        worker.interrupt();       // a polite REQUEST to stop, not a kill
        System.out.println(worker.getState());
    }
}
```

**Interruption is cooperative.** `interrupt()` sets a flag; it does not stop
anything. A method that blocks, such as `sleep`, `join`, or `wait`, notices the
flag and throws `InterruptedException`, and that throw *clears* the flag. Code
that cannot propagate the exception must therefore restore the flag with
`Thread.currentThread().interrupt()`, or the interruption is silently lost. Long
computations should poll `Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()` themselves.

Never swallow an `InterruptedException`:

```java
try {
    Thread.sleep(100);
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    // WRONG: the cancellation request has now vanished
}
```

The old forcible controls are gone for good reason. `Thread.stop()` could leave
an object half-modified while holding its lock, and it now throws
`UnsupportedOperationException`. `suspend()` and `resume()` are deprecated for
removal because suspending a thread holding a lock deadlocks anything that needs
it. Cooperative interruption is the only supported mechanism.

Two more details worth knowing. An exception escaping `run()` kills only that
thread, silently unless you install a handler:

```java
Thread t = new Thread(() -> { throw new RuntimeException("boom"); });
t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((thread, ex) ->
    System.out.println(thread.getName() + " died: " + ex.getMessage()));
t.start();
```

And `setPriority` is a hint the OS may ignore entirely, so never build
correctness on it.

In practice you will rarely write `new Thread(...)` in application code. Tasks
go to an executor, which the last subchapter covers, and that is another reason
`Runnable` is the right abstraction: it is what executors accept.

> Key Takeaways
> - A thread needs a task and an execution mechanism; `Runnable` keeps them
>   separate, `extends Thread` fuses them.
> - Prefer `Runnable`, because it leaves the inheritance slot free and works
>   with executors and lambdas.
> - `start()` creates a new thread; `run()` is a plain call on the current
>   thread.
> - A thread can be started only once, and a second `start()` throws.
> - The six states are `NEW`, `RUNNABLE`, `BLOCKED`, `WAITING`, `TIMED_WAITING`,
>   and `TERMINATED`.
> - `RUNNABLE` means eligible to run, not necessarily executing.
> - `interrupt()` only sets a flag, so cancellation is cooperative.
> - Catching `InterruptedException` clears the flag, so restore it or propagate
>   the exception.
> - `Thread.stop()` now throws, and `suspend`/`resume` are deprecated for
>   removal; use interruption.
> - An uncaught exception kills just that thread, silently without a handler.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write the same task twice, once extending `Thread` and once implementing
>    `Runnable`, then rewrite the second as a lambda.
> 2. Print `Thread.currentThread().getName()` from a task invoked via `run()`
>    and again via `start()`, and explain the two outputs.
> 3. Start a thread that loops until interrupted, printing a counter. Interrupt
>    it from `main` and make it exit cleanly without swallowing the exception.
> 4. Write a program that observes a thread in at least four different states by
>    calling `getState()` from another thread.
> 5. Interview: A colleague catches `InterruptedException` and logs it. What is
>    wrong, and what are the two acceptable responses? (Hint: what happened to
>    the interrupt flag when the exception was thrown?)

<a id="122-shared-state-and-the-java-memory-model"></a>
### 12.2 Shared State and the Java Memory Model

This subchapter covers what actually goes wrong when threads share data, and the
precise guarantees the language gives you in exchange for using its
synchronization tools.

#### Shared Mutable State Hazards

Two threads running independently cause no trouble at all. Every concurrency bug
you will ever write comes from a single source: **shared mutable state**. Both
words are load-bearing, and removing either one eliminates the problem.

- If state is shared but **not mutable**, every thread reads the same
  unchanging value. Safe.
- If state is mutable but **not shared**, only one thread can see it. Safe.
- Shared *and* mutable: every hazard below applies.

That is the most useful fact in this chapter, because it tells you that the
primary tools are not locks. They are immutability and confinement. Locks are
what you reach for when you cannot have either.

The hazards come in exactly three kinds, and mixing them up leads to fixes that
do not fix anything.

| Hazard         | Question it answers                               | Broken example                  | Fixed by |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | -------- |
| **Atomicity**  | Can another thread see a half-finished operation? | `count++` losing increments      | `synchronized`, atomics |
| **Visibility** | Will another thread ever see my write?            | A loop never noticing a stopped flag | `volatile`, `synchronized` |
| **Ordering**   | Can operations appear to happen out of order?     | Seeing an object before its fields are set | `volatile`, `synchronized`, `final` |

**Atomicity** is about operations that look indivisible in source but are not.

```java
public class Counter {
    private int count;

    public void increment() {
        count++;      // THREE operations: read count, add 1, write count
    }
}
```

Two threads can both read `7`, both compute `8`, and both write `8`. One
increment is lost. No amount of `volatile` fixes this, because the problem is
not staleness; the problem is that the sequence is interruptible.

**Visibility** is about writes that another thread never observes. Each core has
its own caches and registers, and the compiler is free to keep a value in a
register rather than re-reading memory.

```java
public class Stopper {
    private boolean stopped;         // not volatile

    public void stop() { stopped = true; }

    public void run() {
        while (!stopped) { }         // may hoist the read OUT of the loop and
    }                               // spin forever, even after stop() returns
}
```

This is not theoretical. Compiled with optimization, that loop commonly becomes
an infinite loop, because the JIT is permitted to treat `stopped` as unchanging
within a thread that never writes it.

**Ordering** is about reordering. The compiler, the JIT, and the processor may
all reorder operations as long as a *single-threaded* observer cannot tell.
Another thread is not a single-threaded observer.

```java
public class Reorder {
    int a = 0;
    boolean ready = false;

    void writer() {
        a = 42;              // these two writes can be reordered,
        ready = true;        // because neither depends on the other
    }

    void reader() {
        if (ready) {
            System.out.println(a);   // may legally print 0
        }
    }
}
```

Here is the shape of all three, with each thread's view drawn separately:

```text
   THREAD 1                MAIN MEMORY              THREAD 2
   +-------------+                                  +-------------+
   | cache/regs  |         +-----------+            | cache/regs  |
   |  count = 8  | ------> |  count=7  | <--------- |  count = 8  |
   +-------------+  write  +-----------+  write     +-------------+
         ^                                                 ^
         | read 7                                          | read 7
         +-------------------------------------------------+

   Both read 7, both wrote 8. Expected 9, got 8: one update LOST.
```

The way out, in order of preference:

1. **Do not share.** Confine state to one thread, or pass copies.
2. **Do not mutate.** Make the shared object immutable.
3. **Synchronize.** If you must share mutable state, every access, including
   reads, must be coordinated.

Point three has a detail people miss constantly: **synchronizing only the writes
is useless.** If a reader does not synchronize, it has no guarantee of seeing
anything. Synchronization is a protocol both sides must follow.

> Key Takeaways
> - Every concurrency bug comes from state that is both shared and mutable.
> - Removing either sharing or mutability removes the problem entirely.
> - The three hazards are atomicity, visibility, and ordering, and they need
>   different fixes.
> - `count++` is a read, an add, and a write, so it is not atomic.
> - Visibility failures are real: a non-volatile flag read in a loop can be
>   hoisted into an infinite loop.
> - Compilers and processors may reorder operations that no single thread can
>   distinguish.
> - Prefer confinement, then immutability, and use locks only when neither is
>   possible.
> - Both readers and writers must synchronize; guarding only writes guarantees
>   nothing.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. For a shared `int total` updated by several threads, state which of the
>    three hazards apply and which single keyword, if any, fixes each.
> 2. Write the `Stopper` class above and run it with a second thread calling
>    `stop()` after a second. Report whether it terminates, then add `volatile`
>    and report again.
> 3. Take a class with a shared mutable `List` field and rewrite it twice: once
>    using confinement, once using immutability.
> 4. Interview: A colleague fixes a lost-update bug by marking the counter field
>    `volatile`. Why does the bug survive? (Hint: which of the three hazards
>    does `volatile` address, and which one is the actual bug?)

#### Race Conditions and Interleaving

A **race condition** exists when the correctness of a program depends on the
relative timing of operations in different threads. The name is apt: two threads
are racing, and the result depends on who wins, which nobody controls.

The crucial insight is that threads do not execute in whole statements. The JVM
may switch threads between any two *bytecode* instructions, so the real
execution is an arbitrary **interleaving** of the participating threads'
instructions.

Consider `count++` in bytecode:

```text
   getfield  count     <- read the current value onto the stack
   iconst_1
   iadd                <- compute value + 1
   putfield  count     <- write it back
```

A switch can occur at any of those boundaries. Interleave two threads at the
worst moment:

```text
   time   Thread A              Thread B              count in memory
   ----   ------------------    ------------------    ---------------
    1     read count -> 7                                    7
    2                           read count -> 7              7
    3     compute 7 + 1 = 8                                  7
    4                           compute 7 + 1 = 8            7
    5     write 8                                            8
    6                           write 8                      8   <- LOST
```

Two increments, one result. And this is not a rare interleaving; with two
threads doing a hundred thousand increments each, you lose thousands.

```java
public class LostUpdates {
    private static int count;                 // shared and mutable

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Runnable task = () -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; i++) count++;    // the race
        };

        Thread t1 = new Thread(task);
        Thread t2 = new Thread(task);
        t1.start(); t2.start();
        t1.join();  t2.join();                // wait for both to finish

        System.out.println("expected 20000000, got " + count);
        // Observed on a warm JVM: 10063454, 10133588, 13173489, ...
        // Almost exactly half is common, because each thread runs mostly alone
        // on its own cached copy and the last writer simply wins.
    }
}
```

The loop count is deliberately large, and that detail is itself instructive.
With only a hundred thousand iterations this program usually prints the
*correct* answer, because once the JIT compiles the loop it finishes in under a
millisecond, which can be less time than starting the second thread takes. The
threads never overlap, so there is no race to lose. **The bug is not in the code
that runs slowly; it is in the code whose threads actually overlap**, which is
precisely why small tests miss it and production does not.

Race conditions come in two recognizable shapes, and naming them helps you spot
them in review.

**Read-modify-write**: the new value depends on the old one, and the pair is not
atomic. `count++`, `balance -= amount`, and `list.set(i, list.get(i) + 1)` are
all this shape.

**Check-then-act**: you test a condition and then act on it, but the condition
may have changed in between. This one is sneakier because each half looks
innocent.

```java
public class LazyInit {
    private Resource instance;

    public Resource get() {
        if (instance == null) {          // CHECK
            instance = new Resource();   // ACT: two threads can both get here
        }
        return instance;                 // and return DIFFERENT objects
    }
}
```

```java
// Check-then-act hiding behind a thread-safe collection
if (!map.containsKey(key)) {        // CHECK: map is thread-safe ...
    map.put(key, compute(key));     // ACT: ... but this PAIR is not
}

// Fixed with a single atomic operation
map.computeIfAbsent(key, this::compute);
```

That last pair generalizes into the most important warning about concurrency:
**composing two thread-safe operations does not produce a thread-safe
operation.** `ConcurrentHashMap` guarantees each individual call is atomic; it
guarantees nothing about a sequence of them. This is why the concurrent
collections provide compound methods such as `computeIfAbsent` and
`putIfAbsent`.

Any group of operations that must appear indivisible to other threads is a
**compound action**, and it must be made atomic as a unit, either with a lock or
with a single atomic primitive.

```java
// Same logic, made atomic by holding one lock across the whole compound action
public synchronized void increment() { count++; }
```

One warning about testing. Race conditions are **nondeterministic**: they depend
on timing, core count, and JIT decisions. A test that passes proves nothing, and
bugs commonly appear only in production under load. Reason about correctness
from the memory model rather than from observed behaviour, and use tools such as
`jcstress` when you need real evidence.

> Key Takeaways
> - A race condition is correctness that depends on thread timing.
> - Threads interleave at bytecode boundaries, not statement boundaries.
> - `count++` is four bytecode operations and can lose updates at any of three
>   boundaries.
> - The two common shapes are read-modify-write and check-then-act.
> - Lazy initialization without synchronization is a check-then-act race that
>   can return two different objects.
> - Composing thread-safe operations does not yield a thread-safe operation.
> - Concurrent collections expose compound methods such as `computeIfAbsent` for
>   exactly this reason.
> - Any group of operations that must appear indivisible is a compound action
>   needing one lock or one atomic call.
> - Races are nondeterministic, so a passing test is not evidence of
>   correctness.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run `LostUpdates` above five times and record the results. Then lower the
>    loop count to one hundred thousand and explain why the bug often
>    disappears.
