```java
CompletionService<String> cs = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(pool);
tasks.forEach(cs::submit);

for (int i = 0; i < tasks.size(); i++) {
    Future<String> done = cs.take();    // blocks for the next COMPLETED task
    System.out.println(done.get());     // process in completion order
}
```

**`Future` has a real weakness: you cannot say what to do next without
blocking.** Reading a result means calling `get()` and waiting.
`CompletableFuture` (Java 8) fixes that by letting you attach continuations, so
the pipeline is described up front and runs as results arrive.

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class Composition {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);

        CompletableFuture<String> pipeline =
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchUserId(), pool)
                // thenApply: transform the value with a plain function
                .thenApply(id -> "user-" + id)
                // thenCompose: chain a call that ITSELF returns a future (flatMap)
                .thenCompose(name -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(
                        () -> loadProfile(name), pool))
                // exceptionally: supply a fallback if anything above failed
                .exceptionally(ex -> "anonymous");

        System.out.println(pipeline.get());

        // Combine two independent futures once both complete
        CompletableFuture<Integer> a = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 20, pool);
        CompletableFuture<Integer> b = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 22, pool);
        System.out.println(a.thenCombine(b, Integer::sum).get());     // 42

        // Wait for a whole group
        CompletableFuture.allOf(a, b).join();

        pool.shutdown();
    }

    static String fetchUserId() { return "7"; }
    static String loadProfile(String n) { return "profile of " + n; }
}
```

| Method              | Purpose                                                    |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `supplyAsync`       | Start an asynchronous computation that returns a value       |
| `runAsync`          | Start one that returns nothing                               |
| `thenApply`         | Transform the result with a function                         |
| `thenCompose`       | Chain another future-returning call, avoiding nesting         |
| `thenCombine`       | Merge two independent futures                                |
| `allOf` / `anyOf`   | Wait for all, or for the first                                |
| `exceptionally`     | Provide a fallback value on failure                           |
| `handle`            | Handle success and failure in one function                     |

Always pass an explicit executor to the `*Async` methods. The default is the
common `ForkJoinPool`, which is shared process-wide and sized for CPU-bound
work, so blocking in it can starve unrelated code including parallel streams.

| Aspect                | `Future`             | `CompletableFuture`         |
| --------------------- | -------------------- | --------------------------- |
| Get the result        | Blocking `get()` only | Blocking or via callbacks    |
| Chain operations      | No                   | Yes, `thenApply` and friends |
| Combine several       | Manually             | `thenCombine`, `allOf`       |
| Error handling        | Catch at `get()`      | `exceptionally`, `handle`    |
| Complete manually     | No                   | Yes, `complete(value)`        |

On Java 21, **structured concurrency** is available as a preview feature and is
worth knowing about. `StructuredTaskScope` ties a group of subtasks to a lexical
scope, so they are all cancelled and joined together, which removes the
leaked-task and forgotten-cancellation failure modes. Being a preview, it needs
`--enable-preview` and may change.

> Key Takeaways
> - `Runnable` returns nothing and cannot throw checked exceptions; `Callable`
>   does both.
> - `submit` returns immediately with a `Future` standing in for the eventual
>   result.
> - `get()` blocks, so prefer the timed overload in production.
> - A task's exception surfaces from `get()` wrapped in `ExecutionException`;
>   unwrap with `getCause()`.
> - `cancel(true)` interrupts a running task, and interruption is still
>   cooperative.
> - `invokeAll` waits for every task, so one slow task delays all results.
> - `CompletionService` delivers results in completion order instead.
> - `CompletableFuture` lets you compose non-blocking pipelines with
>   `thenApply`, `thenCompose`, and `thenCombine`.
> - Always pass an explicit executor to `*Async`, or you share the common
>   `ForkJoinPool`.
> - Structured concurrency in Java 21 is a preview that scopes and cancels
>   subtasks as a unit.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Convert a `Runnable` that prints a computed value into a `Callable` that
>    returns it, and retrieve it through a `Future`.
> 2. Submit a task that throws, then write the `try`/`catch` that prints the
>    original exception message rather than the wrapper's.
> 3. Submit three tasks sleeping 3 s, 1 s, and 2 s. Print results with
>    `invokeAll` and then with a `CompletionService`, and compare the orders.
> 4. Build a `CompletableFuture` pipeline that fetches an id, loads a profile,
>    and falls back to a default on failure, using an explicit executor
>    throughout.
> 5. Interview: What is the difference between `thenApply` and `thenCompose`,
>    and what goes wrong if you use the first where the second belongs? (Hint:
>    what is the type of the result when the function itself returns a future?)

#### Concurrent Collections Overview

The obvious way to make a collection thread-safe is to wrap it so every method
takes a lock, and Java has done that since 1.0:

```java
List<String> list = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
Map<String, String> map = Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>());
```

This is rarely good enough, for two reasons.

**One lock for the whole collection serializes everything.** Sixteen threads
reading a map take turns, so the collection becomes the serial fraction in
Amdahl's law.

**Compound operations are still not atomic**, and neither is iteration.

```java
// Each call is atomic; the PAIR is not. Two threads can both pass the check.
if (!syncMap.containsKey(key)) {
    syncMap.put(key, value);
}

// Iteration is a long compound operation. Without external locking this throws
// ConcurrentModificationException if another thread modifies the list.
for (String s : syncList) { }

// Correct but coarse: the whole loop is one critical section
synchronized (syncList) {
    for (String s : syncList) { }
}
```

`java.util.concurrent` replaces the single lock with data structures designed
for concurrency from the start.

**`ConcurrentHashMap`** is the workhorse. Instead of one lock it locks
individual hash bins, and read operations usually take no lock at all, so
throughput scales with cores.

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class Counts {
    private final ConcurrentMap<String, Integer> counts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public void record(String key) {
        // Each of these is a SINGLE atomic operation, unlike check-then-act
        counts.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum);
    }

    public void ensure(String key) {
        counts.putIfAbsent(key, 0);                       // atomic
        counts.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> expensive(k));   // atomic, computed once
        counts.compute(key, (k, v) -> v == null ? 1 : v + 1);
    }

    private int expensive(String k) { return k.length(); }
}
```

Two behaviours to internalize. Its iterators are **weakly consistent**: they
never throw `ConcurrentModificationException`, they reflect the state at some
point during traversal, and they may or may not show concurrent updates. And
`size()` is an **estimate**, because computing an exact total would require
locking everything. Two restrictions: `null` keys and values are forbidden,
because `get` returning `null` would be ambiguous, and the function passed to
`computeIfAbsent` must not modify the same map, which can deadlock.

**`CopyOnWriteArrayList`** takes the opposite approach: every mutation copies
the entire backing array. Reads are completely lock-free and iterators are
immutable snapshots.

```java
// Ideal for a listener list: thousands of iterations, a handful of mutations
private final List<Listener> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

public void fire(Event e) {
    for (Listener l : listeners) {   // snapshot: safe, no lock, never throws
        l.onEvent(e);                // safe even if a listener removes itself
    }
}
```

Use it only when reads vastly outnumber writes. A thousand-element list written
frequently copies a thousand references per write.

**`BlockingQueue`** is the coordination primitive that replaces most
`wait`/`notify` code. It blocks a consumer when empty and a producer when full,
which makes the producer-consumer pattern almost trivial and gives you
backpressure for free.

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class ProducerConsumer {
    private static final String POISON = "STOP";     // a sentinel to end cleanly

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        BlockingQueue<String> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(10);   // bounded

        Thread producer = new Thread(() -> {
            try {
                for (int i = 0; i < 50; i++) {
                    queue.put("item-" + i);   // BLOCKS while the queue is full
                }
                queue.put(POISON);
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            }
        });

        Thread consumer = new Thread(() -> {
            try {
                while (true) {
                    String item = queue.take();      // BLOCKS while empty
                    if (POISON.equals(item)) break;  // shutdown signal
                    process(item);
                }
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            }
        });

        producer.start(); consumer.start();
        producer.join();  consumer.join();
    }

    private static void process(String s) { }
}
```

The queue methods come in four flavours for the same operation, and picking the
wrong one is a common bug:

| Operation | Throws            | Returns special value | Blocks   | Times out              |
| --------- | ----------------- | --------------------- | -------- | ---------------------- |
| Insert    | `add(e)`          | `offer(e)`            | `put(e)` | `offer(e, time, unit)` |
| Remove    | `remove()`        | `poll()`              | `take()` | `poll(time, unit)`     |
| Examine   | `element()`       | `peek()`              | n/a      | n/a                    |

Use `put` and `take` for producer-consumer, because they provide the
backpressure. Using `add` on a full bounded queue throws instead of waiting.

The full landscape:

| Collection                | Replaces                 | Characteristics                           |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------- |
| `ConcurrentHashMap`       | `HashMap`                | Bin-level locking, lock-free reads, atomic compute methods |
| `ConcurrentSkipListMap`   | `TreeMap`                | Sorted, concurrent, `O(log n)`              |
| `CopyOnWriteArrayList`    | `ArrayList`              | Snapshot iteration, expensive writes       |
| `CopyOnWriteArraySet`     | `HashSet`                | Same trade-offs                            |
| `ConcurrentLinkedQueue`   | `LinkedList` as a queue   | Unbounded, non-blocking, lock-free          |
| `ArrayBlockingQueue`      | Hand-written buffer       | Bounded, blocking, one lock                 |
| `LinkedBlockingQueue`     | Hand-written buffer       | Optionally bounded, separate head and tail locks |
| `SynchronousQueue`        | Direct handoff           | Zero capacity; each put waits for a take    |
| `PriorityBlockingQueue`   | `PriorityQueue`          | Unbounded, ordered, blocking                 |
| `DelayQueue`              | Scheduling by hand       | Elements become available at a set time      |

Finally, the iteration semantics, which differ from the standard collections:

| Behaviour            | Standard collections           | Concurrent collections                  |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------- |
| Concurrent modification | `ConcurrentModificationException` (fail-fast) | Tolerated (weakly consistent) |
| What the iterator sees | The live collection           | A snapshot, or an approximation          |
| `size()`             | Exact                          | Possibly an estimate                     |
| Needs external locking | Yes, for iteration           | No                                       |

The guidance is simple: **default to the concurrent collections and never use
`Collections.synchronizedX` for new code.** They are faster, they need no
external locking for iteration, and their compound methods eliminate the
check-then-act races that wrappers invite.

> Key Takeaways
> - `Collections.synchronizedX` uses one lock for the whole collection, which
>   serializes all access.
> - Wrapper collections still leave compound operations and iteration unsafe
>   without external locking.
> - `ConcurrentHashMap` locks individual bins and reads mostly without locking.
> - Use its atomic compound methods such as `merge`, `putIfAbsent`, and
>   `computeIfAbsent` instead of check-then-act.
> - `ConcurrentHashMap` forbids `null` keys and values, and its `size()` is an
>   estimate.
> - Concurrent iterators are weakly consistent and never throw
>   `ConcurrentModificationException`.
> - `CopyOnWriteArrayList` gives lock-free snapshot reads at the cost of copying
>   on every write, which suits listener lists.
> - `BlockingQueue` replaces `wait`/`notify` for producer-consumer and supplies
>   backpressure.
> - Queue operations come in throwing, special-value, blocking, and timed forms;
>   use `put` and `take` for backpressure.
> - Prefer concurrent collections over synchronized wrappers in all new code.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Replace a `Collections.synchronizedMap` with a `ConcurrentHashMap` and
>    rewrite one check-then-act block as a single atomic call.
> 2. Iterate a `CopyOnWriteArrayList` while another thread adds to it, then try
>    the same with an `ArrayList` and compare what happens.
> 3. Implement producer-consumer with an `ArrayBlockingQueue` of capacity 5, two
>    producers, and three consumers, terminating cleanly with a sentinel.
> 4. Benchmark `ConcurrentHashMap` against `Collections.synchronizedMap` with
>    eight threads at 90% reads, and report the ratio.
> 5. Interview: Why does `ConcurrentHashMap` reject `null` values, and why is
>    its `size()` only approximate? (Hint: what would a `null` return from
>    `get()` mean, and what would an exact count require locking?)
